events.title: Oil prices rise after IEA warns on market constraints; Saudi officials say Aramco facilities attacked
events.summary: A Saudi-led coalition reportedly struck Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen. U.S. Central Command rejected Iran's claims that the Strait of Hormuz is under Tehran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk." Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and notable commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on on CNBC's "Squawk Box." Oil prices were higher on Wednesday morning, pulling back from earlier gains, as investors digested the International Energy Agency's latest monthly report on the shape of the oil market. Brent crude futures , the international benchmark, were 20 cents higher at $105.89 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate was up $1.27 to $95.41 a barrel. The IEA's October Oil Market Report, published Wednesday, warned that constraints on diesel markets could continue well into 2027, with fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to derail a recovery on the supply side of the global oil market. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis continues to escalate, with the Saudi Ministry of Energy saying Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco had been attacked overnight. No injuries were reported at the site in Dhahran, a city on Saudi Arabia's eastern coast. It follows a series of Houthi attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh over the past week, including a fatal strike on the city's international airport. According to Al Jazeera, Houthi energy terminals and fuel reserves in Yemen were struck by a Saudi-led coalition, though a spokesperson said that precautions were taken to avoid "collateral damage on civilians." Tensions also continued to simmer between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. Central Command rejected claims by the commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy that the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran's control and that any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk." "RGC's navy commander has no navy," CENTCOM said in an X post , adding that "American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz." Oil may rally another $20-$25 due to the Iran conflict, hedge fund manager and noted commodity trader Paul Tudor Jones said on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "I am long oil... bullish oil...I think it can rally another $20 or $25 bucks," said the founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment. "If something to ameliorate the situation was going to happen, it would have happened already before the midterms," he added.

events.title: Bank of America shares drop 8% after third-quarter revenue miss and regulatory penalty
events.summary: Bank of America's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Revenue was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading. Misses in fixed income and equities trading revenue totaled roughly $750 million. The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%. Bank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected. Earnings per share: 91 cents, may not compare with $1.10 expected by LSEG Revenue: $30.12 billion vs. $30.69 billion expected by LSEG The bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share. Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations. Fixed income trading revenue fell 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate. Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million. Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance. In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter. Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate. The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, will inevitably spark questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets. Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. Now, questions arise as to whether there are any more risk-management issues waiting to be found. The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, adds 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years. Correction: Bank of America reported third-quarter revenue on an FTE basis of $30.12 billion compared with LSEG estimates of $30.69 billion. An earlier version misstated the comparison.

events.title: Merry squishmas: £10 squeezy banana on list of top festive season toys
events.summary: Social media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys says A cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” is tipped to be among the must-have toys this Christmas , according to expert buyers at Hamleys. The £10 “slow-rise, squeezable, sensory” fruit taps into the “squishies” craze that is fuelling a high street boom in toy sales. Hamleys expects to sell thousands of the Big Squij toys, which come in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound, in the coming weeks. Their popularity has been supercharged by social media and a growing army of child and adult collectors. There are more than 260,000 TikTok posts and more than 600,000 on Instagram tagged #squishies. The most popular official brand, NeeDoh, has 1.1m TikTok followers. Victoria Kay, the head of buying and merchandising at Hamleys, said the “squishy craze is only really just getting going”. “The demand is huge. There is a wonderful simplicity to their power whether you are a young child or an adult . Literally once you squeeze one, it’s really difficult to put it down.” Squishies are the biggest toy trend of the year, according to Andrew Murphy, who runs The Entertainer, the UK’s largest chain of toy shops. Some theories suggest their viral success is because of their stress-relieving powers or simplicity, but he suggests the “degree of fanaticism from kids under 10 for these products is not explainable in any rational way. It’s just a real, deep desire”. The squishies craze is good news for independent toy shops, he said: “It will be increasing sales in total by minimum of 30%. Most of their costs are fixed so they’ll probably be doubling the profit for the year.” The craze has been a shot in the arm for UK toy sales this year, which by the end of August were up 13% by value and 19% by volume, according the market research company Circana. Sales of toys that cost under £10 are growing fastest, with an extra £100m worth of these so-called “pocket money” items sold during the period thanks to the clamour for World Cup stickers and squishies. As for Christmas – still 72 days away – Hamleys says this week is when shopping for the festive season “officially” starts, according to a poll of consumers. With that in mind it has produced its annual shortlist of toys to please toddlers through to teenagers and older. At £10, the Big Squij toys are the cheapest. while the remote-controlled flying Thunder Unicorn” is the most expensive at £75. The list of 15 items includes evergreen favourites such as Lego, Barbie, Peppa Pig and PlayDoh. With the upcoming Marvel superhero extravaganza Avengers: Doomsday on the horizon it features two Doctor Doom toys – a £45 Lego bust and a £30 action figure. There is also something for J-Pop fans with a collectible figurine of the computer-generated pop-star Hatsune Miku . The 16-year-old vocaloid – her “voice” comes from music software – is playing London’s O2 arena next month. events.title: NTangible bets it can predict how athletes will perform under pressure
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When collegiate sports programs recruit athletes, they can measure concrete metrics like a player’s sprint speed, throwing velocity, and physical strength. But there has never been a clear way to quantify the mental aspects of sports — how well will this athlete perform in high-pressure situations? Will they stay calm, focus, and give it their best shot? Or will they panic in the spotlight and mess up? NTangible co-founder and CEO Dan Connerty thinks he’s unlocked the secret to measuring if a player will execute in the most important moments. “We really wanted to hyper focus on this idea of clutch performance,” Connerty, a professional baseball player turned sports-tech entrepreneur, told TechCrunch. “Cognitive [science] itself is just this black box that nobody’s wanted to touch, because nobody’s had the ability to measure it accurately prior.” Alongside psychologist Dr. Ed Levine, a professor emeritus at the University of South Florida, Connerty developed a psychological assessment that he says can predict how likely an athlete is to perform under pressure. The Clutch Factor assessment is inspired by the Thematic Apperception Test, a psychological examination in which people are presented with photos of ambiguous situations and describe what they see happening, who they imagine themselves to be in the scene, and what they think might happen next. “There’s no right or wrong answers,” Connerty said. “The key words that you use, the way in which you use those words, and the semantic phrasing associated with it get scored against the neurolinguistic scoring guide that psychologists created, and it shoots out your clutch factor score.” The score is between 0 and 1000 and, according to Connerty, an athlete who scores over a 750 is twice as likely to commit to a Division I school. “What we’ve been able to do is leverage this analysis, where we can show the predictive ability,” he said. “This number can be heavily used in rankings, leaderboards, recruiting conversations, NIL conversations, and scholarship conversations, especially in the crazy wild west that is collegiate sports right now, where we’re writing $4 million checks to quarterbacks.” A possible flaw in the product, however, could be that athletes seeking to impress coaches and recruiters may answer the questions dishonestly to get a higher clutch score. When I took the quiz and answered honestly, I got a below average score of 584, which didn’t surprise me — I dreaded high-leverage situations when I played high school sports. When I took the quiz a second time, answering as I imagined a very level-headed, clutch, top recruit might respond, I scored an 802. Perhaps the platform would work better as a way for coaches to learn more about their athletes and help them improve in weaker areas. Connerty thinks that “clutch” is a skill that can be trained. While he isn’t positioning NTangible as a training platform, he worked with former MLB sports psychologist Howie Schwartz to create a list of exercises that athletes can use as a starting point for upping their mental game. While Connerty’s background is in baseball, NTangible now supports testing for nine sports. He also has ambitions to expand the clutch test to apply to corporate settings, so that HR departments can evaluate employees’ strengths and weaknesses under pressure. The NTerpret assessment translates more directly to the workplace — the respondent answers questions about how they best respond to coaching and feedback, giving management data on how that employee processes instructions and acts on information. NTangible’s most viable business model seems to be selling to sports organizations and companies directly, rather than to individual athletes. The company will elaborate on its strategy on stage on Wednesday at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s currently among the top 20 companies dueling for the grand prize at Startup Battlefield. You can check out the rest of the field, and the investors who will decide the winner, by joining us in person this week at Disrupt, happening Tuesday through Thursday, October 13 to 15, in downtown San Francisco. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Amanda Silberling is a senior writer at TechCrunch covering the intersection of technology and culture. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. She holds a B.A.

events.title: Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
events.summary: Exclusive: Douglas Alexander, on trade delegation to India, talks up economic benefits of joint trading arrangements with Europe Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said. Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer. But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India . When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries. Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position. Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%. But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater. “In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.” He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up. “At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit , you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity. “We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.” Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU. The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses. “There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.” Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products. One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy , which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market. Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

events.title: ‘Ugly’ jump in US inflation, driven by gasoline prices, in blow to Trump before midterm elections – business live
events.summary: Newsflash: US inflation jumped in September, and by more than expected, as the soaring cost of motor fuel pushed up the cost of living. The US Consumer Prices Index roses by 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August. Economists had forecast a smaller rise, to 3.6%. Prices rose by 0.6% in Spetember alone. Gasoline prices jumped by 9.1% in September, and were 34% higher tha a year ago, as motorists across America felt the impact of Donald Trump’s Middle East war at the pumps. Those price pressures prompted Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin last Friday – but as reported earlier , it’s not expected to unlock much extra supplies to the market. 20m ago ABN AMRO predict Fed rate hike in December 1h ago October interest rate hike 'back in play' 1h ago Quilter: 'Ugly US inflation data' is blow to Trump 3h ago Euro hits 16-month low against the pound 3h ago Bank of America earnings hit by $1.2bn fine over money laundering failings 6h ago Diesel shortages could persist well into 2027 7h ago UK bond yields drop with Healey 'to avoid more borrowing' in budget 7h ago China on track for record trade surplus this year 7h ago Ed Miliband: Global financial system is failing developing countries 7h ago Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', Heathrow boss claims 7h ago BoE's Pill wary of predictions of four rate rises 8h ago Bank of England governor and IMF warn of rising cyber crime risks 8h ago IMF's Georgieva urges US to get its house in order 8h ago Introduction: IMF sounds alarm over rising government borrowing costs US bank stocks have hit their lowest level in over four months, Reuters reports , with the S&P 500 banks index down 1.3%. ABN AMRO predict Fed rate hike in December The Fed’s next meeting, on 27-28 October, is just a week before the midterm elections. Rogier Quaedvlieg , economist at ABN AMRO, predicts the Fed will avoid raising interest rates then – but will hit borrowers with a hike in December. September CPI inflation was hotter than expected for the second consecutive month. Core inflation rose by 0.34% m/m, while headline inflation increased by 0.649%, lifting the y/y rate to 3.7%. This was above consensus but in line with our forecast. The core reading was the key surprise, prompting markets to raise the implied probability of an October rate hike from less than 25% to more than 50%. Energy prices are beginning to have a significant impact, including on airline fares. Prices of new and used cars also increased as new model-year vehicles entered the market. The AI buildout again added to price pressures, with large increases in computer software and accessories, as well as computers and peripherals. Although inflationary pressure was broader than in last month’s exceptionally concentrated report, the share of CPI components showing elevated inflation continues to decline. We therefore still expect inflation to ease over the course of the year. We also continue to expect the Fed to hold rates in October before raising the policy rate by a further 25 bps in December. Stocks are falling at the start of trading on Wall Street, as today’s US inflation report disappoints investors. The S&P 500 sharesindex has fallen by 0.4%, shedding 32 points to 7,773 points. The tech-focused Nasdaq is down 0.5%. US government borrowing costs are pushing higher, after today’s inflation report hardened expectations of interest rate rises from the Fed. The yield on two-year Treasury bills has risen by 13 basis point (0.13 of a percentage point) to 4.92%, hitting their highest level since 29 September. Ten-year US Treasury yields are up 9.5bps to 5.3% – towards the 24-year highs set earalier this month. This adds to the fiscal mess facing the US ( something the IMF warned about this morning ); high bond yields push up the cost of servicing the $40tn US national debt, and makes issuing new debt more expensive too. Congressman Brendan F. Boyle is blaming Donald Trump’s trade war, and his war with Iran, for driving up costs for Americans. Boyle , a Democratic member of the House of Representatives, posted on X: President Trump promised to lower costs on “day one,” but American families have already paid $3,500 more due to inflation since he took office. If he cared at all about working people, he would end his tariff taxes and his reckless Iran war. The US dollar has hit an 18-month high, as traders anticipate that today’s inflation reading could prompt an increase in US interest rates. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of currencies, is up 0.5% to its highest level since April 2025. October interest rate hike 'back in play' This jump in inflation increases the chances that the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates later this month. According to CMEFedwatch , a quarter-point Fed rate hike in October is now a 43% chance, up from 22% yesterday.

events.title: Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
events.summary: Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said. Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”. He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU. The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU. It is mainly aimed at China , which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland. “It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry. “We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added. Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France. The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December. Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors. But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director. The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car. Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year. The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time. The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently. Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years. One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

events.title: I live in the Hamptons year-round. Visiting in the offseason is quieter, but comes with trade-offs.
events.summary: The Hamptons are quieter in the offseason, but there's still so much to do. Vanessa Gordon As a year-round Hamptons resident , I love the summers here, but I also appreciate the offseason. Since it's much quieter in the winter, it's easier to get into restaurants and visit the beaches. Although it's cold out, there are countless activities to enjoy, like ice skating and wine tastings. As someone who has lived in the Hamptons for most of my life, I can always tell when summer is over: suddenly, it becomes incredibly easy to get around. In July and August, I automatically have to build traffic into almost everything I do. Drives that should take 15 minutes can take considerably longer, parking becomes challenging, and there are typically long lines everywhere. But luckily, once the fall season settles in and the Hamptons have entered their offseason, I can get in my car and go anywhere I want with ease. Sure, the quiet comes with tradeoffs, but I wouldn't want to be anywhere else in the colder months. The hotels are more relaxing once the summer rush ends. Vanessa Gordon When I take a summer staycation at a hotel in the Hamptons, my schedule is packed with dinners, beach time, events, and shopping. So, if I ever want to really enjoy the local accommodations, I prefer to do so in the winter. Once it gets colder, I can take the time to truly enjoy the property, sit by the fireplace, and have a gourmet breakfast without rushing. Some of my favorite places to stay are the Maidstone and the Baker House 1650, both located in East Hampton. I also love Gurney's Montauk Resort and Seawater Spa, which offers fixed-price meals at the restaurant and hosts mixology classes throughout the offseason. It's also much easier to go out to eat. Vanessa Gordon I don't even attempt to dine out on summer weekends, when many of my favorite spots are packed. However, during the offseason, I love that I can check out restaurants I wouldn't otherwise visit in the warmer months. Even though many restaurants close down during the offseason, I love checking out places that do stay open year-round, including Bistro Été in Water Mill and Almond in Bridgehampton, both of which are among the most popular eateries in the Hamptons. Out in Montauk Village, the Montauk Bake Shoppe is famous for its fried jelly croissants, but during the summer, it can be so busy that I rarely even attempt to get one. In the quieter months, I can stop in without delay. There's still plenty to do — but you need to know where to look. Vanessa Gordon There are considerably fewer events in the offseason, but that doesn't mean nothing is happening. Since the beaches are dramatically quieter in the fall, I love surfing in October and early November, while the water is still warm enough. Later in the season, I like to go on seal-watching hikes and cozy wine tastings . Many establishments also host a variety of events and activities throughout the quieter months. Guild Hall continues to have films, exhibitions, talks, and performances, while Sag Harbor Cinema has screenings. The latter also hosts HarborFrost, a fun outdoor winter celebration that features hot cocoa , ice dancers, and live music. I also enjoy going to Buckskill Winter Club for outdoor ice skating with my family and playing indoor tennis at Sportime Quogue. The holidays are one of my favorite times to be here. Vanessa Gordon Once the Hamptons International Film Festival and Sag Harbor American Film Festival are over in the fall, the community quickly transitions into the holiday season — one of my favorite times to be here. East Hampton, Bridgehampton, and Sag Harbor in particular are very festive. The trees lining the villages are lit, and I always look forward to seeing light displays and holiday decor throughout the community. The hardest part about the offseason is making a living. Vanessa Gordon Because the Hamptons economy remains highly seasonal, there is considerably less work in many industries during winter. Weather events like a snowstorm can create opportunities for people through shoveling and property management work, but it's not really possible to build an entire year around the hope that it'll snow. In my case, I own an event production company, so with the area extremely quiet, I have to get a little creative. Winter is when I do a lot of work to prepare for the summer, including client outreach, partnerships, travel, and planning. During the offseason, I take my work with me to New York City , Miami, Palm Beach, parts of California, and increasingly, internationally. I wouldn't want summer in the Hamptons to last all year. Vanessa Gordon I find it fascinating how often people ask me what it's like to live in the Hamptons year-round. It reminds me of when I visited Block Island in Rhode Island , once in March and another time in August. It was the same place, but it almost felt like two completely different destinations. That's how I think about the Hamptons. Winter has its drawbacks. Farmers' markets close, there are fewer events, some restaurants disappear until spring, and there is less work. That being said, I don't see the offseason as the lesser version of the Hamptons. After all, I can go to dinner spontaneously, play tennis indoors, surf in October, and have a relaxing staycation. I've learned to appreciate the quiet, because in the blink of an eye, the summer crowds will be back and the busy season will start all over again. Read the original article on Business Insider

Around 72 million Americans will see the benefit increases in January, according to SSA. The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. events.title: Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket
events.summary: The consumer price index showed annual inflation of 3.7% in September after rising 0.6% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. The Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, posted an annual reading of 2.6% after climbing 0.3%. Energy prices were a major factor again as gasoline rose 9.1% and accounted for half the increase in the index. However, price pressures were broad-based, with gains in shelter, vehicle costs and apparel. September brought little relief to the accelerating cost of living, as consumer prices increased again and kept the inflation rate well above the Federal Reserve's goal. The consumer price index , a broad measure of goods and services costs across the U.S. economy, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected respective gains of 0.6% and 3.6%. Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core CPI rose 0.3% for the month and was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with respective estimates for 0.2% and 2.5%. The annual rate for headline inflation was 3.4% in August while the core rate was 2.4%. Surging energy costs were again the primary culprit in the inflation picture. The energy index jumped 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending anytime soon. Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for about half the gain in headline CPI, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gas has posted a 34.2% rise while fuel oil has roared higher by 74.2%. Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago. However, shelter prices increased 0.4% and used car and truck prices jumped 0.7%. Apparel prices, which are sensitive to tariffs, increased 0.3% and are up 3.4% on an annual basis. Stock market futures turned negative following the release while bond yields were sharply higher. Futures traders also raised the odds of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Oct. 27-28 to about 54%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds for a rate rise before the end of the year increased to better than 96%, with a near 50-50 chance of the Fed boosting rates by half a percentage point by December. This is the final CPI reading that FOMC officials will get before that meeting. The BLS on Thursday will release the September reading on the producer price index, a measure of wholesale costs. "CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years," said Sonu Varghese, chief macro strategist at Carson Group. "The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom." Inflation as measured by the CPI has surpassed the Fed's 2% benchmark since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, but then spiked following the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran. Over the past few months, the year-over-year trend has moderated but still has held well above target. Fed officials responded in September by approving their first interest rate hike in more than three years, a quarter percentage point move that took the benchmark funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to skip an October increase but to hike again in December. The type of supply shocks that have driven the energy surge generally are considered temporary, and policymakers often will look through them when considering where to set rates. However, Fed officials fear that the longer the war drags on, the higher the likelihood that the spike will make its way through the broader economy and become embedded in consumer and business expectations. Prices also have faced pressure from President Donald Trump 's tariffs as well as demand for goods associated with the artificial intelligence build-out. In recent days, a number of key policymakers have expressed the belief that the Fed doesn't need to rush to implement another hike. However, most say they expect another increase this year. Market pricing implies the Fed could raise rates at least twice more in 2027. Fed officials follow the CPI and a host of other metrics but use the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index as their primary forecast and policymaking metric. The PCE numbers for September won't be released until later this month.

events.title: 10-year Treasury yield jumps as September core inflation comes in hotter than expected
events.summary: The 10-year Treasury note yield rose on Wednesday following the latest U.S. inflation print. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — jumped more than 7 basis points to 5.289% and reached the highest level since Oct. 8. The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury yield — which tends to react most to geopolitical events — was up more than 3 basis points to 5.602%. The 2-year Treasury — which closely tracks the Fed's interest rate decisions — gained more than 10 basis points to 4.895%. Earlier, it hit its highest level since Sept. 29. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely. The consumer price index rose 3.7% year over year in September, higher than the Dow Jones consensus estimate of 3.6%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, came in at 2.6% on an annualized basis, versus the 2.5% consensus estimate. The latest inflation reading comes just two weeks before the Fed's next interest rate decision. With inflation remaining sticky, the central bank may need to raise rates higher and keep them there for longer in 2027, said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The bond bulls have turned around and are running the other way as 10-year yields have shot higher after today's shocking inflation report," he said. "Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates." Odds for an October 28 quarter-point hike in the fed funds rate — currently 3.75% to 4.00% — increased to 43.7% from just 22.1% a day ago, according to futures trading measured by CME's FedWatch tool. There is now a greater than 95% chance of at least one hike before the year is out, and included in that is a 40% chance that rates are higher by a half-percentage point — double the odds one day ago. Looking ahead to the rest of the week, investors also await the September reading for the producer price index, September retail sales data and weekly initial jobless claims figures, all due on Thursday. — With additional reporting by CNBC's John Melloy.

events.title: Netflix is cutting about 1,000 staffers in its biggest round of layoffs in years
events.summary: Netflix is turning to layoffs under co-CEO Ted Sarandos. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Bloomberg/Getty Images Netflix is cutting about 1,000 employees, following in the footsteps of other major media companies. The cuts impact staffers on the product, tech, and HR teams, a person familiar with the move said. Shares of the streaming giant are down significantly this year, and its engagement growth has slowed. Netflix is laying off about 1,000 employees in its biggest round of cuts since 2022, a person familiar with the plans confirmed. Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters notified employees about the downsizing on Wednesday. Netflix is contending with slowing engagement growth and a lagging stock price that's down more than 30% over the last six months and over 40% over the past year. The streaming giant is letting go of staffers primarily across the product, tech, HR, and legal teams, the person said. The Wall Street Journal first reported the news. Other media giants have made cuts in recent weeks. NBCUniversal said in early October that it's parting with a few hundred global streaming tech employees , while Disney did its third round of layoffs in six months in late September. Netflix's cuts come a week before it reports third-quarter earnings, which will be after the closing bell on October 20. Its last major round of layoffs was in 2022, after the company lost subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. Sarandos said at a Bloomberg event in late September that "we're not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster." Paid streamers have faced pressure overall as free services  like YouTube and Tubi have gained popularity. Netflix and its rivals are turning to podcasts and creator content to win over viewers. Disney+ and Paramount+ are planning to add free tiers , and Netflix's Peters said this summer that "a free offering could make sense in some markets." Netflix met Wall Street's earnings expectations last quarter but said it would start posting its detailed engagement report once a year, instead of twice a year. The company told shareholders that "engagement is not just the quantity of view hours, but also refers to the quality and variety of our offering." The reporting change troubled investors, as engagement is generally correlated with subscribers' willingness to stick around and pay higher prices. ( Netflix hiked prices in March to $19.99 a month from $17.99 for its standard ad-free plan and to $8.99 for its ad-supported plan, up from $7.99.) Netflix's viewership grew 2% in the first half of the year. Its 97 billion viewing hours are likely far higher than any of its paid streaming peers, which don't disclose engagement in the same way. Netflix generated 7.8% of viewership on US TVs in July, according to the latest data from Nielsen, below YouTube's 14.2% share but well above third-place Disney's streamers at 4.7%. However, Netflix's streaming viewership share is down from 9% in December, which was its highest mark in more than five years, thanks to hit shows like "Stranger Things." events.title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
events.summary: Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures. But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about." The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn . The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing. Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects. Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them. But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test. Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, previously showed the BBC hundreds of driving tests being offered for sale by resellers on messaging groups Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand." She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks. "On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken." Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure. Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog". A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017". events.title: US consumer prices accelerate in September on costlier petrol; core CPI firmer
events.summary: Petrol prices above US$6 a gallon at a gas station in Emeryville, California on Oct 12. US consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the year, driven by a 7.1% jump in petrol costs, Reuters reported. Core CPI also firmed, rising 0.3% in the month and 2.6% yearly, keeping inflation pressure on the US Federal Reserve and rate rise fears alive. The report hurt Trump politically and will help set 2027 Social Security COLA, with seniors expecting about a 3.5% rise, or US$67.90 a month. WASHINGTON – US consumer prices accelerated in September amid a surge in fuel costs, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later in October back on the radar. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labour Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics said on Oct 14. In the 12 months till September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in the year ended August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would gain 0.6% over the month and increase 3.6% on a year-on-year basis. Petrol prices soared 7.1% last month, data from the US Energy Information Administration showed. The report followed surveys this month showing a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump’s approval rating , driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies, including tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war with Iran, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. n the 12 months ended September, core CPI inflation increased 2.6% after advancing 2.4% in the year to August. The US Federal Reserve tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target. The core CPI measure is lagging behind core PCE inflation, which increased 3% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets. The central bank last month raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4% range, the first hike in three years , and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Prior to the CPI report, financial markets assigned a roughly 22% chance of a rate hike at the Oct 27-28 policy meeting, CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase this month diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rates in December. The September CPI inflation report was keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how much their benefits will increase in 2027. The Social Security Administration uses the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers data from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026 to determine the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programmes benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children. The Senior Citizens League, one of the nation’s biggest seniors groups, projected a 3.5% COLA raise next year. That would be up from 2.8% in 2026, and would lift the average monthly benefit for retirees by US$67.90 to US$2,007. The Social Security Administration will announce the COLA increase for 2027 later on Oct 14. REUTERS

events.title: US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 13:47 BST US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August. Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have spiked following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US. Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%. Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI). It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy. The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change. There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise. If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example. Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices. Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel. Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100. What is the current rate of inflation? Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices. Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months. In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics. Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year. Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%. How have tariffs affected inflation? Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world. While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. US President Donald Trump raised tariffs Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost. In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax. Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas. Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year. What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? Published 22 August While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years. During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up. Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel. Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%. It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace. A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

events.title: Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in 2027
events.summary: Social Security beneficiaries will see their monthly checks increase in 2027. Abdullah Durmaz/Getty Images Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027, following the latest inflation adjustments. The SSA's annual cost-of-living raise means the average monthly check will be $75 larger. Over half of retirees rely on Social Security as their primary income, according to an AARP survey. Older Americans just learned how much to expect in monthly Social Security checks next year. The Social Security Administration announced its latest cost-of-living adjustment on the heels of Wednesday's September inflation report. SSA beneficiaries , who are mostly 65 and older, are now set to receive a 3.6% raise in their benefits in 2027. That's higher than the 2026 increase of 2.8% and will amount to a $900 annual boost for recipients, according to AARP calculations — an average monthly check increase of $75. The consumer price index, which tracks how much prices have changed, is key in determining just how much Social Security checks should go up. The adjustment is calculated based on the increase in prices during the third quarter of this year compared to a year ago for urban wage earners and clerical workers. The Social Security Administration said it will start notifying people about their amount in November via its online portal. While a check bump will likely be a welcome development for many older Americans, it might still amount to a drop in the financial bucket. Over the past few years, Americans 65 and older have increasingly been slipping into poverty after adjusting for transfers like taxes and government programs. An August AARP survey of 1,085 Americans ages 50 and up found just over half of recipients say Social Security is their main source of income; among those who said they were highly reliant on it, 82% said it helps them cover basic expenses like housing, food, and healthcare. Looming over all of that is the concern that Social Security won't be able to pay out full benefits in just a few years; the latest accounting from the fund's trustees found that, unless funding is replenished, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Fund will stop being able to pay out full benefits at the end of 2032. events.title: Trump's diesel dilemma — by the numbers
events.summary: The cut in global supply from the wars in Ukraine and Iran have made wholesale diesel prices more than double since the beginning of 2026. Last week, President Donald Trump lifted restrictions on Russian diesel to ease global shortages. Experts agree that bringing more Russian diesel to market is unlikely to sway near-term prices. Diesel prices are surging as midterms approach – and they are likely to stay high in the near future, according to analysts. The International Energy Agency's monthly report for October, released Wednesday, was the latest to predict that constraints on the diesel market will likely keep prices elevated into next year. The group warned that even if refineries step up production of diesel into the year-end, inventories will likely remain strained until the second half of 2027. Last Friday, President Donald Trump unexpectedly paused sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and announced that he reached a deal with President Vladimir Putin in which the Kremlin would release 4.8 million metric tons of diesel , or nearly 36 million barrels, to the global market. Over the weekend, he took to Truth Social to announce an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine , but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later accused Russia of attacking the country's energy facilities . The foreign policy developments come as rising fuel prices — particularly skyrocketing diesel — have become a major flashpoint ahead of this year's midterm election. But releasing Russian diesel to the global market is unlikely to drop prices in the near term. A note from Goldman Sachs last week even predicted that diesel prices will remain high through 2027 as refineries struggle to meet demand. Here's what the numbers tell us so far: Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine have dramatically cut global supply. Trump has insisted that the war in Ukraine is to blame for high diesel prices. On July 8, Russia banned diesel exports after Ukraine struck its refineries. In the U.S., the price of a gallon of diesel rose nearly 40% between July 6 and Sept. 22. However, the price of diesel had already jumped after the Iran war started and was still 20% above its prewar level when Russia instituted its export ban, making that tightening of supply feel that much more acute. Indeed, both conflicts have created major ripple effects across global energy markets causing major swings, sometimes daily.

events.title: My nanny called in sick on a Tuesday. For the first time, I was excited instead of panicked.
events.summary: The author left her PR career to be more present with her family. Courtesy of the author My old PR career required me to be available well beyond normal work hours. I left agency life because I wanted more control over my schedule. Now I can step away from work without feeling like everything will collapse. My daughter's nanny called in sick . I had my day all planned and mapped out. A full to-do list for that day, but the list did not survive to even 8 a.m. Being in the PR industry , I am very familiar with this feeling. However, instead of feeling a sense of dread about how I would get it all done, I felt excited. Excited that I got to spend time with my daughter instead of being behind a computer. So I put my daughter in the car, drove into town, and left my computer at home . Working in PR means you are always reachable I came up in public relations, and a prerequisite for the job is being reachable. You have your agency touch base on Monday morning and leave with a plan for the week. By Tuesday, the plan is usually gone because a client has news, a problem, or a new opportunity lands on your desk, and everything else gets pushed. You have billable hours to hit on every account, and if you don't hit them inside a normal week, you find the hours somewhere else. Mine were usually after dinner. Ten years ago, during the end-of-month reporting, one week a month, my evenings were filled with grabbing screenshots, finding associated Unique Views per Month, and all that. When a client has a crisis in the middle of the night, nobody has to tell you to pick up. You just do. I was good at the work. That was most of the problem. We left Dallas and moved to a farm The first time I stepped out of that current was in 2020. My husband and I left Dallas , where I had every professional reason to stay, and bought a small farm in East Texas. I kept the same job. It was a good job, good people, and benefits most people would want, and I did it from a place where you swapped concrete sidewalks for literal cattle trails, fluffy cows, and chickens. The author moved from Dallas to a farm in East Texas. Courtesy of the author That part worked. Then I had my daughter, and the choice got made. I didn't leave the workforce because I fell in love with my baby and lost interest in working. I loved my professional self, and still do. The real story is that I wanted to work, but what changed was who I wanted to do it for. My husband was home six days a week because, years before that, he'd built something he could control. I was home two. He hadn't worked less than I. He'd just built the thing that got to decide when he works and when he doesn't. There's no villain in this story. My ambition and my employer's ambition just stopped pointing in the same direction. When you're not writing your own check, you don't get to be the person who fixes that, even if you have the title that should support that. So I left. No agency waiting, no book of business, no plan past figuring it out as I go. The thing my 25-year-old self would find insane isn't that I quit. It's what I do now with the work that comes to me. I keep things intentional now People email me most weeks wanting help at the intersection of affiliate and PR. I keep a few clients I enjoy working with, but honestly hand most referrals to friends in the industry. I refer away more business now, even without a salary, than I ever imagined turning down when I had one. In PR, good clients don't throw money at you. The work can often be hard to come by. Giving it away on purpose isn't something anyone taught me. The author doesn't stress now when her nanny calls in sick. Courtesy of the author The calls I keep are intentional. For now, they're the publicist and agency consulting clients that light me on fire. I finish those calls with more energy than when I started. Nothing at an agency ever did that. It's still work. But it's fulfilling work when you see the puzzle pieces start to click for students and clients. In my 20s, I wanted a great title, to own accounts of my own, and my name on a 30 under 30 list. I got some of that, and none of it changed the pride of ownership like fulfillment does. The view from up there turned out to be the same, only with a constant stream of stress-relief tips on my FYP. I didn't get less ambitious. I stopped assuming that ambition and escalation were the same as my definition of success. Now I'm learning things I'm bad at, which is uncomfortable when you're used to being the one with the answers. I can also process a chicken I raised and have it on a plate by dinner, which my Dallas self would have found completely unhinged. Truth be told, you need to let it set for a few days for the best texture. Ask me how I know! Ha. And when the nanny is sick on a Tuesday, I can be unreachable. The work is still there on Wednesday. events.title: Turkish authorities raid TV channel as press freedom groups warn of a crackdown
events.summary: Authorities have raided Halk TV, one of Turkey's few independent broadcasters, and appointed a trustee manager as part of a corruption investigation ISTANBUL -- Authorities on Wednesday raided the headquarters of one of Turkey ’s few broadcasters not aligned with the government, and appointed a trustee manager to oversee the popular news channel as part of an investigation into alleged corruption. Press freedom groups and opposition parties, however, denounced the move against Halk TV, calling it yet another step by the government to silence opposition voices. Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index. A statement from the Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said an investigation was launched into Halk TV chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over allegations of bid rigging, bribery and money laundering. Detention warrants were issued against 17 suspects and 11 of them were taken into custody, the statement said. Trustees were also appointed to run other companies owned by Mahiroglu. The channel’s broadcasts were temporarily halted. Police surrounded the station’s headquarters while financial crimes investigation teams conducted searches inside, media reports said. The raid on the channel came as Istanbul's imprisoned mayor, Ekrem Imamoglu , was due to appear in court to defend himself against allegations of widespread corruption in a case that critics also see as a politically motivated move against the opposition. Imamoglu, who has been behind bars for more than a year, was considered the main challenger to Erdogan. Halk TV has reported extensively on the trial and other cases against Imamoglu. In a video message posted on X, Mahiroglu condemned the appointment of a trustee for the channel, calling it a politically motivated move and a “dark day for Turkey.” Mahiroglu, who lives abroad, denied the allegations against him as “baseless” and said seven of his relatives were detained. The Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against the channel. “The appointment of a trustee to Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression,” the group said. “This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public’s right to access information, is unacceptable.” Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid amounted to an abuse of power by the government. “Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit,” he wrote on X. “Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country.” Amnesty International urged Turkish authorities to "immediately restore Halk TV’s independent operations and end their attacks on media freedom.” Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship. Last week, two journalists were arrested and two others were placed under house arrest for alleged misleading reports on a recent Turkish investment fund scandal — which has implicated a senior figure from Erdogan’s ruling party. On Monday, international and Turkish human rights groups urged social media platforms, including X, to resist court orders blocking hundreds of accounts belonging to journalists and activists. They also called on the Turkish government to stop issuing orders to block the accounts. The government has cited public safety concerns to justify the restrictions. events.title: Warren Buffett says to 'make money while you sleep.' AI agents may be the answer, Robinhood CEO says.
events.summary: Warren Buffett has long recommended people make their money work for them. Bloomberg/Getty Images Warren Buffett has championed investing as a way to put your money to work and build wealth. Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev says everyone should use AI agents that are "productive while they sleep." Agents might provide a new way to divorce money from work and build diverse income streams. "If you don't find a way to make money while you sleep, you will work until you die." That famous Warren Buffett line stresses the need to invest in businesses, real estate, and other assets that generate passive income such as dividends and rent. Buffett has long warned that if you rely solely on your salary and fail to put your money to work or build other income streams , you'll have to work for a wage your entire life. Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev proposed a new-age alternative during the latest episode of the "Sources" podcast. His "North Star" is that "everyone should have a team of agents that's productive while they sleep," he said. Tenev was referring to AI agents — systems that can autonomously perform tasks by reasoning, planning, using tools, taking actions, and communicating with humans and other agents. Early adopters are using agents to manage their emails and calendars, build apps and websites, and handle a wide range of daily tasks. Tenev's vision is that everyone will have agents w orking for them at all hours, supercharging their productivity and potentially diversifying their income streams. "I see a world where a large portion of the trading volume for an individual investor, for our customer base writ large, is generated by AI agents," he said. Tenev said that's because agents "don't have a lot of the limitations that we have as human traders." They can operate 24/7, trade multiple asset classes simultaneously, and can easily navigate trading opportunities on Robinhood 's app, he explained. However, Tenev also said agents require supervision, suggesting they won't be a set-it-and-forget-it passive income stream. "Each person should be a 24/7 agent manager," he said. "Your job becomes managing your agents ." That sounds much more demanding than receiving a dividend check in the mail. But it's easy to imagine people earning income from multiple sources by allocating agents to different tasks. Buffett hasn't publicly endorsed AI agents as a way to divorce income from work, and there's no guarantee he will. It's worth noting that the legendary investor and former Berkshire Hathaway CEO and chairman was critical of Robinhood during its pandemic boom in 2021. He accused the trading app of encouraging users to treat the stock market like a casino and gamble using options and leveraged positions. A Robinhood spokesperson told Business Insider at the time: "The new generation of investors aren't a 'casino group.' They are tearing down old barriers to investing and taking control of their financial futures. Robinhood is on the right side of history." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How AI apps are offering free substitutes for Big Tech software
events.summary: AI-developed ArtCraft is challenging Adobe after disrupting legacy software’s economic model. As AI development rapidly expands, people are replicating paid-for desktop and mobile apps with free apps, potentially changing the future of legacy software. Last week, a Reddit user named Brandon Thomas shared a project called “ArtCraft” – essentially a free rebuild of the Adobe Creative Suite, which includes programmes such as Photoshop and Adobe PDF. The recreated services have been named PhotoCraft and PdfCraft. list 1 of 3 OpenAI engineer charged after listening device found in meeting room list 2 of 3 AI could self-replicate on home devices within ‘months’, Anthropic says list 3 of 3 Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks This software package usually costs individuals $779.99 per year if paid upfront or $69.99 per month on an annual contract. Earlier this week, ArtCraft also released copies of the Microsoft Office suite. As with the Adobe package, ArtCraft has announced WordCraft, DeckCraft, and GridCraft, taking on Microsoft Word, PowerPoint, and Excel. While the software engineer behind the new packages is based in the United States, the programmes are available worldwide. Who is Brandon Thomas and what did he do? Reddit user “u/ai_art_is_art”, the person behind ArtCraft, has been revealed as Atlanta, US-based software engineer Brandon Thomas. Using AI platform Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Rust software, Thomas said he was able to reverse engineer Adobe’s creative suite. Announcing his project on Reddit, Thomas said that this is not a “one-off flash in the pan that will die”. “I’m not just some casual vibe coder. I’m a 15-year industry veteran who has written everything from six-nines payment rails that move billions of dollars of transaction volume a day to advanced robotics and optics automation. I’ve used Rust extensively for about a decade, and I know how to build and maintain large-scale Rust projects,” he said. “Six-nines payment rails” refers to online payment infrastructure which provides 99.9999 percent operational availability, while Rust is a programming language. Thomas said he had become fed up with being hit with cancellation fees on software products and wanted others to be able to access them for free. He wrote on the social media and news site, Hacker News: “We’ll replace Google Search, we’ll build our own smartphones, we’ll build better infra. We’ll remove all the ads and de-enshi**ify the entire tech world.” What is ‘vibe coding’ and how common is it for app development? While Thomas denies he is “just some vibe coder”, vibe coding is at least partly what he has done. Vibe coding is a new term in software development which refers to prompting AI tools to generate code rather than writing it manually. This means that people who do not have technical knowledge of programming can describe an idea to an AI tool and have it create it for them. According to the IBM technology company, vibe coding is a “shift toward intent-driven software development, where AI systems assist developers by generating code from natural language instructions”. The phrase was introduced by computer scientist and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy in February 2025, who wrote on X that AI users could “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists”. Vibe coding has become more common as AI has taken off and new apps have flooded Apple’s App Store. The New York Times reported that Sensor Tower, a global market intelligence and digital analytics platform, estimates that new apps doubled in the first half of this year to about 560,000. There is a legal grey area around replicating software which has already been established without infringing on intellectual property. On Reddit, Thomas described his Adobe-similar apps as “clean-room” replacements, meaning that they were built from scratch from publicly available file-format specifications, rather than from Adobe’s proprietary source code. However, there is still little information about how much of the code Claude wrote and how much Thomas wrote, according to Technollama, a blog written by Professor Andres Guadamuz, a reader in intellectual property law at the University of Sussex. “We also do not know whether the claimed ‘clean-room process’ stands up to scrutiny,” he said. Could AI coding kill legacy software? The downfall of legacy software is unlikely to make apps like Adobe Creative Cloud or Microsoft completely obsolete, but it could make them far less profitable if there are free-to-use substitutes available.
