events.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI employee who allegedly planted recording device in conference room
events.summary: An OpenAI employee was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found hidden inside the executive conference room. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested in connection with the matter, the DOJ said. Alfozan was fired from OpenAI after the incident, the company said. An OpenAI employee was arrested after a " sophisticated recording device " was discovered inside its executive conference room, according to the Department of Justice and a post by the company. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, who is a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 in connection with the matter, the DOJ said in a release on Tuesday. The company said an employee planted the device a few days before it was found, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "moved quickly to make an arrest," the post said. The employee was terminated. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology." Alfozan is also listed as a partner at Raed Ventures , a venture capital firm that focuses on the Middle East and North Africa, according to its website. The firm announced on Feb. 6, 2025, that H.H. Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, had joined the firm as a venture partner. Alfozan was announced as a venture partner two days later. The Raed announcement for Alfozan lists Meta , Microsoft and SAP as previous roles and said he studied computer science and engineering at MIT. Raed, which is headquartered in the Saudi capital of Riyadh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI said in the post. "We take protecting our technology, data and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance." Alfozan was not authorized to access the executive conference room where the device was found, according to the DOJ. The department said footage showed him near the conference room on multiple days before the device was discovered. The DOJ said that on Oct. 5, he went into the room. The DOJ said a bag was also found in the OpenAI building on or about Oct. 5 that belonged to Alfozan. Inside the bag, security found his wallet, ID and another recording device similar to the one that was in the executive conference room. The department said a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse that "shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan's own chatbot account" was used to get information about continuous audio recording and Wi-Fi. The DOJ said promps were submitted related to "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device." The device was concealed in toilet paper, and its contents were encrypted, according to the DOJ. This security incident comes as the ChatGPT-maker, along with competitors like Anthropic and other big tech names, faces heightened scrutiny over safety protocols after a series of cyber incidents where autonomous agents escaped testing environments and hacked into outside systems. Last week, OpenAI defended its decision to fire three safety researchers, alleging a "significant breach of trust," saying that the researchers "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni raised safety concerns in a letter to OpenAI's leadership, saying that communications around their exits "have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI." —CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this article. events.title: English and Welsh water firms could be forced to return £107m via lower bills
events.summary: Yorkshire and Thames among providers facing penalties for missing performance targets, but bills could rise elsewhere Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and other providers could be forced to cut tens of millions of pounds from household bills after the regulator said they had missed performance targets. Customer bills at Yorkshire Water could fall by £27 on average, while those at Thames could decrease by £7, according to estimates by Ofwat, the regulator of the privatised industry in England and Wales. The water industry has faced growing criticism in recent years amid rising bills , scrutiny over sewage pollution , high levels of debt and underinvestment in ageing infrastructure. As water customers cannot switch away from their provider if it underperforms, Ofwat instead has an “outcome delivery incentives” system of automatic payments or penalties based on agreed targets. Yorkshire and Thames will have to return £75.1m and £45.8m respectively after missing targets in 2025-26, Ofwat said. The payments will add to the financial pressures on the companies. Yorkshire is among the companies subject to enhanced monitoring by Ofwat over its financial resilience, while the government is considering whether to bring Thames Water under public control after years-long negotiations to reduce its crippling debts. The other companies that must return money to customers include: Dŵr Cymru (or Welsh Water), at £16.7m; South West Water, at £16m; and United Utilities in north-west England, at £13.4m. However, some companies will receive a reward payment because they met their targets – covered by higher bills. Severn Trent, which serves the Midlands, south-west England and parts of Wales , and Northumbrian Water are in line to receive an extra £41.8m and £35.9m respectively, Ofwat said. Northumbrian customers’ bills could rise by an average of £21, the regulator said. Severn Trent customers could pay £8 more per year. Overall, the industry is expected to cut its bills by a net £240m for failures during 2025-26. Of this, £107m is expected to be returned to customers via lower bills in 2027-28. Ofwat said at this stage the figures were still at the draft stage and not every household would receive the same change. Bills are “affected by a range of factors and the effect will vary by company and customer type”, the regulator said. It will make its final decision on the payments by 15 December, which will take effect on bills from 1 April 2027. Ofwat recently announced that water companies could increase annual tariffs by an extra £3.4bn, on top of the 36% average rise agreed over five years to 2030. Customer bills are rising to pay for long-overdue investments to fix leaking pipes and treatment works, as well as to pay for new assets such as reservoirs. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Andy Burnham last month said the government would pave the way for public ownership of water firms and promised a 10-year path to a “very different water system in the UK”. The comments suggested the prime minister might opt for a temporary nationalisation of debt-laden Thames Water as the government seeks to make a decision on a £10bn rescue takeover put forward by lenders for the UK’s biggest water supplier. Ofwat’s announcement came after Burnham said customers must not be “treated as a blank cheque” and after the regulator said in August it planned to allow yet more bill increases on top of those already agreed. A government spokesperson said: “This government won’t allow customers to be treated as a blank cheque, and we are committed to protecting households from cost-of-living pressures. We will always challenge water companies where they seek to pass unnecessary costs on to households. “We will deliver a strengthened water bill that puts people first, ensuring affordable access to clean water, driving down pollution, and strengthening public control.” A Yorkshire Water spokesperson said: “We recognise that our performance last year fell short of the standards we and our customers expect in some areas, and we remain focused on improving. “We are already delivering Yorkshire’s largest ever environmental investment programme and with the help of over 1,000 new colleagues, we’ve completed improvements at almost 300 locations across the county.”

events.title: Bilt’s CMO is betting big on marketing that's hard to measure
events.summary: The launch of the Bilt Locals merch collection is part of a strategy to turn customers into willing brand ambassadors. Bilt A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly marketing newsletter . Bilt CMO Zoe Oz thinks traditional advertising is losing its power. Her alternative? Turning customers into willing brand ambassadors. The fintech loyalty platform is investing heavily in entertainment, live experiences, and covetable merchandise — though Oz readily admits these tactics are more difficult to measure directly than paid ads. In September, Bilt launched its Locals Collection, a range of vintage-inspired apparel and accessories that members could purchase with Bilt Points , Bilt Cash, or a linked card. Bilt said an October pop-up event in New York City drew long lines, and most items sold out. The most popular included a motel keychain, diner mug, and $150 "bodega crew" sweater. Since launching the Bilt Collection in 2021, Bilt said members have redeemed more than 70 million points and spent over $800,000 across more than 60,000 orders. "If you're making merch, it really should be something that someone chooses to wear, not just because it's affiliated with the brand, but actually because they want to wear it," Oz told me. The goal, she added, is to create "a tiny moment that Bilt gets mentioned without it having to be Bilt mentioning it ourselves." Selling sweaters and keychains might seem like an unusual move for a company best known for rewarding people for paying their rent. But Oz sees the collection as part of a much bigger ambition: turning Bilt into a lifestyle brand. "We want to be a generation-defining brand," Oz said. "You don't get to do that if you're just providing a financial service and leaving it at that. You really have to spend time integrating yourself into what the member does every single day." 'Do they have the staying power?' Matt Powell, CEO of the marketing agency Moroch, said brands like Red Bull and Soho House have successfully branched out beyond their initial product focus to cement themselves as lifestyle brands. For Bilt, Powell asked: "Do they have the staying power to build this long term? And as their brand extends into homebuyers inevitably, does that approach still work for that audience?" Bilt's ambitions haven't been without their setbacks. Wells Fargo ended a credit card partnership with Bilt earlier this year ahead of the contract's planned expiration date. The Wall Street Journal reported that the bank was losing as much as $10 million a month on the deal. Bilt's subsequent transition to a new credit card program sparked customer complaints over payment issues and other service problems. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau met with Bilt and said in September it considered the matter closed after the company refunded affected customers. Bilt CEO Ankur Jain said in a May interview that the Bilt credit card accounts for "less than 11%" of its business. The bulk comes from the fees it makes on the resident experience and housing payments platform it offers to housing operators and apartment owners, as well as merchant commissions. Bilt, which reached a $10.75 billion valuation at its latest funding round last year, has expanded beyond rent and mortgage rewards to include restaurants, fitness, entertainment, and other aspects of neighborhood life. It's preparing to open its second café, this one in New York's Meatpacking District below its headquarters, designed to offer members a space to hang out day and night. Oz said Bilt has drawn inspiration from entertainment and community experiences popular decades ago, reimagining them for modern audiences. Its social media sitcom , "Roomies," is a riff on "Friends," while Bilt also hosts dining events, parties, fitness classes, and comedy shows designed to bring members together in real life . Oz said that Bilt's emphasis on real-world experiences flies in the face of conventional marketing wisdom, which often prizes efficiency, scale, and measurability. "Live experiences is not an efficient business, it's like the most inefficient, unscalable thing you can possibly do," Oz said. "But we found those to be 10 times more effective than the other ways we used to spend money." Oz said that it's difficult to determine whether activities such as merchandise sales and live events directly increase customer engagement. Bilt can track whether members who buy merchandise also attend events or use its other services, but determining whether those experiences made them more engaged is another matter. The merchandise business remains relatively modest in scale. Bilt's 60,000-plus orders have accumulated over five years, and the company hasn't disclosed how many individual members have purchased items or whether those customers subsequently spent more with Bilt. The company said last month that it had over 7 million members. Thinking beyond traditional advertising Oz thinks traditional advertising is becoming increasingly formulaic. Bilt still runs paid ads and lifecycle marketing, but she considers them "table stakes" rather than the source of its competitive advantage. Oz said that giving members more opportunities to interact with the brand ultimately helps increase their lifetime value to the company, even if the impact of any individual interaction is difficult to isolate. "What's going to create that intangible love? What's going to make someone sit down at dinner and say, 'I love Bilt'?" Oz said. She said her approach requires marketers to be comfortable with launching ambitious ideas that might ultimately flop. "I have a very high tolerance for experimentation. I have a high tolerance for failure. I have a high tolerance for moonshots ," Oz said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs
events.summary: One official claims satellite internet could erode online governance in Iran amid war with the US and Israel. Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have pledged to continue a crackdown against satellite internet service Starlink, along with further restrictions on the global internet as the US-Israel war on Iran continues. Elon Musk’s Starlink, which is free of the heavy filtering and restrictions imposed by Tehran, is outlawed in Iran on national security grounds. The use of satellite-based internet services and the distribution of Starlink terminals are subject to fines and imprisonment. list 1 of 3 SpaceX’s showpiece Starship rocket reaches orbit for first time list 2 of 3 ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan? list 3 of 3 Poland says two Turks arrested over Russia-linked Starlink station fire It is one of the many measures imposed by Iranian authorities since the United States and Israel launched strikes on the country on February 28, leading to a prolonged and economically punishing war between the countries. Iran’s 90 million people have undergone two lengthy state-imposed global internet shutdowns in 2026 – for three weeks during nationwide protests in January and for 88 days at the start of the ongoing war . Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of the Supreme National Cyberspace Council, described Starlink as a “tool of war” for enemies. “It is a tool used for command and control by the enemy, for espionage and information gathering,” he said. “We have several systems for cutting off Starlink satellite terminals.” He did not elaborate on what measures or devices were being used to block Starlink, but one was deployed during the January protests and authorities were prepared to share the technology with aligned countries. Iran is among several countries that have banned or restricted Starlink due to national security concerns. It has set baseline sentences of between six months and two years for using or possessing Starlink. Importing and distributing the devices carry jail terms of up to five years. If paired with national security or espionage charges, individuals can even face the death penalty. Aghamiri has called on Iranians to use domestic platforms, supported by what the authorities call the National Information Network. He also backed a tiered-access model, which envisages protected international access for selected groups – such as traders, researchers and journalists – during periods of internet restrictions. A Tehran-based internet and telecommunications expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Al Jazeera that Iranian authorities use a combination of measures to block Starlink connections. This includes the use of multiple jammers with different configurations to disrupt services, along with spoofed GPS locations to slow new devices being set up. They can also identify Starlink-associated internet protocols if they connect to local applications and services. Authorities also try to physically intercept terminals using patrols and drone searches, or raid locations selling the terminals. In June, Israeli politician Naftali Bennett claimed that Israel had smuggled tens of thousands of Starlink devices into Iran when he was prime minister, between 2021 and 2022, to aid antigovernment protesters. Since 2023, Iran has also pursued the matter at the International Telecommunication Union’s Radio Regulations Board, trying to pressure the US and Norway, which plays a role in the satellite network’s regulatory filings, to halt transmissions. On October 4, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned the Norwegian ambassador in Tehran to protest against what it described as a failure to act over unauthorised Starlink operations. During a governance meeting at the end of September, Deputy Technology Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami had warned authorities that Starlink could signify “the last nail in the coffin of the [cyberspace] governance” of Iran if it becomes prevalent, due to the unfettered internet access it provides. He pointed out that the government blocked the messaging app Telegram after the cost-of-living protests in 2017-18, but had to resort to a weeklong internet shutdown for the first time during the nationwide protests in 2019 . WhatsApp and Instagram were blocked after the 2022-23 protests, which preceded the near-total shutdown during the January 2026 protests. “If this trend continues, in the next crisis we will have to cut electricity, because Starlink, as a new tool of evading state governance, is fundamentally not even dependent on our network,” Hakami said. Starlink has allowed Iranians to send out videos of the protests abroad since 2022 despite state restrictions. Tens of thousands of terminals are believed to have been smuggled into the country since, but exact figures are unknown.

events.title: Qatar’s wealth fund keeps spending as war slashes government revenue
events.summary: The News Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund isn’t slowing its dealmaking, a senior executive said, even as the Iran war gutted the state’s revenue by 42% in the first half of the year. The war “hasn’t impacted our progress,” Mohsin Pirzada, head of funds at Qatar Investment Authority, told Semafor. “We continue to invest, we continue to deploy.” “We’re obviously very mindful that we manage the surplus wealth for the state of Qatar, and that is largely derived by LNG exports,” Pirzada said. The sovereign fund has remained an active investor, with its funds division deploying billions of dollars already this year. QIA announced a $20 billion investment partnership with JPMorgan last month, following a $25 billion agreement with Goldman Sachs just before the Iran war began. While no new fund deals are “on the radar” now, Pirzada said, QIA “will have a handful of strategic platform arrangements with managers or institutions like JPMorgan, or like Goldman Sachs,” focused on firms that the fund has had long-standing relationships with.” Know More Before the war, QIA said it planned to invest $500 billion in the US alone over the next decade. The fund had expected to nearly double in size, boosted by an 85% expansion of its liquefied natural gas (LNG) output by 2030. That gas expansion has now been delayed — an Iranian attack on the Ras Laffan complex knocked out about 17% of its existing capacity. Qatar’s economy is expected to contract 15.6% this year , and the government will likely post a deficit. QIA, with around $580 billion in assets, is a significant backer of Wall Street firms and US technology. Its appetite mirrors that of its Gulf peers: with the exception of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, all are on track for one of their most active years of dealmaking ever, according to fund tracker GlobalSWF. Qatar has been one of the most impacted Gulf countries by the US-Iran war. Unlike some of its neighbors, it has no export routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, and has been reluctant to move LNG tankers — which are more flammable and expensive than crude carriers — through the strait. Despite the disruptions, there are signs of recovery. QatarEnergy Chief Executive Saad al-Kaabi said last month that the expansion project is expected to begin production in the first half of 2027. Meanwhile, an LNG export facility in Texas, majority owned by QatarEnergy in a joint venture with ExxonMobil, shipped its first cargoes in April. Notable Qatar cut government department budgets by around a third and funding for overseas aid by about 85% to cope with the financial strain of the war , the Financial Times reported. A “dinosaur” gas tanker is one part of an ambitious effort to revive Qatari energy shipments , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: More expensive gas, semiconductors likely pushed up inflation last month
events.summary: U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections WASHINGTON -- U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas , clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability. The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday , up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month. The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices. Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low. Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%. Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year. By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago. Gas prices jumped more than 9% from August to September, Wednesday's report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy. Prices at the pump have ticked lower in the past two weeks to a nationwide average of $4.33 a gallon, according to AAA, though they remain higher than a month ago. Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients. The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones. Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple's newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade , though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities. events.title: I don't regret leaving New York City for a small Italian village — but I've had to adjust to some big lifestyle changes
events.summary: I've found that in my Italian village, building relationships can help you get tasks done. Camellia Phillips About three years ago, I moved from New York City to a small Sicilian village . Grocery shopping and running errands are very different here. However, I've grown to appreciate many of the ways my lifestyle has changed. I recently walked into the macelleria in our Sicilian village — a combo butcher, deli, and corner store — and started babbling excitedly that my favorite cheese was back in stock. One of the owners joked in Italian that "Camellia moved here just for the food." She wasn't completely wrong. After 20 years in New York City, my husband and I moved to a small town in Italy for some of the more classic reasons: quality food, a slower pace of life, and community-oriented culture. Now that we've lived here for nearly three years, though, we've also experienced the reality behind the tourism taglines. Our village has its own rhythm — one I've learned to appreciate, even when it's pushed me to change and adapt. The food system is hyper-local and seasonal I buy produce from a local food truck that frequently comes by my village. Camellia Phillips Buying food here looks very different from the way we shopped in the US. With no large grocery store within a 40-minute walk, we shop hyper-local. This includes the macelleria, weekly outdoor market, and vendors who drive our narrow streets selling fruit, vegetables, eggs, fish, fresh bread, and more. Each truck passes by only on certain days and times — and the schedule isn't written down. We had to learn it by living it. We've now gotten to know local vendors and farmers, and we message them in advance to find out what's available. We eat what's in season, like broccoli and citrus in winter, or melon with prosciutto in summer. Some specialties, like prickly pears, fresh figs, and wild asparagus, are only available for a few weeks each year. This hyper-local food delivery system can be a lifesaver, too, if you have limited mobility. Our older neighbors lean out their balconies to call down orders for eggs and artichokes. Everything closes for 3 hours in the afternoon Many businesses in our town tend to slow down in the afternoon. Camellia Phillips If you're trying to pack in an afternoon of errands on your own schedule, small-town Sicily is not the place to do it. Where we live, most businesses and public offices close for around three hours every afternoon. Especially in the hot summer months, the streets are nearly deserted between 1 p.m. and 4 p.m. each day. At first, this caught me off guard. I'd head out to grab a prescription or a quick lunch , and find everything closed. Then I realized this was what a "slower pace of life" actually entails. Taking an afternoon break to eat, rest, and step away from your work is the norm, not the exception. But the break doesn't mean people don't work exceptionally hard. Our village comes back to life in the late afternoon, and then, many businesses stay open until 7 or 8 p.m. My husband and I have grown to appreciate this rhythm. Most evenings after work, we head out for a long walk, do our shopping, and chat with people along the way. Relationships are essential to getting things done Since moving here, I've relied less on apps to schedule appointments and complete paperwork. Camellia Phillips In New York, we could use an app to schedule an appointment or get groceries delivered. Here, getting things done requires building personal relationships. As newcomers, that's meant showing up in person — a lot. When we first moved, we started our residency and immigration paperwork at the vital records office at city hall. But here's the thing: It's only open to the public one morning and one afternoon each week. To learn the schedule, we had to go in person. Then, we had to show up on the right day with initial questions … and return another day to submit our forms. If you're used to taking care of business from behind a screen, this can seem inefficient. Now that I've adjusted to it, though, I'm convinced this system is actually a feature. Yes, tasks can take more time, but showing up in person has helped us connect with people in our community. And it can pay off in unexpected ways. When my husband's distant cousin recently visited from the US, we stopped at city hall to show them the beautiful, historic building . A staff member recognized us — thanks to all our visits — and offered an impromptu private tour! Personal connections can also turn into support when you need it most. Now, I feel comfortable using WhatsApp to send urgent questions to our pharmacist and doctors, even on weekends. Adapting to Italian culture takes time and intention Before moving, I imagined I'd fall naturally into an Italian pace of life . But I've learned that we carry our habits and personalities with us — the good and the bad. I spent 20 years as a deadline-driven nonprofit fundraiser, and even though I thought Italy would help me slow down, I found myself reproducing that same workaholic approach here. Changing took longer than I expected, but I've learned to prioritize connection over the illusion of efficiency, and I've become more intentional about balancing urgency versus patience. Now, I try to live by the common saying here — "piano piano," or "little by little" — and trust that what's important will get done in its own time. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in Manchester
events.summary: Company hails first step in rolling out technology across UK as first autonomous vehicles take to city’s streets Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK. The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe’s first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Uber said it was “excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK”. In social media posts, Verne said it had “started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester”, while Pony said there were “plans to bring robotaxis to the city” and that testing was under way. The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers. Limited passenger services started last month in London , but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London’s licensing rules for private hire vehicles. The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital’s politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected. A critical report from London assembly’s transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. It said there was “considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far, and the vehicles are operating under government licence via the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) and the Department for Transport . A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it wanted the city’s taxis to be the safest in the country. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “New technologies play an increasingly important role in the growth of our city region,” they said. “But they need to be introduced responsibly, safely and with real thought about what it means for our residents. “Although no applications have been made to operate driverless taxis in the Greater Manchester, we’re aware of potential interest from companies to do so. “Safety will always be our top priority, and we will need strong assurances that no vehicles will operate on our roads that pose any risk to residents.” Uber said it expected to offering robotaxi trips in as many as 15 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, mainly in the US and the Middle East.

events.title: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million
events.summary: Morgan Stanley topped expectations on the top and bottom lines for the third quarter. Results were powered by equities trading, which exceeded revenue expectations by $909 million. Still, the results were good, not great, as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, according to Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo. Morgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Earnings per share: $3.03 vs. $2.91 LSEG estimate Revenue: $20.34 billion vs. $19.95 billion LSEG estimate The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue climbed 12% to $20.34 billion. The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million. Morgan Stanley cited widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere. Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations. Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower IPOs and a decline in fixed income underwriting. Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note. events.title: I eat the same dietitian-approved lunch almost every day. It's got fiber and protein — and is a breeze to prep in advance
events.summary: My husband and I eat the same lunches nearly every single day during the week. Rachel Hosie I meal-prep the same protein- and fiber-rich lunch for my husband and me every single week. Because I mix up the ingredients, dressings, and seasonings for the grain bowls, they never get old. The nourishing bowls are Mediterranean diet-friendly and help me follow the 80/20 principle . When I lived in a big city, I used to love treating myself to lunches at trendy salad spots. Although these take-out meals were tasty, they were terrible for my wallet. I've since turned into an avid meal-prepper and frequently make my own lunch — almost always a fiber- and protein-packed grain bowl — for a fraction of the price. The recipe I use aligns with the 80/20 nutrition principle I follow, meaning I eat nutrient-dense foods 80% of the time and don't worry about nutrition for the other 20%. The grain bowls are so nourishing that I feel relaxed about occasionally going out for a slightly less nutrient-dense lunch, since I know I'm hitting my nutrition goals most of the time. Here's how to make the go-to lunch that helps me stay on track. These grain bowls are easy to prep and customize The grain bowls are nearly impossible to mess up and highly customizable. Rachel Hosie I play around with the ingredients I put in my grain bowls every week, but they always follow the same formula: My grain-bowl ingredient checklist: Grains, such as quinoa, wholegrain rice, or buckwheat Beans or legumes, such as chickpeas, edamame, or lentils A protein source, such as tofu or chicken Raw vegetables, such as chopped cucumber, tomatoes, beetroot, or scallions Roasted vegetables, such as butternut squash, bell peppers, cauliflower, broccoli, or zucchini A flavorful add-in, such as crumbled feta, avocado, or hummus Greens, such as lettuce or spinach Spices and herbs of choice Seeds and nuts of choice A dressing of choice The recipe is flexible, so there's no need to add ingredients in a specific order. It's truly hard to mess up. You can also adjust the quantity based on your needs. I typically make six portions — three for me, and three for my husband — because there's usually a day or two during the week when we eat with colleagues or friends. Plus, after three days of eating the same meal, I'm typically ready to mix it up. I drizzle a tahini mixture over my bowl for added flavor. Rachel Hosie To add variety to my days, I prep these with varying dressings and protein sources. My favorite dressing is a creamy tahini mixture. To make, I combine tahini, lemon juice, Greek yogurt, garlic granules, salt, pepper, water, and olive oil until it's a dressing-like consistency. I also like making a satay-style sauce with crunchy peanut butter , soy sauce, ginger, garlic, sesame oil, and lime juice. Chickpeas and avocado are delicious, filling protein sources. Rachel Hosie There's also flexibility when it comes to protein source in these bowls. Nichola Ludlam-Raine , a dietitian and the author of "How Not to Eat Ultra-Processed," recommends adding oily fish, such as salmon or tinned mackerel , for omega-3s, which can help support heart and brain health. When I include meat in the grain bowls, I typically use a modest portion, since I always add plenty of plant-based protein, too. This approach keeps the ingredient list affordable and provides a fiber boost from plant-based proteins. If you're predominantly eating plant-based, make sure you're getting enough iodine by using dairy yogurt in your dressing or swapping in the occasional white fish. Having a balanced lunch prepped and ready to go helps me stay consistent Incorporating a mix of roasted and raw vegetables adds texture to the bowls. Rachel Hosie My grain-bowl formula has lean proteins, produce, legumes, and whole grains — all the workings of the Mediterranean diet . According to Ludlam-Raine, "It's essentially a Mediterranean-style pattern of eating in bowl form, which is linked with better cardiometabolic and long-term health outcomes." The well-rounded meal also has fiber-filled whole grains, slow-release carbohydrates, protein for satiety and muscle maintenance, legumes for plant protein and additional fiber, vegetables for polyphenols and micronutrients, and healthy fats from seeds, nuts, and olive oil. We store the bowls in our refrigerator throughout the week. Rachel Hosie Strategizing my meals in advance helps me maintain a healthy, balanced diet throughout the week, and this grain bowl is the backbone of my meal plan. "Overall, what you've got is a brilliant example of a practical and sustainable approach to meal prep . It's balanced, fiber-rich, protein-sufficient, and easy to adapt week to week, which is key for long-term adherence," Ludlam-Raine told me. "You're making the healthy choice into the easy choice." The best part is that I don't get bored with eating the same thing on repeat. This story was originally published on March 12, 2026, and most recently updated on October 14, 2026. events.title: Redwood Materials has a new business: Helping AI data centers avoid America's backed-up electric grid
events.summary: JB Straubel, co-founder and chief executive officer of Redwood Materials. Bloomberg/Getty Images Redwood Materials wants to help AI data centers get electricity faster. It plans to combine retired EV batteries with solar and other on-site power sources. Redwood is working with Rivian and has built a battery system for Crusoe in Nevada. Redwood Materials wants to help companies sidestep years-long waits for electricity by building on-site energy systems with recycled EV batteries, according to CEO JB Straubel . The battery recycling startup is expanding beyond collecting and processing old electric-vehicle batteries. It's increasingly pitching itself as a way for AI data centers to get power faster, without waiting for new connections to America's backed-up electric grid. "Connecting to the grid can take years," Straubel wrote in a blog post on Wednesday. His solution is what the industry calls " behind-the-meter " energy systems, which operate without needing to connect to the grid. Redwood would combine second-life EV batteries with solar panels and other on-site power sources, allowing customers to generate and store electricity at their own facilities. A battery storage racking system from Redwood Materials Redwood Materials The company is already putting the idea into practice with Rivian. Redwood recycles used batteries from the EV maker and is installing energy storage systems at Rivian's manufacturing plants, building on a 10-megawatt-hour installation at the company's Illinois factory. Redwood is also packaging the batteries with its own power electronics and software, turning what began as a recycling business into a broader energy offering. The company launched its Redwood Energy division last year on the premise that EV batteries still have years of useful life after they're retired from cars. It has already built a large battery system for a Crusoe data center. Straubel's latest post makes clear where Redwood sees its biggest opportunity. "The underlying problem is speed to power," he wrote, referring to the AI-fueled race to secure electricity. That marks another step in Redwood's evolution. Investors originally backed the company to recycle batteries. Today, it's increasingly selling something different: a faster way to bring power to energy-hungry AI data centers. events.title: Exclusive: Honeywell Technologies launches a ‘brain behind the building’ with Nvidia and Dell. Its CTO says humans will run it for now
events.summary: Honeywell Technologies’ new AI platform can run in three modes: manual, semi-autonomous and autonomous. The company’s chief technology officer hasn’t switched on the third. “We have not opened up an autonomy right now,” Suresh Venkatarayalu told Fortune in an interview ahead of Wednesday’s launch of Forge Cognition. The platform, built with technology from Nvidia and Dell, puts AI agents and digital twins on top of the systems that heat, cool, secure and power buildings. Honeywell’s launch announcement says the agents can “autonomously coordinate actions across existing systems.” Venkatarayalu says people will stay in the loop for now. “Maybe we will start running in this mode for probably next two to three years,” he said. After that, customers decide when to make the switch. “For me, I wouldn’t deploy these agents without my control system in place,” he said. That gap between what the software can do and what Honeywell will let it do is the bet. Forge Cognition is the first major product from the slimmed-down Honeywell, which spun off its advanced-materials and aerospace businesses over the past year and now sells automation for buildings, factories and process plants. It is also an early test of a question facing every company putting AI agents into physical operations: how much control do you give software that runs equipment people depend on? Venkatarayalu calls the platform “a brain behind a building.” For now, that brain advises, and the operators decide. Nvidia’s 90-day test The project started with a challenge at CES in January. As Venkatarayalu tells it, Nvidia’s leadership heard Honeywell’s pitch for autonomous buildings and asked the obvious follow-up: “Who is your lighthouse customer?” In other words, where’s the real building that proves it works? “We don’t believe in just POCs,” Venkatarayalu said, meaning proofs of concept. Honeywell CEO Vimal Kapur turned the question around and asked Nvidia, “Why can’t you be my lighthouse customer?” Nvidia took the challenge. Within 30 days, Venkatarayalu was in Santa Clara pitching Nvidia’s operations and real estate team. The two companies then set a 90-day target: show meaningful results at Voyager, Nvidia’s roughly 750,000-square-foot headquarters building, in time for Honeywell’s investor day in June. Nvidia’s head of operations and real estate, Scott Ekman, wanted more than a demo, Venkatarayalu said. He had his own business objectives. The teams agreed on five performance targets, measured where the building stood, and tracked progress week by week across about 900 pieces of equipment. By late April, Honeywell had enough to show investors a three-minute live demonstration. The first target was alarms. Building systems are designed to err on the side of caution, so they flag everything. In Voyager’s security and access-control system, Venkatarayalu said, close to 90% to 95% of alarms were false, and Nvidia had eight or nine people per shift clearing them. Honeywell took Nvidia’s open-source Nemotron model and trained it on Honeywell’s own engineering knowledge to sort real alarms from noise. Honeywell says the result at Voyager is up to a 90% reduction in unnecessary alerts related to the Building Management System. Operators can check every call the agents make. Operators can open each alarm the system classified and mark whether they agree. “That’s all about bringing in an operator in the loop,” Venkatarayalu said, so the operator can learn to trust it. The second target was energy. The agents broke Voyager’s utility bill down by floor, zone, and peak and off-peak hours, then flagged a pattern in how the building was heated. Venkatarayalu said they looked at how many zones in the building were running the heating system at a standard, “something like 58 degrees throughout the year, “and then it wasn’t really sensing the external temperature that goes beyond 58. Why should I be running the heating system?” “We have identified close to 10% of energy efficiency,” he said. That figure is potential savings Honeywell and Nvidia have identified through more intelligent understanding and optimization of operating conditions; it hasn’t been achieved yet. Talking to a building In its simplest mode, Forge Cognition is a chatbot for infrastructure. “Can I talk to the building? Can I talk to a physical asset?” Venkatarayalu said. Operators can ask about performance and trends, then click into a digital replica of Voyager, built with Nvidia’s Omniverse simulation software, down to a single floor, zone or machine. Dell supplies the servers that run it on site. Venkatarayalu frames the shift as a change in what the system does. Traditional building automation could “see and act”: sensors collected data, and operators responded. The new version adds “think” and “learn”: AI models trained on Honeywell’s installed base and engineering documents interpret what the sensors pick up, and operator feedback improves them over time. “Autonomy for me is automation plus plus,” he said. The learning works differently from site to site. At Honeywell’s campus in Bangalore, the goal was energy savings. At Voyager, Venkatarayalu said, Nvidia’s leadership told him, “For me, comfort is more important.” The agents have to learn what each operator is trying to achieve as well as how the equipment behaves. He sets a high bar for moving to full autonomy. Before a customer makes that call, he said, the system should have “10 out of 10 accuracy all the time.” The skills gap Venkatarayalu presents the product as help for operators. “At least I do not think as replacement,” he said. “In an industrial environment, I need a co-pilot that aids and directs me and helps me to do my job better.” In the U.S., he sees a labor shortage. Elsewhere, it’s a shortage of skilled operators. He said Nvidia’s operations chief described the same problem. As Venkatarayalu tells it, Scott said the system now performs on par with his best-trained building operators, a team he spent 10 to 15 years building. As Nvidia adds more large, complex buildings, Scott told him, it won’t be able to hire and train that talent fast enough. Predicting equipment failures matters for the same reason. Some replacement parts take six to 18 months to arrive, Venkatarayalu said, so knowing early what will fail is how operators plan ahead. Nvidia also wants its own people trained. According to Venkatarayalu, Nvidia will sign a service contract only after Honeywell’s forward-deployed engineers train its operations team and chief engineer to keep giving the models feedback. “Physical AI is bringing new intelligence to the complex systems that run our buildings and industrial facilities,” Deepu Talla, Nvidia’s vice president of robotics and edge AI, said in the launch announcement. events.title: Fragment raises $12 million to help keep AI agents from going rogue with company money
events.summary: Keeping the books straight is a business headache. As companies turn to AI to automate routine financial tasks, they face a new worry: whether they can trust bots with company money. Fragment, a New York-based startup, is developing software designed to reduce costly accounting errors. Founded by serial entrepreneur and CEO Thomas Neckel and CTO Varun Mohan, a former Robinhood engineer, Fragment announced on Wednesday that it raised a $12 million Series A round that closed in mid-2025 to build software that lets AI agents safely handle billing and accounting. Early-stage venture capital firms FirstMark and BoxGroup co-led the financing. The round follows an $11 million seed round led by payments company Stripe, with participation from BoxGroup and tech executives including Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi and Plaid CEO Zach Perret. Neckel declined to disclose the company’s valuation following the Series A. It works like this: Developers plug Fragment’s tools into their software. The system uses double-entry accounting, a centuries-old method that records where money comes from and where it goes, to check that the numbers balance before money moves. “Just like Claude Code or Cursor is a set of software blocks for agents to automate coding, we are a set of financial building blocks or financial primitives to automate commerce,” Neckel told Fortune . Fragment’s push is part of a broader shift toward agentic commerce, in which AI agents shop and make payments on users’ behalf. In June, Visa announced a partnership with OpenAI to let agents make purchases within spending limits set by users, while Mastercard introduced a service that lets AI agents more easily pay each other. Three months earlier, Stripe and Tempo launched a shared standard that lets agents pay to access online tools and data without a person completing checkout. But giving AI agents more control can also expose businesses to costly mistakes. In July 2025, an AI agent from software development platform Replit reportedly deleted a live database despite instructions not to make changes. Concerns about whether humans can trust AI also surfaced after OpenAI said that its experimental agents had bypassed restrictions during tests in July 2026 and accessed systems at Hugging Face, a platform where developers share AI models and training data. Fragment says its accounting tools can give businesses the confidence to expand AI commerce. It has roughly 50 to 60 paying customers, including corporate card startup Ramp, financial software company BILL, and digital marketplace Whop. They use its software as a shared transaction record, reducing the need for staff to manually check that numbers match across different financial systems. “We think that this ecosystem is about to explode, and so that’s really the goal: becoming the standard toolkit that anybody uses for bringing financial capabilities to their agents,” said Adam Nelson, a managing partner at FirstMark, who co-led the Series A round.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: AI agents are on a shopping spree: Total payments on Base blockchain eclipse 138 million, Chainalysis finds
events.summary: The field of agentic commerce , which describes the use of AI agents to carry out Internet transactions, is rapidly maturing, and crypto is fueling the boom. That’s according to a new report by the blockchain analytics platform Chainalysis, which found developers are increasingly giving AI agents their own budgets to buy the computing power, live web data, and code tools they need to complete tasks. The growth of agentic commerce over the past 15 months has been steep. On Base, the Coinbase-incubated blockchain, cumulative payments through the x402 protocol—which lets bots automatically pay for online services using crypto—rose from about 1,500 in mid-2025 to more than 138 million by the third quarter of 2026. In practice, agentic commerce entails providing an AI bot with an allowance:  A developer funds the bot’s wallet with stablecoins—typically Circle’s dollar-pegged USDC—and the bot pays for services as it works, without asking a person to approve each purchase. When it needs help with a task, it can pay to get up-to-date information, ask a more capable AI model for help, or use an automated tool to check software code for security flaws. More than 87% of these payments were for less than 10 cents, per the report. At those amounts, the fee for processing a credit card payment can cost more than the service itself. That makes blockchains an ideal alternative for bots buying services in small amounts, according to Eric Jardine, head of research at Chainalysis. “You have this perfect combination of speed plus low cost to settle, and that’s the sort of thing that you would need if you were doing true AI-to-AI commerce,” Jardine told Fortune . “The trend is likely to be exponential “ Agentic commerce has proliferated over the past year, and its use cases have spanned from online shopping to travel booking and payments settlement. It has also given AI systems a bigger role in deciding what to buy and how to pay. For consumers and businesses, this means handing AI systems not just tasks, but also spending decisions. Crypto companies have played a key role in spurring their popularity in the United States. Chief among them is Coinbase, which introduced x402 in May 2025 and later teamed up with cloud security firm Cloudflare to support its development. The protocol’s foundation launched under the Linux Foundation in July with 40 members, including Visa, Mastercard, Stripe and Google, extending its backing beyond the crypto industry. Chainalysis centered its research on x402 because the protocol was purpose-built for agent-to-agent commerce. Beyond transaction growth, the report shows that bots are putting funds to work sooner. The median time between a wallet receiving its first deposit and making its first payment fell from 73 days in late 2025 to 18 minutes by the third quarter of 2026. Roughly two-thirds of new wallets now spend within an hour of receiving funds. Repeat funding has also become more common. Around 90% of qualifying active wallets received another deposit within 30 days, up from roughly 71% a year earlier, suggesting that developers are funding ongoing tasks rather than using them for one-off experiments.  Given agentic commerce’s exponential growth so far, Jardine expects this bot-driven economy to keep expanding as more online platforms accept payments from AI agents. “I would hazard that the trend is likely to be exponential,” Jardine said. “As activity increases, there’s network effects, and those network effects tend to act like magnets for more activity,” he said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: A former Ukrainian officer goes on trial over sabotage of Nord Stream pipelines
events.summary: Defense lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial HAMBURG, Germany -- Defense lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial. The trial that opened Wednesday in Hamburg centers on undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany in what is considered one of Europe’s biggest acts of sabotage since World War II. Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure. His lawyers, making the motion for dismissal, argued that Kuznietsov was still an active duty soldier and as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for reasons of secrecy linked to national security. As the proceedings got underway at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court, Kuznietsov, dressed in a gray suit and dark tie, kept a calm expression as he sat between two lawyers in black robes. From the dock, Kuznietsov glanced over to a packed visitors area and exchanged smiles with two people. He did not speak during Wednesday’s proceedings, which lasted about two hours, and listened to simultaneous translation from German into Ukrainian through white headphones. After the charges were read out, a judge asked whether Kuznietsov wanted to comment, and his defense lawyers said he did not. They went on to request that all the charges be dismissed. Kuznietsov’s legal team said allegations of war crimes would be better targeted against the Russian forces acting on orders from President Vladimir Putin during the 4-1/2-year-war, citing examples like atrocities in the Ukrainian town of Bucha and the kidnapping of Ukrainian children . The defense team also disputed the accusation that the attack was sabotage of civilian infrastructure, with defense lawyer Nicola Canestrini saying the pipelines “were a weapon in the hand of the Russians.” But the crux of their call for dismissal was that Kuznietsov had to keep quiet as a Ukrainian officer. “He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers,” defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court, adding that under German law: “Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted.” Meyer-Lohkamp also decried the detention conditions of his client, likening them to solitary confinement: “He is brave, but he is locked up for 23 hours a day and suffers because of it. He has no opportunity to participate in social life.” The trial of the suspect , who is alleged to be the ringleader of the attack, is being held under strict security measures. While international observers initially blamed Moscow for the blasts, investigators later found suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies. More than 100 media representatives from around the world, including Britain, China, France, Ukraine and Russia, have been accredited to cover the case, according to the court. Pro-Ukraine protesters gathered outside the courthouse as attendees filed into the building, holding up placards and signs that carried messages including “Russia is a Terrorist” written in red. Ivan Kuritsyn of Citizens’ Initiative Vilni De Ua, a nonprofit formed by Ukrainians displaced by the war, said the demonstrators were on hand “to show our solidarity with Serhii Kuznietsov and to support him.” Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says “I want to emphasize here that we in no way question the court’s decision, because only the court can decide whether Serhii is guilty or not, but we must support him regardless,” Kuritsyn added. According to the charges, the defendant was allegedly involved in causing the Sept. 26, 2022, explosions that damaged pipelines built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations. The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that departed from the German port of Rostock. It had been rented from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries. Kuznietsov’s lawyers argued that his fingerprints were not on the yacht and no witnesses spotted him on it.

events.title: I moved from Texas to Europe 11 years ago. Here are my 5 biggest pros and cons of living abroad.
events.summary: Leah Young. Courtesy of Leah Young Leah Young moved from Texas to Spain in 2015 to become a teaching assistant. What was meant to be a one-year stay has turned into a permanent life in Europe. Young, who now lives in France, said living abroad has come with its ups and downs. Leah Young always dreamed of moving to Europe , but when the opportunity finally came, taking the leap was terrifying. "I had never lived abroad , and I didn't know anyone else who had," Young, 34, told Business Insider. "I remember thinking, 'How practical is this, really?'" It was 2015, and she was moving to Spain , a country worlds away from Texas, to work as a teaching assistant. It didn't matter that she had never been there or worked as a teacher before or that the $700 a month she would earn might not cover all her living expenses. For her, it was a chance to finally live abroad. What was meant to be only a year away from home turned into another year, then another, and more. During that time, she lived in Spain and traveled through Germany, Argentina, and Brazil. Last year, she moved to Lyon, France , a place she says finally "feels like home." Young says she has become an expert at starting over after going through all its ups and downs. Here are five of the biggest pros and cons of living abroad, according to Young. Living abroad makes you a more well-rounded person… Young at the Eiffel Tower. Courtesy of Leah Young Growing up in Texas , Young's worldview was shaped by the people and places around her. But after 11 years of living abroad, she has a completely different understanding of how the world works and how people live in it. "I didn't even realize how small my world was before," she said. "We often see our own culture and hear our own language, and we have limited access to different ideas and perspectives." Being surrounded by new people has challenged the way Young thinks about planning her life, from earning money, building her career, and planning for retirement. "That has been so valuable because you can't really get that just from reading or watching TV or movies," she said. "I think it makes you a more well-rounded person." …but it takes time and effort to adapt to a new culture. The Basilica de Fourviere, a famous landmark in Lyon, France. Sergi Formoso/Getty Images Adapting to a new culture can take time — and a lot of trial and error. "When you move outside your own country , you're entering a place with a different culture, language, and social norms," Young said. "Even if you study up a little bit, you'll run into things that are embarrassing, awkward, or really difficult." Manners can be especially hard to understand. "It's the little things that can be the most confusing, like who serves themselves first at the table, who opens the door for someone, or all those small social rules," she added. Over time, those small uncertainties can become frustrating. "They add up day to day, and all of a sudden, you're having to think about whether every little decision or action is appropriate," she said. "Sometimes you get pushback for that, and it can be really humbling and uncomfortable." Moving to a new country can inspire you to forge a new path in life… Leah Young. Courtesy of Leah Young One of the biggest questions Young had to answer when she moved abroad was what she wanted for her life. Having the freedom to choose a path different from the one she was born into has meant everything to her. "When you grow up in one place, there kind of tends to be a mold or a standard for how things go, like where you're going to live, the kind of transportation you take, the kind of marriage you might have, what career you'll have," she said. "But when you move abroad, everything changes." …but being independent is both a blessing and a curse. People dining outside restaurants in Lyon, France. Gary Yeowell/Getty Images Young moved abroad without knowing anyone. Each time she has relocated to a new country or city, she has had to figure out where to live, find work, and make friends all on her own. For her, the experience has been both a "blessing and a curse." "You're completely starting from zero, and so you have to have this feeling of, 'I'm going to get strong and do this myself,'" she said. "It's really stressful at the beginning, but the more things that you take on yourself, the stronger you become. It really gives you this intense feeling of self-reliance." While the experience has made her feel more competent and "tough," she still wishes she had someone she could rely on. "If I need to carry a really heavy package, I don't have anybody to call and help me, or if I'm having trouble with my electric bill, I'm going to have to be the one who calls, even if it's in a foreign language," she said. "You realize that you're really on your own." Through it all, distance makes the heart grow fonder. TK Courtesy of Leah Young Young's family and many of her closest friends still live in Texas , more than 5,000 miles away and in a different time zone. "It hits really hard, especially during that first week away," she said. "Almost as soon as you arrive, when you get to your hotel or Airbnb, you realize, 'Oh my gosh, I am completely isolated here.' It's pretty freaky." For Young, spontaneous hangouts or nights out with loved ones have been replaced by phone calls, video chats, and messages. While she still visits them in the US when she can, the trips never seem long enough. "That is something you can't really change," she said. "In an ideal world, they would be coming with me, but they can't. You can only see them so many times a year." The distance is particularly hard during the holidays and challenging periods in life. It's made Young even more appreciative of the time they do have together. "For me, it has been kind of a blessing in disguise," she said. "I started having much more frequent phone calls with my best friend. With my mom, we call almost every single day, and I don't know if that would be happening if we lived in the same place." events.title: Malawi launches black market fuel crackdown as prices soar
events.summary: Malawi launched a nationwide crackdown on fuel hoarders and black market sellers as the nation struggles with shortages that have left truckers queuing for up to a week and bus fares doubling on some routes. Diesel and petrol have been scarce for weeks because the country lacks the hard currency to buy fuel supplies, sparking a scramble for dollars that has seen the central bank sell off gold to pay suppliers and the government return to the IMF for a bailout. Malawi, which has among the highest fuel pump prices in Africa at more than $3 a liter, highlights the impact of a $100-plus per barrel crude price on import-dependent economies with thin buffers. Unlicensed resellers face arrest , and stations caught hoarding can lose their license under the new measures. The IMF last week said it was making “ considerable progress ” in designing a “package of macroeconomic policies.” Its last program was a $175 million loan that expired in May last year, the latest in a string of support packages for one of the continent’s poorest countries, whose agriculture-based economy has been hit hard by extreme weather patterns. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

Insecurity has complicated DR Congo’s hopes of profiting from rising demand for copper, coltan, and cobalt used in digital infrastructure and the energy transition. events.title: How CFOs at Chevron, ServiceNow and Nasdaq decide which AI bets create value
events.summary: Good morning. AI projects must earn their share of corporate budgets. “It doesn’t get a free pass just because it’s got AI on the front of the opportunity,” Eimear Bonner, CFO of Chevron , said during a panel session I moderated at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit in Santa Barbara on Tuesday.  “It’s got to compete for capital.” Bonner’s test: a clear path to value, a transformative target and results that show up on the bottom line. “It can’t be a science experiment,” she said. Gina Mastantuono, president and CFO of ServiceNow , agreed with Bonner’s viewpoint, and noted that the way CFOs calculate ROI is moving beyond just measuring potential gains in revenue and profitability. Finance chiefs must also weigh the cost of inaction: falling behind competitors that adopt AI, with long-term competitiveness at stake, she said. ServiceNow funds projects that strengthen competitive differentiation, solve a customer problem and deliver measurable value on a clear timeline, she said. “I don’t think the winners in AI are going to be the ones that spend the most,” she said.  Mastantuono urged measuring outcomes, not activity—”not how many AI pilots you have,” but whether AI lifts revenue, efficiency and speed. ServiceNow expects $500 million in savings this year, largely from using its own products. Sarah Youngwood, EVP and CFO of Nasdaq said during the panel session that the company categorizes investments into “horizon zero”—foundational needs like cybersecurity—followed by short-term return initiatives, medium-term bets, and longer-term R&D. Nasdaq’s decade-old investments in cloud and algorithmic AI, Youngwood said, position it to serve clients today. “It’s all about the gold standard data that we have,” she said, pointing, for example, to data across 3,500 institutions representing $12 trillion in assets. Youngwood oversees Nasdaq’s AI KPIs, tracking inputs such as training and platform engagement alongside outputs including coding speed, client retention and token costs. For Bonner, who becomes president of Chevron’s oil, products and gas business on Jan. 1, discipline also means regular check-ins with project teams to remove barriers and confirm progress. AI is helping the company find oil and gas faster, recover more from reservoirs and anticipate maintenance needs, Bonner said. Chevron is also on the supply side of the AI boom: It plans to power a Microsoft data center in West Texas through a 2.67-gigawatt natural gas project. events.summary: Manchester City have contested the guilty verdict and the appeal will be heard by mid or end January. Manchester City’s appeal after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules is expected to be heard by January, according to the chair of English football’s independent regulator. “The Premier League has said that they want to get this resolved within the season, and actually, of course, it’s not the Premier League, it’s an independent commission that’s actually going to hear this, made up of three retired judges or lawyers,” Independent Football Regulator (IFR) chair David Kogan told Times Radio on Wednesday. list 1 of 4 Yamal magic helps Barcelona beat Galatasaray in Champions League list 2 of 4 Manchester United’s Martinez blasts board’s lack of investment list 3 of 4 Bayern’s Michael Olise sent off for ‘super dumb’ yellows within seconds list 4 of 4 Arsenal beat Lille 3-0 as perfect Champions League start continues “My understanding is that there is a prescribed process, which is 12 weeks, and so people are assuming this will actually be heard by the middle or the end of January,” he added. “But as I say, it’s not our process, it’s that of the Premier League’s independent commission. What I don’t think we can do is take any judgment until we’re quite clear.” City, who have repeatedly maintained they are innocent of any wrongdoing , are currently top of the Premier League table with six wins out of six following Sunday’s 3-0 defeat of Liverpool. No sanction has been announced, but City could face a heavy points deduction leading to relegation. There has even been speculation they could be stripped of the three Premier League titles they won between 2009 and 2018. IFR’s Kogan said on Tuesday he would resign if there was political interference in any future IFR investigations of City. An independent commission found the club guilty on charges of breaking financial rules between 2009 and 2018. It had been accused of using ‘sham’ contracts to artificially inflate revenues and reduce reported costs by more than 900 million pounds ($1.2 billion). British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for his initial comments on the case, saying he would be “really concerned” if City’s Abu Dhabi owners left the club following the verdict. Downing Street later had to backtrack, saying no one was “above the rules”. Burnham, who was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to June 2026, has since published all of his dealings with the City hierarchy. “We’ve had absolutely no interference from anybody since we created the regulator a year ago,” Kogan said. “We cannot, when regulating football, be subject to political interference on decisions we make about owners, directors or anything else.” “And I won’t actually be prepared to run an organisation which is subject to that degree of interference,” he added. Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca said last week he “completely trusts” the club and believes it will win its appeal.
