U.S. President Donald Trump said American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm elections in early November. Saudi officials said Wednesday that Saudi Aramco facilities had been targeted overnight. Saudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom. The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Energy. The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi Arabian targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday. Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.–Iran war. Iran 'counting the moments' until it can attack U.S. ships Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media. "If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview. "We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens." CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as it prepares its population for renewed war in the coming weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3. On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports. Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile." In a post on X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control. "IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait."

events.title: IMF chief urges wealthy nations to rein in debt to ease global economic pressure
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund says the United States and other wealthy nations must urgently tackle mounting global debt, which is weighing most heavily on low-income countries BANGKOK -- The U.S. and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing most heavily on low-income countries and straining the global financial system, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other U.S. leaders recognize that the federal deficit and national debt are too high. But economic growth alone would not be enough to address the country’s more than $40 trillion in national debt, she said. Meanwhile, rising bond yields , reflecting higher premiums demanded by investors for taking on greater risk, have been disrupting financial markets. “We believe that growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. “There is no magic,” she said, adding that other measures would be needed. “You have to go in a direction of tightening, bringing it down, bringing the deficit down.” Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war , have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world’s poorest nations. Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call “fiscal consolidation” have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since. “Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries,” said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. “And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world.” “Among the world’s poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance,” the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said. That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. “The Global South is paying the price for rising interest rates in wealthier countries,” U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at an event on the sidelines of the IMF meetings. “We need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space,” he said. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The median developing country pays three times as much in interest as developed countries, said Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). On average, nearly 10% of government spending goes toward debt repayments. High fuel and fertilizer prices, the effects of the El Niño weather phenomenon and rising borrowing costs have left many low-income countries with little room to recover. “I mean, we don’t see really a light at the end of the tunnel,” De Croo told The Associated Press. Creating jobs is another top priority, particularly as the growing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce over the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest only 400 million net new jobs will be created. The UNDP this week announced its “Jobs for Prosperity” initiative to bring together governments, development banks — such as the World Bank — and private businesses to encourage investment in sectors such as tourism, healthcare and food processing. The initiative and related efforts will help countries attract investment by strengthening governance and policies and developing pipelines of “investible projects,” De Croo said. “These are things that are feasible. It’s been proven that you can do it in many places of the world,” he added. Separately, the IMF, Bank of Thailand and World Bank Group announced a “Bangkok Blueprint” on Wednesday to combat cybercrime, financial fraud and online scams. The announcement came a day after cyberattacks caused refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France. Associated Press journalists Haruka Nuga and Tian Macleod Ji contributed to this report. events.title: 'Office' is actually having a scarcity problem
events.summary: The office market posted its fifth consecutive quarter of positive net absorption, with occupiers adding 6 million square feet in the third quarter of this year, according to a new report from JLL. This all comes at a time when supply is falling — and falling faster than demand is recovering. There is currently just 23 million square feet of new office space under construction, and with demand for premium office surging, this new space is becoming increasingly scarce. A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. Barely a few years after what some saw as a pandemic-driven collapse of the U.S. office market, the sector is roaring back to health at an unexpectedly fast clip. That speedy recovery is resulting in a shortage, especially of premium space. The office market posted its fifth consecutive quarter of positive net absorption, with occupiers adding 6 million square feet in the third quarter of this year, according to a new report from JLL. And employers are expanding, with signed leases now averaging a 13% increase in footprint. Just two years ago, the main theme in office was downsizing. This all comes at a time when supply is falling — and falling faster than demand is recovering. Just 3.5 million square feet of new office space was delivered in the third quarter, which matches the near-record low supply seen in the second quarter. At the same time, 9.6 million square feet was removed through either conversions or redevelopments. The inventory of office space nationally has lost 45 million square feet since the end of 2023. There is currently just 23 million square feet of new office space under construction, and with demand for premium office surging, this new space is becoming increasingly scarce. JLL deems it a "flight to scarcity." As a result, rents are finally rising. Effective rents for first-generation trophy space are now up more than 20% compared with the third quarter of 2025. The lack of available trophy space is now pushing more occupiers to second-generation space. In turn, rents for that sector are up 10% annually. "Office, which is having a real renaissance right now … If you own, if you bought that 18, 24 months ago, you've done incredibly well in office in San Francisco and New York," said Willy Walker, CEO of Walker & Dunlop, a commercial real estate finance and advisory firm, on CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime ." There are, as always, stronger local drivers to different metropolitan markets. Tech is leading the way with the highest net absorption in San Francisco and Austin. Sun Belt markets have also seen strong demand, with gateway area leasing volume up 13% from a year ago. Smaller, tertiary markets have come back to roughly 95% of their 2019 leasing volume. With supply shrinking and demand rising, construction should be picking up, but it's not. "Now is the perfect time to be putting a shovel in the ground, except no one's going to do it," said Walker, noting that this year office construction is at about 9% of its normal annual supply. "It's a perfect time to start projects to be delivered in the next two or three years. The problem with it is back to equity capital. You're not finding the equity capital going towards it right now, and as a result of it, we will be in a supply-constrained market, which, what will that do? It'll push rents up." events.title: Companies may be held liable when AI harms their clients and customers
events.summary: When AI messes up on a tax return or in a court filing, it's no laughing matter. DigitalVision Vectors/Getty Images Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from a novelty on the job to a common workplace tool. Gallup found that 52% of U.S. employees and 68% of professional services workers were using AI by February 2026. Thomson Reuters similarly found in spring 2026 that 74% of professionals use AI several times a week for work. This widespread use shouldn’t surprise anyone. For accountants, attorneys, consultants and other professionals, AI can accelerate research , summarize complex information and assist with writing and other forms of communication. But its rapid adoption has a big downside – AI can produce information that sounds authoritative and looks polished while being completely wrong . And when AI generates mistakes, responsibility for those errors belongs to the professional or business relying on the AI output – not companies that develop AI systems. AI errors have led to lawsuits, court fines, financial consequences and public embarrassment from fabricated citations, nonexistent sources and inaccurate AI-generated information. These cases raise an increasingly important question: How can professionals benefit from AI without outsourcing the judgment their work requires? Fake citations We are two certified public accountants who research tax accounting . In the September 2026 issue of Journal of Accountancy, we examined what happened in Clinco v. Commissioner , a case before the U.S. Tax Court where an attorney submitted a brief to the court with allegedly fake citations. The Tax Court is a specialized federal court that resolves disputes between taxpayers and the IRS. This case involved a restaurant owner accused of underreporting more than US$2 million in business receipts and claiming unsupported depreciation deductions on rental properties. The main issue concerned Clinco’s accounting records used to determined how much of their income to tax. The taxpayers’ attorney, Abraham Wagner, cited four cases to support his argument that an IRS notice assessing additional taxes was invalid. The court determined that three of the citations appeared to be AI-generated hallucinations that cited nonexistent Tax Court cases. The court rejected the taxpayer’s argument and warned Wagner that submitting fake citations could lead to sanctions from the court, including financial penalties or disciplinary action against Wagner. Ultimately, the court did not sanction Wagner in the case, but the decision stands to put attorneys and other professionals in Tax Court on notice that AI hallucinations will not be tolerated. Using AI for audits and other professional work may save time but also poses some legal hazards. iStock/Getty Images Plus When AI gets it wrong AI errors made on behalf of clients are not limited to briefs drafted by attorneys. Nor are these mishaps limited to the United States. When Deloitte produced a 237-page report in 2025 for the Australian government examining its automated system for penalizing welfare recipients who failed to meet job-seeking requirements, it contained nonexistent academic citations and a fabricated quotation it attributed to a federal court judgment. The global consulting firm later issued a revised version of the error-ridden report. Deloitte blamed generative AI for the errors in the original and agreed to partially refund its fees. Like most airlines, Air Canada has a chatbot on its website to respond to its customers’ questions. The chatbot told a customer in November 2022 that he could buy a plane ticket under a bereavement policy and be reimbursed later. This was not company policy, and Air Canada refused to honor what the chatbot had told the customer. The customer sued the airline and won 812 Canadian dollars in damages. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada had failed to take reasonable care to ensure that its AI bot provided accurate information and agreed with the customer that the airline had negligently misrepresented the bereavement policy. AI lawsuits There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers. In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages. There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC , that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026 the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable. Hallucinations and ‘confabulations’ Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible. The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations” – the confident presentation of erroneous or false information. Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way. Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid. AI errors in the workplace A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency. Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use. As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work. AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops. The University of Dayton is an academic partner of The Conversation. Kaitlin Newkirk is affiliated with the Ohio Society of CPAs.

events.title: Delta's business-class revamp: New seats, menus, plates and more Porsches
events.summary: Delta is overhauling its top-tier cabin with new suites for its largest A350 plane, starting next year. The company is also ordering more Porsches to take its highest-end customers from the terminal to aircraft transfers. Delta is also rolling out a new dining menu, adding Blanton's bourbon, debuting new crockery and making other additions. Delta Air Lines , the country's most profitable airline, has a problem serving its top-tier customers: not enough Porsches. The airline uses a fleet of 40 of the luxury vehicles to drive its high-value flyers right to the plane. "What's happened over the last several years is the demand has continued to rise, and we realized that the 40 cars that we have weren't enough to meet the demand. So we're moving that fleet to 70," Ranjan Goswami, Delta's chief marketing and product officer, told CNBC. It's just one of many changes Delta is making for customers who fly in its most luxurious and expensive cabin, known as Delta One . The Porsche service is part of a VIP add-on option. The carrier on Wednesday unveiled new crockery for the cabins, new Missoni mini pillows and fresh food and beverage menus, including Champagne served over sorbet and Blanton's bourbon. Many of the new items will appear on flights originating in Los Angeles later this month and on other routes in the coming months. Delta is also planning to debut updated suites with a bigger screen and a more cushioned, lighter lie-flat seat when it starts flying its first Airbus A350-1000 planes early next year. Delta didn't announce changes to the coach and premium economy cabins. The airline's executives said the company is already thinking about adjustments on other aircraft, including smaller Airbus jets and on Boeing 787 Dreamliners that Delta has ordered and that will come in the next decade. Delta has invested heavily in premium service for close to two decades, and United Airlines has followed suit for a little over 10 years. Other carriers are also leaning into demand for higher-priced options. Alaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel race Budget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgrades United ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layouts Caviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are here American Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up? First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanes Airlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first class "You got to keep looking at the next cycle of what customers want, and you got to start planning for it now," Goswami said. He said Delta focused on details and quality with its latest project for Delta One so that the items, from sliding suite doors to new Delta-logo-emblazoned dinnerware, are made to last. The company tested some of those items to check for chipping, but there are other challenges, like customers liking them too much. "I think people are going to love a couple of items, although we hope they don't steal them," he said. events.title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The US military’s race to make fake blood In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply. Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.  The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives. Discover how the military hopes to make blood last longer . —Andrew Rosenblum This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday, October 21!   10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges. Explore WeLion’s push to make safer, higher-capacity batteries . —You Xiaoying Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from geothermal power plants to carbon dioxide batteries .  MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process. Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.  The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. events.title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 10:24 BST Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds. The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said. Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £48,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships. It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate. Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment. Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA. The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds. Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March. The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added. The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%. The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing . Eight firms under investigation over online pricing Published 18 November 2025 AA and BSM ordered to refund learner drivers for hidden fees Published 15 April A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers". Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead. Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics. "When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added. Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics. "Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines." Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, praised the CMA's response. "The refunds secured by the CMA are a much-needed win for consumers at a time when household budgets are under strain," she said. The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways. Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers. However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false. Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines. Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said. events.title: Sharjah turns to AI to identify foreign investment opportunities in seconds
events.summary: Sharjah is using artificial intelligence to help foreign investors identify investment opportunities within seconds, as the emirate seeks to attract more foreign direct investment despite mounting geopolitical uncertainty . A new AI-powered platform, called Najm, will initially help investors find sites for factories and warehouses across the emirate. It was launched by the emirate's investment promotion agency, the Sharjah FDI Office, also known as Invest in Sharjah. The AI agent is designed to help investors make “informed investment decisions”, Mohamed Al Mushrrakh, chief executive of Invest in Sharjah, said at the Sharjah Investment Forum on Wednesday. For the introductory phase, Invest in Sharjah has teamed up with property portals Bayut and Property Finder, as well as e-commerce platform Dubizzle . Najm will use commercial and industrial real estate data from the online portals and will provide instantaneous information to investors. “Investors could struggle to find information they need to make an investment decision, so we asked ourselves a simple question: how can we deliver the right information at the right moment, when they need it,” Mr Al Mushrrakh told delegates at the Sharjah Investment Forum. “Najm is the answer to that question. It is Invest in Sharjah's new tool for global investors.” The launch of the AI agent is driven by the need to cut the noise around the investment ecosystem in Sharjah and find new ways to bring foreign direct investment to the emirate. Sharjah, the third largest emirate in the UAE after Abu Dhabi and Dubai, is home to 33 industrial zones. Sharjah’s real estate sector recorded more than 16,000 transactions during the first half of this year, with the emirate’s Muwaileh commercial area accounting for the highest value and volume of deals in the first six months, according to Invest in Sharjah data. Sharjah received Dh7.74 billion in FDI last year, an 8.8 per cent increase on an annual basis. The count of projects in the emirate that received FDI also soared by 45 per cent year-on-year, to reach 142 developments, data showed. In the second phase, the Najm platform will expand its sector horizon to cover a broader range of assets and investment opportunities in the healthcare and education sectors, Mr Al Mushrrakh said. “What you have seen today is just the beginning ... Najm stands to cover investment opportunities across multiple sectors from industry to education and technology and beyond,” he said. “We will continue to invest in human capital, technology, infrastructure and partnerships between the public and private sectors. "Through these efforts, we can build a resilient economy, attract new investments into opportunities that we will build together."

events.title: A quarter of financial firms tie pay and promotions to AI proficiency: survey
events.summary: Tokenmaxxing may have been the shortest-lived corporate try-hard hustle in history, but many of Wall Street’s year-end bonuses still hinge on AI use. Applicants’ AI skills are nearly four times as important in hiring decisions as where they went to college, and a quarter of US financial firms have tied raises, promotions, and bonuses to AI proficiency , according to a survey of 500 companies by financial recruiting firm Selby Jennings. Breathe easy, bulge-bracketers: The practice is more common among fintech startups and smaller firms than brand-name banks and trading houses, Jacob Summers, Selby Jennings’ head of tech recruiting, told Semafor. Nearly a third of firms surveyed have created new roles or departments to track AI use, where total token burn is less important than wringing some actual value out of all the token use. (“Tokenmaxxing is dead, long live valuemaxxing,” proclaims an IBM blog post from June.) But in many organizations, monitoring that work falls to managers, turning them into part-time AI accountants. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Saudi set to drop plans for five 2034 World Cup stadiums
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund is preparing to inform organizers of the 2034 men’s soccer World Cup that it plans to drop five new stadiums it proposed to build to host the tournament, according to people familiar with the matter. Public Investment Fund will likely narrow its focus to three new stadiums as it cuts spending on some of its signature domestic investments, the people said. Dropping the five venues would leave the kingdom with 10 stadiums for World Cup matches. The changes are part of a revised plan the kingdom is preparing to submit to FIFA, the tournament’s organizers, the people said. PIF is looking to drop plans to develop stadiums in King Abdullah Economic City and Qiddiya Coast, both near Jeddah; Roshn and New Murabba in Riyadh; and NEOM, in the kingdom’s northwest. Several of the cancelled stadiums are attached to broader real estate projects that have been halted or where work has slowed. Saudi Arabian officials are still working on the updated proposals and the plans could change, the people said. PIF and the Saudi Ministry of Sport didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More Reuters earlier reported on the cancellation of the NEOM stadium, which was envisaged as being on the roof of The Line, a 500-meter-tall skyscraper. Work on The Line has effectively ground to a halt , and NEOM has not allocated any funding for the project until after at least 2030, Semafor previously reported. Saudi Arabia had also proposed a 45,000-seat stadium at Qiddiya Coast, a planned entertainment and tourism destination north of Jeddah. That development has also been put on hold. Another 45,000-capacity stadium in Riyadh’s New Murabba district is also set to be dropped. Work on the wider development has slowed after the departure of Chief Executive Michael Dyke and the suspension of work on the project’s centerpiece, a 400-meter-tall, cube-shaped skyscraper with screens lining its interior, similar to The Sphere concert venue in Las Vegas. The kingdom is still proceeding with plans for other new stadiums including one in Dhahran being developed by Saudi Aramco, and the King Salman International Stadium and Prince Mohammed bin Salman Stadium in Riyadh. The cuts could leave Saudi Arabia developing just six new stadiums and refurbishing four existing ones for the World Cup. Four of the stadiums it plans to use in 2034 are also due to host matches for the 2027 Asian Cup, which starts in January. The outlook for that contest going ahead in Saudi Arabia has been thrown into doubt by the kingdom’s involvement in the war in Yemen against Houthi militias. The group has launched multiple attacks against Saudi cities in recent weeks, shutting down the capital’s airport and killing at least 18 and injuring hundreds. Qatar also previously dropped four of the stadiums it had planned to build for the 2022 World Cup as it got closer to the tournament. events.title: Fulham manager Arbeloa fined for Man Utd refereeing outburst
events.summary: Alvaro Arbeloa fined $33,000 for remarks made after Fulham’s 1-1 draw against Manchester United in September. Fulham coach ‌‌Alvaro Arbeloa has been fined $33,163 ⁠⁠and given ⁠⁠a warning for comments he made after his side’s 1-1 draw with Manchester ⁠⁠United in September, when he suggested officials would not allow United to lose. The English Football Association (FA) announced the sanction on Wednesday. United rescued a point at ⁠⁠Craven Cottage on September 20, with Matheus Cunha’s deflected equaliser arriving in the 89th minute of the Premier League fixture. Speaking after the match, Arbeloa said: “I knew after ‌‌the game against Manchester City that they don’t let Manchester United lose here.” The former Real Madrid coach was referring to one of United’s previous league matches, when Erling Haaland scored the winner in 10-man City’s 1-0 victory at Old Trafford. The ⁠⁠strike was initially disallowed for offside ⁠⁠before being awarded following a lengthy and contentious VAR review. “It was alleged that the Fulham head coach acted in an improper ⁠⁠manner by making comments in a post-match interview that imply bias and/or question ⁠⁠the integrity of a match ⁠⁠official,” the FA said in a statement. The FA added that Arbeloa admitted the charge. The 43-year-old Spaniard, who took charge of Fulham ‌‌in July, is still searching for his first league win with the London club, who sit bottom ‌‌of ‌‌the standings with two points from six matches.

events.title: Saudi national arrested over alleged planting of recording device at OpenAI
events.summary: AI agents, meet double agents. OpenAI said it identified, fired, and reported to the FBI an employee who bugged its office. The employee, a Saudi national later identified by law enforcement as Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested last week and charged with illegally recording company communication. (He appears to have some ties to members of the Saudi business elite.) Among the evidence against him: chatbot logs about how to install recording devices. Startup espionage has been pursued for far less (see: the Deel-Rippling drama over corporate HR software), but the FBI’s quick work and public rollout of the arrest shows how high the stakes are for the US government and frontier labs. The arrest comes days before the White House AI task force’s first meeting . Its chair, Jay Clayton, cited the case as proof the group is needed. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Even more borrowers choose riskier mortgages, as higher interest rates crush affordability
events.summary: The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.50% from 7.49% The ARM share of mortgage demand increased to 10.5%, the highest in a year. Applications to refinance were less than half of what they were one year ago. Mortgage rates moved to the highest level in nearly three years last week, causing overall demand to drop. Riskier mortgages, however, continue to gain a growing share of what demand there is. Total mortgage application volume dropped 2.7% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. It is also 37.5% lower than the same week one year ago. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased to 7.50% from 7.49%, with points decreasing to 0.83 from 0.84, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. The rate was more than a full percentage point higher than it was a year ago. "As a result, borrowers continue to rely more on ARM [adjustable-rate mortgage] loans to help lower their monthly payments," said Joel Kan, an MBA economist, in a release. "The ARM share at 10.5 percent was at its highest level since October 2025." ARMs offer lower interest rates and can be fixed for up to 10 years, but then they adjust depending on future interest rates. That is why they are considered riskier. Applications to refinance a home loan have been hit hardest by higher rates, as a shrinking pool of borrowers can now find much relief. These applications declined 0.4% for the week and were 56% lower year over year. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 4% for the week and were 16% lower than the same week one year ago. There are more homes available for sale now, but mostly on the higher end of the market. Supply is also rising not because of new listings, but because of slower sales. Home prices also continue to rise. While closed home sales increased very slightly in September from August, according to a report Tuesday from the National Association of Realtors, those sales were based on market conditions over the summer, when rates were lower. "Despite the small monthly gain on a seasonally adjusted basis, August and September marked the two slowest months for home sales this year," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist, in a release. "Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home." Correction: Total mortgage application volume dropped 2.7% last week compared with the previous week. An earlier version misstated the figure. Closed home sales increased very slightly in September from August. An earlier version misstated the timeline.

events.title: Billion Dollar Boy just made an acquisition that points to influencer marketing’s next hot opportunity
events.summary: Creator Authority is joining Billion Dollar Boy. Pictured: Creator Authority's Brendan Gahan and Cassie Jackson with Billion Dollar Boy Group CEO Ed East. Billion Dollar Boy Group A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly marketing newsletter . A new M&A deal signals that "business-to-business" could be the next hot growth area in the creator economy. The social and influencer marketing company Billion Dollar Boy Group exclusively told CMO Insider that it acquired the B2B influencer marketing agency Creator Authority. Creator Authority connects brands with content creators, providing services that include contracts, licensing, and campaign management. The companies declined to disclose the specific financial terms, beyond that it is an all-cash, "multimillion-dollar" deal with an earnout component. Following the acquisition, BDB Group said it forecasts its 2027 revenue will exceed $100 million. BDB Group said its global revenue has grown 24% in the past 12 months. The deal started with a LinkedIn DM. In 2023, BDB Group cofounders Edward East and Thomas Walters were lapping up Brendan Gahan's content on LinkedIn about how B2B creators were finding success on the platform. Gahan hadn't yet launched Creator Authority, but was increasingly becoming a B2B influencer himself. East got in touch to arrange an intro call, and they kept in touch for regular catch-ups before the conversation evolved into takeover talks. The LinkedIn message Billion Dollar Boy Group's Ed East sent to Creator Authority's Brendan Gahan that laid the early groundwork for the deal. Courtesy of Ed East "I'm so excited about the B2B space," Gahan, who will take the role of senior vice president of B2B at Billion Dollar Boy, told me. "It feels like YouTube in 2010; there's this moment when it just explodes, and I'm excited to grow with it." The creator economy gets a B2B infusion Dealmaking in the creator economy has been accelerating. There were 70 creator economy M&A transactions in the first half of 2026, according to the advisory firm Quartermast Advisors . That was up 23% year-over-year, making it the busiest first half of creator deals on record, with agencies accounting for around a fifth (21.4%) of transactions, per Quartermast, which advised Creator Authority on the sale. Notable recent deals include Accenture Song's acquisition of the creator and social agency Whalar in July, Publicis Groupe picking up the French creator agency Point d'Orgue in August, and the influencer and social agency SAMY's purchase of Atlanta-based social and digital agency Get Engaged last month. BDB Group's acquisition of Creator Authority — its first-ever acquisition — marks a new phase of consolidation as agencies that made their names in the consumer space seek to capitalize on the growth of B2B creator marketing. In a survey commissioned by BDB Group and conducted by Censuswide in September of more than 1,000 marketing decision-makers in the US and UK, 20% said they invested in B2B creator marketing in 2026. Architecture, engineering, and building (33%), manufacturing and utilities (24%), and retail, catering, and leisure (23%) were the industries where B2B creator marketing investment was most prevalent. On the platform side, LinkedIn has been making big investments in the influencer marketing space. This summer, it introduced a creator marketplace to help advertisers identify creators relevant to their sectors and desired audiences. It's enhanced its BrandLink program that lets publishers and creators receive a share of the revenue generated by ads placed in their videos. Last year, it launched a slate of original video shows from business-focused creators . East told me the Creator Authority team will increase from around 15 people currently to around 30 to 40. BDB Group plans to shift some of its existing staff to work with the Creator Authority team. That will expand Creator Authority's global presence to New York and London from its current bases of Los Angeles and Austin. BDB Group will benefit from Creator Authority's status as an official LinkedIn Marketing Partner and inherit a client roster that includes Amazon, Adobe, and Mastercard. "Creator marketing is an emerging channel for B2B brands, and it's one of the most significant growth opportunities in this space, without a shadow of a doubt," East said. events.title: It’s BlackRock vs. Apollo in war to bank corporate America
events.summary: A little-noticed deal this week for senior-care clinics is the first shot fired in a Wall Street turf battle. BlackRock’s HPS credit arm is essentially lending $2.8 billion to Humana, marking Larry Fink’s entry into a space that Apollo has had to itself until now. Apollo’s dryly named “capital solutions” business, launched in 2024, was a bet that asset managers could cosplay as banks. Their money could go places that banks’ deposit funding couldn’t, especially after post-2008 regulations. Apollo has since made big loans to companies including Intel and Keurig Dr Pepper, notching $800 million from the business last year on its way to a $1 billion target . Two years ago, I wagered that BlackRock and Apollo would be the winners of the weird debt world that limped, then sprinted, out of the global financial crisis. Apollo got there first, but BlackRock just threw its hat in the ring. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Othello uses AI to tell salespeople what to say during calls. See the pitch deck that helped it raise $8 million.
events.summary: Othello, cofounded by Jared Zelman and Raphael Assor, just raised an $8 million seed funding round. Othello Othello gives salespeople real-time, AI-powered recommendations to improve their sales calls. It uses reinforcement learning to coach reps in pitches modeled on their company's top performers. Othello just raised $8 million in a round led by A16z Speedrun and Owl Capital. Jared Zelman has been honing his sales pitch since college, when he spent his spare time cold-emailing billionaires and prominent investors , hoping to forge a connection. His extracurricular activities helped lay the groundwork for his current startup, Othello, a platform that uses AI to give salespeople real-time coaching tips to improve their sales calls. Othello exclusively told CMO Insider on Wednesday that it had raised an $8 million seed funding round, led by Andreessen Horowitz 's startup accelerator A16z Speedrun, and Owl Capital. Othello listens in on video calls and uses AI trained on a company's uploaded sales and product materials to suggest questions to ask, answer tricky queries, and flag missed opportunities in real time through an on-screen overlay. "Too many good deals are killed by bad calls," said Zelman, who is now 24 and was using Othello to help respond to questions during our interview. Zelman said he evolved the idea for Othello at his second startup, Cicero, which created AI avatars for prominent authors and podcasters. Zelman said he struggled to sell the idea to enterprise prospects and used to have a friend stand behind his computer holding up cue cards to help steer him through his sales calls. "I was like, 'Hey, I'm just going to build this for everybody,'" Zelman said. "In sales, you can outsource and use AI to do everything except for the one important part of the job, which is the sales call." Othello says its AI models are trained on 20 million hours of recorded sales calls and that its platform can be integrated with business software platforms such as Google Workspace, Salesforce, Slack, and ServiceNow. The company says customers' data is not used to train AI models shared with other businesses. Its customers include Microsoft and Capital One. Othello isn't the first company to use AI to help salespeople. It's a much smaller challenger to rivals such as Gong and Salesloft, which offer tools to analyze sales conversations, with Salesloft also providing real-time coaching. Gong and Salesloft have raised hundreds of millions of dollars and have multibillion-dollar valuations. Zelman said Othello's advantage lies in the speed and accuracy of its proprietary AI models, which deliver recommendations in milliseconds and improve from recorded sales calls using reinforcement learning . He said its singular focus on offering this type of in-call solution will also give it an advantage if an enterprise tech company like Salesforce or HubSpot chose to launch a similar product. "Providing real-time recommendations is so damn hard because if it's too slow or not smart enough, it's really unhelpful and very, very distracting," Zelman said. Othello could also prove useful for chief marketing officers , Zelman said, by helping ensure salespeople actually use the materials created for them, while giving marketing teams insights into which messages are most effective at converting customers. Othello plans to invest the funds in growing its engineering team. Zelman said he anticipates increasing the company's head count to around 80 employees, from 20 currently. The startup is also planning to improve the product to focus on coaching individual sellers on their strengths and weaknesses, beyond optimizing its recommendations based on learnings from a company's best performers. In the future, he envisioned the product being used for in-person meetings via smart glasses . A group of individual investors including DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, Hugging Face cofounder Thomas Wolf, Chime cofounder Ryan King, and Ripple founder Chris Larsen invested in the funding round. Check out the pitch deck Othello used to secure its $8 million seed investment, shared exclusively with CMO Insider. Some of the slides have been omitted or redacted. Othello describes itself as a 'real-time sales augmentation layer.' Othello It cites stats from a Gartner report on the sales industry. Othello The 2025 Gartner study found that salespeople drove 60% of business-to-business revenue, a contribution that is forecast to increase to 75% in the following four years. It also cites research from The Bridge Group that found it takes the average salesperson 13 months to reach productivity, which is 32% slower than four years ago. A separate report from The Bridge Group found that 35% of sales reps leave each year, double the rate of attrition reported three years ago. Othello says there will always be human salespeople. Othello "People like to play golf," Zelman told CMO Insider. Othello says while other AI tools save time, its platform helps close more deals. Othello This slide shows the Othello platform in action. Othello Its overlay prompts sales reps on which questions to ask and provides information about the company they are pitching and the pain points raised in the conversation. Othello says it's focused on providing insights while a call is happening. Othello It provides prompts for discovery questions, responses to technical queries, and case studies. Othello Othello says it has more than 50 large enterprise customers. Othello This slide offers stats on how Othello can improve sales team performance. Othello The company said a subset of its customers that had more than 20 reps using Othello for more than a quarter achieved 15% higher win rates and 45% faster ramp-up times. "Ramp-up" refers to the time it takes a new sales rep to reach full productivity. Companies often define this differently, but it could include reaching $1 million in revenue or achieving another specific performance goal. 'Everyone sells better with Othello,' the company says. events.title: We’ve raised $8m to use generative AI to save our kids from YouTube
events.summary: It was on a flight to Cleveland from San Francisco a couple of years back that I had the idea for my startup. My two-year-old daughter was running up and down the aisle — raising hell as kids often do — and my wife and I looked at each other and knew: it was iPad time. Flicking through the various options on Netflix , I stopped on a popular kids cartoon that you’ve heard of but that I’m not going to throw shade at here.  As I watched my daughter watching these characters bounce around the screen, it was the pace that bothered me: fast cuts, constant scene changes, another burst of action before the last one had settled. I wanted her to have room to wonder what might happen next, and a chance to decide. I’m in my 40s, so I grew up in a world of Sesame Street, Mister Rogers, Bob Ross reruns — and when we weren’t glued to these shows we were reading Choose Your Own Adventure books like Journey Under the Sea . The ’80s weren’t perfect, but it was a golden age for kids’ TV. But this? What bothers me about YouTube Shorts is the habit it encourages: the moment something loses your attention, swipe to something else. We worry about our children’s ability to concentrate, then give them feeds that offer an escape from every moment of boredom. My own doomscrolling is on me. Choosing that experience for my daughters is on me, too. I want their screen time to give them reasons to stay with an idea, ask another question and see what they can make of it. A 2025 Common Sense Media report found that 58% of American 4-year-olds have their own tablet, rising to 68% of 8-year-olds. Children ages 5 to 8 average nearly three and a half hours of screen time a day. What happens during those hours deserves as much scrutiny as how many hours we allow. Before Giant, I founded Apartment List, which now accounts for 3% of U.S. rental moves. Becoming a father gave me a different problem to work on. My co-founder, David Silverman, and I started Giant to let children create characters, explore ideas and shape stories as they unfold.  We hike around the Bay Area, ride bikes and scooters, play sports, go to ballet and hip-hop classes, and sing and dance in the living room. We’ve been camping a dozen times. I’m an Eagle Scout, so yes, I’m the dad who considers sleeping on the ground a vacation. After all that, I’m perfectly happy letting my daughters spend some time on an iPad. I’d just rather they bring their own ideas to life than passively watch someone else’s. I loved Choose Your Own Adventure books because my decisions changed the story. Generative AI can take that further: children can invent a character, introduce an idea or take the adventure somewhere its creators never anticipated. It doesn’t have to be an algorithm that decides what you watch next. Children shouldn’t have to be passive consumers of content, they should be active creators of it.  Rejecting AI in entertainment hands another advantage to the giants that can already afford to make it. For a startup, AI makes it possible to compete. For the audience, it makes something entirely new possible: a show or movie that unfolds in real time, driven by your imagination. You create the characters, shape the world and decide what happens next. That’s worth the price of admission. I approach this as a father first. Giant is COPPA certified, but privacy is only part of keeping children safe. We’ve built systems that flag unsuitable content and give parents visibility into everything their children create. We also think carefully about what our characters say, what they generate and how they respond to a child. And we have no ads. Parents deserve that visibility without an advertiser competing for their child’s attention. On that flight to Cleveland, I wanted something better to put in front of my daughter. Today, I can see what that could look like: a dragon from her sketchbook, a journey to the moon, a story that changes because she has an idea. We still set limits on screen time. Within those limits, I want her imagination and curiosity to have somewhere to go.  The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Why travelers are switching their favorite brands
events.summary: For years, loyalty in travel was built around a relatively predictable formula: earn a customer’s trust, reward repeat purchases and create enough value to keep them coming back.  Airlines created frequent-flyer programs. Hotels accumulated points, tiers and perks. Brands invested heavily in personalization, rewards and direct-booking strategies designed to make customers choose them again and again.  Agentic AI  is changing the equation and all stages of the customer journey, from earliest discovery through long-term loyalty and retention. That creates new challenges and opportunities for travel brands. Loyalty is no longer only about being remembered. It is increasingly about being relevant.  Latest Accenture research,   Win the AI agent, win the traveler,  suggests that travelers are increasingly making decisions based not on long-standing brand relationships, but on which company can help them achieve their goal fastest and with the least effort. The survey of more than 5,000 travelers across 12 markets found that 96% would switch away from their preferred travel brand if another provider offered a significantly easier and faster experience. The vast majority ( 91%) are willing to pay more for an option that reduced the time and effort required to plan and manage a trip.  Those figures challenge one of travel’s longest-held assumptions: that loyalty alone can protect brands from competitive disruption. In fact, according to  Accenture’s Consumer Pulse 2026 , 36% of loyal travelers (those who typically choose from 1-3 preferred brands within a particular category- hotel/airline) would let an agent switch from their favorite brands for a better fit.  Travelers don’t want more choice. They want convenience Despite years of technology innovations, 94% of travelers describe the booking process as moderately or very complex. Nearly two-thirds use four or more platforms before ultimately making a purchase.  They may begin on a search engine, continue onto a hotel website, compare options through an online travel agency, check reviews on social media, and then switch between multiple devices before finally booking.  Every additional click, comparison and handoff introduces friction, and that friction can risk revenue and damage relationships/loyalty. More than 83% of travelers report abandoning a booking because of payment-related challenges such as unexpected fees, declined cards or limited payment options. Nearly half say the payment experience strongly influences which provider they ultimately choose.  The industry’s challenge is no longer simply attracting attention. It is removing obstacles. Consumers increasingly know where they want to go and have more inspiration, information and options than ever before. What often stands between intent and action are the countless friction points along the journey: complex booking processes, disconnected systems, unclear pricing, fragmented loyalty programs and the effort required to plan and manage travel. As AI takes on more of the discovery and decision-making process, travel brands have an opportunity to eliminate that complexity and make every step feel more seamless, personalized and intuitive.  The next loyalty test may happen well before the traveler even experiences a brand Generative AI is beginning to change how people discover and compare travel options.  Instead of searching separately for hotels, amenities, locations and prices, travelers can increasingly describe what they want in a conversation:  Find me a family-friendly hotel in Amsterdam for a weekend.   I need a hotel in Paris with a spa near the Eiffel Tower.   The important shift is not simply that AI can answer these questions faster. It is that AI can increasingly influence which options the traveler considers in the first place.  A traveler may no longer browse dozens of websites or compare options themselves. They could simply tell an AI agent what they need, and that agent might recommend another brand if it better matches the trip they’re trying to take.  The race is on to show up in AI recommendations and search results. This means travel companies need to rethink what it means to be discoverable.  For years, brands optimized their websites, search rankings, mobile apps and distribution relationships. Now, they will also need to ensure their content, inventory, rates, amenities and booking capabilities can participate effectively in AI-driven discovery.  Radisson’s ChatGPT experience  is an early example of this shift: instead of asking travelers to navigate its digital ecosystem, it allows them to describe what they need and brings relevant Radisson properties into that conversation.   The significance goes beyond adding another way to book a hotel. It is about meeting travelers in the moment when they articulate their intent.  For brands, the question becomes: when a traveler asks an AI agent for the best hotel for their needs, is the brand’s information accurate, accessible and relevant enough to make the shortlist?  In this environment, a strong brand still matters. But it increasingly needs to be backed by strong data, connected commerce capabilities and an experience that can deliver on the promise.  Making travel simpler, faster and easier The travel companies that thrive in the coming decade will likely be those that recognize a simple truth:  convenience is becoming a major driver of loyalty. AI agents may influence discovery and booking, but what ultimately drives preference is a brand’s ability to execute. That requires accurate inventory, seamless booking and payment systems, personalized offers, reliable service delivery and loyalty programs that provide meaningful value. As travel becomes more digital and interconnected, operational excellence becomes a competitive advantage. The brands best positioned to win will be those that pair a compelling brand with the infrastructure, partnerships and customer experience needed to deliver consistently across every touchpoint.  Success will require more than adopting AI. It means rethinking the customer journey to reduce friction and help travelers move seamlessly from intent to booking. Ultimately, travelers aren’t looking for more channels to navigate. They want faster, simpler, and more intuitive experiences. And the rise of agentic commerce offers the industry a powerful opportunity to deliver exactly that.  The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
events.summary: Kashim Chowdhury allegedly juggled five government jobs Published 14 October 2026, 12:40 BST A civil servant is accused of earning almost £350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload. Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £350,000 overall. The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin. Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care. The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave. Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs. Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell. "This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit." Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother. But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered. The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers. Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them. events.title: Wall Street’s big banks deliver mixed earnings. Executives bet the IPO lull won’t last
events.summary: Big week for Wall Street’s largest banks and for finance nerds like myself. Morgan Chittum here. I’m Fortune’s new senior finance reporter, and Allie’s asked me to write Term Sheet a few days a week (Dream gig!) A bit about me: I love reporting on big banks, asset managers, and other financial firms that have an outsized influence on our lives. So, what better way to kick off my first-ever newsletter than with a debrief on bank earnings?  It’s been a mixed bag of reports. Bank of America posted a third-quarter profit drop this morning while Morgan Stanley beat on the top and bottom lines. The latter was largely expected: Citigroup did the same yesterday. Wells Fargo , however, missed on revenue despite surpassing earnings estimates. The bank reported revenue of $21.87 billion, lower than consensus of $22.31 billion. It’s the third time in the past four quarters that Wells has done so. The real surprise came from JPMorgan, the nation’s largest bank by both assets and market cap — about $881 billion. On Tuesday, JPMorgan missed on revenue and earnings for the first time in nearly three years, weighed down by rising expenses and weaker fixed-income trading.  Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs , often seen as JPMorgan’s dealmaking peer, crushed estimates for both revenue and earnings per share.  After their releases, I was inundated with messages from colleagues asking the same question: Why did JPMorgan’s earnings disappoint while Goldman’s blew past expectations? Aren’t they peers? It’s a little more complicated than that. Like JPMorgan, Goldman saw some relative weakness in fixed income, currencies, and commodities, but the firm was able to offset that because of its enormous equities business, where revenue surged an eye-watering 72%. But this is a deals newsletter, after all—so what does all of this mean for the dealmaking backdrop? We’ve recently seen a slew of IPO delays. Oura postponed its plans in late September. Bamboo Insurance and Holtec Nuclear did the same shortly before that.  Still, bank executives say that won’t last for long. JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on a media call that IPOs are being “delayed rather than cancelled,” describing the firm’s pipeline for deals as “very, very strong.” “There are a lot of deals that need to get done that want to get done,” he told reporters. “Maybe in moments of a little bit of market turmoil, you see, especially in the capital markets space, the gap between buyers and sellers can widen temporarily before we find a new level. So we’ll see how it goes. But overall, the conditions remain very supportive.” Goldman CEO David Solomon on the earnings call acknowledged that activity got “a little bit softer” in September. “The IPO market was wide open,” he told analysts. “It’s just if you expected a valuation and you got something 10% to 15% less, you might choose not to go forward–you might choose to wait.” Matt Kennedy, a senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, told me something similar. “After an active summer, suddenly we’re now in a rising-rate environment and investors are questioning AI valuations,” he said. “So, I think the IPO pipeline will take some time to digest that new reality compared to the enthusiasm they were seeing earlier in the year.” Kennedy added: “It’s not like companies are canceling their IPOs. I think they’re prepping them, filing confidentially, selecting banks, and giving themselves optionality for when market conditions are ripe.”  To this end, Kennedy added: Despite these mixed earnings and a string of IPO delays, 2026 is still on pace to beat last year’s deal count, according to Renaissance Capital. And the year has already set a record for IPO proceeds–even without SpaceX’s blockbuster June offering.   Looking ahead, one of the “single-biggest catalysts” for a pickup in IPO activity would be an end to the Iran war , according to Kennedy. “That would bring down oil prices and maybe kickstart some of that deal flow again,” he said. “It might help with inflation and the rate environment too. A lot of these things are connected.” (A successful Anthropic IPO next month, per Kennedy, would also be a positive.) See you tomorrow, Morgan Chittum X: @morgan_chittum Email: morgan.chittum@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . Joey Abrams curated the deals section of today’s newsletter . events.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn for money laundering failures
events.summary: Third largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings Bank of America (BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators for widespread failures to detect ‌potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings. The treasury department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report more than $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, including $1bn that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks. “Financial institutions are on the ​front lines of protecting our economic and national security,” the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said in a statement. “When a bank of this size ​fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the ⁠entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.” The treasury said the bank “prioritized its revenues” in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries ​from outside parties such as law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. The consent order requires Bank of America to hire an ​independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that the bank failed to detect at the time, and report those transactions to FinCen. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of ​employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised ​by our regulators.” The spokesperson added that the bank’s third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2bn, which will reduce quarterly net income ‌by approximately ⁠17 cents a share. Analysts have estimated adjusted EPS of $1.10, according to mean estimates compiled by LSEG, but that excludes one-offs like this fine. The penalty is likely to add to negative investor sentiment and raise concerns about higher expenses and whether Bank of America can maintain its roughly $6bn quarterly share buyback pace, the UBS analyst Erika Najarian said in a note. With earnings due ​on Wednesday, “we think shares likely underperforming at ​open,” she said. She noted there ⁠was no asset cap, a regulatory penalty that would limit how large the bank could grow. As part of the fine, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency levied a $750m civil ​penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money ​laundering programs that were ⁠identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog. The regulator said the bank’s compliance program was “deficient and ineffective”, and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions. In addition, the bank paid an $11.6m fine to the Office of Foreign ⁠Assets Control ​for over 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The treasury said the bank mistakenly ​processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran. The fine comes days after American Express was also hit with a $350m penalty for similar anti-money ​laundering shortcomings.
