events.title: These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.
events.summary: They were victims, not abusers. That’s what they told police officers, attorneys, visitors and anyone else who would listen. It didn’t matter. The women were all taken to a sprawling immigration detention center in the woods of west Michigan and handed thin jumpsuits — red, to mark them as a high security risk. Inside the North Lake Processing Center, they talked about the men whose calls to police landed them there. The boyfriends or husbands who threatened to get them deported and cut them off from their children. The men, or sometimes women, who hit them, pulled their hair or choked them, bruising their throats. They didn’t know where to go for help before, but now, in the confines of a cold cellblock in a former prison, the women helped one another. If one spoke to somebody on the outside who could connect them with advice, legal aid or money for the commissary, she’d pass around a tablet used for calls so others could tell their stories. Migladys Bermudez, an immigration attorney in southeast Michigan, remembers a call in May from a Peruvian woman detained at North Lake. Her name was Pilar, and she’d heard about Bermudez from a fellow detainee who had been a client. Pilar told Bermudez about the boyfriend she tried to escape before her arrest, when she used makeup to cover the marks she said he left on her face. But he had accused her of being the abuser, resulting in her arrest. Pilar handed the tablet to a Cuban woman named Leya. Over the echoes of the other detainees’ chatter, she described how her boyfriend insulted her, isolated her and gave her a black eye. Then, after grabbing him by the arm during an argument, she was the one behind bars, separated from their nursing daughter. On video calls, the girl didn’t seem to recognize her mother anymore. She stopped calling her “Mamá.” Bermudez was taken aback. All three women in that chain — the former client, Pilar and Leya — said they were trying to get out of abusive relationships when they were arrested by local police on domestic violence allegations. In all three cases, the charges were dropped or never filed at all. The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained the first woman during a routine check-in a few months after her charges were dropped. The others were handed over to ICE by local officials.  It’s long been intimidating for immigrants who suffered abuse to call 911, regardless of who was in the White House. They knew — and their abusers knew — that their immigration status made them vulnerable. But previous administrations treated victims as just that, people who needed help, not as targets for deportation. Bipartisan coalitions in Congress have long supported the Violence Against Women Act, which creates a pathway toward legal status for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence or other serious crimes. Now, under President Donald Trump, all bets are off. On inauguration day, his administration rescinded guidelines that largely prevented immigration agents from making arrests at sensitive locations — including domestic violence shelters and hospitals. About a week later, the administration eliminated key protections granted to VAWA applicants and other crime victims. For the first time in decades, immigration authorities could disregard those protections and more freely arrest, detain and deport immigrant victims. Life became more harrowing in other ways for immigrants who were victims of domestic violence. Federal immigration agents made arrests outside specialized domestic violence courts. And the administration persuaded more and more local police and jails to carry out the president’s mass deportation campaign, sweeping still more immigrants into custody.  Even communities without these so-called 287(g) agreements are helping the government round people up. In west Michigan’s Kent County, where Pilar and Leya were arrested, the county jail turned over more immigrants to ICE in the first six months of 2026 than it did during the entire Biden administration. Advocates across the country say they’re seeing signs of an alarming increase in the numbers of domestic violence victims who are detained and deported. And many immigrants are staying in abusive relationships, fearful of calling for help or even stepping outside their homes. “It’s just probably the most dangerous time for immigrant women right now who are victims of domestic violence,” said Bermudez, who took on Leya’s immigration case. The arrest and detention of domestic violence victims is, in part, an unanticipated consequence of an effort meant to keep them safe. In much of the country, law enforcement officers are encouraged — or even required — to make an arrest when they have probable cause to believe that a domestic violence assault has taken place. Sometimes victims are mistaken as the abuser and taken into custody. Then, if they’re immigrants, they can be turned over to ICE — even if they were never criminally charged. There’s no comprehensive way to track how often this happens or how many domestic violence victims have been detained by ICE or deported. But ProPublica spoke with a half-dozen alleged victims who were locked up together in a single facility, North Lake, and reviewed police records about others who were there, too. Their stories offer a picture of why Congress created programs like VAWA in the first place, and what’s at stake when those guardrails are taken away.  A coalition of immigrant survivors and advocates have sued the Trump administration, saying changes to how immigrant victims are treated not only undermined public safety, but also broke promises enshrined in federal law and policy. “We were seeing our clients be more scared, be systematically targeted, be arrested, and deported very quickly,” said Kathleen Rivas, supervising attorney of the survivors team at Public Counsel, a law firm that’s involved in the litigation. In May, a federal judge ordered the government to restore protections while the case played out. The Trump administration has appealed the order.  White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” But Leya, Pilar and other immigrants we interviewed have no criminal records. And advocates said communities are less safe now because immigrants are afraid to call police when their partners hurt them. This gives more ammunition to the threats of their abusers, said Casey Carter Swegman, director of public policy at the Tahirih Justice Center, a national nonprofit that advocates for immigrant survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault and human trafficking. “Certainly more immigrant survivors are feeling like the violence and abuse

After Mark Zuckerberg’s cautious-looking sip of stout on Stripe cofounder John Collison’s "Cheeky Pint" podcast became a social-media talking point , a new debate has emerged: which tech leaders can actually hold their drink? Soon after Zuckerberg's much-memed appearance, ETN, a tech podcast, built what it called the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," publishing a leaderboard of guests' Guinness consumption, measured to the nearest sixth of a pint. events.title: Getty Images to go private under ‘pre-packaged’ bankruptcy
events.summary: Getty will continue to operate normally throughout the process, citing up to US$143 million (S$184 million) in financing from Koch, as well as cash from ongoing business. Getty Images will go private through a “pre-packaged Chapter 11 filing” after agreeing a debt restructuring with major lenders and new equity of up to US$533 million. The company says it will keep operating normally, with up to US$143 million from Koch and no expected impact on contributors, partners, customers or staff. The move follows a warning that its shares would be delisted from the New York Stock Exchange after falling below US$1, after a US$206.1 million loss in 2025. NEW YORK – US photography company Getty Images announced on Oct 12 it reached an agreement with major lenders to restructure its debt, take the company private and undertake a “pre-packaged” bankruptcy. Getty, which partners with AFP among numerous other media companies, said members of the Getty Family and affiliates of Koch Equity Development will invest up to US$533 million (S$683 million) o f new equity to pay down debt under a restructuring. Getty “reached agreement with all of its major financial stakeholder groups on the terms of a comprehensive restructuring,” the company said. Getty will continue to operate normally throughout the process, citing up to US$143 million in financing from Koch, as well as cash from ongoing business. “There is no anticipated impact on content contributors, partners, customers, or employees across the Company’s worldwide network,” Getty said. The company plans a “prepackaged Chapter 11 filing” to win court approval of the restructuring. “The requisite majority of creditors have committed to vote in favor of the Plan,” said Getty, which expects the restructuring to be complete by end 2026. The announcement came after Getty disclosed in a securities filing earlier in October that it had been notified of plans to delist its shares from the New York Stock Exchange because they had fallen below US$1. Getty reported a loss of US$206.1 million in 2025. AFP

events.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh
events.summary: Saudi civil defence says danger passed after it issued two warnings through its national early warning platform. The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, as the Yemeni armed group said it carried out more attacks on the kingdom. Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki on Wednesday announced the thwarted attack on X, days after two separate strikes hit Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, killing 14 people and injuring hundreds. list 1 of 3 The escalation in Yemen is a turning point list 2 of 3 How the Middle East conflict is threatening data centres, internet cables list 3 of 3 Yemeni government launches air strikes on Houthi positions The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defence also issued two alerts through its national early warning platform, later saying the danger had passed. One alert was for the Al-Kharj governorate in Riyadh province, and the other for the capital. The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for supporters of God), issued a statement saying they targeted facilities of Saudi ⁠⁠Arabia’s national oil company Aramco in Dhahran, an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, and the capital’s King Khalid international ‌‌airport. Overnight, the Saudi Ministry of Energy confirmed that the administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit. Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital Doha, said any notion that the Saudi-led coalition could contain the conflict to Yemen had been shattered over the last 10 days, which saw the targeting of several sites in Saudi Arabia. Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports , including the Abha international airport, where two people were killed, and on Aramco facilities. Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive in Yemen to retake coastal territory from the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital maritime trade chokepoint. Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces escalated sharply last month, shattering a United Nations-brokered ceasefire that had largely held since 2022. The Houthis have controlled Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, since seizing the city in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to flee to southern Yemen. The Muslim World League on Wednesday condemned the continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they deliberately target civilians and civilian sites. The league’s secretary-general, Sheikh Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, said their nature confirms “the criminal approach of this terrorist militia in deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure”. Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah television reported that four air strikes hit the Harib district in the country’s Marib governorate. The results of the attacks were not immediately clear. Nawaf Obaid, a security and intelligence analyst and senior research fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that while air strikes are intensifying, the “actual ground war hasn’t really begun” for the Saudi-led coalition. Obaid broke down the phases in which such an operation could unfold, saying the first phase would be “to hit at basically the power and the energy source that’s allowing the Houthis to operate … tanks, armoured vehicles, trucks”. Phase two would be to look at the “systematic increase of Houthi control in the region, which is critical,” he said. Phase three would involve a discussion on how “to start taking back these territories that the Houthis have gained since the beginning of the war”. Obaid said these “multipronged phases” would include “extra-specialised” troops, especially in mountain warfare, because the Houthis are taking the battlefield into difficult terrain.

events.title: Kenya clears path for Dangote refinery IPO investment
events.summary: The News Kenyan investors hoping to participate in the Dangote refinery initial public offering now have access through a financial instrument being used for cross-border African investment for the first time on Nairobi’s bourse. The use of global depositary receipts (GDRs), which allow backers to buy a stake in a foreign company without leaving their home market, bypasses regulatory barriers that have held up intra-African investment. The use of GDRs offers a template for exchanges across the continent to expand pan-African trade and broaden their investor bases. After an extension of the IPO period was announced on Monday, Kenyan individuals and institutional investors will have until Oct. 27 to buy into their country’s $300 million allocation of Africa’s largest public offering. The minimum entry price in Kenya was slashed from $824 to $4.12, matching what Nigerians were being offered. Announcing the extension, Dangote said he wanted greater African participation and highlighted the Kenyan arrangement that he hoped could be replicated. African policymakers are keen to deepen capital markets as a way to mobilize more of the continent’s domestic resources to fund infrastructure projects and reduce borrowing costs. Know More The refinery’s stock market debut was touted as a way for African investors to own a stake in the continent’s largest refining plant. But the prospectus for the $1.6 billion share shows it was not registered as a public offering outside Nigeria, Reuters reported. That has left investors relying on their own country’s regulations or finding workarounds using the few eligible online financial platforms. Reuters reported patchy take-up outside Nigeria , reflecting low levels of cross-border investment. The Nairobi Securities Exchange’s (NSE) approach is structured around Standard Bank’s Kenya subsidiary Stanbic, which will hold the shares and issue the GDRs. These will be traded on the NSE in Kenyan shillings, and Stanbic will manage the foreign exchange conversion and pay out dividends. Karimi Warui, vice president of investment banking at Renaissance Capital, which is overseeing the IPO in Kenya, told Semafor that the Dangote Group initially intended to pursue a conventional cross-listing approach to get on the NSE and other stock exchanges, but ultimately settled on GDRs for ease. Trying to deal with the rules and regulations of 10 different jurisdictions “became a bit onerous for them,” she added. She said this approach in Kenya could inspire others. “I wouldn’t be surprised if companies that are already listed like [Kenyan telecoms company] Safaricom pursue GDRs in the future to tap into markets like South Africa and Nigeria,” she said. “I actually think we will see more of this now,” saying the IPO would “show regulators the need to work with financiers and issuers” to accelerate growth and integration of Africa’s financial markets. Warui also emphasized the need for regulators to customize policies to fit African markets instead of copying Western regulators. The use of GDRs comes amid a significant push to enhance retail investing in the country. Safaricom this year rolled out NSE trading on the mobile money service M-Pesa, helping drive retail participation in the IPO of the state-run Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) . Warui told Semafor that Renaissance Capital was copying the KPC blueprint for the Dangote IPO — with an online platform for share purchases during the offer period, and trading on the M-Pesa platform expected once it is listed on the NSE. Besides Kenya, Uganda’s markets regulator has approved a restricted offer limiting participation to high net-worth individuals and professional investors. Botswana has been selected to host the southern African portion of the public offering, Bloomberg reported. Step Back Some analysts have cautioned that the GDRs could leave Kenyan investors exposed to FX risks as the GDR tracks the Lagos share price, which is in naira, meaning currency devaluation could significantly affect investors. Acknowledging the concerns, Warui noted that Dangote Refinery’s revenues were dollarized and that dividends could also be paid in dollars, mitigating the potential impact of naira devaluation. Previous GDR listings by African companies have been outward, where issuers list the underlying shares on exchanges outside the continent — mostly on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) to attract Western capital. Room for Disagreement Sultan Mwangi, a Nairobi-based investor and financial researcher, predicted that participation in the Dangote IPO among Kenyan investors would be far lower than expected, especially among retail investors. He attributed this to the handling of the IPO which he said had left investors “disappointed” despite initial excitement. Among issues he cited were inadequate investor education and a need to address concerns regarding the use of GDRs, especially over whether this will leave people exposed to fluctuations in the value of the naira. According to Mwangi, the extension of the IPO offer as well as lowering the minimum investment were a response to low uptake among retail investors. “People were not convinced, and the amount of time available to explain it has not been enough,” he told Semafor. Dangote Industries has yet to respond to enquiries from Semafor on whether the lowering of the minimum investment was a response to underwhelming participation among Kenyan retail investors. Notable African nations should turn to an estimated $4 trillion in capital held by domestic institutions, such as pension funds, to develop infrastructure, the Africa Finance Corporation has said.

events.title: It’s a different oil crisis, but Saudi Arabia will still pay
events.summary: Wael’s view In June 2008, I sat in a Jeddah Hilton conference room packed with ministers from more than 100 countries waiting for King Abdullah to arrive. Oil was closing in on a record price. Saudi Arabia’s message that day: The world had enough oil. It offered a modest increase in output and told governments to cut taxes and rein in speculators. Less than three weeks later, on July 11, crude hit about $147 a barrel. This week in Riyadh, another ministerial gathering took place. The man now leading the kingdom’s response, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, was an assistant oil minister two decades ago. This time the crisis is different — and so is his answer. Then, the argument was about speculation. Saudi officials said investors had pushed prices well past what supply and demand justified, and that financial trading in oil had grown many times larger than the physical market. Washington thought OPEC should pump more. Riyadh replied that it would not build capacity for buyers who did not exist. Now the argument is about geography. Gulf crude is trapped behind the Strait of Hormuz, and the kingdom’s answer is to build around it. Prince Abdulaziz told the World Petroleum Congress that Saudi Arabia may lift its East-West pipeline capacity from about 7 million barrels a day to 10 million within three years, and he wants more international involvement. His logic is that the more countries have a stake in the line, the better it is protected. Both responses share one feature. Saudi Arabia cannot solve the crisis alone, and it ends up paying for the attempt. In 2008 it built rarely used spare capacity and has carried its cost ever since. A new pipeline will follow the same pattern. When the war ends it will not run full, and Riyadh will keep it as insurance. The oil market has also shifted. In 2008, OPEC was dominant and no one else could add meaningful supply. Some consumers searched for substitutes, and ethanol was an answer then. Today, it’s the electric vehicle. But neither remedy has removed the need for fossil fuels and no price spike has changed the thirst for oil. The biggest difference is Washington. In 2008, the US relied on OPEC’s oil. Today, it has plenty of its own, a reality that may not be felt by Americans paying more at the pump. If America needed OPEC barrels as badly as it did in 2008, the politics of this current crisis would look very different. Geopolitical risk has been the main factor driving $100 oil this year, with shipping and insurance comprising more than a third of the price of the global crude benchmark. Even if Hormuz is opened tomorrow, the new logistics of moving crude will weigh on producers. It will also change the relationship between states: Iraq is planning to build a pipeline through Syria to the Mediterranean, while Kuwait and Qatar may lean on their Gulf neighbors to reach ports outside the strait. Ultimately, much of the bill will go to the same address: Riyadh. The kingdom has carried the cost of a largely idle pipeline for decades, and will soon have to revert to its role as the global swing producer, keeping prices fair to producers paying for new infrastructure, and consumers who won’t tolerate high prices forever. Notable Saudi Arabia’s oil supply could still be threatened even after the end of the war. This report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies looks at what options there are. Despite the oil shock, the Saudi economy can remain resilient, according to t his briefing from the Atlantic Council .

events.title: Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again
events.summary: Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran. Iran’s military said it has expanded its surveillance of the Strait of Hormuz by deploying new units to target ships, amid a desperate tussle between Tehran and Washington to control the waterway, among the world’s most important passages for energy transport. With the United States naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has repeatedly said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the strait. list 1 of 3 Trump says Houthis trying to increase oil prices before US elections list 2 of 3 How Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ is reshaping southern Lebanon list 3 of 3 How do Iranians move money abroad to avoid US sanctions? Tehran’s latest announcement coincides with a surge in attacks in the waterway and a fall in oil transit after crude flows had risen back to pre-war levels in September. Chris Featherstone, a political scientist at the University of York in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera the increased attacks and their impact on energy flows demonstrate the fragility of the strait as a key pathway for oil exports. So, what’s going on and who controls the Strait of Hormuz now? What has Iran said about expanding its presence in Hormuz? Iran’s Navy said it has deployed operational units in a new formation “east of the Strait of Hormuz and across the Sea of Oman and the Arabian Sea, after identifying a tanker that sustained damage and caught fire”, according to a report by the Iranian news and documentary network Press TV on Tuesday. The navy said these units would maintain “real time surveillance of enemy activities and maritime traffic in the region”. It also warned vessels not to switch off their transponders and urged them to coordinate with Iranian armed forces for safe passage through the area. Separately, an Iranian official told the Reuters news agency that Tehran had started ⁠using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. The strategy includes a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the November midterm elections in the US, according to the official. Attacks in Hormuz rise to record levels Ships in the Strait of Hormuz have been experiencing the worst spate of attacks since the start of the US and Israel’s war on Iran in late February. According to maritime tracking firm Kpler, 10 tankers were struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, followed by another strike on October 5. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre has separately recorded 15 other attacks between October 6 and October 14, with 11 of them occurring in just the past four days. They include a container ship and a tanker hit by unknown projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, UKMTO said. Iran maintains that its attacks and restrictions in the waterway are a matter of national security and self-defence in response to the US-Israel war. Iranian authorities have also signalled they intend to disrupt a US-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the strait during the war. In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) noted that the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level. Attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), “attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said. UAV stands for unmanned aerial vehicle, or drone, while VHF hailing refers to Iranian forces using standard marine radio to verbally contact, track, and intimidate passing merchant ships on international communication channels. How have attacks affected oil flows? Before the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies. In retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait and has stepped up attacks on vessels trying to break its regulations. Meanwhile, Washington has also maintained a blockade on Iranian ports. In September, however, Gulf oil flows through Hormuz, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, Kpler reported . Shepherded by the US Navy, more and more oil tankers had started passing through.

events.title: Job cuts could fund diesel price drop says deputy
events.summary: Prices at the petrol pump in Guernsey have reached record highs A Guernsey deputy has said leaders could fund a fuel price drop for drivers by cutting civil servant posts. Deputy Neil Inder said he plans to submit two amendments around the cost of fuel in relation to the upcoming States budget amid "exceptional circumstances due to global events". The proposed amendments are to freeze fuel duty and to also cut the cost at the pumps of white diesel - used by cars, trucks and buses - by 5p. Asked how the States would fund this, he added: "What the States needs to start looking at properly is reducing the size of the civil service." Deputy Neil Inder said rising fuel price rises were set to get worse amid global unrest In the 2027 budget, fuel duty is due to increase by inflation (4.3%) from 1 January 2027, increasing duty rates to 94.4p per litre. With the war continuing in the Middle East, fuel prices have increased across Europe, with diesel prices hitting an all-time high, according to the RAC motoring organisation. It comes as fuel prices recently hit record highs across Guernsey, and the price of diesel hit £2.00 per litre in the UK. White diesel, used for regular road vehicles, is subject to the standard fuel duty rate, while red diesel, used in industries including farming and fishing, is a rebated fuel that is duty-free or has a heavily reduced tax rate. "I think we've got to realise what's happened to the world diesel prices," said Inder. Listen to the latest news for Guernsey "There's been an unreasonable spike in diesel prices over the last three or four months and it really is set to get worse." He said this would inevitably impact the cost of living and added: "Whether we like it or not diesel really does make the world go round and the wheels turn in Guernsey." Inder said under "normal circumstances" he would probably go along with the P&R proposal to "up duty on the diesel", but said the global climate called for greater consideration. "In reality the biggest cost to the States is the amount of people we employ," he said. "Given the cost of the revenue they would gain, all that really is, is four or five civil servants - stop employing them, those that retire, don't replace them." "There's only one budget a year and this is the time to address it," added Inder. The BBC has asked the States for comment. events.title: Anthropic urges court in Washington, DC, to rehear appeal of Pentagon blacklisting
events.summary: Anthropic is asking a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models. The Defense Department labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk in March, and the AI company sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's decision. Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C., to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models. "The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation." The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models . Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional. Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety." In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation. Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed. A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. A Pentagon spokesperson told CNBC in an email that the agency doesn't comment on pending or ongoing litigation. — CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this report. events.title: How top brands are hunting for the next breakout influencer
events.summary: Marketers at CMO Insider's "The AI Marketer: Creator and Influencer Edition" roundtable held during Advertising Week New York shared their strategies for discovering the next breakout influencer talent. Derek French A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly marketing newsletter . Marketers are getting smarter about finding their next influencer partners . At a CMO Insider roundtable during Advertising Week New York, top marketers told us how they're using AI-powered platforms , social listening tools, and some surprisingly old-fashioned tactics to discover new creators and niche communities. Meredith Diehn, SVP of marketing at Goodwipes, said her company recently adopted the influencer discovery tool Modash, which has significantly reduced manual work in identifying potential partners, freeing up the team to review creators' previous content and determine whether they're a good fit. Goodwipes' searches using Modash are remarkably granular, Diehn said. "I'm going to find a creator who is a girl with IBS who lives in Nashville," she said. Diehn's team is also using a social listening tool called Nectar to uncover microcommunities already talking about the brand that might not have been obvious targets. Diehn said Goodwipes is exploring opportunities to reach communities like postpartum mothers, whose needs can make flushable wipes particularly useful. Alicia Latoya Richardson, head of community and partnerships at the creator membership community FiveTwoNine, said brands are finding success using a tool called Companion, from its parent company Billion Dollar Boy Group, to search for creators across different geographies and demographics and assess their potential value. For its client Adobe, for example, FiveTwoNine has used Companion to analyze posts created by attendees at its events and estimate the resulting earned media value . (EMV is a measure of what the same reach or engagement would have cost if bought through paid ads.) "AI has definitely elevated the way we report to clients on value," Richardson said. Mars Pet Nutrition is also using AI-powered creator-discovery tools to help it cast a wider net when searching for creators and narrow the pool to candidates most likely to deliver reach and engagement. But there are still some areas where the tech falls short, said Paolo Narag, creative excellence lead at Mars Pet Nutrition. Earlier this year, while he was working on its Sheba brand, Narag's team launched a campaign called "Ignored to Adored." The campaign played on the insight that cat owners often feel ignored by their pets, despite loving them, and leaned heavily on content creators who shot candid videos of being snubbed by their feline companions. The creator who "popped" was the American figure skater Ilia Malinin , who already had two cats and was about to adopt a third. While AI filtering helped Mars find the right influencer, the team had to dig deeper to uncover the actual storyline that ultimately worked. "We still have the human discernment to say, 'OK, let's work with their management teams,'" said Narag. "Let's talk to their creators. What are the stories that they have that we can then jump on and amplify?" Sometimes it pays to just ask Another way to discover promising creators is simply to ask different communities which influencers they trust, rather than relying solely on algorithms, said FiveTwoNine's Richardson. FiveTwoNine hosts creator events on subjects such as AI, Pinterest, and fashion. "We will ask that community that is engaged: Who are you listening to? Who are you following? Who are you paying attention to?" Richardson said. Alicia Latoya Richardson of FiveTwoNine advised marketers to poll communities they're trying to reach on the creators they are paying attention to. Derek French Authenticity is a major consideration when selecting a creator partner. A Morning Consult survey of about 2,000 US adults in September, conducted exclusively for CMO Insider, found consumers ranked creators expressing genuine opinions (33%) and demonstrating they actually use a product themselves (30%) as the top factors that make sponsored content feel authentic. Kate Ridley, chief brand officer of Stanley 1913 , said she prioritizes working with creators who genuinely appreciate its products. She added that the brand hasn't necessarily codified a tried-and-true way to identify new talent because the relevant microcommunities can change so quickly. Ridley said her approach is one of "constant listening," followed by being ready to make "quick and agile decisions" about how to tap in. "We don't have a formula, and if I'm being really candid, frequently feel lost in it," Ridley said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tech giants race to get AI gadgets on shelves for holiday rush
events.summary: Apple, Amazon and Microsoft have all announced new devices in the past week with the aim of bringing generative artificial intelligence firmly into the home. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, leading consumer tech companies are touting improved personal assistants and speedier on-device chips with AI capabilities. "This is really about getting devices into consumers' hands, into consumers' homes, slowly teaching them how to use it, and getting feedback from them," said Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at IDC. With the holidays just months away, tech companies are betting this is finally the year that AI starts showing up under the Christmas tree. Apple , Amazon and Microsoft have all announced new devices in the past week with the aim of bringing generative artificial intelligence firmly into the home. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the leading consumer tech companies are touting improved personal assistants and speedier on-device chips with AI capabilities as they try to sell new laptops, tablets, phones and smart home computers. Success is far from guaranteed. In addition to the weakest consumer sentiment data in 12 years due largely to stubborn inflation, and growing fears about the potential safety risks of AI, there's a learning curve that comes with the new technology. Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at IDC, said tech companies want to introduce AI to consumers to lay the groundwork for more aggressive device launches in the coming years. "This is really about getting devices into consumers' hands, into consumers' homes, slowly teaching them how to use it, and getting feedback from them," Ubrani said, adding that new gadgets from Apple, Amazon and Microsoft aren't expected to sell in large volumes, at least not yet. Getting affluent early adopters on board now could be considered a win given the macro headwinds. Hardware prices across the board have risen, driven by soaring costs for components, especially memory and storage, as power-hungry AI servers suck up most of the capacity. Those price hikes have led to plunging shipments this year of new smartphones and laptops. Microsoft kicked off the launches last week by showing off an Nvidia -powered Windows laptop starting at $2,599, based around an AI chip called RTX Spark that can run powerful AI without relying on the cloud. Amazon followed by releasing Alexa tablets , the company's first pieces of hardware named after its smart assistant. The largest Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs $550, compared to $155 for its predecessor, the Fire HD10. And on Tuesday of this week, Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub, powered by Siri AI. The $299 devices include a 7-inch screen that can be mounted, along with facial recognition software so it can be personalized for multiple family members. Analysts applauded Apple for introducing HomeView at a reasonable price given all the component shortages. "Apple has prioritized ecosystem adoption over immediate high hardware margins, delivering a local-AI hub at a price point that undercuts what a spec-heavy machine should logically cost," said Mohit Agrawal, who specializes in AI at CounterPoint Research, in an email. Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester, said the shopping season will mark an early test of consumer demand for a new class of gadgets. "I think consumers are interested in what AI can do," said Chatterjee. "What's less clear is whether they are interested in buying hardware specifically because it is an AI device." Despite the many economic headwinds, the spending outlook heading into the holidays remains robust. Nearly half of U.S. consumers expect to spend the same or more this year compared to last year's holiday season, according to a McKinsey survey published in August. And Bain published a report last month, predicting that U.S. retail sales over the holidays will set new records and top $1 trillion for the first time. However, analysts cautioned "more than half of the nominal sales growth will come from higher inflation" pushing up prices. The firm predicted that sales in some electronics and appliances will remain flat. "In a time when folks are being a little money conscious, you say, 'Do I really need the next one of those, or could I drag out the replacement cycle on whatever it is?'" said Aaron Cheris, head of Bain's global retail practice, in an interview. "We've seen things that are discretionary purchases drag out longer." All three producers of the new AI gadgets emphasized their increasingly intelligent assistants, as well as more powerful chips to run them. Amazon said it's ditching the budget-friendly Fire family of devices in favor of three new Alexa Tablets that feature a more premium design with its souped-up AI assistant front and center. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to summon the assistant and ask questions, get personalized recommendations or control their smart home.

events.title: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China’s grip on critical materials with AI
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startup Scimplify has raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense, and energy emerging as key growth markets. The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from $150 million after a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation. The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process. In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview. Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing, and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch. “Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.” Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries. About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said. The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Scimplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago. Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said. Energy, electronics, and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry. Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare-earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China. The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project. events.title: Dubai and Abu Dhabi among top destinations for next-generation wealth, Savills says
events.summary: Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tensions, according to Savills. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, the London-based consultancy said in its Spotlight on Wealth Trends report on Wednesday. Next-generation wealth refers to individuals under 40 who have inherited significant wealth or have accumulated it through entrepreneurial success. Dubai and Abu Dhabi benefitted from a slew of government initiatives that support economic and societal growth, including favourable tax environments, business-friendly policies and significant infrastructure investment “with a sophisticated luxury offering”, Savills said. In particular, Dubai's entrepreneurial ecosystem, global connectivity and lifestyle appeal attract international talent and capital. Abu Dhabi complements this with its growing financial centre, a rising number of family offices, expanding economic opportunities and a high quality of life, the study said. Those are “reinforcing the UAE's position as a compelling destination for globally mobile wealth”, Kelcie Sellers, associate director for world research at Savills, wrote in the report. In the wider Gulf, “economic diversification and succession planning are becoming more prominent, with growing focus on family governance, next-generation involvement and the long-term deployment of capital within the region”, Ms Sellers said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and the flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country is a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as for global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as institutional partners. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a report this week by Boston Consulting Group found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report said. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. New York leads globally New York topped the Savills list, followed by Miami, London, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Singapore, Hong Kong and Monaco at ninth. Dubai and Abu Dhabi were the only Gulf cities on the list, which ranked more than 100 destinations worldwide. Cities in Europe, the Middle East and Africa accounted for 16 of the index’s top 30 locations, driven by lifestyle and sporting events, which include major golf and tennis tournaments and Formula One races. In terms of the number of sporting events, Dubai was number one in the Emea region, while Abu Dhabi, home of the season-ending F1 race, was sixth. “The defining characteristic of Emea is the diversity of its wealth proposition. Global business centres, leading educational institutions, major sporting and cultural events, coastal retreats and mountain resorts are all within reach,” Ms Sellers said. Global wealth continues to grow rapidly. Total personal wealth jumped by nearly 11 per cent in 2025 to create about one million more millionaires, according to industry tracker Altrata. More than 510,800 are now ultra-high net worth individuals, or those with a net worth of $30 million or more, holding around $60 trillion in combined wealth – which is greater than the combined economies of the US and China, Altrata said. “Location decisions are becoming a core component of wealth planning … at the same time, new fortunes generated by technology and artificial intelligence are reshaping global wealth hubs,” Ms Sellers said. “As a result, many wealthy families are adopting multi-jurisdictional lifestyles, balancing residence, education and wealth structures across multiple markets.”

events.title: Singapore marine fuel supplier Equatorial eyes higher LNG bunker demand from 2028
events.summary: Vessels including oil tankers in the Singapore Strait. The Republic is the world’s biggest refuelling hub for ships, supplying an average 4.7 million tonnes of bunker fuel monthly so far this year. Equatorial Marine Fuel Management plans to use part of its 2026 profits to expand into LNG bunkering, with demand expected to rise from 2028 as more LNG capacity and dual-fuel ships come online. The Singapore supplier won one of eight LNG bunker licences in July and is talking with LNG cargo suppliers and shipowners. Its first new LNG bunker barge should arrive in late Q3 2027. Singapore LNG bunker sales reached 487,100 tons in January to September 2026, up more than 21% year on year. Equatorial says demand is resilient, while biofuel demand has slowed because of delays to the IMO net-zero framework. SINGAPORE – Equatorial Marine Fuel Management, a top Singapore bunker supplier by volume, plans to channel part of its 2026 profits to fund its expansion into supplying liquefied natural gas (LNG) to ships as it positions for higher demand from 2028, its executives said. The company, which was one of eight suppliers awarded an LNG bunker licence in late July, is in discussions with LNG cargo suppliers and shipowners for collaboration, its executive director Choong Zhen Mao told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore International Bunkering conference (SIBCON) 2026. “The opportunity that we see in LNG still seems to be growing, even in this climate. I think that’s where we see the market moving,” he said, referring to the surge in LNG prices after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted exports from the Middle East. The company will be receiving its first new-built LNG bunker barge in the later part of the third quarter in 2027, he added. Singapore’s January-to-September 2026 LNG bunker sales totalled 487,100 tonnes, up more than 21% from a year earlier, data from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore showed on Oct 14. Equatorial’s chief operating officer (COO), Choong Sheen Mao, expects a more notable increase in Singapore’s LNG bunker demand from 2028, as more LNG production capacity and dual-fuel vessels come online globally. Equatorial currently supplies about 10% of total bunker volumes at Singapore, the world’s biggest refuelling hub for ships, according to its executives. The city state has supplied an average 4.7 million tonnes of bunker fuel a month so far in 2026, official data show. The company’s year-to-date profits for 2026 have exceeded last year’s level, the executives said, though they did not disclose the figures. Bunker fuel prices surged after US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February drove oil prices higher, and have remained volatile since then. The ensuing disruption to shipping routes supported refuelling demand in key hubs including Singapore. “Demand looks to be resilient,” said executive director Choong. “When there is uncertainty, sometimes people tend to purchase a bit more, fill their tanks a bit more... people tend to break a voyage down into smaller trades these days to ensure availability and cargo security.” Equatorial owns eight fuel oil barges, seven marine diesel barges, as well as four chemical bunker tankers that meet the International Maritime Organization’s type 2 standard to carry methanol or biofuel blends up to 100% biofuel content. Some of the chemical bunker tankers have been repurposed to supply conventional fuel this year amid a slowdown in marine biofuel demand, COO Choong said. “Demand for biofuels has slowed this year because of the delay in the IMO’s net-zero framework, while current prices are not competitive,” he said. Depending on the blend and delivery window, biofuel blends command premiums of at least US$100 per tonne over conventional low-sulphur bunker fuel oil, according to industry sources. REUTERS

events.title: Mary Chia insolvency proceedings dismissed, but $350,000 loan dispute remains unresolved
events.summary: As part of court-given directions, Mary Chia transferred $651,498.97 to the court’s account on Oct 6. Mary Chia’s insolvency proceedings were dismissed after it paid $651,498.97 into court and $13,900 in costs, but a High Court dispute over two loans remains unresolved. The company still contests the claimed balance, including default interest, late payment interest and restructuring fees on loans with a combined principal of $350,000. Fullink had sought about $902,640. Mary Chia also plans to raise $1 million through share subscriptions for working capital and expansion, while five subsidiaries face separate CPF arrears cases worth $103,727. SINGAPORE – Insolvency proceedings brought against beauty and wellness group Mary Chia Holdings and three other parties have been dismissed, although a legal dispute over two loans totalling $350,000 remains unresolved. The Catalist-listed company announced on Oct 14 that the court had confirmed the dismissal of proceedings brought by Fullink Capital on Oct 13, following compliance with court directions issued on Sept 30. As part of these directions, Mary Chia transferred $651,498.97 to the court’s account on Oct 6. The amount had previously been placed with the company’s solicitors as security. It also paid $13,900 in court-ordered costs to Fullink’s solicitors on Oct 9, with receipt confirmed on Oct 12. The proceedings involved Mary Chia Holdings, Organica International Holdings, Mary Chia chief executive Ho Yow Ping and chief financial officer Su Jun Ming. Despite the dismissal, the $651,498.97 will remain with the court pending the outcome of an ongoing High Court case concerning amounts claimed by Fullink. Mary Chia stressed that placing the money with the court “does not constitute an admission of liability” in respect of the disputed amounts. The company had earlier paid $343,829 on July 21, representing the amount it acknowledged was due. It continues to contest the remaining sums claimed by Fullink, including disputed default interest, late payment interest and restructuring fees arising from two loans with a combined principal of $350,000. These issues have yet to be determined by the court. Fullink issued statutory demand seeking $902,640 The dispute dates back to March, when Fullink issued a statutory demand seeking about $902,640 over loans extended to Organica, a wholly owned Mary Chia subsidiary. Mary Chia had provided a corporate guarantee for the loans, while Ho and Su were personal guarantors. Fullink subsequently commenced winding-up proceedings against Mary Chia and Organica, as well as bankruptcy proceedings against the two executives. At a hearing on Sept 30, the High Court directed that the insolvency proceedings be dismissed once the secured sum of $651,498.97 was paid into court. Separately, Mary Chia said it had entered into subscription agreements on Oct 6 to raise $1 million in gross proceeds through a proposed share subscription. The funds are intended to strengthen the group’s financial position, with net proceeds earmarked for working capital and business expansion in China and Thailand. The proposed fund raising remains subject to shareholder approval at an extraordinary general meeting, regulatory approvals and other conditions. The latest development comes as five Mary Chia subsidiaries face separate court proceedings over unpaid Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions. In an Oct 9 filing responding to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation, the group disclosed that the five subsidiaries owed a combined $103,727 in CPF arrears , based on the CPF Board’s revised computation. Mary Chia also admitted that it had failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four subsidiaries in an earlier announcement, attributing the omission to shortcomings in its internal reporting and disclosure processes. In its Oct 14 media release, the group said it had worked with the CPF Board to establish a monthly payment arrangement for its outstanding contributions. It added that the first monthly instalment had been “paid in full”, and that the relevant subsidiaries would continue making payments according to the agreed schedule. The five CPF-related cases have been adjourned to Nov 12.

events.title: I moved from the US to Spain and lost over 15 pounds without dieting. I still eat bread and pastries and drink beer.
events.summary: The author moved her family from Connecticut to Spain. Courtesy of the author I moved my family from Connecticut to Spain and lost over 15 pounds without trying. I still eat bread and pastries and drink beer, but I walk much more than I did in the US. The lifestyle change has improved my physical health and helped me feel less anxious. I moved my family of four from Connecticut to Spain in August 2025. Since then, I've lost more than 15 pounds. I didn't go on a diet. I didn't start a workout plan . I didn't give up bread, beer, or pastries. I simply changed where I lived. I drove almost everywhere in the US Before we moved, my husband, our boys, and I lived in a town where you needed a car to get almost anywhere. I worked from home as a copywriter, and on a typical day, I averaged about 3,000 steps. For years, I tried to change that. Every few months, I'd start a new fitness plan or decide to eat differently. I bought a Peloton. I even got an under-the-desk walking pad so I could get steps in while I worked. At one point, I added a weighted vest. I was constantly trying to fit healthy habits into a life that left little room. I'd stick with something for a while, fall off track, and then get frustrated with myself for not being disciplined enough. The author walks more now that she has moved to Spain. Courtesy of the author It wasn't just exercise. Most days, I felt like I was racing something. There was always another email, deadline, or thing I should have been doing. I was running a business, taking care of kids, managing a household, and trying to squeeze my own health somewhere into the margins. I was also taking medication for anxiety . I'd been on it for a couple of years, and questioned if it was helping at all. I constantly felt on edge. Like I was never doing enough, I couldn't relax. Then we moved to Las Rozas de Madrid. I walk 12,000 steps in Madrid For the first time in my adult life, I don't have a car. Our boys' school is in another town, so we walk to the train, then switch to a bus, for drop-off and pickup. Our neighborhood is walkable — the grocery store, pharmacy, library, and hair salon are all within about 10 minutes of our flat. These days, I average around 12,000 steps a day without even trying. That's four times what I was doing back in Connecticut. We live at the top of a hill, so I walk up it sometimes several times a day. I carry groceries home. I walk to appointments. I walk because I need to get somewhere, not because I scheduled it. In Connecticut, exercise was something I had to make happen. I had to find the time, put on workout clothes, get on the Peloton or the walking pad, and convince myself that this was the part of my day when I was supposed to be active. Here, movement is just part of getting through a day, and I've come to genuinely enjoy it. Most mornings, I walk through Calle Real, the pedestrian street running through the center of town. Elderly men sit together on benches talking. People connect over coffee or a beer in cafés. Kids weave through on scooters or kick a fútbol against the edge of the amphitheater. I love being one more person in the middle of it all. The sun is out most days, and it lifts my mood almost instantly. I still eat all the things I love My relationship with food has changed, too, though probably not in the way you'd expect. I still eat pastries. I still drink beer. And I eat more bread than ever. But the food I eat is fresher, made with fewer ingredients, and less processed. And I'm not sitting at my desk all day, grazing between meetings. I'm moving throughout the day instead of spending most of it in one place. The author eats more bread than before. Courtesy of the author I wasn't consciously trying to lose weight, but this lifestyle change made it nearly effortless. Somewhere along the way, I realized something else had changed. I wasn't anxious all the time anymore. That heavy feeling, like an anvil on my chest, was gone. I no longer take medication for anxiety. Spain isn't some magic place that takes away all of life's stresses. I still have work. I still have two kids. I still have bills, deadlines, and frustrating days. But the pace of ordinary life is different. Shops close in the middle of the day. If you're sitting in a restaurant, the check doesn't arrive until you ask for it. If you need a bus or train, you wait for it, because there's no faster option. There are more pauses in the day. And somewhere in those pauses, I stopped feeling like I needed to constantly chase the next thing. For years, I thought taking care of myself meant finding the discipline to exercise, eat better, slow down, and make time for myself. I kept trying to become the kind of person who "does it all." It turns out, discipline was never really the problem. I needed a life that asked less of me. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Israeli plan to reopen settler ‘Route 463’ threatens to isolate Ramallah
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? The move to open Route 463 for Israeli settlers threatens to isolate Palestinian villages and severely fragment the Ramallah governorate. The Israeli army is reportedly preparing to reopen Route 463 to settler traffic, a move that threatens to isolate eight Palestinian villages and two large residential neighbourhoods in the occupied West Bank. The areas that would be most affected by the reopening of the road would be northern Ramallah and el-Bireh, a suburb of Ramallah city. It would separate the northern and southern parts of the Ramallah and el-Bireh Governorate. list 1 of 3 Palestinians dream of returning home after Israel raids West Bank camps list 2 of 3 Jerusalem Daily: Israeli forces raid NGOs in Ramallah list 3 of 3 Israeli attacks kill one in Gaza, wound journalists in occupied West Bank The road extends for about 10km (6 miles) from el-Bireh and the Jalazone refugee camp in the east to Ein Qiniya in the west. It was originally constructed in the mid-1990s to connect the Beit El settlement, north of Ramallah, to Dolev, another settlement to the west of the city. Following the outbreak of the Second Intifada in 2000, the Israeli army barred both settlers and Palestinians from using the road for a period. The reopening of the road is part of a 1.075-billion-Israeli-shekel ($355m) settler infrastructure budget, aimed at connecting settlements in the occupied West Bank, illegal under international law. While there is no timeline for the reopening of Route 463, the far-right Israeli government is pushing for it to be implemented before Israeli elections on October 27 . The law will bypass the Knesset in an apparent attempt to speed up the process. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, a monitor affiliated with the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), warned that the plan falls under a “systematic policy to dismantle Palestinian geographic and demographic contiguity” in a governorate home to nearly 400,000 Palestinians across 80 communities. If reopened, tens of thousands of Palestinians would be forced to use an old alternative road near the Jalazone camp, north of Beit El, which is already heavily congested and would be unable to accommodate any increase in traffic. Jamal Juma, coordinator of the Popular Campaign to Resist the Wall and Settlements, a coalition of independent Palestinian civil society groups, said the reopening of the road will completely encircle the western side of Ramallah. The villages affected will include Surda, at-Tira, and Wadi at-Tira to the north of Ramallah, and Ein Qiniya, Ras Karkar, Deir Ibzi, and Ein Arik to the west. The impacted zone would extend southwest to Beitunia and the Fruits Roundabout, southwest of Ramallah, connecting to the town of Safa and Route 443, a main artery between Jerusalem and Israel. Road closures to the east have pushed the urban expansion of Ramallah, the administrative capital of Palestine, westwards over the past two decades, making one continuous urban block between the city and neighbouring areas such as Birzeit and Surda. Opening the road to settlers will impede this expansion, separating Ramallah from its surrounding villages. Turning a route used by the inhabitants of heavily populated West Bank villages into a “settler road” will likely be accompanied by more military checkpoints, watchtowers, and widespread land confiscations, Juma warned, all affecting Palestinians. There could also be more home demolitions and restricted access for farmers under the pretext of “settler security”. Settler roads are a major component of a network that connects settlements and outposts while separating Palestinian communities. As of March 2026, settler roads occupy more than 3 percent of the occupied West Bank’s area, with many more swaths of Palestinian land affected by their presence. The commission noted that out of 173 military and security orders issued between October 2023 and April 2026, 66 were dedicated to constructing settler roads. During the first half of 2026 alone, the Israeli occupation issued 40 military land seizure orders targeting 611 dunams – a dunam being 1,000 square metres – to build 16 security roads. The push to reopen the road follows a wave of pogroms across the occupied West Bank by settlers, in coordination with the Israeli military. On September 8, settlers closed a roundabout near Ein Ayoub in the Ras Karkar area, pelting Palestinian vehicles with stones. The attacks and the push for the reopening of the road coincide with a tightening of restrictions on Palestinian movement in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began. Munif Treish, the mayor of el-Bireh, told Al Jazeera that 95 percent of the road’s route falls within Area B, which according to the 1995 Oslo II Accords is under Palestinian civil administration and joint Israeli and Palestinian security control.

events.title: Russia’s arrest of Japanese journalist: Why are tensions rising?
events.summary: Japanese journalist Imai Yuki arrested on Sakhalin for allegedly spying on Russian defence capabilities, says the FSB. Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist from Sakhalin Island after accusing him of spying and gathering information on its defence capabilities. On Tuesday, Russian news agencies reported that the reporter, working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was arrested by the Federal Security Service (FSB) as he was preparing to leave the next day. list 1 of 3 ‘New tactic’: Russia expands deadly attacks on Ukraine’s transport system list 2 of 3 Poland says two Turks arrested over Russia-linked Starlink station fire list 3 of 3 Ukrainian ex-officer goes on trial in Germany over Nord Stream blasts According to the TASS news agency, the FSB said the journalist, Imai Yuki, was arrested in the Sakhalin region and taken to Moscow after being accused in a “criminal case”. The arrest of the Japanese citizen comes amid deteriorating relations between the two countries as Tokyo joined Western sanctions against Moscow due to the invasion of Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s August visit to Iturup Island, which is part of the Kuril Islands archipelago, drew sharp reactions from Japan. The two countries have a longstanding territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands dating back more than a century. Here’s what we know about the arrest: Who is the arrested journalist and what is he accused of? Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova, during a press briefing on Tuesday, said Yuki was accused of espionage. “Tokyo’s attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country’s security are regrettable. We cannot help but point out that today’s incident is not an isolated one,” Zakharova said. “Given the overall decline in bilateral cooperation caused by the Japanese authorities’ anti-Russian policies since the start of the Second World War, as well as Tokyo’s reluctance to listen to Moscow’s concerns regarding Japan’s remilitarisation policy, which affects our legitimate security interests in the Far East, we are forced to note that this development will further darken the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations.” Zakharova called on Tokyo to “come to its senses and change its approach, abandoning hostile steps towards Russia”. According to Russia’s Interfax news agency, Yuki will be remanded until December 12 before the trial begins. On Wednesday morning, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Tokyo had requested the “prompt provision of information” from Russian authorities over the arrest. “As well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” he added. Japanese media have also reported that the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs would summon the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a protest over the arrest, but no official confirmation has been released so far. The Hokkaido Shimbun, where Yuki worked, said it was still confirming details and added that it would “respond with the reporter’s safety as our top priority”. What’s the history of Russia-Japan tensions over Sakhalin Island? While Russia administers the Kuril Islands archipelago, Japan claims the four southernmost islands – Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets – calling them the Northern Territories. The Kuril chain of islands sits between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. The dispute began in 1855, after Russia and Japan established their first diplomatic and trade treaty, which also drew the Russo-Japanese border in the Kuril Islands, with Iturup under Japanese control and the islands to the north under Russian control. Russia took control of the Kuril Islands after the 1945 Yalta agreement, which was signed by United States President Franklin Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. Following Japan’s surrender in the final weeks of World War II, Moscow seized the entire archipelago and expelled about 17,000 Japanese citizens. In the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty, Japan renounced the Kurils but maintained that the four southernmost islands were part of its territory. However, Russia never signed the treaty. Because of the ongoing dispute, Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty to end World War II. What’s behind the recent rise in tensions? In August, Putin visited Iturup on his first-ever trip to the disputed islands. He was the second president to visit the islands after his predecessor, Dmitry Medvedev. But Putin’s visit caused uproar, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling it “absolutely unacceptable”. Takaichi told reporters at the time that Putin’s visit had “worsened Japanese sentiment towards Russia”, adding that the chain of islands was a “unique territory of [Japan] historically and under international law”.
