events.title: How Trump’s tariffs and Iran war are becoming liabilities in Michigan’s Senate race
events.summary: Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers is distancing himself from President Donald Trump on tariffs and the Iran war as economic concerns dominate the battleground race. Republican candidates are largely leaving Trump out of their general election ads after leaning heavily on him in the primaries, with just 4.3% mentioning him now, down from 47.1%, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The Michigan contest could help decide control of the Senate, making Rogers’ effort to hold Trump’s base while appealing to swing voters a key test for the GOP. Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers sat at a neighborhood bar, a bottle of Canadian Labatt Blue pilsner in hand, and delivered a message that would have been hard to imagine just weeks ago. "Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," Rogers says into the camera in an advertisement released Oct. 7. "We need to end this tariff war now." He never mentions the man who started it: President Donald Trump . It's a dramatic reversal for Rogers, who spent months defending Trump's tariffs , saying as recently as September that " Trump is right to put America first " by imposing duties. But in Michigan, where farms, factories and tourism rely on Canadian trade, Trump's trade fight and Ottawa's retaliation have become a political quagmire three weeks before an election that could decide Senate control. Rogers is locked in a dead heat with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed . The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates the contest a toss-up, with neither candidate emerging as a clear favorite. Polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne has El-Sayed with a four-percentage-point advantage over Rogers. And Rogers' omission of Trump – mirrored in an earlier ad calling for an end to the war in Iran – reflects broader GOP anxiety heading into November's election. Even as Trump urges voters to " pretend I'm on the ballot ," many battleground Republicans are barely talking about him in general election ads, with some using them to tacitly break with his signature policies. Fifty-seven of 1,324 Republican candidate ads in the general election period mention Trump – 4.3%, down from 47.1% during the primaries, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The analysis counts distinct ads, rather than how often they aired, and includes spots scheduled through the end of October. Democratic candidates are invoking Trump far more often. He appears in 20.9% of their general election ads, nearly five times the Republican rate. "Republicans needed to toe the Trump line to win the base in the primaries, but they need independence to survive November," said Ron Bonjean , a Republican strategist and partner at ROKK Solutions. Michigan conducts roughly $80 billion in annual trade with Ontario, according to the Michigan Chamber of Commerce. Canada is also Michigan's top export market, buying $23.2 billion in goods last year, roughly 39% of all state exports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. The relationship is especially important to automakers , whose parts routinely crisscross the border before final assembly. The Detroit Three – General Motors , Ford and Stellantis – reported roughly $6.5 billion in combined tariff-related costs in 2025, according to a CNBC analysis of company financial disclosures. "You can't slap a tariff on goods crossing that bridge without immediately inflating the cost of every vehicle rolling off a Michigan assembly line," said Richard Czuba , founder of the Glengariff Group, a Michigan polling firm. Trump escalated the trade fight with Canada again in August. After negotiations collapsed, the U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, hitting steel, aluminum and manufacturing inputs on top of existing duties on lumber and autos. Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs . The new duties landed as Michigan was already feeling the strain. The state reported Michigan's agricultural exports to Canada fell 12.3% in 2025, while Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's administration estimated tariffs were averaging Michigan households about $1,000 a year . "Republicans in tight races like Rogers are largely avoiding Trump's priorities — or breaking with him, especially on tariffs — because the cost of living is such a potent issue," said Erika Franklin Fowler, a Wesleyan University professor and co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project , which tracks political advertising. An early September WDIV/Detroit News poll by the Glengariff Group found 64.2% of likely Michigan voters opposed Trump's Canadian tariffs, with nearly 62% saying they hurt the state's economy. Against that backdrop, Rogers pivoted. After calling tariffs " necessary " in late August, he was on the air by October demanding an end to the fight " to lower your prices ." "Mike Rogers was a free-trade Republican until being a free-trade Republican put him at odds with Trump," Czuba told CNBC.

events.title: Aldar's international unit plans to deliver 9,000 homes in next five years
events.summary: London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties , plans to deliver about 9,000 homes in the next five years in the UK capital with a total development value of £5 billion ($6.6 billion), as demand remains resilient. The homes will be built across about 30 sites, with the company targeting buyers in the affordable segment as well as international investors. More than 3,600 homes will be for sale, 1,538 will be for build-to-rent and another 3,575 will be sold in the affordable segment, in which government support helps people to buy a home. London Square plans to start work on 12 sites this year with 65 per cent of those affordable, said chief executive Adam Lawrence. “There's always demand for affordable housing, it is a huge market and a huge need,” he told The National. There is also international demand from buyers in Turkey, Hong Kong and Middle East countries, he added. “Turkey is really strong at the moment. We've opened an office in Turkey, in Istanbul, recently, and we're seeing, within days of opening, we're into double-digit sales there. Hong Kong's been very quiet, but that looks like it's coming back.” The company, which was acquired by Aldar in 2023, has delivered 5,000 homes across 46 sites with a development value of £2.9 billion ($3.8 billion) since London Square was founded in 2010. “Under the Aldar banner, our sales have actually been better than they were historically and in the current market have been outperforming all of our peers,” said Scott Brown, chief financial officer of London Square. “Through our involvement with Aldar, we've not only been able to drive the capital but we've also been able to drive our sales.” London Square, which regenerates former industrial sites, is behind projects such as the Nine Elms development, which features more than 750 residential homes and 21,500 square feet of commercial and retail space. It is also transforming the former headquarters of Surrey County Council into a premium 292-home development, which includes the restoration of old structures. The company aims to complete 600 homes this year, up from 398 last year, with sales backlog to reach £1 billion by the end of 2026. “Most of this year will be on the affordable market rather than the build-to-sell market … about 30 per cent of what we're building is affordable,” Mr Brown told The National in London. He did not provide details on the total sales the company expects this year. London Square reported sales of £251 million for the first half of 2026, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf. Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity, says Naomi Minegishi, London Square international sales director. “International demand is being driven by investment opportunity, safe haven of their capital and a strong legal framework,” Ms Minegishi said. “Families also want to have a second home to spend time in summer, as well as to have a home to support their children as they enrol them in school or universities to study in London.” London's property market has been affected by geopolitical uncertainty that is pushing inflation higher. In the third quarter, the average home price in London grew modestly by 0.4 per cent annually to £529,720, as demand remained subdued amid higher borrowing costs, according to the Nationwide Building Society. However, fundamentals remain strong on higher investment activity, lifestyle vibrancy and a diverse population, said Sharief Ibrahim, executive director and head of residential agency at CBRE. “There is real cause for optimism. There are countless examples of schemes that are performing really well, many in the London Square portfolio in terms of the volume of apartments being sold and the value being achieved,” he said. “London is a resilient place. It's been through economic downturns, shocks to the economy and the system and the appeal of London has endured throughout that period. It's a global powerhouse and one of the, if not the most, successful city in terms of inward investment globally.” It projects home transaction volumes to be around 6,000 to 7,000 this year and 7,500 to 8,000 next year.

events.title: My wife and I have a 30-year age gap and run a dating site together. I've been divorced 3 times — there won't be a fourth.
events.summary: Brandon Wade and his wife, Dana. Courtesy of Seeking Brandon Wade met his wife on the site he founded, formerly known as Seeking Arrangements. A self-professed nerdy guy, he wanted a dating site that let him highlight his ability to provide. He was a multimillionaire when they met, but the couple doesn't have a pre-nuptial. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Brandon Wade, co-CEO of Seeking . It has been edited for length and clarity . When I met my wife, Dana, back in 2020, I wasn't in a good place. I had just celebrated my 50th birthday alone. I'd already been married and divorced three times , which was quite painful. I no longer believed in love. I was immediately attracted to Dana — with online dating , attraction is very important. The day after she messaged me, we talked on the phone for four hours. A few days later, I flew from my home in Vegas to Florida to meet her. We discovered that — despite our 30-year age gap — we have similar values and upbringings. Dana is hugely ambitious and wasn't afraid to ask me hard questions, like "What's your biggest fear?" Loneliness is my greatest fear. But when I met Dana, I realized it didn't need to be my fate. I felt left behind by dating sites When I was a younger man, I felt left behind by the dating industry . I was successful and nerdy — an MIT grad. I'd focused so much on academics and success that my social skills suffered. Picking up women wasn't something that came naturally to me. I wanted to design a dating site that let men like me flex what we really have to offer: our competency, capability, success, and ambition. I launched Seeking Arrangements in 2006. We were clear about our intention to match younger women with successful men. A lot of people thought this idea had a negative connotation. Most of the judgment was directed at the women. But women shouldn't be judged for wanting more from life, and from who they're dating. Wanting a generous, successful, ambitious partner isn't a moral or ethical failing. My parents have been married for nearly 60 years In 2019, my company rebranded as Seeking and banned transactional dating. To me, transactional dating means setting concrete parameters, such as "If you give me X, I'll do Y." All relationships are transactional in some ways, but there shouldn't be scorekeeping. As Seeking, the company still aims to connect successful, ambitious people. Most of the women on our site are ages 18-35, while the men are ages 30-60. An age gap as big as mine and Dana's is uncommon, though: the average age gap on our site is 12 years. Seeking allows men like me to highlight what makes them attractive: their wealth, lifestyle, and accomplishments. In a sense, we're more willing to explicitly say what's often unsaid in dating: women value success in their partners. My parents have been married for nearly 60 years. One of the things that attracted my mom to my dad back in Singapore was that he drove a car, not a motorbike. That showed her he could provide for the family she wanted to raise. My in-laws are about 3 years older than I am Today, Dana and I are co-CEOs of the company. She's Gen Z, I'm Gen X, which gives us a good multi-generational perspective . In a way, we're the biggest success story Seeking has had, and now we're co-pilots in helping other couples find their match. When Dana and I married in 2022, we didn't get a prenup . I was a multimillionaire; Dana came from a middle-class family. We both wanted to show our family and friends that we were fully in this. There would be no fourth divorce for me. Once Dana's parents saw how playful and natural we are together, I think any doubts they had about us disappeared. I call her parents Mom and Dad, even though they're only about three years older than I am. Dana and I don't have kids yet, but we want them. When our kids ask how we met, I'll tell them it was a match made in heaven, but that it came with a lot of effort. The dating industry didn't offer me a solution to find love, so I created one. I want my future children to know that if you're willing to work hard and solve the problems before you, you can always have what you want. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: WFH helped create the AI revolution. RTO could pose its biggest problem.
events.summary: Maskot/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . A baby boom, cleaner air, and AI. The work-from-home revolution might be over, but its impact is still being felt. Many of us have settled into some type of hybrid setup, balancing our days in the office with at least one spent at home. But even if you're in the cubicles every day — God bless — the WFH revolution has still affected you. Nick Bloom, a Stanford economist who's a leading expert on remote work, spoke to BI's Aki Ito about six ways the WFH era fundamentally changed things for us all . Some are a bit … personal. Remote work led to a 5% increase in fertility in the US and Northern Europe, according to Bloom's estimates. He summed it up with a line from a friend: "My wife and I discovered she can't get pregnant by email." Other effects were more widespread, such as a reduction in nitrogen dioxide in major cities thanks to the new hybrid world. But the biggest residual from the WFH era is what's dominating our current workplace convos: artificial intelligence. Bloom makes a strong case for why WFH crawled so AI could walk. Digital communications surged when we abandoned our offices, creating a treasure trove of data for models to learn on. The casual water-cooler conversation became a documented Slack thread that could be fed into an LLM. Now that most of us are in the office at least part of the time, that raises questions about how companies will source more training data. Having picked the internet to pieces, AI companies are getting desperate for training data . They've gone so far as to create virtual workplaces . Granted, people still Slack each other in the office. (I've fired off messages to colleagues sitting a few feet away. Sometimes you've got to see if you can actually make them "lol" IRL.) There's still a level of communication that goes undocumented, though. The quick coffee chat to brainstorm an idea. The impromptu deskside conversation. That's why executives were pushing us back to the office in the first place. For the organic collaboration and innovation that can only occur when rubbing elbows with colleagues. That RTO push could now pose real problems for AI's development. Companies could bug their own offices, making sure they pick up every little conversation, however benign, between workers. But that comes with plenty of legal and regulatory issues. And at a time when workers are already on edge about losing their jobs to AI, actively recording their every word to improve models won't do much to ease concerns. Still, with billions of dollars invested and the fate of the stock market depending on the tech realizing some big ROI, AI companies will have to figure something out. At least we've got some WFH babies joining the workforce in a few decades as reinforcements. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Diesel supplies to remain ‘tight’ into 2027: IEA
events.summary: The IEA predicted that refining capacity will recover and lead to a surplus on the diesel market in the first quarter of 2027. PARIS – Diesel supply disruptions in the Gulf stemming from the US war against Iran will keep the market tight into 2027, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Oct 14 , as it will take time to rebuild depleted stocks. “The gasoil market balance will remain tight well into 2027 and is dependent on a recovery of product supply from the Middle East,” the Paris-based agency said in its monthly energy markets report. Diesel prices have hit record highs across Europe and in the US in recent weeks, due to both reduced oil exports from the Gulf and damage to refineries in the region from retaliatory attacks by Iran. Governments have responded by reducing fuel taxes or providing subsidies, and by releasing strategic reserves that will need to be rebuilt. The IEA predicted that refining capacity will recover and lead to a surplus on the diesel market in the first quarter of 2027 , “lifting stocks broadly in line with normal seasonal patterns”. But that will not fully compensate for the deficit accumulated since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, which sent energy prices soaring around the globe. And if Gulf supplies do not return to normal levels soon, “further demand reductions and the heavy economic costs these will entail may be needed to balance markets”, the IEA warned. AFP

events.title: Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research
events.summary: Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research. The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released. Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”. Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face , a tech startup. Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London. The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips. “The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.” Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”. On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access. The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said. Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.

events.title: Caregivers are facing a "generosity paradox": Paying for loved ones but not wanting their kids to do so for them
events.summary: Barbara Marcanti, Carla Bacon, and Kathleen Korpela have all navigated caring for their aging loved ones. Barbara Marcanti/Carla Bacon/Danielle Barnum Photography Caregivers risk financial security to support older loved ones, creating a "generosity paradox." An Edward Jones report reveals caregivers spend $8,700 yearly, sacrificing savings for loved ones. Long-term care costs strain families, with many spending six figures on nursing facilities annually. Many caregivers for older loved ones are stuck in a painful dilemma: They're willing to put their financial security at stake to care for loved ones today, but that leaves them at risk of being a burden on their families later on as they age. This "generosity paradox" is at the heart of "The Financial Impact of Caregiving" report by Edward Jones, Age Wave, and The Harris Poll, which was shared exclusively with Business Insider. The report found 87% of caregivers providing financial assistance agreed that they didn't want to feel like a burden, while 81% said they were willing to put themselves in a less secure financial position to support their loved ones. These results are based on over 5,000 adults in the US and Canada who are financial caregivers of people aged 65 and over or aged 18 to 64 with disabilities. It's a contrast that, according to dozens of caregivers who have spoken with Business Insider, has weighed on them emotionally. Many told reporters that reducing their financial security puts them at greater risk of needing support as their health declines , making them feel like a burden. They hope their children won't need to support them to the same extent that they supported their parents. We are inviting readers to share their stories with Business Insider reporters to help us assemble a comprehensive look at long-term care costs. We want to know how much caring for an older loved one has cost you and your family. Please fill out this form to participate. The costs of caregiving have increasingly fallen on family and friends, both financially and personally. As the population ages, people are battling health conditions for longer, while support for long-term care has been more strained. Medicare doesn't support most long-term care costs, while Medicaid eligibility varies by state and is at risk in some pockets of the US. Long-term care costs have skyrocketed, and some families told Business Insider they're spending six figures annually on nursing facilities or home health aides. "An overwhelming number of people want to continue to do this for their loved ones, but they don't want their own family members, their own children, to go through the same thing that they're going through right now," said Vanessa Okwuraiwe, principal at Edward Jones. Barbara Marcanti's 102-year-old mom would've needed care costing about $20,000 monthly at a skilled nursing facility, but because she couldn't afford that, Marcanti moved her mom in with her in 2025. Marcanti said she has gladly provided for her mom, but said that her selflessness has affected her aspirations and family. "There's still a lot I want to do on my bucket list," Marcanti said. "I feel like I'm often passed over by my friends because 'Barb's got to deal with her mom.' I don't want my mom to be my date every time I go out." The "generosity paradox" can be seen in how caregivers view themselves. Edward Jones found that only 57% consider themselves "financial contributors" to their loved ones, even though 91% support their care using their own money. Meanwhile, 84% of caregivers are financial contributors, and they devote over $8,700 on average each year. It's led about 70% to sacrifice their savings by cutting back on or pausing their savings contributions. Many caregivers view their work as done out of love and fulfillment. The survey found that 85% said that caregiving gives them a sense of purpose, while 61% feel guilty that they can't give more of their time and energy to caregiving. More than half of caregivers support one of their parents, while 16% provide care for a grandparent, according to the report. Nearly half care for both an older loved one and children simultaneously. These sandwiched caregivers devote just over 100 hours a month supporting older care recipients. Spousal caregivers provide the most care hours a month at 189. Caring for a spouse can have its own challenges, balancing one's own health against one's partner's needs. A few years after her stroke, Carla Bacon, 69, became a caregiver for her 70-year-old husband after his own stroke. Between shifts at her full-time office job, she does everything for him as he builds up the strength to walk again. Hiring a CNA costs them $5,000 a month, and medical supplies run $500 monthly. They've paid out of pocket for a Hoyer lift, a mobility van, a therapy bike, and a special shower. "I operate on a hope and a prayer," said Bacon, who lives in Oklahoma. "I keep reminding myself that I'm 69. What's life going to look like over the next five years?" In many cases, adult children struggle to reverse roles with their parent. Kathleen Korpela wished her family had been more prepared when her father was diagnosed with Alzheimer's , including having conversations with her dad and understanding Social Security and all the other financial information she would end up "very quickly and very painfully" catching up on. "It was extremely challenging to navigate the transition from adult child to effectively parenting my parent," Korpela said. "It was definitely a challenge to navigate that dual role identity without losing myself." The report encourages people to plan ahead much earlier than they anticipate. Okwuraiwe said that families should have conversations early about preparing for when their loved ones will need part-time or full-time care, making everyone more confident. In one case, someone Okwuraiwe knows didn't have the right documents in place before their parent's Alzheimer's developed. "Now, they have statements from 10 different financial institutions, and the poor parent is going through Alzheimer's, and their short-term memory is gone," Okwuraiwe said. "They're not able to give guidance as to what they want done with this money." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s how | Richard Wilson and Clara Long
events.summary: AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s how A fight over a datacentre in Utah has been a testing ground for citizens’ assemblies, paving the way to oversight What’s your “(p)doom” – the percentage chance that rogue AI will create an existential catastrophe? Judging by their recent warnings, it is rising among tech bosses. On 25 September, OpenAI paused training of its latest frontier models as reports of AI agents going rogue mounted. A day later, Australia’s Senate asked the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic to appear before an inquiry after rogue OpenAI agents broke into US government websites and an Australian health portal. Both declined. Bill Gates, meanwhile, has warned that AI in the wrong hands could “cause a billion deaths”. “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said. Days before, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, the chief executives of Anthropic and OpenAI, appeared before the UN security council . Amodei warned that AI could become “a risk to humanity as a whole”. Altman said that “if AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone”. Doomsday scenarios aside, AI is already disrupting schools, workplaces and public services, with the most marginalised often feeling the impacts harder and faster. If democracy is to matter in this era of tech power, surely we must try to democratise AI. But how? Utah offers a glimpse. Proposals for a datacentre more than twice the size of Manhattan provoked a furious backlash over energy use and the potential impact on the state’s stressed water supplies and Great Salt Lake ecosystem, all while people felt excluded from having a say. On 18 and 19 September, Utah Common Ground convened 38 residents selected by civic lottery to consider what role the public should have in shaping decisions about AI technology and infrastructure. Despite their political differences, participants overwhelmingly agreed on the need for greater public control. Their 10 recommendations included public hearings and independent environmental assessments for hyperscale datacentres, community-led AI literacy programmes and tighter transparency rules. Every recommendation received at least 82% support. In a polarised state, that is a mandate legislators should struggle to wave away. Globally, there have been more than 80 public participation projects focused on AI over the past five years, involving more than 200,000 people in more than 95 countries. In Switzerland, a citizens’ assembly demanded privacy, transparency and meaningful human control. A Belgian citizens’ panel called for AI that serves everyone and leaves nobody behind. At present, however, this work is fragmented and largely ignored by decision-makers in government and the labs. The Citizens’ Track on AI , a decentralised network of assemblies rooted in communities but connected to the institutions where consequential decisions about AI are being made, intends to change that. The Bloom Project , which helped convene the Utah assembly, is building one part of that network: a series of US local and state assemblies intended to feed into a national citizens’ assembly on AI in 2028. At the global level, the ambition is to connect assemblies across countries into the UN’s emerging processes for AI governance, while also creating direct lines of accountability to the AI companies. A bridge built by the powerful can be withdrawn by them. That is why Utah matters. Its forum was rooted in civic groups that will outlast the forum itself, though it has no guaranteed hearing yet. Durable civic power needs both: communities that keep convening and decision-makers who have to answer them. The same principle underpins proposals published last week for a standing global citizens’ assembly on AI : combining the independent moral authority of globally representative, self-governing citizens with legislated powers to hold AI companies accountable for their safety and alignment practices. None of this is easy. Yet deliberation need not be slow: Taiwan went from citizens’ panel to law in months in an effort to address scam advertising. It is also hard to buy: lobbyists can buy policy influence, not the outcome of a citizens’ assembly. Can any of this protect us against AI being used to launch a cyber-attack, develop a biological weapon or escape human control altogether? Not by itself. But how much risk society should accept isn’t an engineering question – it’s a political one. Citizens’ assemblies can give governments the mandate, and the cover, to impose the testing, red lines and stop buttons that companies won’t impose on themselves. The danger is not only that AI may escape human control. It is whether the humans controlling it are a tiny group of elite executives, investors and politicians vulnerable to corporate capture. Altman was right: decisions of this magnitude cannot remain inside laboratories in San Francisco.

events.title: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | Anonymous
events.summary: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system. In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere. Our sector is carrying more risk than we realise. The warming global climate has caused more frequent high-intensity storms, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires and drought. While the immediate impact of these events is plain to see, the long-term effects will be compounded as insurers withdraw from affected areas, leaving the economy in freefall and people’s day-to-day lives in ruins. As a modeller, it is my job to look objectively and scientifically at the data to calculate an expected loss from a natural disaster, which affects the price of the premium for a given policy. Our industry says it holds those numbers as sacrosanct, but as my analysis shows higher and more volatile risk, the price rises with it and we lose customers. So modellers like me are coming under pressure to reduce their projected losses. In the most basic terms, we are collectively fudging the numbers and taking on more risk than we should for a lower price than the expected loss demands. Sometimes I will forecast losses that would normally be seen as much too risky for us to insure, but we offer the policies anyway. This will eventually lead to a sector built on “competitively priced” contracts that underestimate risk, leaving gaping holes in the safety net that insurance is supposed to provide. For example, if subsidence – which is made worse by drought – damages a number of homes in your area, insurers may exclude this from your policy, so you won’t be covered if subsidence then hits your house. When that happens to an entire community, businesses leave, investment dries up and the local economy tanks. Now imagine this happening in multiple towns around the country, at the same time. And subsidence is just one such issue, alongside wildfires, coastal erosion, wind and floods – and that’s just in the UK. I have respect for underwriters who are just doing their jobs, and I know that no single individual is responsible. My concern lies with the attitude of much of the industry towards modellers, actuaries and researchers: there is a sense that we are an inconvenience to the deal-making process, rather than an essential part of risk management. We are the failsafe that stops our industry from reckless gambling. At the largest scale, misquoted insurance can damage insurers, companies, their employees and the communities that rely on them. The upshot is that our customers are likely to be much more exposed to climate-related risks than they realise. People are not budgeting for a major increase in their insurance premiums or planning for their homes becoming uninsurable, but many of them absolutely should be. If the worst happens, the insurance industry may not have the money to pay every claim when a major disaster hits. That would have profound consequences for the economy as a whole – businesses could go bankrupt, the housing market could seize up and, if people couldn’t pay their mortgages, banks would fail. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more As natural catastrophes continue to become less predictable and more severe, the foundations of our entire economy will only become more fragile. Our customers deserve to know. The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of their Secret Source series , a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

events.title: You bailed on TV. But politicians are still spending all their money there.
events.summary: Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Sebastián Vivallo Oñate/Agencia Makro/Getty Images; Gary Miller/Getty Images; Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images; BI Audiences have been leaving TV for the internet for a very long time. Most advertisers have figured that out some time ago. But not political advertisers: They still spend the majority of their money on TV. Political consultant Rob Flaherty explains why. If you ask pundits, 2024 was the Podcast Election (which also means it was the YouTube Election ). And maybe 2026 is the Influencer Election . One thing the chattering class won't call it is the Television Election — because everyone knows everyone has stopped watching TV. Except that's not how political campaigns are run, at all. Even in 2026, more than 60% of the estimated $11.6 billion spent in this election cycle will go to good ol' fashioned broadcast and cable TV. Another 20% will be spent on streaming TV. If you think that doesn't leave a lot of room for things where you and most people you know spend a ton of time — YouTube, Reels, TikTok, etc. — you're right. Political pros know it, too. So why isn't that changing? I asked Rob Flaherty , who has spent most of his life doing digital politics for Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and, most recently, Kamala Harris . Flaherty offered up a bunch of reasons why TV remains so dominant in political spending, even as it gets less relevant to voters. But a base reason is simply that political operatives spent money on TV because other political operatives spend money there: Flaherty even admits that in his current work — co-running an anti-AI super PAC — he has been buying some TV time just so other people in politics will take him seriously. You can hear our entire conversation about how campaigns work in the TikTok era — and how they ought to work — on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt of our chat. Peter Kafka: You said that when you were working on the Harris campaign, you spent roughly 50-50 between TV and digital — but that most campaigns still spend 70% of their budget on TV. Make the best case for why a campaign should still spend half or more of its money on TV. Rob Flaherty: Well, I would not advocate for that. But I think the steelman case that you would hear is: Digital political ad inventory is actually quite limited. There are only so many places you can spend. Social media is not a mind-changing surface; it's a base-building surface. Meanwhile, television is concentrating on a smaller number of higher-view surfaces. So you actually want to spend more money on TV because it's more expensive to buy against an NFL game than it was just to buy across from the local news and in prime time. That sounds a lot like the TV industry's own argument for years: "Yes, ratings are down, but that means the shows people are still watching are more valuable." Look, this is an industry that has a nobody-ever-got-fired-for-hiring-McKinsey problem. If you do the same thing everyone else does and you lose, then you did everything right. And if you try something different and you lose, it's you who made bad decisions. I'll even say candidly: I run Tomorrow Together , a new super PAC where we just launched a bunch of ads. We're advertising against people who don't want AI regulations . And even I — Mr. F—ing Digital — felt this pull, like I needed to have pretty significant TV spending. Because otherwise the industry won't view it as legit, because TV is legit. We still spent mostly on digital, largely because it's a super PAC and we're spending late. But I prioritized making sure we had some TV in there, because otherwise people don't think it's real. And also, the way a lot of this works is: The general consultants who are the top consultants to the candidate, very often are economically tied to the margins of TV. Spell that out. You're running a campaign. Why do you have an economic incentive to buy TV? Because you get a cut of the buy. The more TV a campaign buys, the more money you make. Basically. Usually, the general consultant hires up all the other consultants. Those consultants get a cut, either a fee or a cut of media spend. TV margins are great. They are really, really great. They are better than digital margins. For the consultant, you're making 10%, 15% on a TV buy. And by "margins," you mean the money the person buying the ads gets from the campaign? Yeah. You make more money because there's just less staff time. The other thing that's crazy is a lot of the big TV firms don't actually do the buying. They subcontract to one of three or four buying shops. So everybody's just making money all over the place. There's a rent-seeking thing: The most senior consultants who have been around for a while came up in TV. They talk to the candidates. They push them to spend more on TV. And then you have campaign managers who are typically relatively more junior, particularly on Senate races, who don't want to mess up. They don't want to do something different and radical, and they have to convince the candidate and the general consultant anyway. So you end up in this place where the easiest thing to do is just sort of the same thing. The broader media business had the same problem: Advertisers took a long time to follow consumers to digital. They were still spending on TV when people were leaving in droves. Does politics eventually catch up? If you talk to any politician, they would tell you digital is very important. It's the internet. And then you look at their media mix, and it's not that. I do think presidential primaries are what drive innovation in politics. I do think you're going to see some people try a bunch of new stuff, and then that will lead to a more cogent theory of how you spend more of your campaign dollars on the places where people actually are. I'm hopeful that change is coming. But so much of the way that media gets spent is profit-seeking and rent-seeking that you do have to break through that. It has the entrenched layer of political power on top of it, and that is one of the reasons. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: South Texas Latino voters who flipped for Trump in 2024 are up for grabs in 2026
events.summary: Some Hispanic and Latino voters who were a boon for Republicans and President Donald Trump in 2024 now appear to be moving back toward Democrats ahead of the 2026 midterm election. Republicans are hoping to hold on to narrow majorities in the U.S. House and Senate despite Trump's unpopularity and widespread economic anxiety. In South Texas, three House races in majority-Hispanic border districts could decide control of Congress. TEXAS — Tano Tijerina had a confession to make. "I want to tell you something I never thought I'd have to say from a stage like this," Tijerina, a former minor league baseball player and a Texas GOP congressional candidate, said during a speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. The line was hardly a bombshell. Tijerina had been elected three times for Webb County judge — in 2014, 2018 and 2022 — on the Democratic ticket. And he's made his 2024 defection a key part of his campaign in the majority-Latino, South Texas border district in which he's running. But Tijerina's admission elicited shouts of "No!" and boos. Just to be sure, he quickly made clear he had kicked his old Democratic habits. "I'm a beef-eating, truck-driving, gun-slinging, … Bible-thumping, Jesus-loving, calloused-hand cowboy that's going to fight like hell for South Texas," Tijerina — looking like a Texas brawler in a beige cowboy hat and a tight blue suit that hugged his biceps — thundered over a hearty round of applause. Tijerina is part of a coalition of Hispanic and Latino voters who have long leaned Democratic but have more recently shown a willingness to vote for both parties. The group could be critical in deciding control of Congress this November. Hispanic and Latino voters nationwide moved rightward in 2024 in surprisingly large numbers and helped deliver a second presidential term to Donald Trump . In the congressional district in which Tijerina is running, Texas' 28th, voters opted for Trump by 7 percentage points , after backing President Joe Biden four years earlier. However, they stuck with their Democratic congressman, Rep. Henry Cuellar , whom Tijerina hopes to pick off in November, reelecting Cuellar to an 11th term. Riding high after their 2024 romp, in which Republicans won control of the White House and both chambers of Congress, there was optimism in the GOP that the rightward turn among Hispanic voters could reflect a permanent realignment . In the past two years in Texas and Florida — states with large Hispanic populations— Republicans redrew congressional maps , banking on their continued support. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' But amid anxiety over high consumer prices , Trump's persistently low approval ratings and sentiment that immigration policies have overreached — even in South Texas, where support for a secure border is strong — enthusiasm for the GOP appears to be waning with less than a month to go before the 2026 midterm election . The districts in play there are among a small number across the U.S. that could help decide control of the next Congress. And a recent survey conducted for the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter found Democratic statewide candidates in Texas were leading their Republican opponents by a 2-to-1 margin among likely Hispanic voters. And an NBC News/Telemundo poll of Latino voters across the U.S., released Oct. 4, found 27% of those surveyed approved of Trump and 59% said they'd prefer Democrats control Congress. Trump, at a White House Hispanic Heritage Month event in September that was meant to shore up support from the demographic, invited attendees to tour the construction site for his new ballroom, while largely glossing over election issues such as immigration and the economy. "Latino voters are pissed," Chuck Rocha, a Democratic political strategist who is consulting for campaigns in Texas, including for state Rep. James Talarico in his run for U.S. Senate, told CNBC. "Right now, we benefit from them being pissed at Donald Trump." This could spell trouble for candidates such as Tijerina, whose district is listed as "lean D" by the Cook Report . It's also a challenge in other majority-Latino border districts for Republicans such as Rep. Monica De La Cruz and Eric Flores. Flores is an Army National Guard veteran and former assistant U.S. attorney who is hoping to oust Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in the 34th District. De La Cruz is attempting to stave off a potent challenge in the neighboring 15th District from Tejano music star Bobby Pulido , who is barnstorming the district one quinceañera at a time . The Flores-Gonzalez and De La Cruz-Pulido races are both "toss ups," according to the Cook Report.

events.title: Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? | Arwa Mahdawi
events.summary: Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? Airports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozing G reat news for everyone who is soon to fly via a US airport: the Trump administration has just elevated the travel experience. You still risk getting arrested by immigration agents and thrown into a detention centre, but never mind that! Instead, luxuriate in the fact that none of the poorly paid Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff with whom you interact will be sitting down. The government recently got rid of all the chairs at travel document checking stations, arguing that “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism” and strengthens “our security posture and … commitment to hospitality”. Funnily enough, border patrol and customs officers have not adopted the same policy. Perhaps because their job tends to involve being as inhospitable as possible. TSA agents aren’t the only US workers getting sore calf muscles during their shifts. Unlike their European and British counterparts, cashiers at US supermarkets have traditionally been forced to stand while working . The US’s upright obsession seems to be down to a Protestant work ethic and a lack of labour laws . Sitting apparently conveys laziness to the discerning American consumer. Over the years there have been numerous right-to-sit lawsuits pushing back on mandatory standing but, while things are shifting slightly, seated supermarket cashiers are still unusual. One exception is Aldi, which has been expanding aggressively in the US. Cashiers get chairs at Aldi because (surprise) it’s more efficient when your workers’ feet aren’t aching all the time. While seated cashiers and TSA agents may be looked down on by the US establishment, it’s a different story for high-flyers. Rather than “maintaining a standing posture” to “reinforce professionalism”, the US president often looks as if he is snoozing at his desk. Which, to be fair, is probably because he regularly stays up all night posting extremely important memes on the internet. Having their chairs seized isn’t the only indignity that TSA agents have faced recently: along with other federal employees, they had to work without pay for several weeks during government shutdowns in Trump’s second term. Members of Congress on the other hand? They could continue to collect their generous salaries during the shutdown unless they explicitly chose not to . Americans should not take this injustice sitting down. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: New Mexico and El Paso Spent Millions on Climate Plans. Three New Data Centers Could Undo Them.
events.summary: Meta is building a massive data center on the northeast edge of El Paso, Texas, on the New Mexico border. Paul Ratje for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.  Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.  Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.  A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso. The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters. The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months , as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune .  But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year. They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside.  “The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said. Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately. “We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.” The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.  Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not. A truck sprays water for dust suppression at the construction site of Project Jupiter in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.  Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said. “This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?” Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.  State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break , which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.  New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.  The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019 . (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)  “This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University. “This is a huge source.” Homes in Chaparral, New Mexico, sit adjacent to Meta’s data center, just over the state border in El Paso, Texas. events.title: 'It's definitely tight trying to budget on maternity leave'
events.summary: Sara Ody was among the first customers at a new community food pantry in Sheffield Almost 50,000 households in Sheffield are struggling to make ends meet and cannot pay their bills, according to a new cost of living report by the council. Described as having a "negative budget", these people are unable to afford the necessary costs even after all benefit entitlements have been claimed and their outgoings have been reduced to the bare essentials. In the same week the report was published, a new food pantry opened in the Woodseats area of the city, offering low priced food for anyone struggling with the cost of living. Within the first hour 14 people called in, with 37-year-old Sara Ody among those through the door. "There's always a thought process, 'can we afford this? do we have to sacrifice this to be able to afford food, childcare and clothes?' It's definitely tough," she said. The Community Grocery pantry, run in partnership by The Message Trust and Ikon Church at Woodseats, offers membership for £1 per year, with food and household staples from just 50p. Sara said her finances were especially tight now she is on maternity leave from work. "There's four of us now, and I've got to the point in my maternity leave where there is not really any money coming in, so it's definitely tight trying to budget, especially in the run up to Christmas," she said. "It's frustrating because I saved up so much money while I was working to be able to still have opportunities and do things while on maternity leave, but you have to budget all the time. "We're finding food is so expensive and every week it seems the prices are going up and up so things like this are amazing. We can get definitely some staple bits to see us through winter." According to the report to Sheffield City Council , external , Citizens Advice estimates 47,500 people in Sheffield have negative budgets. It says that poverty in the city predates the cost-of-living crisis and reflects longer-term inequalities in income, employment, health, housing and opportunity. However, it says years of financial pressure have also left some households with depleted savings, debt and arrears, reducing their ability to absorb further shocks It adds that children are particularly affected, with approximately one in three children in Sheffield living in poverty, "substantially above" the national rate. John Lawson is from The Message Trust John Lawson is the regional lead for The Message Trust, which has 35 stores nationwide, and is based in Sheffield. He says community grocery stores can bridge the gap between food banks and supermarkets, as they offer a variety of food but at a fraction of the cost. "We opened here after seeing the need on the doorstep and the challenges that people are facing with the cost of living," he said. "Even a lot of the community who wouldn't necessarily have been struggling five years ago are now finding themselves living paycheck to paycheck." The store is open to everyone and there is no means testing. Lawson added: "We want to make it accessible for everyone, so if someone is passionate about saving food from landfill, they should shop here. If someone's in crisis and needs free food, they can come here. "Or if someone just wants to be in the community, in an amazing space like we've got here, they can come and hang out. "We want to create an opportunity and a resource where anyone can come and access healthy food and wraparound care so we can holistically look after the whole person with mental health support, debt advice, cookery courses or just simply offering a social space for people to come together." Another customer Debbie Schofield, 44, said she thought the pantry would help people realise they are not alone. "I think Woodseats needs this community hub where people can get some cheaper resources and have a chat somewhere warm," she said. "I like the concept of the community pantry. I think everybody's struggling with the cost of living, everything has gone up quite considerably, but I also feel like social media isolates us in our own homes. "I don't feel there's a sense of community like when I was growing up, like in the 1980s and 90s. It's really important for these pantries to exist because they bring neighbours together and then people in the wider community start to recognise each other.

events.title: I'm a CEO and a mom. I built AI agents to help run my household — and save hours every week.
events.summary: CEO Carrol Chang built AI agents to help run her family life and said they save her hours every week. Courtesy of Andela Carrol Chang, CEO of Andela, uses AI to manage her family's hectic schedules in New York City. An AI agent creates her kids' sports calendars and accounts for commuting times. Chang used to spend about five to eight hours a week on parenting admin. Now it's about two. Carrol Chang is the CEO of Andela, which helps companies implement AI by connecting them with technical talent. The wife and mother of three, who lives in New York City, built AI agents using several models to help coordinate her family's schedules and manage school emails. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. That first year of my second child's life was joyous in so many ways, but it was also the hardest of my life. It almost broke me, and I have a wonderful husband. I was privileged to be in a stable, senior job at a supportive workplace, and it didn't matter because the weight of the calendar management , the sick pickups, being the person that the school or the day care would call, trying to organize holiday gifts for the family, and booking family travel was crushing to me. A lot of this mental load has been lifted , so I'm grateful. I now have three kids and agents for their sports and school, and for meal planning. With their sports, the games are always on different days and in different boroughs. In the past, I would have had to look them up on Google Maps and map out the commute. Is it subway? Is it bus? Is it walking? Is it taking an Uber ? I'd put that commute time on the calendar with enough of a buffer to get there before the game. Then I'd do the same thing on the way home. If there's a conflict with the kids' schedules, you have to reconcile which parent is going to go to which game. Now the agent does it for me, and it saves me so much time. The agent set up everything I'm not an engineer, so I said to AI, "Talk to me like I'm a seventh grader and teach me step-by-step what I should do in order to accomplish this task." Then I had two open browsers, and I followed the instructions. Then, it magically runs. The agent set up everything and sent me around 60 calendar invites for my kids' soccer games and back, and it was all expertly done. One says, "Uber to game, 23 minutes." I think a lot of parents are finding the time in late nights and early mornings to do this kind of admin stuff, and that's not really what we want to do. What we want is to spend time with our families. I remember calculating this, and it was about five to eight hours a week of mental labor . It was calendar management, meal planning, paying our nanny, messaging people to confirm what time to arrive for what, and ordering and unpacking groceries. Now, I probably spend two hours a week doing this stuff and checking on the agents. If you go into this thinking that AI is not going to make a mistake , you will get so frustrated that you'll give up too early. People also make mistakes, so you just have to have a system of checking the AI. It helps me stay on top of emails I also created a school agent. I instructed the agent to read the school emails, pick out information, and add calendar events as needed. First and foremost, I need it to flag school closures and add them to the calendar. I've instructed the agent to only care about events that apply to my kids. My kids go to a bilingual school, with a Spanish track and a Mandarin track. My kids are in the Spanish track, which means I want the agent to ignore the Mandarin events. The agent will look at whether an email was sent to the listserv or whether it's from an individual. If it's an individual, it has to come through to me because the teacher is emailing my husband and me directly, so we should obviously pay attention. An agent plans our dinners My husband has also taken on a lot, and we now use an agent for meal planning. There are food allergies we have to take into account. I have a note in my phone with 15 dishes that would rotate every three weeks because we found our thing, and I didn't want to spend any more time thinking about this, so we're just going to do kale sausage pasta and eggplant moussaka. Now, we don't have to do that because AI suggests new menus that meet everyone's requirements. Then it gives us instructions on what to shop for. These shopping apps have integrated AI, which makes it even easier. With the extra time I have , I sleep more, and I get higher-quality sleep. I am less stressed and more pleasant to be around. The time I spend with my kids and family each day is more enjoyable for everyone. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How a radio glitch triggered a false hijack alert in Germany
events.summary: Authorities scrambled fighter jets to escort a plane on its way from Corfu to Nuremberg after a pilot sent a hijack alert. German authorities briefly closed an airport and scrambled fighter jets to escort a passenger plane on Tuesday following an emergency alert indicating a hijacking was taking place on board. However, the alert had been accidentally triggered by a radio “malfunction”. Corendon Airlines said its Boeing 737-800, which was en route from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to Nuremberg, Germany, sent out an emergency code while it was flying over Croatia “due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system”. In a statement, the airline said that “no emergency situation occurred”, and the 178 passengers, flight crew and aircraft had not been in danger at any point. The plane landed safely in Nuremberg. German police said Corendon Airlines flight XR456 “inadvertently” sent out an emergency “squawk” alert with the code 7500 while flying over Croatia on Tuesday. A squawk is a four-digit code a pilot sends via the jet’s transponder to air traffic control. The code 7500 tells air traffic controllers that a hijacking is in progress. However, air traffic controllers were unable to make contact with the pilots or crew, causing the alarm to be raised further. It is unclear why this happened. “The aircraft could no longer be reached by radio to clarify the situation”, prompting warnings to be activated in several European countries, police said. A Rafale fighter jet was scrambled from Croatia to intercept the Boeing passenger jet, while the German military also dispatched warplanes. Police cordoned off the Albrecht Dürer airport in Nuremberg as a precaution until they knew the reason the pilot had sent the hijack alert. Police spokesman Michael Petzold explained that authorities had “received a code directly from the cockpit that suggested a hijacking”. “Since we were then unable to reach the cockpit, and the tower was also unable to contact the cockpit, we had to assume the worst – that it might indeed be a hijacking,” Petzold said. The incident disrupted flights, with six flights delayed and two inbound flights diverted to other airports as a precaution, a Nuremberg airport spokesperson said. Why are aviation authorities so concerned? The hijack scare has come amid heightened concerns about aviation security after the copilot on board a Flydubai jet bound for Israel from Dubai attacked the captain with an emergency crash axe, forcing the flight to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on September 30. On Friday, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said the copilot was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv and called the incident a “terrorist attack”. Also, before the false hijack alert in the early hours of Tuesday, flights had been briefly disrupted at Nuremberg ‌airport after pilots reported suspected drone sightings. Authorities across Europe have already stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks after a series of mostly mysterious drone incidents and concerns about Russian hybrid warfare. Western nations, including Germany, have accused Moscow of launching a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disruption to undermine European support for Ukraine and destabilise the continent. Several German airports have had to suspend operations for brief periods in recent months due to drone activity, with suspicion often falling on Russia. Last month, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August using a drone laden with explosives. Berlin closed the Russian consulate among other measures. Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin “fabricated” the evidence. However, in light of the concerns, NATO’s top general told the Warsaw Security Forum earlier this week that the alliance has a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on its members, embedding lessons learned from the Ukrainian front lines. How common are radio glitches and false hijack alerts? Radio glitches are common, but incidents rarely escalate to major security events because pilots use back-up radios to communicate with air traffic controllers when they lose communication signals. In 2019, a pilot flying an Air Europa jet from Amsterdam to Madrid accidentally transmitted hijack alert 7500. For half an hour, aviation authorities thought the alarm was a genuine emergency and followed safety protocols, which disrupted flights and led to the evacuation of part of Schipol airport in the Netherlands. In 2011, a flight from Chicago to Germany was diverted to Toronto when a pilot spilled coffee and accidentally set off a hijack alarm. The spill caused distress signals to go out, including the 7500 transponder code.

events.title: No forms, no fuss: Abu Dhabi wants AI to eliminate government paperwork
events.summary: Abu Dhabi wants to become the world’s first “AI-native” government, harnessing artificial intelligence to personalize services and manage straightforward tasks. Backing the ambition is a 13 billion dirham ($3.5 billion) investment to transform the emirate’s digital services by 2027. Western governments, often tech-phobic, will be watching. Speaking at the Ai Everything conference in Abu Dhabi last week, Ruba Al Hassan, director general of strategic affairs and future foresight at Abu Dhabi’s Department of Government Enablement, described a government gearing up to handle more of the paperwork it usually expects residents to do.  In October 2025, the government launched AutoGov through its TAMM app—a unified digital platform that centralizes over 1,000 smart government services for citizens, residents, businesses, and visitors in Abu Dhabi.  AutoGov takes care of regular tasks like renewing licenses, paying bills, and booking routine health appointments. The goal is to spare residents the inconvenience of repeatedly visiting government offices, particularly when little has changed in their circumstances. Al Hassan wants the government to handle car registrations so seamlessly that you forget it needs to be renewed. Instead, residents can authorise the TAMM services app to handle the task. “I enter my preferences, give my consent, and then I forget about it,” she explained. “I don’t ever have to think about my car registration ever again. It just happens.” The initiative relies on residents being comfortable with the government acting for them. When asked about potential trust issues, Al Hassan pointed to the government’s history of completing projects and handling emergencies, like the pandemic. “That comes from when we say something, we do it. We get it done,” she said. “It comes because we’ve proven time and time again that we can deliver on our promises”.  In Edelman’s 2026 Trust Barometer, 86% of people in the UAE said they trust the government to “do the right thing”, compared with 53% in 28 other countries surveyed. It helps that the emirate’s services are centralised. For example, licensed health facilities must join Malaffi, Abu Dhabi’s health information exchange, unless exempt (failure to join can prevent license renewal). By August 2025, the exchange reported 3.5 billion clinical records from over 3,000 facilities. The use of AI predictive technology highlights risks like diabetes, heart failure, and kidney disease. Al Hassan describes a doctor’s appointment where the doctor can review the patient’s history and risk information before deciding on treatment. “So the doctor doesn’t waste time on paperwork and looking for information, and can just focus on spending time with you,” she said.  However, diagnosis and treatment are still the doctor’s job, “because the doctor can add context.” Diagnosing  problems early could prevent expensive complications, but only time and use of the system  will reveal how much money or how many hospital visits it has saved. Al Hassan says using AutoGov is optional. Abu Dhabi’s rules allow medical data to be shared through Malaffi without written patient consent, but it’s unclear what permission is needed for subsequent use by AI. Patients can ask the provider who collected their records to limit sharing, but it’s not clear if they can refuse AI analysis while still allowing their records to be used for treatment. Getting different departments to work together can be another challenge. Al Hassan said the common question that government delegations visiting from Europe or South Asia often ask is: “How did you get everyone to come together and cooperate?” By contrast, she references her own experience, in which meetings with eight government groups are held, during which the shared goal is agreed upon before talks even start. “There is no more fighting. There is a discussion,” she said. Years of integrating  services, supported by money and the authority  to require involvement, help explain Abu Dhabi’s progress. Sometimes the problem is more simple . Al Hassan remembers showing a group of visitors TAMM’s feature for taking pictures and reporting potholes. One of the visitors, she said, quickly saw a problem: “We can’t do this. There are too many potholes. The city will be overwhelmed.” An app can make it easier to report a problem without giving the city the ability to fix it. Looking ahead, Abu Dhabi will need to assess whether the investment leads to both time and cost savings. Britain’s 2025 Copilot trial, with 20,000 civil servants, showed workers saved about 26 minutes a day. Turning those minutes into cost savings depends on how staff use the extra time, after paying for software, training, and reviewing its results. Earlier this month, the emirate launched AiNative, a program with OpenAI, Microsoft and Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, to train 20,000 government workers in practical and responsible AI use by the end of the year. Al Hassan says workers’ skills must keep up with technology; just calling the government “AI-native” won’t be enough. “It’s not the final goal. It will keep changing.” For residents, her long-term goal is easier to imagine. When a passport is about to expire, the government already knows the owner will need a new one. Al Hassan wants renewal to happen automatically without needing to apply. “Why would I even have to request it?” she asks. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Political fallout from Trump’s Russian diesel deal overshadows price impact
events.summary: President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s deal to deliver Russian diesel to global markets may be sending shockwaves through the GOP — but don’t expect it to do the same to prices. Already, multiple House Republicans ; key GOP candidates ; and two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the move. The planned imports will “have very little unnoticeable impact on domestic US diesel prices, even if it happens — and I think that’s a big if,” given legal complications and Russian constraints, Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations, told Semafor. He said that the amount of diesel Russia has pledged to release for the month of November represents only “one day of US diesel demand.” He pointed to heating oil futures, observing that “traders appear to be pricing in very little near-term impact.” The White House pushed back: One official insisted to Semafor that “massive amounts of supply will lower costs for American farmers, truckers and workers.” “They’re not releasing that [diesel] to us, they’re releasing it to the entire world,” Trump told reporters Tuesday. “Because the world market suffered with high prices — and when you knock out diesel refineries, that’s not a great thing.” — Eleanor Mueller
