events.title: A growing security premium threatens Saudi Arabia’s investment project
events.summary: Welcome to this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief. We’ll be covering:   Saudi special report: we assess the outlook for the kingdom’s economy   Abu Dhabi teams up with OpenAI and Microsoft to train government employees   SoftBank in talks for $100 billion Gulf investment for new AI fund  And, the three things we enjoyed reading   The attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company Aramco on Tuesday evening as part of a suspected Houthi missile strike marks the latest blow to the kingdom’s image as a safe and viable place to do business.   While there was no official comment from Aramco, the kingdom’s energy ministry confirmed the strike had caused a limited fire but no injuries or fatalities , though it was unclear whether the building in the eastern city of Dhahran had been hit directly by a missile or by falling debris. Authorities also reported drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed near the capital, Riyadh, and the country’s southern region.   On Wednesday, the Houthis ​vowed to press on with attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities. As the kingdom’s conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis intensifies, questions are mounting over whether its much-vaunted Vision 2030 is increasingly out of reach.  For a country whose future hinges on diversifying away from oil and attracting foreign investment to help it do so, the spillover effects of the conflict pose a significant setback to its ambitions.  “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the World Petroleum Energy Congress in Riyadh on Monday. “Our response must be equally serious while remaining focused on the decades ahead; Vision 2030 must continue, investment must continue.”  Exactly what a “serious response” entails remains unclear, but what is immediately apparent is that investor sentiment has already been rattled.   The CEOs of Shell, TotalEnergies, BP, and ExxonMobil had all been due to attend this week’s WPEC but are conspicuous by their absence.   I was due to travel to Jeddah this week for interviews and an event, but, like many others, plans were canceled given the security situation.  According to the Wall Street Journal , the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has been moved between heavily guarded palaces fitted with bunkers by a handpicked security team.   During the course of the last week, many of the kingdom’s most strategic assets have become high-profile targets. Most notably, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh suffered four attacks in the space of five days. The Saturday attack marked the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade, killing 13 people and injuring 309.   James Reeve, a Saudi macro consultant who formerly worked as a senior director for the kingdom’s Public Investment Fund, told me that foreign investments already made in Saudi are unlikely to be reversed in the near term. “I think more troubling for the Vision 2030 story is the impact on new FDI (foreign direct investment) inflows,” said Reeve.   “For foreign firms weighing up significant capital investments in the kingdom, the images of missiles falling apparently unhindered on the capital’s airport will be shocking and difficult to forget. Those contemplating investments in tourist infrastructure will also have to weigh the impact on tourism inflows.”  On Monday, Saudi authorities extended the airport’s closure until Saturday , and regional carriers have temporarily suspended flights.   Meanwhile, Air France-KLM has suspended flights to Riyadh until 31 October and Delta Air Lines has delayed planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on October 23, until March 2027.  “In the short term, this is clearly damaging,” Andreas Krieg, a Middle East security analyst at King’s College London, told me.   “The important effect is not simply physical damage to an airport or the cancellation of individual flights. It is the return of a security premium to doing business in Saudi Arabia. The immediate consequences are likely to be delayed investment decisions, higher required returns, and greater dependence on state capital.”   As one of the principal gateways into the Saudi capital and a foundation stone of the entire Vision 2030 project, the Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s airport directly threaten the kingdom’s economic strategy. It wants to become a global centre for business, logistics, tourism, hospitality and major global events; it has been chosen as host of both Expo 2030 and the FIFA World Cup in 2034. Before the current attacks, the airport handled roughly 110,000 passengers a day—similar in scale to Miami International airport. It is also the base of Riyadh Air, a new airline backed by Saudi’s PIF, which seeks to establish the city as a major transport hub to rival Dubai and Doha. These latest developments come as Riyadh is already grappling with rising fiscal challenges.   The kingdom recorded a fiscal deficit of 160 billion riyals ($42.7 billion) in the first half of 2026, up 71% from 93 billion riyals a year earlier, as it increased spending to prop up growth amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran war.  Earlier this month, the Finance Ministry raised its estimated 2026 budget deficit by 48% to 245 billion riyals ($65.33 billion), equivalent to 4.9% of GDP.   Such revisions and forecasts may now be due for another downgrade.   However, Krieg said it is premature to start calling into question the credibility of Saudi’s long-term economic plans.   “I would not extrapolate from several weeks of disruption to the collapse of Vision 2030,” he said.   “Saudi Arabia has enormous fiscal resources, deep domestic capital pools and the ability to keep strategic projects moving even when private capital becomes cautious. The long-term effect depends almost entirely on duration.”   Reeve also said that the extent of damage to investor confidence will be directly linked to the duration of the conflict and that the onus will now be on the government to reassure investors.   “Foreign investors are unlikely to up sticks at this point,” he said. “They will want to see how long the strikes last and how the government and PIF might respond in terms of loosening the purse strings to shore up confidence.”   But he was more pessimistic overall, adding: “All in all, I think current events are quite a big blow to the Vision 2030 thesis.”   The kingdom’s flagship business summit, the Future Investment Initiative (FII), dubbed ‘Davos in the desert’ is due to be held in under two weeks. events.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
events.summary: Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a...smart display? Why it matters : Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future. It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday. Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: Getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts. Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices. "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios. Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners. HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other, a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4. Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri. The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: Making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets. Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making . Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm , a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses. Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand. U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana. "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon. Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones. Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it remains unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market. "The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios. The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

events.title: Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI
events.summary: Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence . You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton? In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton. There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist. Compared to women , “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.) While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides. Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men. Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women. “Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says. Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did. In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty. “We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says. events.title: Ukraine warns Starlink limits are disrupting military operations as Russia pounds its energy infrastructure
events.summary: For the second time this week, Ukraine didn't receive advance warning from partners of Russian ballistic missile attacks, President Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy's defense tech advisor Serhii Beskrestnov suggested limits on SpaceX's Starlink were to blame for the lack of advance warning. Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians are without power as of Wednesday morning after Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure overnight, despite Trump's "energy ceasefire." Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, disrupting Ukrainian military operations. It comes as Russia intensifies attacks on the country's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's proposed "energy ceasefire." Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces, disrupting some missions. Meanwhile, Russia unleashed an attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, leaving at least 600,000 people without power in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, raising further questions about the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Sunday. "There is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector," Zelenskyy said in a post on X early Wednesday. He highlighted a targeted ballistic missile strike against the energy infrastructure that Zelenskyy said should have been covered by the "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy said. The attack comes after the Ukrainian president on Monday accused Russia of violating Trump's proposal that the adversaries stop attacking each other's energy facilities to help bring down the cost of oil and diesel. Both Russian and Ukrainian authorities initially denied any knowledge of an energy ceasefire agreement. Ukraine has since welcomed such a deal, while Russian authorities said talks are ongoing, without confirming whether they have reached an agreement. Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday: "Regarding the status of this agreement, we can refer to Zelensky's reaction. When asked the same question, he said he had not heard of such an agreement, would welcome clarification and was ready for a ceasefire," according to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Zelenskyy also said that for the second time this week, Ukraine received no advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches. The latest unflagged strike on Kyiv damaged a residential building and killed one person and injured six, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine's Beskrestnov said that the Starlink speed restriction currently applies to the StarShield military service package and is set at 100 mph, or about 160 km/h. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram. "SpaceX is likely to have taken such measures at the request of the Trump administration," he added in a separate post. SpaceX and the White House have been contacted for comment. events.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
events.summary: Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond. Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action. U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study . Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat. Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap." The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next. "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study. State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models. Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here." Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions. The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings. Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans. Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes. Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions. She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning. One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a PhD student in Cornell's Information Science Department. What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions. AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said. That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said. The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

events.title: Former Cathay cinema operator mm2 Asia, subsidiary still owe over $219k in CPF arrears
events.summary: Cinema operator mm2 Asia formerly operated Cathay Cineplexes, which ceased operations in Singapore on Sept 1, 2025, after its four remaining outlets closed amid mounting financial difficulties. mm2 Asia and its subsidiary mm2 Entertainment still owe over S$219,000 in CPF arrears, while founder Melvin Ang says restructuring makes further repayments hard. The court heard mm2 Entertainment paid S$20,203.50 but still fell short, and it must pay at least S$80,000 before the next hearing on Nov 11. mm2 Asia’s restructuring plan includes a S$15 million share placement, a rights issue of up to S$10 million, and debt-for-equity conversion after Cathay Cineplexes closed in 2025. SINGAPORE – Former Cathay Cineplexes operator mm2 Asia and its subsidiary still owe more than $21 9,00 0 in Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions, with their founder telling a court that demands for further repayments are difficult to meet while the companies undergo a restructuring . Th e St ate Courts heard on Oct 14 that mainboard-listed mm2 Asia owed $8,633.50 while its wholly owned subsidiary mm2 Entertainment had an outstanding amount of $210,843.50. Their founder, Melvin An g, who represented both companies in court, said mm2 Asia could settle its outstanding arrears in full by the next hearing on Nov 1 1. During the hearing for mm2 Entertainment, the prosecution said the company made a payment of $20, 203 .50 on Oct 13, but had fallen short of the $5 0,0 00 it was previously directed to pay. Ang said the company hoped to settle all its outstanding contributions by D ec 31, after completing its restructuring. However, when asked how much it could pay in four weeks, he said it hoped to make another $20 ,000 payment. $20k to $40k repayments will prolong the matter The prosecution said repayments of between $20,000 and $40,000 would prolong the matter, given the substantial amount still outstanding. The court subsequently directed mm2 Entertainment to pay at least $80,000 before its next hearing on Nov 11. Ang pointed out that the company had been granted a moratorium by the High Court and said there had been no staff complaints to the Ministry of Manpower over the CPF arrears. He said mm2 Entertainment would struggle to meet a court direction to pay at least $ 80, 000 by the next month , citing its financial difficulties and ongoing restructuring efforts . “Asking us to pay $80k by next month before the scheme of arrangement is completed is really difficult,” he said. Separately, during mm2 Asia’s hearing, Ang initially told the judge that the company had paid “everything” in full on Oct 13, after making an $11,000 payment. However, the prosecution said records showed that $10,438.50 had been paid, leaving a discrepancy of $561.50. The prosecution suggested that part of the payment might have gone towards other statutory obligations, including Skills Development Levy payments. Ang said the discrepancy could have been an error and undertook to settle the remaining $8,633.50 before the Nov 11 hearing. At an earlier hearing on Sept 16, the court was told that both companies owed about $213,000 in CPF contributions. Ang, who had also represented the company then, had cited financial difficulties and an ongoing scheme of arrangement when seeking more time to pay. “There is no fund in the company,” he had said then, adding that mm2 Entertainment proposed to begin repaying its arrears from January 2027. mm2 Asia faces three charges over unpaid CPF contributions for one employee between November 2025 and January 2026, while mm2 Entertainment faces eight charges involving four employees for November and December 2025. Both companies are seeking to restructure their debts through proposed schemes of arrangement , which allow financially distressed companies to negotiate repayment terms with creditors, subjected to creditor and court approval . What are some aspects of mm2 Asia’s proposed restructuring On Sept 18, the High Court granted both companies permission to convene creditors’ meetings to vote on their proposals. It also extended a moratorium protecting them from creditor enforcement proceedings by two months to Nov 21 , giving them more time to complete the restructuring . According to court documents filed on Sept 3 and seen by The Straits Times, mm2 Asia’s proposed restructuring includes a $15 million share placement to MMRA, a subsidiary of private equity fund Hildrics Asia Growth Fund. The proposed investment involves the issuances of approximately 16.34 billion new shares, alongside cash distributions and debt-for-equity conversion for creditors. The company also proposes a rights issue to raise up to $10 million. On Sept 22, mm2 Asia announced that the Securities Industry Council had granted MMRA a conditional waiver from making a mandatory general offer for its remaining shares, subject to conditions including independent shareholder approval.

events.title: Bank of England and IMF bosses warn of cyber threat to trust in financial system
events.summary: Kristalina Georgieva says online fraud could lead people to opt out of system and turn to ‘shoeboxes under their bed’ The heads of the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund have issued a stark warning that rising cyber-attacks risk undermining trust in the financial system. Speaking on a panel about online fraud at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, pointed to alarming headlines about self-replicating AI agents hijacking personal devices , and the French supermarket hack that heated fridges up to 50C . “If you try to say what’s at the heart of this debate about AI – for me, it’s about trust in technology and it’s about human control to achieve that trust in technology,” he said. Pointing to the key importance of technology in underpinning today’s financial system, he added: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.” Echoing his concerns, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva , said the toll of cyber-fraud was now so great that people could decide to opt out of the formal financial system altogether. “I was born and grew up on the other side of the iron curtain,” the Bulgarian economist said. “We didn’t trust the system. What did we do? I would have my dollars in a shoebox under my bed. “And I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve, given the speed, the scale and the cost of fraud growing up, we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds.” She said this threat was particularly acute for people on the fringes of the financial system. “Imagine what would happen if trust disappears or is eroded to a point that people no more have the courage to be included,” she said. Her comments followed a warning from the IMF on Tuesday that the possibility of a big cyber-attack was one of the factors raising the global financial stability threat level to “elevated”, alongside higher borrowing costs and the risk of an AI share price crash. Bailey stressed that fraud was now frequently committed via social media platforms and apps, not just traditional financial channels – and urged big tech to take responsibility. He contrasted today’s environment with the legal status in the UK of outlets such as newspapers, which are responsible for the veracity of everything they publish. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Instead, the governor said: “We’ve moved into quite an extreme position of, well, these platforms are open to everybody and there’s no real liability to the provision of the platform to what’s on it. Guess what? Everything’s on it. You know, the good, the bad and the incredibly ugly and downright criminal and terrible.” He added: “I don’t go around pointing the finger at people and saying: ‘You’re bad.’ What I have said is: ‘Look, there is responsibility all around.’ And we need to evolve to a world where everybody understands this responsibility, and everybody is then a part of addressing the problem.” He added: “We must get the social media companies involved because a lot of this fraud is transmitted through those channels.” Bailey called for the same tools that are being used by cybercriminals to be put to work protecting the financial system. “I’m going to use a sporting metaphor: this technology is arming the offence but it can also arm the defence, and it must do.” The panel event at which the pair were speaking was to launch a new set of international principles for avoiding cyber-fraud in financial institutions, called the Bangkok blueprint.

events.title: NoonTalk needs continued financial support from CEO Dasmond Koh, auditors warn
events.summary: Auditors said NoonTalk will continue to require financial support from CEO and controlling shareholder Dasmond Koh to continue operating. NoonTalk Media faces serious financial trouble, with auditors warning it may not continue operating because of losses, cash outflows, and debts above assets. CEO and controlling shareholder Dasmond Koh has promised 12 months of financial support, including help from his listed shares and a $1.8 million loan conversion. The company hopes new China marketing income, cost cuts, and extra fundraising will improve cash flow, while it will keep quarterly reporting because of the uncertainty. SINGAPORE – NoonTalk Media’s financial difficulties appear to remain unsolved despite financial support from its chief executive and controlling shareholder Dasmond Koh. Auditors flagged significant uncertainty over the talent management, multimedia production and events firm’s ability to continue operating, citing its losses, cash outflows and liabilities exceeding assets. The warning was disclosed in an Oct 14 announcement on its audited financial statements for the year ended June 30. Koh has given a written undertaking to provide the necessary financial support for 12 months from Oct 14 to help the company meet its debts as they fall due, NoonTalk said in the statement. The support will come mainly from Koh’s holdings of Singapore-listed shares, which can be converted into cash when the company calls upon him. It follows Koh’s conversion of a $1.8 million loan to NoonTalk into company shares in July. This comes as the auditing team highlighted several factors that could cast significant doubt on NoonTalk’s ability to continue operating. The group reported a loss of $2.55 million for the financial year ended June 30, and used $2.16 million in cash in its operations. At the end of June, its total liabilities exceeded its assets by $2.93 million. Its short-term liabilities also exceeded its short-term assets by about $2.93 million. Short-term liabilities are obligations due within a year, while short-term assets include cash and other assets expected to be converted into cash or used within that period. The auditors added that the assumption that NoonTalk could continue operating depended on continued financial support from Koh. Besides Koh’s support, NoonTalk said it expected income from a new platform marketing business in China. Its subsidiary Ruiqi Zhongxin (Chengdu) Culture Technology has entered into a framework agreement with a third party to carry out promotional campaigns and place advertisements on ByteDance’s Ocean Qianchuan platform. The board said its cash flow forecast, which took account of potential income from the marketing services, and planned cost reductions, indicated that the group could generate positive operating cash flows. NoonTalk is also evaluating options to raise or obtain additional funds for its day-to-day operations. For now, the board said sufficient information had been disclosed for trading in NoonTalk’s shares to continue in an orderly manner. The Catalist-listed company will also continue reporting its financial results quarterly instead of twice a year because of the material uncertainty over its ability to continue operating.

events.title: Is the modern economic system broken? These urban beekeepers think so – and this is their solution
events.summary: At Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere? T he bees at Bybi, a collective of beekeepers in Copenhagen , live on the roof. Their home is a complex of Victorian buildings, right in the centre of the city, that looks like an idealised vision of the modern social enterprise, ennobled by the architecture of the past. It’s a place of cottage industry in concert with nature, where the marginalised are brought in from the fringes and corporations stand waiting to help, where jobs happen but a lot of the work is done by volunteers, and where – this bit is important – a lot of time is spent discussing ideas. Oliver Maxwell, Bybi’s 48-year-old founder, encourages me to examine the buildings more closely. They were once a prison, a workhouse and a hospital; their functions today – a homeless shelter, a young offender institution and, until recently, a job centre – are not so different. Denmark’s Victorian transformation, from “agricultural backwater to industrialised agriculture”, was reflected in how they treated people, Maxwell says. In the middle of it all is the collective, which looks like a lot of things – a commune, a kitchen-table business, an art space. Everything smells of honey. Long drapes in earthy colours frame the entrance to a space where volunteers jar honey by hand. Small pots are stacked against a window in what appears to be a random formation, but this turns out to be a stylistic map of the city: each jar is from a particular street, with its own shade and its own taste, thanks to “the flowers people planted, the weather, the bees’ own decisions and choices”, as Maxwell puts it. “Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection, a place asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?” he says. Between 40 and 50 volunteers come in and out throughout the year, with a core team of 15 undertaking practical, honey-related tasks and events. They have 80 to 100 colonies, not just on this rooftop, but all over the city, on businesses and conference centres, schools, municipal buildings, restaurants. They produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year. How that turns into money really depends. Sometimes they give it away, at weddings and festivals. “Honey is an invitation,” Maxwell says. “It wants you to come in as a co-creator, with a joint responsibility for its health. We ask that you share it with someone you care for. And you plant a flower to help the bees.” Sometimes they sell it in the old-fashioned way, at a couple of boutique delicatessens around the city. Sometimes they ask people how much they want to pay; some are generous, some are not. Sometimes they discuss it in a reverse haggle, sitting in a group where they, as sellers, start low; the bidders tend to drive the price higher by thinking deeply about what went into the honey. Maxwell, an anthropologist, is originally from the UK. He spent time in Vietnam doing forest protection, some more in Brighton training social enterprises, then arrived in Denmark in 2007, setting up Bybi along similar lines in 2010. The plan was to employ homeless and other marginalised people, who would then be absorbed back into society. Honey would be made at the same time. Bybi also employed a social worker, “who was always a really nice person”. The problem is, “it just doesn’t work”, he says. “The bottom half of the jobs market has fallen out and everyone else has to run faster and faster. The moment you make contact with the market economy, everyone just melts. We’re sitting here with a crisis of community, a loneliness crisis , a crisis in the meaning and purpose of work. People need to do stuff – we’ll find stuff to do. But the labour theory of value, where you create worth with your time, your boss takes it and gives you some back that you can live on? That does not work.” They abandoned the “giving homeless people jobs” agenda. Now, people come because they want to, not because they’ve been forced to by the job centre. Five or so people are employed, with more in the summer; there are scores of volunteers, including disabled people who pack flower seeds. “They do it as slowly as they like and we give most of the seeds away for free,” Maxwell says. “It’s outside the logic of work.” And yet jobs are found. Maybe that, like the honey, is a byproduct of the bees. Back on the roof, 53-year-old Aref Haboo, the principal beekeeper, is looking for the queen amid sheets of honeycomb. The Syrian Kurd, who came to Denmark in 2014, finds her first time with an instinct gleaned from 18 years doing this job in the Afrin province of northern Syria, before he was displaced by Islamic State. Bees can recognise faces , apparently; they can also count and maybe even dream.

events.title: Trump plays Russian roulette on eve of midterms
events.summary: President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions. Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters. Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues. On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader. On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington. On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets. On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary." Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes. For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war. For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment , as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. For Republicans: With control of Congress hanging in the balance, Trump is embracing a dictator viewed unfavorably by 81% of his own 2024 voters, according to a January YouGov poll . The big picture: Trump's warm relationship with Putin has haunted his political career since 2016, when Russia interfered in the presidential election to help him defeat Hillary Clinton. From the Mueller investigation to the Helsinki summit , Trump's deference toward Putin has long divided Republicans and put him at odds with his own national security establishment. A decade of investigations, scandals and Washington outrage has done little to shake that affinity. If anything, the scrutiny appears to have hardened Trump's determination to defy the foreign-policy consensus. What they're saying: On Monday, Trump again suggested that Russia was more interested in ending the war than the country it invaded, telling reporters: "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky." "The President's diesel deal will help lower prices for farmers, truckers, and families across the nation as he simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement. The bottom line: Losing control of Congress could paralyze Trump's legislative agenda and expose his administration to years of investigations and subpoenas. But as polling alarms pile up , the president appears increasingly willing to follow his raw political instincts, regardless of the consequences for Republicans fighting to keep him in power. In a Truth Social post Tuesday, Trump made clear that he sees himself as personally immune from the results of the midterms, writing: "I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE."

events.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
events.summary: Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows. Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work. The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic. Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios. That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt. It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker backed AI safety group, which has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4). The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike. OpenAI President Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI. Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void. Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future. Eliosoff, an active participant in New York's effective altruism community, said he didn't want to see a repeat of 2024, where crypto industry funding had outsized influence on the regulatory positions of most candidates. "If politicians feel like they can't say anything because there's a very deep-pocketed and ruthless political entity that's going to go after them, that motivates me to step in," Eliosoff said. Between the lines: Eliosoff has donated to Democrats and Republicans who he says appear to be open to taking AI risks seriously and could be well positioned to pass regulation. Donors told Axios they are not primarily motivated by party affiliation or specific policy positions but by fears that industry spending will silence candidates on an unpopular technology. The other side: Leading the Future had retained more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has supported more than 15 Democrats and more than 25 Republicans. In a statement, the group said AI regulation will need 60 votes to pass in the Senate, so anyone serious about safety "and harnessing the benefits of AI for all Americans should be focused on building a broad coalition for action." What's next: This cycle will be a test of whether candidates who take AI industry money and oppose real regulation lose and whether that is clearly understood as a central factor in their loss, Guardrails Alliance Executive Director Shaunna Thomas said. "Republican leadership and the Trump administration are on the other side of the majority of Americans on AI," Thomas said. "That's a very important place for Democrats to be stepping into – boldly." Yes, but: Guardrails faces pushback from some Democrats who warn its strategy, which includes opposing some Democrats, could help elect Republicans less inclined to regulate AI. The bottom line: Trump allies have opened a new front against Anthropic and safety advocates affiliated with the EA movement, but their political giving — as well as the insistence of AI insiders — shows that the political clout of pro-safety AI advocacy is set to grow.

events.title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
events.summary: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off.  As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed.   Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer. Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide. A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it. The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons. Globally, that figure is likely in the millions .  One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem. Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline. But that’s an imperfect solution. The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less. Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation. Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says.  A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started. That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems. He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”). Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer. Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals.  KaloCyte techs use a device called a tangential flow filtration machine to process unencapsulated hemoglobin. MATT ROTH After processing, the hemoglobin is concentrated and then freeze-dried to make it shelf-stable. MATT ROTH With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has.  Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage. Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says. After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”   In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit. Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s. On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding. In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors. But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products. Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians.  As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success. Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles. The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets. The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale. Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic. Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane. For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible. Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage . It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict. events.title: Scott Bessent's growth plans aren't enough to tame surging deficit and debt pile, IMF chief says
events.summary: Georgieva said growth alone cannot deliver the required fiscal adjustments fast enough, calling for measures to rein in U.S. federal deficits. Bessent has argued that sustained growth above 3%, with spending restraint, can lower the debt-to-GDP ratio. The IMF projects U.S. gross debt reaching 142% of GDP by 2031, while the deficit is expected to top 6% of GDP in fiscal 2026. BANGKOK — The head of the International Monetary Fund has urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to trim the deficit, warning that his plan to lean on growth to tame U.S. Government debt isn't sufficient. "Growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel Wednesday at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "Some [fiscal] measures would be necessary." Georgieva said Bessent recognizes that federal deficits and overall debt have grown "too high," and that measures to improve the budget balance and reduce the debt are necessary. But "the authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to bring them down, she said. Bessent and Trump administration officials have touted resilient economic growth , driven by the artificial-intelligence build-out, reshoring manufacturing and tax cuts for consumers, as crucial tools to improve the U.S. fiscal posture. "With 3% growth, we grow our way out of this," Bessent said last month. He has argued sustained growth above 3%, combined with spending restraint, could lower the debt ratio and bend the debt-to-GDP curve. U.S. federal debt has exceeded 100% of gross domestic product, once an unthinkable threshold, with the country's public debt load surpassing $40 trillion and on track to break a record set in the aftermath of World War II. The U.S. government has historically spent more than it collects through taxation, committing to unbalanced spending in the decades since President Bill Clinton briefly managed to balance the budget in the 1990s. But debt-financed spending has sharply accelerated in recent years. Trump cut taxes in his first term and signed the first Covid relief packages in 2020, which Joe Biden followed with a $1.9 trillion stimulus in 2021. That federal spending helped stave off a recession but also fueled inflation that still weighs on American households and businesses. Before his appointment, Bessent had said he wanted Trump to cut the deficit to less than 4% of GDP by the end of his term, and said in August that the U.S. budget deficit had likely peaked . The U.S. Treasury market has been battered this year with yields climbing to multidecade highs, as investors bet that surging energy costs and heavy AI spending will keep borrowing costs higher. Benchmark 10-year yields hovered near their highest level since 2002, standing at around 5.2% on Wednesday. Although the budget figures for the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30 have not yet been released, the deficit is expected to top 6% of GDP, compared with 5.8% in fiscal 2025 . "With the government running an annual budget deficit of 6 percent of GDP, the debt will rise another $7 billion by the end of today—and each subsequent day," Benn Steil, senior fellow and director of international economics at Council on Foreign Relations, said in a Sept.25 note. Steil also warned that it could be "reckless" for Washington to declare the debt crunch solved by supporting unsupported projections, pressing for spending and revenue reforms. The IMF, which released its October World Economic Outlook on Tuesday, forecasts U.S. growth of 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, and projects U.S. gross government debt reaching 142% of GDP by 2031 . IMF chief Georgieva has also urged governments to set credible medium-term plans to control deficits instead of relying on stronger growth alone, as global public debt heads toward 100% of GDP before the end of the decade, the highest since World War II. Bessent reportedly missed this week's meetings to attend to "domestic engagements."

events.title: Former Canadian official says Europe erred on Trump tariffs
events.summary: Europe made a “historic” blunder by caving to the Trump administration on tariffs during Trump’s second term, the former Canadian trade minister who helped negotiate the US-Mexico-Canada deal during the first Trump administration told Semafor. “A real problem for the Western alliance has been the decision by the UK and by the EU to give in to the Trump bullying on tariffs,” Chrystia Freeland said. “People thought appeasement would win a reprieve for us all.” The EU and UK have each negotiated with the administration following the imposition of unilateral tariffs, and the former agreed to a pact that went into effect this year. US trade relations with Canada, meanwhile, have broken down, and Ottawa has announced counter-tariffs following US pressure. Freeland, who is out with a new book , said it’s “possible” albeit difficult for the US and Canada to return to a constructive relationship. That might need to wait until Trump is out of office, though. “There would have to be a clear break because the problem is: How do you do a deal with someone who already broke the deal that you did with them?” she said.

events.title: AI task force readies for first meeting
events.summary: All eyes are on the first meeting of the White House’s AI task force this week as groups and members of Congress try to influence the newly formed body. Americans for Responsible Innovation, former Oklahoma Democratic Rep. Brad Carson’s nonprofit focused on federal AI safety regulation, is pushing the task force to “explore the need for Congress to develop new laws that provide for enforceable safety standards and public transparency” into AI development. Voluntary commitments will not be enough, the group argues, and the task force should make specific recommendations to Congress. Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., also wrote to the task force asking for more resources for the National Institute of Standards and Technology and its in-house testing lab. They also want the task force to ensure that the Energy Department’s National Labs can test AI independently and to mobilize the technology to guard against cybersecurity incidents. Meanwhile, the FBI arrested a Saudi national Tuesday for allegedly secretly recording conversations at the offices of his employer, OpenAI. It’s still not clear what exactly will be discussed at the task force’s first meeting, as the group scrambles to organize following its formation earlier this month. Industry watchers are awaiting any official guidelines for enforcement of its new directive, which may come from the Office of Director of National Intelligence (headed by task force chair Jay Clayton) and the Federal Trade Commission. — Ashley Gold

events.title: OpenAI says Saudi citizen arrested over hidden recording device in office
events.summary: An OpenAI employee has been arrested and charged with using a hidden recording device in a San Francisco office, according to the artificial intelligence company and the US Justice Department. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen, was arrested on October 9, more than a week after staff at OpenAI discovered an audio recording device in the back of a television in an executive conference room, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. Mr Alfozan, who is accused of planting the device, is currently in custody having appeared in court in San Francisco on Tuesday. Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said. The incident is poised to heighten concerns about security at top technology companies at a moment when nations are competing aggressively to develop more powerful AI systems. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” the company posted on social platform X on Tuesday. OpenAI said one of its security teams discovered the device on September 30 during a sweep of a company conference room. According to details and images released by the Justice Departmen t, the device was plugged into a USB port in the back of a TV in the room and covered with toilet paper to disguise it. An image released by the Justice Department showed a small, black device with the text “Seeed Studio” on it. The agency said OpenAI determined it was planted around September 28. OpenAI said it used its AI models to understand more about the device and identify who placed it. Mr Alfozan did not have approval to access the conference room, which typically hosted meetings involving “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information”, according to the complaint, which references an unnamed AI company with offices in San Francisco. The company said it uncovered evidence that Mr Alfozan had planned to use other recording devices to secretly record meetings in other parts of the office. Early this month, according to the Justice Department, OpenAI security employees found a similar recording device in a bag he had left inside one of its corporate buildings. According to a LinkedIn profile connected to Mr Alfozan, he worked as an engineering lead at OpenAI on AI agent software. The profile says he has worked part-time as a partner at Saudi Arabia-based venture capital firm Raed Ventures since 2025, and previously as a senior systems engineer at Meta Platforms. Mr Alfozan attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 2011 to 2016 where he studied computer science and engineering, and the University of California, Berkeley, from 2023 to 2025 to study for a master’s degree in data science, the profile states. OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI and that the investigation is continuing. According to the FBI’s criminal complaint, the device was a Seeed Xiao ESP32-S3 Sense, which was described as a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage”. A device by that name and description appeared to be for sale for $14 from the website seeedstudio.com as of Tuesday. Lennart Koopmann, founder of cyber security firm Nzyme, said the device Mr Alfozan allegedly used appears to be built on “a hobbyist circuit board”, and noted features such as the microphone, and the ability to save recordings to a memory card and send audio wirelessly over short distances via Wi-Fi. “That makes it cheap and easy to hide, and catching one takes either equipment that watches the airwaves for unfamiliar devices or, if its wireless is switched off, someone physically searching the rooms,” Mr Koopmann said. Mr Alfozan is scheduled to appear before Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse in federal court in San Francisco on October 19.

events.title: Hongkong Land in talks with Ong Beng Seng’s HPL for stake in Orchard Road buildings: Sources
events.summary: The assets under discussion are (from left) the HPL-owned voco Orchard hotel, Forum The Shopping Mall and HPL House. Hongkong Land is in early talks with HPL to buy a majority stake in three Orchard Road properties, comprising voco Orchard, Forum mall and HPL House. The deal could value the assets at over $2 billion, but talks may still fail. HPL has faced pressure after Ong Beng Seng’s 2025 conviction and leadership changes. HPL plans to redevelop the site into a mixed project, but investors worry about high costs, lost income and the theatre's weak profits. Hongkong Land would strengthen its Singapore retail presence. SINGAPORE – Hongkong Land Holdings is in discussions with Ong Beng Seng’s Hotel Properties Ltd (HPL) to buy a majority stake in three buildings in the Republic’s Orchard Road shopping belt, according to people familiar with the matter. A potential deal could involve the developer, controlled by Hong Kong’s Jardine Matheson Holdings, investing in the three adjacent properties earmarked for development, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters. The assets comprise hotel voco Orchard, shopping mall Forum, and HPL House, which houses the group’s headquarters and Hard Rock Cafe. Discussions are still at an early stage and could conclude without a deal, the people said. A stake sale will likely value the assets at over $2 billion, although that is subject to change, they said. A Hongkong Land spokesperson declined to comment. Christopher Lim, HPL’s group executive director, declined to comment when contacted by phone. A successful transaction will mark a respite for HPL, which has faced challenges after its co-founder Ong was convicted in 2025 in a scandal that led to the imprisonment of a former senior politician in Singapore. The Malaysian tycoon, who controls the firm with his wife Christina through a roughly 60% stake, relinquished his decades-long tenure as managing director of the company, citing medical conditions. Ong, who was then 79, avoided a jail sentence as the judge exercised judicial mercy owing to his ill health and fined him the maximum $30,000. HPL has been looking to reduce its stakes in the voco hotel and Forum mall, excluding HPL House, people familiar with the matter said last year. The firm is now including the building in the assets put up for sale after talks with other interested parties fell through, the people said. HPL was given provisional government approval in 2023 to redevelop the three properties into a mixed project comprising a hotel, retail, office and residential components, as well as a rooftop garden and a performance theatre. As the sale of assets got under way, the redevelopment plans made some potential partners baulk due to uncertainties, the people said. These include concerns over the theatre’s profitability, and the lack of income for years arising from a big transformation, which is already likely to require significant capital outlay, they said. HPL’s Lim said at a shareholders’ meeting in April that the company was evaluating the redevelopment carefully as it would involve giving up recurring income from the properties. It was “focused on optimising development potential with the relevant authorities, including seeking revisions to certain approved parameters”. The company swung to a net loss of $39.1 million in the first half of 2026, compared with a profit of $11.4 million a year earlier. Its shares have fallen 6% over the past 12 months, compared with a 25% gain in the benchmark Straits Times Index. For Hongkong Land, a purchase of the assets will expand its presence in Singapore’s retail strip. A new fund backed by the firm said in July that it was buying Wheelock Place mall for $1.1 billion from longtime owner Wharf Real Estate Investment Co. Wharf’s controlling shareholder Hong Kong billionaire Peter Woo also owns about a fifth of HPL’s shares. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Wealthy investors can trust Singapore to manage their assets: Gan Kim Yong
events.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong speaking to Bloomberg TV on the sidelines of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi on Oct 14. DPM Gan Kim Yong said wealthy investors can trust Singapore with their assets, as the city-state works faster to stay a top global wealth hub. He said Singapore must build supply chain resilience by diversifying gas supplies, studying nuclear energy, and preparing for climate and geopolitical shocks. Gan said the ASEAN Power Grid will be a long, complex project, while Singapore’s 2027 ASEAN chairmanship will focus on trade and digital economy deals. NEW DELHI – The rich can trust Singapore with their assets, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, as the Republic seeks to strengthen its position as a global wealth management hub. He was speaking to Bloomberg TV on the sidelines of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi, India, on Oct 14. Gan is on a three-day visit to India from Oct 13 to Oct 15 to strengthen bilateral economic cooperation. “You can trust Singapore to manage your wealth. This is where the wealthy people want to put their assets,” said Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) . Asked how Singapore compete s with the likes of Hong Kong and Dubai as a wealth hub, he said that Singapore has to work faster and harder. “Competition is a given. We continue to make sure that our regulations and rules are up to date and facilitate many of these operations for wealth management. We continue to improve ourselves and make sure that we are efficient,” he said. Earlier in the day, he also spoke on a panel with India’s Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal, DP World group chief executive officer Yuvraj Narayan and Canada ’s Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu. Gan said it is important for Singapore to invest in supply chain resilience amid geopolitical uncertainties and climate change. Citing the Covid-19 pandemic and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz , Gan said that “the cost of disruption may be higher than the cost you are paying for resilience”. “In time to come, it may not be the Strait of Hormuz, it may not be geopolitics, it may not be (a) pandemic. It could be climate change. It could impact on supplies. We just have to prepare for the new future,” said Gan. To build supply chain resilience, the Republic is diversifying natural gas supplies and studying nuclear energy as an option, said Gan. “We are looking at different sources of natural gas, so that we don’t depend on a single source for our supply of natural gas,” he said. On the feasibility of nuclear energy , Gan said: “We are still studying today. We have not made a decision, but it’s important for us to keep pace with the development of technology, so we know what is available, and we continue to keep our options open. I think this is something that we consider very seriously.” Asked about the ASEAN Power Grid, he noted that while it is a major challenge for countries to come together to decide and to implement the initiative, there is a need. The ASEAN Power Grid is a regional energy integration initiative to connect electricity networks across ASEAN member states for cross-border power trading and clean energy security by 2045. “With the need for green energy, the interest in developing this project is there. It is going to be very complicated because it will involve cross-border electricity trading, and this is something that we need to develop,” said Gan. Acknowledging that it will be a multi-decade-long project, Gan said the countries “have to look at it from an incremental point of view”. “First, for example, Singapore will connect ourselves with Malaysia, with Indonesia. Next, Malaysia will connect to Thailand and the rest of ASEAN. It’s going to be a step-by-step, phase-by-phase approach and component by component. It’s also important to upgrade the internal domestic power grid in order to be able to carry that,” he noted. This comes ahead of Singapore assuming the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, taking over the role from the Philippines on Jan 1, 2027, and serving through Dec 31, 2027. Gan said the priorities are implementing regional trade and digital economy agreements such as the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which ASEAN is expected to formally sign in November under the Philippines’ chairmanship , and the Trade in Goods Agreement. Gan noted that he is optimistic that the upgraded Trade in Goods Agreement will facilitate further intra-regional trade. “This will also benefit our trading partners because we are able to trade among ourselves more efficiently. Other countries who are trading with us will find that their goods will be able to move more freely within ASEAN so it’s mutually beneficial for all.”

events.title: India's Bank of Baroda to 'defend interests' after BR Shetty's $15bn lawsuit
events.summary: India's Bank of Baroda on Wednesday ​said ​it would protect ​its interests, a day after UAE-based ⁠businessman and founder of NMC Health BR Shetty filed ⁠a $15 billion case against the lender and ​25 other defendants at Bombay High Court. Mr Shetty alleged ⁠the Bank of Baroda and several current and former employees helped facilitate a fraud that contributed to the collapse of the Middle East healthcare group, according to a ⁠court filing reviewed by Reuters. The firm, then the Gulf's largest private healthcare provider, ​was ⁠placed under administration in 2020 ‌after months of financial mismanagement and disclosed debts of $6.6 billion, way above previous estimates ​of $2.1 billion. Representatives for Mr Shetty did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a stock exchange notification on Wednesday, the country's second-largest state lender said: “The bank has not been served with such a suit and cannot comment on the contents of pleadings, which are untested in court. If and when the bank is served, the bank will defend the suit firmly and take all steps necessary to protect its interests.” The Bank of Baroda added that it was pursuing recovery and enforcement proceedings in India and the UAE against Mr Shetty for outstanding dues of 28 billion rupees ($294.5 million) and had obtained several decrees against him. The lender will ​not bear any immediate liability until any order is ‌passed or until it ⁠is required to make a provision on ​account of potential damages, the lender said. Bank of Baroda ​shares dropped ‌2.6 per cent on Tuesday after the legal action was reported. The lawsuit, which centres on the bank's lending to ⁠NMC Health and affiliated entities in the UAE, comes three months after the lender agreed to pay $600 million to settle claims brought by administrators of NMC. Mr Shetty alleged that bank officials enabled round-tripping transactions, ignored repeated anti-money laundering warnings and ​accepted documents bearing forged signatures. He is seeking $5 billion in direct damages, $5 billion in consequential damages and an additional $5 billion for reputational harm, the filing showed.
