events.title: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
events.summary: Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired? Published 14 October 2026, 00:04 BST Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job? We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates , external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason. But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating? Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager. He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI. "Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that." Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on. He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates . "That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening." This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process". According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions. However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments. On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market. EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem. EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year. Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process. "What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't." Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible. It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates. But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews. "A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script." AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff' Published 25 March 2025 AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts Published 5 March Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI Published 21 May One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews. While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would. "I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?" According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

events.title: Singapore’s PDG seeks US$1.2 billion loan for Malaysia data centre
events.summary: A worker walking past a data centre in the state of Johor, which has become South-east Asia's fastest-growing data centre hub, on May 7. Princeton Digital Group is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion to fund a 198.8MW data centre campus in Johor, Malaysia and refinance debt. HSBC, Maybank Investment Bank, OCBC Bank Malaysia, Standard Chartered Bank Singapore and UOB are the lead arrangers for the three-year loan, Bloomberg reported. The move shows rising AI data centre borrowing, but investors are becoming cautious as high rates and market volatility hit demand and some IPO plans. SINGAPORE – Asian data centre operator Princeton Digital Group is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion (S$1.54 billion) to fund its Malaysia build-out , according to a source familiar with the matter, as the debt binge to finance artificial intelligence infrastructure continues. HSBC Holdings Singapore branch, Maybank Investment Bank, OCBC Bank (Malaysia), Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore), and United Overseas Bank are the mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for the three-year loan deal, said the source, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Proceeds from the loan to be taken by the company’s subsidiary, Princeton Digital Group Labuan Alpha, will be used to fund a 198.8MW data centre campus project in Johor, Malaysia and to refinance existing debt, the source said. Standard Chartered declined to comment. Representatives for Princeton Digital Group, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC Malaysia and UOB didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Data centre companies across the world have been taking on debt as they seek to raise capital to meet growing AI demand. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt. But there are signs global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations as evidenced by the collapse of Nvidia-backed data centre operator Firmus Grid’s initial public offering earlier in October. Data centre firm AirTrunk, which counts Blackstone as a key investor, was reported to delay its planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027 as higher interest rates and market volatility temper investor demand. Headquartered in Singapore, Princeton Digital’s top shareholder is Warburg Pincus, and other investors include Stonepeak Partners, Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala Investment and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board. The firm, founded in 2018, operates more than 1.8GW of data centre capacity across Asia including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, according to its website. PDG has been on a borrowing spree as it seeks to expand across Asia. In May, the firm said it raised around US$856 million for its data centre build-out in Indonesia. Earlier in 2026, the company said it was targeting to raise US$5 billion in debt to support regional expansion plans. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Ossoff rejects 2028 buzz amid bruising night of Senate debates
events.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced. Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected. "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia. The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington. In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded , referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer. Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein. "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back , pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state. Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects. Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage. In his closing statement , Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger." In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge , as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points. Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel , saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine. Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war. Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

events.title: John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget
events.summary: Move aimed at firms such as Amazon and eBay could raise up to £1bn more for Treasury, says report A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget. The chancellor is said to be preparing to announce that online marketplaces will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by all retailers selling on their platforms. Marketplaces have been required to collect VAT for overseas businesses selling into the UK since 2021 but some foreign operators have posed as British retailers, using shell companies or other techniques to avoid this rule. Under the proposed change, websites would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, no matter where they are based. Healey is expected to announce this change will be made to fund cuts to business rates for high street shops, the Times reported. The government ran a consultation over the summer on changing the “deemed reseller” rules, saying “non-compliance persists among both overseas and UK-based businesses, distorting competition and disadvantaging compliant firms online and on the high street”. It consulted food delivery platforms as well as retail marketplaces, suggesting it was considering drawing them into the system. Amazon said it welcomed the prospect of a change to deemed reseller rules. “Closing this loophole will raise significant revenue for the exchequer and simplify compliance for both HMRC and legitimate sellers,” the UK’s biggest online marketplace said. The development comes as pressure continues to grow on Andy Burnham and Healey to relieve struggling small businesses on the high street before the budget on 28 October. Before he was elected in Makerfield, Burnham said he would increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high street retailers would not pay the tax. The government is facing calls from many factions to cut tax, with large retailers pushing for changes to national insurance to boost youth employment, for example. However, this week the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned Healey that his budget risks being a “ work of fiction ” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The IFS said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. In a boost for the Treasury, this week the International Monetary Fund upgraded its GDP growth forecast for the UK this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from its previous update in July . However, the IMF also cautioned that Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances. Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

events.title: Houthi attack hits Aramco's historic nerve centre in Saudi Arabia
events.summary: A missile attack on an administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state energy company Aramco hit the historic centre of the kingdom's oil industry , sparking a fire that authorities said caused no casualties. The strike by the Yemeni Houthi rebels hit a complex that serves as the nerve centre of the world's largest oil exporter, housing key research and development site, energy operations and thousands of employees and their families. People living near the building described moments of terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. "This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life," one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area following the attack. While no further details have been released about the incident, the site is a key one for Aramco, serving as its central hub for oil, gas, and energy operations. More than an HQ Aramco, at the time known as the Arabian American Oil Company, moved its headquarters from New York City to Dhahran in 1952. Dhahran was where the kingdom’s first commercial oil was found in 1938, at Dammam No 7, the “Prosperity Well". The Saudi government gradually acquired the company, completing a full buyout in 1980, before it was renamed the Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Aramco) in 1988. Aramco’s headquarters is situated within a vast complex spread across 58 square kilometres, with a large residential area housing a reported 11,000 people, including employees and their families. The Dhahran district also has a research and development centre and the Expec Advanced Research Centre, which was inaugurated in 2008. Expec has been upgraded with a building to focus on upstream research and development. The Dhahran complex also houses a large-scale cooling plant, operated by Saudi Tabreed, with a 32,000 refrigeration-tonne capacity that includes thermal storage tanks for energy saving. The chilled water piping network stretches 16 kilometres to reach sites, meeting Saudi Aramco's requirements for cooling. The area also includes Ithra, the King Abdulaziz Centre for World Culture, which was built by Aramco as a cultural and creative destination for the public. The centre has attracted more than four million since its opening in 2018. Previous attacks The Dhahran area was attacked on February 25, 1991, during the Gulf War, when an Iraqi Scud missile struck a US Army barracks, killing 28 American soldiers and wounding 110. Aramco’s other sites in the Eastern province have also faced attacks in the past. Several drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing centres on September 14, 2019, knocking out about 50 per cent of the country’s crude oil production. The 17-minute strike by 18 drones and three low-flying missiles, claimed by the Houthis, caused a surge in oil prices and shut down more than 5 per cent of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia said about two weeks later that it had fully restored oil output. In March 2022, an Aramco plant in Jizan was also attacked by the Houthis with a drone laden with explosives, with a gas station in Khamis Mushait and a power station in Dhahran also hit. In early March this year, after the start of the Iran war, a fire broke out at Aramco’s Ras Tanura refinery , the kingdom’s largest, with 550,000 barrels per day of capacity, due to drone attacks. Operations were halted for 16 days. Ras Tanura, on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast, hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports. Other sites hit this year include Satorp in Jubail, a joint venture between Saudi Aramco and TotalEnergies processing 465,000 bpd and one of the world's largest export refining platforms, as well as Samref in Yanbu, a 400,000 bpd Aramco-ExxonMobil joint venture. Earlier this month, Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser said ​the company had ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required. Aramco can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million bpd available ⁠within days, ​he ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “Our system is intact,” he added. Aramco, which is listed on the Tadawul exchange, is majority owned by the Saudi government. It is due to release its third quarter financial results on November 3.

events.title: Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts As Australia considers copyright reforms, Pope Leo's AI adviser Father Paolo Benanti issues a warning Father Paolo Benanti has a background in engineering and is an advisor to Pope Leo XIV on artificial intelligence. ( Getty Images: Massimo Di Vita ) The AI adviser to Pope Leo has praised Australia for taking a considered approach to tech companies. Father Paolo Benanti warned Australia that changes to copyright laws to allow AI training would be risky. He believes tech companies openly court religious leaders to protect their business interests. Australia risks reviving a "new form of colonialism" if it allows AI companies to train on copyrighted work without permission and send profits offshore, warned an influential AI adviser to the Vatican. Asked about Australia's consideration of copyright changes to attract AI training, Father Paolo Benanti compared the risk with Europe's history of taking resources from other countries and profiting from them elsewhere. "You go, you take resources, and you monetise it outside the place where the resources [were]," he said. He said Australian writing could become another resource used by foreign companies, with the money and tax revenue ending up overseas. Father Benanti warns AI companies mining creative work risks repeating old patterns of colonial exploitation. ( Supplied: Microsoft ) “Is it ... a new form of colonialism from foreign power that could ... exploit from the resources and monetise it outside of the place where they are taken?" he asked. Those were questions he said he would ask before voting on such a change. Last month, the ABC reported that the Attorney-General's department was quietly consulting on changes that would mean AI companies could train on copyrighted content unless its owner had opted out. In June Attorney-General Michelle Rowland told 7.30: "This government has repeatedly said that there are no plans to weaken copyright protections when it comes to AI." Earlier this week, the federal parliament's AI committee took the unusual step of pre-empting its own process to write a letter that urged reforms to pave the way for AI training. Father Benanti praised Australia's efforts to regulate social media and AI when he met Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week, and told 7.30 other countries should follow Australia's lead in reining in tech companies with policies like the teen social media ban. On his visit to Australia as a guest of the Italian Embassy, he described the country as being at the "foremost frontier" and defended it against aspersions about the effectiveness of laws like the social media minimum age. He said that the essential democratic principle was that "no one should be above the law". Father Benanti had a meeting with Anthony Albanese during his visit to Australia. ( Supplied: Instagram ) That included overseas social media companies, which he said could rely on protections in their home countries to avoid other governments' rules. He said Australia's first steps were important, and hoped other countries would follow. Working together would give governments more power to make technology companies comply with the rules in countries where they wanted to do business, he said. Father Benanti studied engineering before becoming a Franciscan friar and a professor specialising in the ethics of technology. He advised Pope Francis on artificial intelligence and now advises his successor, Pope Leo. Pope Leo's first encyclical, titled Magnifica Humanitas, focused on the rise of artificial intelligence. ( Reuters: Guglielmo Mangiapane ) In May, Pope Leo presented his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas , a major papal letter sharing his teachings about humanity in the age of AI. The landmark document made global headlines for criticising autonomous weapons, as well as algorithms that could deny people access to healthcare, employment or security. Father Benanti said the encyclical resonated beyond the Catholic Church's followers because it addressed moral questions they were already asking about how technology could change their lives. The encyclical urged governments to slow the development of AI systems. ( Reuters: Yara Nardi ) He said its appeal came from keeping those questions open for public debate and allowing society to shape how AI is governed. Father Benanti's concerns about AI extend to the emotional attachments people can form with the technology. He is concerned that companies exploit loneliness and romantic attachment to their products to make money from people's emotions. "Those are not neutral things, but are things that are designed by someone," he said.

events.title: New bridge linking China and North Korea will open more than a decade late
events.summary: A new bridge linking China and North Korea is set to open more than a decade after the Chinese side of it was built, in the latest sign of closer ties between the two countries BEIJING -- A new bridge linking China and North Korea is set to open Thursday after more than a decade of delay in the latest sign of closer ties between the two countries. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported Wednesday that both sides will hold a ceremony for the launch of the New Yalu River Bridge. The four-lane, 3-kilometer (1.8-mile) bridge will connect the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju. The bridge initially was expected to enter use in 2014 after China apparently completed construction of access roads, customs facilities and other related infrastructure on its side. But the date passed with no sign of an opening and without North Korea doing corresponding works on its side. At that time, it prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city. A lack of substantial work on the North Korean side prompted speculation that North Korea was wary of an increase in economic dependence or was unhappy with China voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program . Some observers said North Korea and China also differed over the location of the bridge. The new link is expected to lessen the burden on an existing yet aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70% of official trade between the two countries. The old bridge built in 1937 carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time. The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border stretching more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles). The new bridge’s opening will likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually. But in the short term, trade won't likely result in a sharp increase in Chinese exports to North Korea as Beijing would take Pyongyang's interests into consideration to some extent, according to a recent report by Gyubeom Kim, an expert at Seoul’s state-run Institute for National Security Strategy. North Korea’s export of processed goods, food products, cosmetics and alcoholic beverages to China could increase, Kim said. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says The bridge’s opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a 1-kilometer (0.6-mile) road bridge over the Tumen River as part of their efforts to cement relations. Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about the opening of the North Korea-Russia bridge, which the Russian government said would allow daily passage of up to 300 vehicles through a newly built border crossing point. The North Korea-China bridge is much bigger and likely capable of carrying round-the-clock, two-way traffic including containers and heavy cargo trucks, according to Jeong Eun-i, an analyst from South Korea’s Institute for National Unification. China has long been North Korea's biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has prioritized Moscow , sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine , apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance. Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve the economy and build a front against the United States. China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China. The bridge’s opening has been anticipated since Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit , Xi expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority. events.title: Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 00:03 BST About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year. The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance. The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases. Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service. Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26. It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds. But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class. "I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out." A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time. Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs Published 7 days ago Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time Published 29 May Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say Published 16 February Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload. We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day. Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare". "We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands. Bryn Dymott says he is speaking out now because he wants people to know what's really happening Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas. "People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered." Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening. He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise." So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices. Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems. The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others. "Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU. The union believes most Royal Mail workers leaving the company are new starters on part-time contracts, but also says there has been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing. Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas. It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses." The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period. The BBC saw returned post that couldn't be delivered so ended up back on the frames in a Royal Mail office Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027. The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out. The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.

events.title: How To Define CPU And Software Stack Performance For Agentic AI
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Measuring the performance demands of agentic AI; assessing CPU bottlenecks, SW stack efficiency, and system-level tradeoffs. Agentic AI changes the CPU performance problem. A completed task can involve repeated model calls, retrieval, state management, tool execution, application interactions, policy checks and validation loops. Accelerators remain central to model execution, while CPUs coordinate and execute much of the surrounding system path from user intent to completed work. This paper proposes a use-case-driven framework for evaluating that CPU contribution. It separates CPU-visible work into two complementary areas: common agentic framework functions and use-case-specific tool workloads. Five representative workload archetypes are used to capture distinct deployment venues, tool classes and CPU stress profiles. The paper then describes two complementary measurement approaches: component benchmarking, which emphasizes reproducibility and attribution and end-to-end benchmarking, which emphasizes realistic task-level outcomes. The objective is not to prescribe a finished benchmark suite or a single figure of merit. It is to define the measurement boundaries, workload categories and methodological gaps that need industry agreement. In particular, replayable agent trajectories offer a path to separating CPU work from model and network effects while reducing the run-to-run variability introduced by non-deterministic agent behavior. Combining light-based components with traditional electronics is not straightforward. Conventional electronic design automation (EDA) workflows were never built to handle the complex physics and deep integration demanded by photonics. Driven by exploding bandwidth demands, power and latency constraints, and the rapid adoption of silicon photonics, EPDA is no longer optional — it is essential for delivering scalable, manufacturable electronic photonic systems. Today’s multi-chip and chiplet solutions are leading the way for the “More than Moore” vision, with companies leveraging packaging technologies to create value and differentiate themselves from their competitors. Through-silicon via (TSV), wafer-level packaging (WLP), and 3D stacking technologies offer a wide range of packaging options for all form factors. Figure 1 illustrates a common example of 3D die/wafer stacking vs the traditional 2D system-on-a-chip (SoC). Fig. 1: Common example for 3D die/wafer stacking. Source: Cadence As semiconductor packaging technologies such as chip-on-wafer-on-substrate with redistribution layer (CoWoS-R) and local silicon interconnect (CoWoS-L) increase in complexity due to the rapid growth in the number of signals and the integration of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), high-speed interface areas are a key focus for design and analysis. This complexity challenges traditional design and analysis workflows, as importing large designs into analysis tools and managing redesigns can exceed project time constraints, making it difficult to meet deadlines. This white paper presents a comprehensive methodology that enables early and iterative optimization of IC package designs. By integrating in-design analysis (IDA) directly into the design environment and leveraging scalable multiphysics simulation engines, IC package engineers can compress design cycles, reduce late-stage surprises, and achieve confident sign-off on complex advanced package designs. events.title: Why Heat Is Becoming A Bigger Chip Design Issue
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Complex designs now require voltage, timing, resistance, power, and temperature to be analyzed together, and in the context of each other. Vertical scaling will require new materials and cooling options. Agentic AI could help engineers cross traditional discipline silos, which will be necessary because thermal is a system-level problem. Experts at the Table : Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the growing thermal challenges and trade-offs as dies are stacked, vertically integrated, and harder to cool, with Lang Lin, director of product management at Synopsys ; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci ; Chris Mueth, director of new markets management at Keysight EDA ; and John Ferguson, senior director of product management at Siemens EDA . What follows are excerpts of that conversation, which was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Lin; Vinci’s Radhakrishnan; Keysight’s Mueth; Siemens’ Ferguson. SE: One of the big trade-offs in advanced designs is voltage versus current. How do you balance that? Lin : If you reduce the voltage, it will change your timing and reduce the performance. But it also reduces heat. If you keep running the chip fast, you will run into a lot of thermal problems. These are conflicting physics. You need to find the sweet spot for your chip. You need to try the real combination of, say, this voltage versus this timing budget. And you need to do a loop of timing, thermal, and supply voltage or power integrity co-optimization. You have to close this loop and run a couple different workloads to make sure there is not a failure or any other problems. We don’t have a tool yet to do this big loop, so the engineer may be asking how to solve their place-and-route problem while also running timing, thermal, and voltage. And then, they still have to make sure they can close the design. Radhakrishnan : Along with thermal, you also have the resistance change because of the temperature. You need to understand the dynamics of a temperature-based transient. As you pass the current, the temperature rises and the resistance changes. Are you going to keep the same performance? Are you going to change the total current. How much power do you budget? That’s where the coupled nature of the entire simulation is going, and that’s where a lot of focus in the industry will be. As power rises, temperature rises, so you’re going to allow more cooling, and you’re going to push up the power. All of this is going to be coupled, probably starting next year. SE: So given all these issues, is a full 3D-IC possible? Mueth : It’s just a matter of time. We’ll solve a lot of the problems. That will require a lot of materials science, which needs more investment. For the aging problem, we will use specialized materials science types of solvers, which need to be extended to achieve that. There are exotic things you can do, like stacked intercoolers with fluid circulation. Of course, that means it’s going to be incredibly expensive to make those, and you’re only going to use them for high-performance applications. You’re not going to use them for everything else. Radhakrishnan : People are already talking about 3D DRAM and 3D-IC. From a thermal view, there are different techniques like a cooled interposer, but the industry is going more toward a 3D-IC where everything is stacked together and you have optics coming in on the side. It will be more expensive, though, so maybe you need to start with a narrow application. Mueth : One thing that hasn’t been mentioned yet is heterogeneous technology, and how you can bring that in to use the right modal technologies for the right application and integrate that stuff together. SE: For full 3D-IC, or 2.5D or 3.5D? Berg : Well, you can call a stack of 16 HBMs in a single package a 3D-IC. So, depending on your definition, we already have it. And then we say, ‘Well, that was great, but now I need it to be faster. Now I need better signal intent.’ Now, as we bring in the MCPs (Model Context Protocols), it’s not just bringing in the intelligent people. One of the things we need to think about in this industry is that we’re looking at each thing almost in isolation. Here we’re talking about thermal. What are the thermal impacts? events.title: Scale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppers
events.summary: Declining stocks and increased fishing pressure have led to lower sustainability ratings for two popular cod alternatives UK shoppers have previously been urged to avoid UK-caught cod and to buy European hake or coley instead – but now these fish are in trouble, too. The Marine Conservation Society (MCS), an environmental charity, publishes its Good Fish Guide to help consumers and businesses make sustainable seafood choices. It uses a traffic-light system to rate seafood according to the health of fish stocks and environmental impact. On Wednesday, the MCS downgraded the ratings for European hake caught in the North Sea, Celtic Seas, or Bay of Biscay from green to amber owing to declining stocks and increased fishing pressure. Meanwhile, the rating on coley caught around the UK (North Sea, West of Scotland, Rockall and Skagerrak) has fallen from amber to red – the worst rating – meaning it is a “fish to avoid”. Of the 10 coley fisheries rated by the guide, two are still green while the other eight are amber. Kerry Lyne, the Good Fish Guide manager, said the “status of fish stocks are continuously changing” and a “fish that was a good choice a few years ago is not necessarily a good choice everywhere today”. Most of the seafood consumed in the UK is made up of just a few different species, known as the big five: cod, haddock, salmon, tuna and prawns. This puts a lot of pressure on a handful of wild stocks. Cod populations have been in decline since 2015. The main cause is overfishing, although changing sea temperatures and other ecosystem pressures have affected breeding and juvenile survival. “The best thing we can all do if we eat seafood is diversify our seafood choices and avoid those most under threat,” Lyne added. With that in mind, the charity has suggested wild-caught sea bass from around the UK as a more ocean-friendly alternative to cod. Similar to cod, sea bass is a mild white fish with a flaky texture that can be swapped like-for-like in any recipe. The guide is updated twice a year and of the 727 ratings, the latest review has 29 downgrades and 11 upgrades. On the good news front, UK Atlantic bluefin tuna, which has shown huge signs of a population recovery , has a brand new green rating. Chris Graham, the charity’s head of ocean regeneration and sustainable seafood, said one of the factors behind the resurgence was better fisheries management brought in more than 20 years ago. LED lights inside the pots to attract scallops mean the new technology has a much lower impact on the seabed than traditional dredging.

events.title: China’s trade surplus hits $938 billion for Jan-Sep
events.summary: China’s customs agency says the country's exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier HONG KONG -- China’s exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said Wednesday, bringing it on track to exceed last year's record trade surplus as pressure ramped up from its trading partners, including the European Union, to rebalance trade. The exports data, which was better than what economists had expected, accelerated from the 25% growth in August. High-tech goods such as semiconductors and autos have helped fuel its rising shipments overseas. September's export growth pace was the fastest since February, according to FactSet data. Imports climbed 31% in September year-on-year, also accelerating from August’s 28.2% rise. Still, China recorded a $133.5 billion trade surplus last month, widening from $119.1 billion in August. For the first nine months, China’s trade surplus reached $938 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s full-year $1.2 trillion record . Strong exports have helped drive China’s overall economic growth this year, at a time when domestic consumption and investment remained sluggish, weighed on by a yearslong real estate sector downturn . However, China’s export resilience is now faced with mounting challenges, said Ecaterina Bigos, a senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “While U.S.-China trade tensions have eased somewhat, the EU’s push to rebalance directly targets high-value exports,” she said. The U.S. has launched an ongoing probe against China and other trading partners this year on their excess industrial capacity, although Washington and Beijing last month reached an agreement to extend their trade truce and cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods . The 27-nation EU has particularly been struggling to rebalance a trade deficit exceeding $1.1 billion a day with China. EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič, following his visit to Beijing where he met his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao last week, said a deal has been reached with Beijing, including halving Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU over the next few years. Many of China’s trading partners are facing weak growth prospects and are fearful of their manufacturing industries being overrun by exports from China , said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University. China has said it has “no need or intent” to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation and that its trade growth has been driven by its industrial competitiveness in the global market. Between January and September, China’s semiconductor exports soared 108.1% year-on-year in terms of value, customs data showed. Its exports of automatic data processing equipment and parts jumped 54.6%, while auto exports rose 54.3%, driven by an increased global demand for Chinese electric vehicles and hybrids. China’s trade surplus and its high-tech export model depend on open markets, Bigos said, and while diversifying its exports into markets such as Southeast Asia and Latin America can help, it cannot fully substitute for Western demand. The country’s reliance on high-tech exports, meanwhile, could face challenges as some U.S. technology industry leaders called for a global slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence over safety reasons. “A slowdown in the global AI investment cycle could pose a greater threat to China’s export growth than trade restrictions imposed by other countries,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board. Chinese leaders have set an annual economic expansion target of 4.5%-5% for 2026. It is set to release its July-September quarterly economic growth figures next week. This week, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5%, down 0.1 percentage point from its previous projection, as it warned that the country's robust exports were unable to fully offset domestic weaknesses. While Chinese officials have highlighted the need to bolster domestic demand, analysts believe that has yet to become a priority for this year even after authorities recently rolled out new measures to help lift its economy, including subsidies for homebuyers’ mortgage interest payments. events.title: China’s September exports soar, putting $1 trillion trade surplus in sight
events.summary: Exports soared 36.3% from a year earlier, outstripping August’s 25% rise and far exceeding expectations for 25.5% growth, customs data showed on Oct 14. China’s September exports rose 36.3% year on year, and imports grew 31.0%, widening the trade surplus to US$133.53 billion and putting a US$1 trillion surplus in sight. Semiconductors, green-tech goods and cars drove trade growth, while the US and EU surpluses stayed large. Analysts said demand should remain strong through year-end. The strong trade performance may help China meet its 4.5% to 5% GDP target, but it could also deepen trade tensions and raise the risk of new export curbs from major partners. BEIJING – China’s trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass 2025’s record surplus and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners. Global demand for semiconductors and green-tech products has helped keep China’s factories humming, easing pressure on policymakers to shore up economic growth against subdued domestic demand and investment. September’s growth was the fastest since February when exports expanded 39.6%. Imports also remained robust, up 31% compared with 28.2% growth in August and economists’ forecasts of a 24.5% gain. Wang Jun, a vice-customs minister, said at a press briefing there would be external uncertainties including geopolitical conflicts that might affect trade, but added there was foundation and support for continued growth in exports and imports in the fourth quarter. Analysts expect trade to remain buoyant, with tech products continuing to drive exports and imports. “Key trade ties look set to remain stable through the year end , which should keep this year’s key growth engine humming,” said Lynn Song, ING’s chief Greater China economist. China’s trade surplus topped US$1 trillion (S$1.28 trillion) in November 2025 and posted a record US$1.189 trillion for the whole year. The surplus reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of 2026, putting the manufacturing powerhouse on course to hit the US$1 trillion mark sooner unless exports slow sharply in the final quarter. For now, such a slowdown appears unlikely. September’s trade surplus widened to US$133.53 billion, helped by a 20-month-high US$34.01 billion surplus with the United States and a larger US$34.8 billion surplus with the European Union. A deal with the EU to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc, announced earlier in October, is likely to weigh on China’s booming auto trade over time. But with the trade measures likely being laid out in December, exporters may drive up shipments to beat the deadline. “The widening trade surplus with Europe could spur broader EU restrictions beyond last week’s narrow deal, though we expect the resulting economic fallout for China to be small,” said Capital Economics’ China economist Nguyen Hoang Nam. President Xi Jinping’s September summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington secured an extension to their tariff truce and an agreement to cut tariffs on US$30 billion worth of goods from each side. High-tech goods and cars continued to underpin shipments, with semiconductor exports rising 108.1% year on year in value terms in the first nine months. Auto exports expanded more than 50% in both value and volume terms. With the global build-out of AI infrastructure showing little sign of slowing, analysts expect demand for Chinese-made technology products, including semiconductors, to remain robust. China’s factory-gate prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September, separate data showed, while consumer inflation edged up but lagged behind forecasts, underscoring an uneven recovery. The Canton Fair, China’s largest trade exhibition, kicks off on Oct 15 for Chinese manufacturers to showcase their products to foreign buyers. In commodities, September crude oil imports fell 21.5% year on year in volume terms, while soya bean imports were down 7.7% from the same month in 2025. The strength in exports indicates that policymakers could still rely on moderate policy support to meet China’s 4.5% to 5% annual gross domestic product growth target. Risks of curbs on Chinese exports loom as China continues to defend its industrial and monetary policies, which Washington and Brussels blame for Beijing’s massive trade surplus. China’s central bank last week pushed back against criticism of its exchange-rate policy with a lengthy statement, arguing that it never pursued competitive depreciation and rejecting claims that China keeps the yuan artificially weak to gain a trade advantage. Any major hit to exports, a key growth engine, could prompt policymakers to step up stimulus measures to address weak domestic demand and the years-long property market downturn. REUTERS

events.title: Public Media Co’s bridge fund for nonprofit radio stations turns from rescue to reinvention
events.summary: Public Media Co. celebrated its 25th anniversary with a $10 million donation from the Knight Foundation Public Media Co. celebrated its 25th anniversary Tuesday night with a $10 million donation from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation to support its transformation into a major grantmaker — a role that would have been unthinkable two years ago. As recently as 2024, the nonprofit consultant that works to strengthen public radio stations reported $3.42 million in revenue, according to tax filings. Public Media CEO Tim Isgitt said he was proud of his “small, but mighty team” and the impact that they had on the sector. Then came the federal funding cuts . One day in June 2025, Isgitt told a roomful of funders that federal cuts to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting could create a “doom loop” with catastrophic effects on the entire public radio sector, requiring them all to act immediately. The next day, the House of Representatives voted to rescind all of CPB’s funding , about $1.1 billion that stations were already promised. Within weeks, the Senate followed suit. “It felt just like a wave that washed over us all of a sudden,” Isgitt told The Associated Press. Isgitt and Public Media were quickly pressed into service. His idea to help was suddenly in demand. “PMC had never been a grantmaking organization before, but everybody was saying, ‘You’ve got to do this,’” he said. “So we sort of turned ourselves inside out, hired some staff and became a grantmaking organization.” By August 2025, Public Media had organized a fundraising bonanza. It created the Public Media Bridge Fund to raise and quickly donate $100 million to stabilize public radio stations that depended on CPB funding for more than 30% of their annual budgets and were in danger of closing after the federal cuts. The fund launched with $27 million, including an initial $10 million donation from the Knight Foundation and support from Pivotal and the Ford, MacArthur, Robert Wood Johnson and Schmidt Family foundations. By December, it had distributed all $27 million to stabilize endangered stations. Stations with support from other sources, including the Bureau of Indian Affairs for tribal stations and the state of New Mexico for stations there, did not receive funding. “That was a good thing,” Isgitt said, “because we committed every dime that we had.” The Public Media Bridge Fund has raised about $87 million and stabilized 186 public radio stations that serve about 30 million people in the United States. The Knight Foundation’s additional $10 million donation, announced Tuesday, is part of PMC’s new $38 million fundraising effort to help stations become more financially sustainable without federal funding. Knight Foundation President and CEO Maribel Perez Wadsworth said she was impressed with how quickly and effectively Public Media deployed funds last year. “Now, it is really turning all of its attention to sustainability and the things that are critical to sustainability,” said Perez Wadsworth, adding that PMC’s focus on fostering collaboration between local news organizations can “drive the kind of business model change that will hopefully support sustainability in the long run.” The bridge fund will still support stations with unstable budgets; the fund is now also looking at projects with broader impact, Isgitt said. “Our attention now is more on the nationwide system and how it can sort of re-engineer itself to work more efficiently,” he said. The public radio network is a collaboration of three Maryland nonprofit stations owned by Salisbury University and the University of Maryland Eastern Shore. Cost-cutting and increased donations allowed Delmarva Public Radio to use part of its Public Media Bridge Fund grant to modernize equipment and purchase new marketing database software. events.title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
events.summary: Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work — and the scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems. NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research. In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize , joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges. Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households. Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems. In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients. Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence. Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed. Apian , Synnovis and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care. Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback. On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K. Digital Jersey , Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services. In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions. Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling. Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM , a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure. NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations. Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift. Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems. Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups. events.title: Saudi Ministry of Energy reports limited fire in building at Aramco compound targeted in attack
events.summary: The Saudi Ministry of Energy says a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province CAIRO -- A limited fire broke out Tuesday in an administrative building at Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in an attack in the country’s Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said. The ministry said no injuries were reported. The attack came as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition fighting them exchanged attacks Tuesday night. The fighting marked a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region, and the capital Riyadh. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes. The coalition of forces in Yemen led by Saudi Arabia carried out new airstrikes Tuesday on the Houthi rebel-held Yemeni capital, the Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah and residents said. The strikes came shortly after a coalition spokesman urged residents to evacuate the area for their safety. Witnesses reported hearing strong explosions in Sanaa hours after the coalition struck the Subaha fuel facility west of the city. In a rare statement earlier, the coalition had urged civilians in the Houthi-controlled capital to leave the Yemeni Oil Company site, on a hill overlooking the capital, and nearby storage areas ahead of a possible strike. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the facility and its underground fuel depots for their arsenal of missiles and drones. Houthi officials appeared to have anticipated the attack. The oil company said its storage facilities were empty and that a Saudi strike would not affect oil reserves or supplies for residents. Still, witnesses in the city said lines of cars formed at some gas stations amid fears of a shortage. Shortly after the warning, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that any Saudi attack on Sanaa would be met with a “firm and painful” response in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Hours later, Saudi Arabia issued alerts for incoming missiles heading for Riyadh and the Eastern Province but quickly said the danger had passed. The coalition said it had intercepted a series of Houthi-launched ballistic missiles, drones and cruise missiles in multiple areas in the country, including Riyadh and the southern province of Wadi al-Dawasir. Riyadh residents reported hearing loud explosions. Airlines moved a number of their planes out of Riyadh on Tuesday on the advice of insurers and government officials because of the threat of additional attacks. They needed to transfer the planes to other airports in the country so they can keep flying passengers to their destinations, said Osprey Flight Solutions Chief Intelligence Officer Matthew Borie, whose company advises airlines, insurers and countries on flight threats. “It’s not abnormal for this to occur especially in this day and age with the types of conflict zone situations that have occurred in the region,” Borie said. More than 3,120 flights scheduled to depart from airports across Saudi Arabia since Oct. 8 have been canceled or listed as not operating, representing about 41% of scheduled departures, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. That includes more than 300 flights that had been scheduled to depart Wednesday. Several airlines have suspended service to the kingdom because of the Houthi attacks on airports. It was unclear whether the Tuesday strike in Yemen was a signal of military escalation or a carefully measured response to recent deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport. The warning and the attack show “the Saudis’ aims of upping the ante and striking deep in the heart of Houthi-controlled territory while attempting to control the narrative by presenting themselves as more careful and humanitarian actors than the Houthis,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Washington-based New America institute. Saudi Arabia is still scrambling to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis , including an attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300.

events.title: NVIDIA Commits $250 Million to Advance UK Agentic Safety and Security Research Over the Next Five Years
events.summary: NVIDIA announces a compute donation valued at $250 million over five years to support U.K. agentic safety and security research. The program will support the wider U.K. research community, with a proportion of the commitment supporting BOLD, SOFAIR and Imperial College London across fundamental agentic foundation models and robotics safety. Compute access will be delivered through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners, supporting the nation’s research capability and compute ecosystem. NVIDIA today announced a five-year compute donation valued at $250 million to strengthen the United Kingdom’s agentic safety and security research capability. The commitment will provide $50 million in compute access annually to support agentic safety and security research across the U.K. The majority will support the wider U.K. AI safety and security research community, with a proportion supporting work with the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab (BOLD), the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab (SOFAIR) and Imperial College London. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “The U.K. brings world-class scientific rigor to this essential engineering challenge. With this $250 million commitment, NVIDIA will put accelerated computing in the hands of U.K. researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI. This is how the U.K. turns research leadership into real-world solutions — and scientific progress into a future that benefits everyone.” “This commitment is a vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research — and, in particular, frontier AI safety that is becoming ever more important as AI’s capabilities develop,” said U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan. “NVIDIA’s donation will help Britain’s AI innovators access the resources they need to bring their ideas to life — and, in the process, help build a distinctly British AI future that is safe, secure and that serves people’s best interests, objectives that will be central to the U.K.’s G20 presidency.” “To realise the opportunities of AI, people need to feel the technology is safe and secure. The government is committed to ensuring AI can be securely harnessed to fuel new discoveries and drive growth,“ said U.K. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. “NVIDIA’s investment will help British researchers continue to lead the world in that effort — accelerating the breakthroughs that build trust and help us deploy AI safely.” Strengthening UK Leadership in Agentic Safety and Security Compute provided through the initiative will be dedicated to agentic safety and security research. The program will connect complementary areas of U.K. research, including in AI safety and security. BOLD, led by the University of Oxford, is developing approaches that help AI systems learn, adapt and operate alongside people. SOFAIR, led by UCL, is exploring new open source AI architectures and more accessible ways to develop and deploy AI. Imperial’s work will include safety engineering and robotics. “We are experiencing a critical moment where AI safety as an afterthought is no longer appropriate for the open-ended, evolving world,” said Jakob Foerster, founding director of BOLD. “This compute will help us explore transparent and human-centric approaches to AI that allow us to collectively rise to the challenge by building in governance and human-AI co-improvement from the ground up.” “The next frontier of artificial intelligence is physical — robots, autonomous systems of agents that perceive, reason and act in the real world,” said Alessandra Russo, director of Imperial Frontier AI Research Lab and convening co-director of Human and AI, School of Convergence Science. “With NVIDIA and our industry partners, Imperial is working to ensure that safety and assurance is at the heart of this revolution, ensuring the U.K. leads not only in developing physical AI but in making it trustworthy for the communities and industries that will depend on it.” NVIDIA will fund compute access through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners , with infrastructure hosted in the U.K. This will support the U.K. compute ecosystem and provide a domestic platform for research. Provider selection, technical architecture and commercial terms are to be agreed. As part of the wider initiative, research programs will focus on secure agents, open-model security and real-world threat mitigations. The work will support secure sandboxes, reproducible research and safety assessment benchmarks, including research conducted using NVIDIA OpenShell™ open, secure runtime software and the NVIDIA Sentry reference design . Findings are intended to inform safeguards across the wider computing ecosystem. The commitment builds on NVIDIA’s collaboration with the U.K.’s research community, including on the University of Bristol’s Isambard-AI supercomputer, powered by NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchips. events.title: Energy bills through the roof? Five signs your house is leaking heat
events.summary: From finding draughts to buying a thermal leak detector – there are simple, cost-effective ways to start sorting heat loss How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences 1. Cold draughts around windows, doors and loft hatches Pick a day when there is a good breeze, and heat the house to its usual temperature. Then wander around with a candle or smoke pen (about £20). Alternatively, buy a thermal leak detector. This flashes blue for cold, green for normal and red for warm. 2. Water trapped between window panes “Misting or water trapped between the panes of double glazing can point to a failed sealed unit,” says Antony Heath, the marketing and development director at Glevum Windows. “Once the seal has broken, the window may no longer insulate as effectively.” Condensation on the inside of windows, particularly first thing in the morning, can indicate cold surfaces where heat is escaping, says Oliver Novakovic, technical and innovation director at Barratt Redrow. It can have several causes, including poor ventilation. Older single-glazed windows allow more heat loss, which exacerbates the problem. 4. The heating is always on, but your house still feels cold If your home struggles to maintain a comfortable temperature, it may be losing heat through walls, floors or the roof. Uneven room temperatures can also be a sign that radiators are not working or heat is escaping faster in some areas. “The better a home is at retaining warmth through good insulation and airtightness, the less energy is needed to keep it comfortable,” Novakovic says. If snow melts quickly on your roof while nearby properties remain blanketed – or it is a hotspot for birds – this can be a sign that heat is escaping. An older or uninsulated home can lose 25% of its heat through the roof.
