events.title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
events.summary: Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently. Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive. Software partners including ABA Technology , Akila , Galene AI , Honeywell Technologies , K2K , Linker Vision , Milestone , Onetera , ThinkDeep and Younite are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services. NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. NVIDIA Nemotron open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere. In the U.K., the Liverpool City Region , K2K is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The Island of Jersey is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management. In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or , Akila and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale. In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials. In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI , Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data. At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges , Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce. In the Nordics, Younite is developing a digital twin experience with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival. These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw. Elsewhere in the region, Honeywell Technologies is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations. Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies. Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents. System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations. Nebius and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow. Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress , running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona. events.title: Demand for air-con servicing hots up amid worsening haze in S’pore
events.summary: The increase in demand comes as a combination of hazy conditions and hot weather prompts more families and businesses to check that their air-conditioners are working properly. PHOTOS: WIRA AIRCON SERVICES, AIRCON UNCLE, IAIRCON SINGAPORE Requests for air-conditioner servicing surged in September as the PSI first entered the unhealthy range in Singapore, with demand continuing to climb in October. Service firms said customer queries and bookings increased by 15 to 30 per cent, as homes and businesses checked units for poor cooling, dirtier filters and better sleep comfort. Job ads for air-con technicians more than doubled, but hiring remains difficult because suitable candidates are scarce; some firms are holding prices and staffing steady for now. SINGAPORE – More job postings for air-conditioner technicians surfaced in the l ast quarter, as demand for air-conditioner servicing rose sharply across residential and commercial venues. Requests for air-con servicing surged in September, when the PSI first entered the unhealthy range in Singapore , with demand continuing to climb in October. Sushil Acharya, co-founder of home services platform StringsSG, said September recorded the sharpest increase in requests for air-con servicing, coinciding with the onset of the haze. There were 792 requests in September, up from 297 in the same month in 2025. In October, the volume of requests increased further, in line with the worsening air quality across the island . He noted that requests received from Oct 1 to 10 were 23% higher than those received during the same period in September and October 2025. “In September, the number of requests generated per dollar of customer acquisition spending increased by 64% compared with in August,” he said. Air-con servicing companies told The Straits Times that customer demand and queries on air-con servicing have risen sharply, by up to 30%, in recent months. For Rafiuddin Ismail, sales operations manager at Wira Aircon Services, the prolonged haze and hotter weather mean handling a surge in customer queries about air-con performance. There has been about a 30% increase in new customers, he said, adding that he has observed more residential and commercial customers including hotels, shops and offices “experiencing insufficient cooling rather than reporting actual equipment faults”. Rafiuddin said: “We have also received more inquiries from customers who have not been using their air-conditioning units regularly and now want to have them checked before using them more frequently, especially at night. “Many are looking to ensure their units can provide a comfortable sleeping environment.” Similarly, Aircon Uncle operations manager Jeremy Chng has seen a clear uptick in bookings from households and businesses. “(They are) asking questions and looking for dependable support to keep their units running well,” he said. He added that customer demand and engagement have grown by about 20%, reflecting a heavier reliance on air-conditioning in Singapore’s climate as well as a growing awareness that regular servicing can prevent costly breakdowns later. A spokesperson for iAircon Singapore, who wanted to be known only as “Uncle Eric”, said demand for servicing has increased by 15% to 20% lately, with most customers having blower fans and filters that are “much dirtier than usual”. The company is able to monitor the cleanliness of the units closely as many of its customers have signed up for annual maintenance packages with quarterly servicing, he said. FastJobs founder and chief executive Julian Tan said job postings for air-con technicians have more than doubled in the last quarter, but the figure remained below that for the corresponding period in 2025. “Hiring for air-con technicians on FastJobs typically picks up in the hotter July-to-September period, and this year was no exception,” he added. There are typically more job postings for air-con technicians on recruitment platform FastJobs during the hotter July-to-September period. But employers have faced challenges finding suitable candidates. Tan said he has heard from recruitment partners that suitable technician candidates are difficult to find, with some agencies scaling back on these roles as a result. To this end, more air-con and maintenance companies are hiring directly rather than through recruitment agencies, he noted, adding that “roles posted directly by employers nearly doubled compared with the same period last year”. Despite the surge in demand, several air-con firms said they have not increased their prices and are not looking to hire more technicians for now. Wira Aircon Services’ Rafiuddin said: “Our current two teams of four air-con technicians each are sufficient to accommodate our customers’ requests, although we continue to monitor demand. “Hiring additional technicians comes with significant costs so we have to be careful with our recruitment decisions.

events.title: Rare earths company could be nationalised as China-linked investors fail to divest
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Northern Minerals is seen as vital to developing alternative sources of dysprosium and terbium, which are used in renewable energy and military technology. ( ABC Rural: Matt Brann ) China-linked investors are defying federal government orders to divest from a Perth-based rare earths company. Northern Minerals is seen as a key player in efforts by both the US and Australia to break China's stranglehold on the critical minerals supply chain. Resources Minister Madeleine King said "one option" is to nationalise the company, given the strategic national interest. The Resources Minister Madeleine King says nationalising a Perth-based heavy rare earths company is an "option" for the government as China-linked investors continue to defy orders to divest from the strategically sensitive miner. In May, federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers ordered six investors which hold around 17 per cent of Northern Minerals to divest by July 2 from the company, which is developing the Browns Range project in Western Australia's east Kimberley region. But Northern Minerals told the ASX later in July that the companies still held most of the shares they had been ordered to sell. Northern Minerals is seen as a key player in efforts by both the US and Australia to break China's stranglehold on the critical minerals supply chain and is already on track for about $500 million in funding from the Export Import Bank of the United States. Madeleine King told the National Press Club on Wednesday that the uncertainty was "holding up" the development of the project, which is vital to developing alternative sources of dysprosium and terbium, critical minerals which are used in both renewable energy infrastructure and advanced military technology. The minister also appeared to leave the door open to nationalisation when asked if the government would be willing to take that step — although she stressed that no decisions had yet been made. "I guess it is one option, but I wouldn't want to advance on any decision we're making there," she said. She also appeared to confirm that the companies had failed to pay the fines imposed by the federal government for non-compliance. Madeleine King says the critical minerals are important for Australia's national security. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Ms King said the government was "very active knowing what is going on" when it came to the project, and took aim at the China-linked investors refusing to sell, saying "failure to follow through or pay respects, quite frankly, to Australian government decisions, is a very serious matter we are looking at". "There have been a number of decisions made by FIRB [the Foreign Investment Review Board] but also divestment decisions as well, and that has not been done by those who hold those shares," she said. The comments from the minister come after a rolling series of government interventions designed at protecting the company from Chinese entities stalking it. In 2023, Mr Chalmers blocked a Chinese-linked investor Yuxiao Fund from boosting its stake in the company, and in 2025 he ordered another five companies linked to China to divest from it. One of those Chinese investors launched an unsuccessful bid earlier this year to topple the company's leadership. And at least some of the Chinese companies blocked from Northern Minerals seem to have made multiple efforts to circumvent federal government orders to divest from the company. Earlier this year the Foreign Investment Review Board wrote to Northern Minerals, saying three of the blocked investors last year had simply transferred their shares to Hong Kong Ying Tak Ltd, one of the six companies ordered to divest earlier this year. The Resources Minister said the saga highlighted the need for the federal government to press on with its review of foreign investment laws, which is due to wrap up next year. The ABC has approached Northern Minerals for comment.

( ABC News: Kimberley Putland ) Mining giant BHP has confirmed job cuts at its iron ore operations in Western Australia. The ABC understands around 300 jobs will be axed across BHP's South Flank, Mining Area C, Jimblebar and Newman operations in the state's Pilbara. In a statement, a spokesperson said the miner was making changes to ensure the business could continue to "make a significant contribution" to the region and the state, but did not specify how many jobs would go. "As we always do, we will seek to redeploy people into other roles elsewhere in the business where possible," the spokesperson said. Jimblebar iron ore mine, 41 kilometeres east of Newman in the Pilbara. Minister for the Pilbara Amber-Jade Sanderson said the decision was very disappointing. "We strongly urge BHP to redeploy these workers, these are highly needed skills across the sector and across our economy," she said. Amber-Jade Sanderson says BHP's decision is disappointing. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) "But we will be working as a government ... to make sure that we have the jobs and skills centres ready to support these workers as they need to transition into new industries." WA Electrical Trades Union (ETU) state secretary Adam Woodage called the cuts a "senseless attack". "This is another sad reflect of a once-great Australian mining company that has lost its way and forgotten its values," Mr Woodage said. "The fact that this has been announced in the media flouts the requirement to consult with workers and their representatives before taking an action like this. "The ETU's engagement in that consultation will be robust, and we will require the company to provide proof that every redundancy is genuinely required." But BHP denied the union had been ambushed. A spokesperson said consultation with workers started on October 5, and unions were told on the same day. Mr Woodage suggested BHP could instead cut costs within executive bonuses and corporate lobbying. Adam Woodage said there were other ways BHP could cut costs. ( ABC News ) The Western Mine Workers Alliance (WMWA) — a Pilbara-based partnership of the Australian Workers Union and the Mining and Energy Union — flagged the cuts on social media, stating the miner had begun "major structural changes". The cuts come amid an ongoing dispute between BHP and unions over pay and conditions at its Port Hedland operations that has included a series of recent strikes. The unions have lodged an application with the Fair Work Commission in a bid to settle the matter. BHP electricians on sites near Newman have also lodged an application for supported bargaining with the commission. events.title: Forcing gas producers to sell to Australia won't 'crash' prices, King says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gas reservation laws won't cause wholesale price 'crash', King says Madeleine King says the government has struck a careful balance in its bid to push down wholesale gas prices while keeping the sector profitable. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The resources minister has declined to detail how far she expects gas prices to fall under a proposed reservation law, saying the government's modelling is commercially sensitive. Madeleine King has introduced legislation to create a gas reservation scheme she says will create a "modest" domestic oversupply. The Coalition has indicated it will work with the government to pass the laws, but says questions remain about how future supply and investment will be assured. The resources minister says gas prices will not crash under national reservation laws, but refused to say how much they will fall as the industry warns the government is pushing too hard. Madeleine King said she wanted the proposed laws to make prices fairer while ensuring new gas projects would still be profitable enough to proceed. "Allow me to be clear: we need gas to support the rollout of renewables. We need gas to have a strong Australian manufacturing industry. We need gas to continue heating our homes," she said. The legislation introduced to parliament this morning would force producers to sell up to a fifth of their gas slated for export to Australia, pushing down wholesale prices by sparing the country from having to compete with the international market for its own resource. How much gas producers will be required to sell to Australia each year would be set by the energy regulator, with a target amount of 110 per cent of Australia's actual needs. The government says the "modest oversupply" will put downward pressure on prices for consumers. But after being burned by its failure to meet a previous promise to cut home power bills by $275 through renewables, which was thrown off course by Russia's invasion of Ukraine driving up gas and fuel prices globally, the government has been reluctant to put a price tag on how much prices would be expected to fall under the scheme. The resources minister told the National Press Club that the rules for gas producers had been carefully balanced, but that information was commercially sensitive. "We have done a lot of study and a lot of analysis and, I might add, that so has just about everybody else in relation to this," Ms King said. "A lot of the modelling that we have done, or the analysis that we have done, is commercial-in-confidence, so it is difficult." She said the government would release an impact assessment related to its gas reservation laws, but did not commit to that including estimated impacts on wholesale gas prices. "Our focus is on making sure there is this modest oversupply, and that demand calibration is really important, as well, in this," Ms King said. "We all know having too little gas to firm renewables or provide for the manufacturing industry is as dangerous as having a massive oversupply which crashes the market, but also it can undermine investment in renewables, so it is a really fine balance we have got to achieve here." The resources minister said the bill's focus was to make gas cheaper for heavy industry and energy generation, but added that an important element was ensuring cheaper gas prices "will be felt by the consumer". 'Sugar hit' will hurt in long-term, industry says The gas industry has warned that the government's plan could force the sale of gas at rates that are cheaper than it costs to produce. It says the scheme might provide a "sugar hit", but would make future gas projects unviable and dry up supply in the long-term. "The government cannot expect industry to invest billions of dollars in new gas supply while introducing policies that fundamentally undermine the commercial viability of those investments," Australian Energy Producers chief executive Samantha McCulloch said. "Any price impact is likely to be temporary because of the impact this is going to have on investment and future gas supply. "The [Australian Competition and Consumer Commission] has said that the marginal cost of new supply is somewhere between $9.50 and $13 [per gigajoule]. You need a price within that range to encourage investment in new supply." Australian Energy Regulator data shows wholesale gas prices have been between about $10 to $11.50 per gigajoule, depending on jurisdiction. events.title: Barriers facing black and south Asian music events ‘cost London up to £141m a year’
events.summary: Exclusive: Investigation finds racial inequality in live music industry rife and many genres labelled ‘high risk’ despite lack of evidence Black and south Asian music events in London face disproportionate cancellations, restrictions and licensing barriers compared with white events, according to a two-year investigation into racial inequality in the capital’s live music industry. The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report, led by Black Lives in Music, estimates that cancellations, displacement and events prevented from taking place cost London £127m to £141m annually, with projected losses exceeding £650m over five years. The report found that genres including Afrobeats, drill and dancehall are routinely labelled “high risk” despite a lack of credible evidence, while indie, pop and rock events face comparatively little scrutiny. Other events facing stringent restrictions included reggae gatherings aimed at older audiences, jazz nights and community events. The research raised concerns over the use of unverified police intelligence, with promoters describing events being cancelled based on undisclosed information, online searches or unrelated incidents. Charisse Beaumont, chief executive of Black Lives in Music, said that although the investigation focused on London, the problems it uncovered exist nationwide. “As soon as we put the report out there, the call for our survey, people were upset that they couldn’t complete the survey because they were outside of London,” she said. For Beaumont, the discrimination extended far beyond specific music genres. “It’s about race. And that’s what’s so deeply sad about it.” The two-year study was commissioned by the mayor’s office and included collaboration by the Greater London Authority (GLA), the Metropolitan Police Service, UK Music, LIVE, the Musicians’ Union and a wide network of promoters, artists, venue operators and community representatives. The findings suggest that the legacy of the Metropolitan police’s controversial Form 696 persists. Introduced in 2005 as a risk assessment tool, it was scrapped in 2017 after criticism that it discriminated against black music events. Hakeem Stevens, the report’s lead researcher, said police scrutiny had become harder to document. “Back in the day when emails were sent and faxes were sent, we had documented evidence. Now what’s happening is it’s whispers, it’s phone calls, it’s conversations, verbal conversations that can’t be recorded.” He said black and Asian performers faced disproportionate scrutiny, adding: “You’ve got white artists that perform black music, and they don’t get given that level of scrutiny.” Researchers found that promoters received little explanation for cancellations, faced substantial security costs and had limited opportunities to challenge decisions. Stevens said the financial and reputational consequences could severely affect mental health. Beaumont highlighted the case of the Colour Factory, a black-owned venue whose licence was suspended after an incident outside its premises that was reportedly unrelated to the venue. She said the owner successfully challenged the decision but faced significant financial losses, including legal costs and staff redundancies. “In the end, they won, but they didn’t get their money back,” she said. The report also found that when incidents occur, many white-owned venues are supported back into business after incidents, while black-owned venues are forced to close for prolonged periods. Kwame Otiende, a venue owner, promoter and Green councillor, said the additional scrutiny discouraged venues from hosting certain events. “Venues will have known that they get a lot more grief from whatever relevant authorities they need to go through to get a temporary event notice,” he said. Instead, he suggested, venues may opt for safer commercial choices: “I could just put your very sort of middle-of-the-road chart music … and I’ll still make the same amount of money.” The report sets out 19 recommendations, including calls for more transparent, evidence-based licensing decisions, alongside an independent review, clearer evidence standards, better reporting of licensing outcomes and stronger accountability. Beaumont said: “Success would be for me, the ability for any artist from any background, particularly Black and south Asian, to be able to perform and put on events at any venue without barriers, so they too can make money “They’ve got an album out, they do a tour, they might be able to do a 1,000-capacity venue, but can they progress from 2,000 to 5,000 to 20,000 to stadium? That doesn’t happen for us.” The Met police commander Neerav Patel said the force would carefully consider the reports finding.

events.title: Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot
events.summary: Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence Tom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employer W hat a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson asks : “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble. But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who once took on the Murdoch empire , would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not have taken a job as a senior vice-president at Palantir. Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to a deep investigation by Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have made abundant use of the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantir now employs . Palantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include an unrecorded meeting between Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it charged only £1 . The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, has criticised such loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price. Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantir secured a £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender. Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was on unpaid leave from the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Times reports that Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department. There have been repeated allegations that some of Palantir’s products are rubbish . But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee warns , government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop. Thiel, has claimed that “the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE find undocumented people . It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”, he replied : “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.” This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, it turns out that NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is a huge issue .

events.title: Rex grounds two routes 10 months after $60m rescue package
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fuel costs blamed as Rex suspends Orange and Port Macquarie services Regional Express has announced it will suspend two regional NSW services in late October. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) Rex Airlines will suspend its Orange and Port Macquarie services from October 25. The decision comes less than a year after the carrier was sold in a deal that featured a $60 million rescue package and a further $108 million to restructure Commonwealth debt. The airline says it will monitor fuel costs and reinstate the routes it becomes commercially viable. Less than a year after it was sold with the aid of a federal government rescue package, embattled airline Regional Express (Rex) has grounded flights to two NSW destinations. The carrier announced that flights to and from Sydney and Port Macquarie on the Mid North Coast and Orange in the Central West will be indefinitely halted from October 25. Independent MP Andrew Gee, whose federal electorate takes in Orange, described the decision as a "real shock". "It feels like a slap in the face or a kick in the guts for the whole region after everyone called for so much support and so much pressure was put on the government to deliver it," he said. Andrew Gee says Rex's decision comes as a blow after the effort put into ensuring its survival. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) A Commonwealth bailout allowed the airline to keep flying its regional routes and, in late 2025, it was bought by US-based air services company Air T . The sale was endorsed by the federal government, which backed the bid with a $60 million support package and an additional $108 million to help restructure existing Commonwealth debt. In exchange for that support Air T made commitments to increase the number of aircraft in service, maintain an ongoing level of service to regional Australia, and increase frequencies of profitable flights across its network. The ABC has contacted Air T for comment. A spokesperson for Federal Transport Minister Catherine King issued a statement acknowledging the Rex decision would be "be disappointing for many". "In return for support from the Australian Government, Air T agreed to a set of regional commitments aimed at maintaining Rex's services to regional Australia," the spokesperson said. "Notwithstanding these changes, Rex continues to operate one of Australia's largest regional air networks. "The Government continues to work closely with Rex to understand market challenges and to monitor Rex's compliance with regional commitments." The statement noted that customers in both regional destinations would still be able to fly to and from Sydney on different carriers. A spokesperson for Catherine King says the government is continuing to "work closely" with Rex. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) A statement issued by Rex said the suspensions were indefinite, and affected customers would be offered "refunds or re-bookings". "The environment of entrenched high fuel prices driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, together with lack of demand, do not make these routes commercially viable at this time," the statement said. REX said it would monitor the situation and consider reinstating the routes "once fuel prices decrease to a level that makes it commercially viable for flights to resume". The carrier said it remained "committed to serving regional and remote Australia". In May, the airline cut two services in Tasmania and scaled back a service to Mildura in Victoria's north-west. Rex has blamed soaring fuel costs for the suspension of the flights. ( Supplied: Rex Airlines ) Port Macquarie Mayor Adam Roberts said the area's $700 million annual visitor economy would be hit by the Rex decision. "The reality is that it has a significant flow-on effect to our community," he said. "Living in a regional area, we absolutely need these vital services." Cr Adams said whether airport staff would lose jobs remained unclear, but discussions were underway to mitigate impacts. "The state and federal governments need to look at what's happening here and ask the question [whether] they could potentially help us stabilise our potential for travel," he said. "If it's a grant fund or if it's a carrot to entice more airlines to use this airport, we're already having some peripheral conversations." Orange Mayor Tony Mileto is pessimistic about the prospect of the service ever being reinstated. "I don't think they'll be backflipping on the decision," he said. Cr Mileto said there was clearly demand among the other airlines that serviced the airport, including Qantas and Link Airways.

events.title: Geeing up for 6G: What the next mobile standard promises and challenges it faces
events.summary: Over the past weeks, UAE telecom operators etisalat and du have announced further progress in their march towards 6G, the next generation of wireless communication. The industry is accelerating its preparations for the technology that being presented as vital to the world becoming more connected, underpinned by increasingly intelligent devices and services . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi's etisalat – which recently rebranded back from e& – said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. What is 6G and when would it be available? 6G promises faster speeds and efficiency than the current 5G mobile phone technology, which also has more advanced forms under names such as 5G+, 5G Advanced and 5.5G. Historically, new generations of wireless technology have emerged with every new decade, suggesting 6G could become available in the early 2030s. This is a widely shared industry expectation. The US introduced the third generation in 2002, the fourth in 2010 and 5G in 2018. The second and first generations were in the 1980s and early 1990s, respectively, with the “zero G” before that. While a 6G rollout is predicted in the early 2030s, not all of its features are expected to be available at launch, as the industry would continue testing its deployment. How fast is 6G? 5G's maximum transmission speed is 20 gigabits per second, which is already 20 times faster that 4G's 1Gbps rate under ideal circumstances. However, 6G's theoretical maximum compared to 5G, has varied from anywhere between 50 times faster, or 1 terabit per second, to 1,000 times, or 2.5 terabytes per second. One can only imagine how much that will increase transmission speeds. A multi-gigabyte file that used to take seconds or a few minutes to download could be done in a snap. Where is 6G use ideal? The consumer proposition of 6G will always be front and centre, especially as digital consumption and reliance on connected devices will only become more widespread. But on an industrial scale, 6G is expected to power advanced iterations of immersive and mass communication, ubiquitous connectivity, integrated sensing and communication, low-latency and hyper-reliable communication and artificial intelligence communication, according to the International Telecommunication Union, which leads the framework and standards-setting of wireless communications. Communications, business and economic gains aside, the power of 6G will also play a critical role in society by enabling affordable, resilient and energy‑efficient networks for health, education, agriculture and disaster response, the Geneva-based UN agency said. “Advanced networks also present a way to close the persistent digital divide that today leaves many people in low-income countries behind,” it added. Transport, home appliances and security, payment networks, financial transactions and a host of other products and services expected to be highly connected in the future will also rely on the speed 6G would offer. The challenges There are a number of issues that need to be addressed to ensure the reliability of 6G networks. Arguably the biggest challenge is to build 6G networks resilient to any AI-induced compromises. Networks of the future should be able to detect threats and adaptive enough to respond to them, according to the EC-Council University in New Mexico. Encryption, especially that which can protect against quantum threats, and integration to blockchain would also be important to avoid unauthorised data access and manipulation, the university added.

events.title: Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow boss
events.summary: Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned. Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion. The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year. The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps". A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment". They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around £40 billion in economic benefits across the country". Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners. Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer". Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation. "If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said. "It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country." A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost £33bn to build. Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built. This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs. The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues. Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners". "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month . Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions. Thomas Woldbye, seen here speaking to the BBC last year, has stressed the importance of Heathrow's third runway He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK." Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks. Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue". "My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said. Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow Published 27 September Woldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full". "That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government says perpetrators of financial abuse will be pursued in court under sweeping reforms The federal government will introduce new laws cracking down on perpetrators of financial abuse. ( ABC News: Patrick Thomas ) Perpetrators of financial abuse who use the tax and social security systems to create debts as a form of coercive control could soon be held liable. The federal government today announced consultation over whether courts should be given greater flexibility to transfer a tax or social security debt to the spouse responsible for financial abuse in family law proceedings. ABC News last month flagged that Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino was taking a range of steps to combat financial abuse. "Financial abuse is often one part of a broader pattern of coercion, control and abuse designed to remove a person's independence and limit their choices," Mr Mulino said. He said the effects could follow victim-survivors for years after a relationship ended, through debts, financial insecurity and lost opportunities. Family and domestic violence support services: If you need help immediately, call emergency services on Triple Zero. 1800 Respect National Helpline : 1800 737 732 Men's Referral Service : 1300 766 491 The Kids Helpline : 24-hour support on 1800 55 1800 The reforms form part of the federal government's response to the Parliamentary Joint Committee (PJC) inquiry into financial abuse. Reforms to stop death benefit payouts and super rollovers Other reforms announced include preventing perpetrators of family and domestic violence from receiving victims' superannuation death benefits, with draft legislation to be released later this year. The government also wants to stop coerced directorships, including providing protections for victim‑survivors pressured into company directorships and associated liabilities. Daniel Mulino says he wants to stop financial abuse through the tax and super systems. ( ABC News: Stuart Carnegie ) Mr Mulino said draft legislation would be released for consultation later this year and supported by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). The government would also give the ATO powers to prevent rollovers into newly established self‑managed super funds, where there are concerns of fraud, financial abuse, misconduct, or potential consumer harm. ASFA chief policy and advocacy officer James Koval said currently a super fund may be legally obligated to pay a member's death benefit to a person who perpetrated family and domestic violence against that member. He welcomed moves to end it as well as stop rollovers of super in cases of abuse. "Once money leaves the safety of larger institutional super funds and moves into a self-managed fund, it can be very difficult to recover," he said. Perpetrators of domestic violence would be punished rather than rewarded for their actions when committing abuse against their former partners through the tax and super systems. Super Consumers Australia's director of advocacy Lily Jiang said the announcement was a positive step towards addressing the devastating impacts of financial abuse. "We need to address the risks built into the system, identify abuse before people's savings are transferred, and make sure the professionals people rely on aren't enabling that abuse," she said. Lily Jiang wants professionals who facilitate abuse to be held accountable. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Mr Mulino said the government would invest more than $180 million to reform the child support system and close loopholes that facilitated financial abuse and coercive behaviour, including through legislation it introduced in September. Government proposes crackdown on economic abuse The federal government is consulting on major reforms to reduce financial abuse, including making it harder for directors to be appointed without clear consent. It would also expand Services Australia's powers to waive social security debts incurred as a result of family and domestic violence. Ann Kayis-Kumar, the founding director of UNSW's tax and business advisory clinic, noted one in six women and one in 13 men were impacted by "this insidious form of abuse" and hoped the law changes would soon be implemented. She has long been calling for the ATO to waive debts in cases of financial abuse. Ann Kayis-Kumar wants to see the ATO waive debts in cases of financial abuse. events.title: Chinese companies seek Gulf partnerships as physical AI takes shape
events.summary: Chinese robotics companies are looking to the Gulf as a possible manufacturing centre for the next generation of AI-powered machines, as the region's capital, energy resources and industrial ambitions create opportunities for partnerships. Beijing-based robotics company LinkerBot is among those exploring opportunities in the UAE, where it is in talks with major institutions on potential partnerships, Weber Su, the company's vice president and head of global markets, said during the AIM Summit in Dubai on Tuesday. One model being considered would involve Chinese companies supplying advanced robotics parts, while the UAE provides capital-intensive assembly and automated production. Such an arrangement could allow Gulf countries to take part directly in making advanced robots, rather than mainly buying the technology. “That could be the business model that we are exploring with Middle Eastern countries, particularly in UAE,” Mr Su said. LinkerBot specialises in dexterous robotic hands, enabling machines to grasp and manipulate objects. It has expanded into components including reducers and micromotors that control robotic movement. The potential collaboration reflects a broader trend in which Asian companies seek international manufacturing partners, while Gulf economies use their capital, energy and infrastructure to build higher-value industries. In September, Chinese electric and extended-range vehicle maker ROX Motor began producing vehicles in Abu Dhabi . The UAE, meanwhile, is also boosting manufacturing and under its Operation 300bn strategy aims to increase the industrial sector's contribution to gross domestic product to Dh300 billion by 2031. The country's industrial exports rose 25 per cent last year to a record Dh262 billion, with medium and high-technology exports increasing 42 per cent to Dh92 billion, according to the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology. The UAE is also investing in automation to improve manufacturing competitiveness. Mr Su said Chinese companies could increasingly focus on specialised robotics parts, while Gulf partners develop the capital-intensive assembly operations needed to bring those technologies to market. Turning that potential into commercially successful partnerships will require investment agreements, viable production models and sustained demand for AI-powered machines. The next wave of AI? The potential partnerships come as the technology industry moves towards what investors and developers describe as the next stage of artificial intelligence: physical AI. Chinese AI developers including DeepSeek , Zhipu AI and Moonshot AI are becoming increasingly competitive with their US rivals, offering advanced models at lower costs, according to Joseph Zeng, founder and chief investment officer of Hong Kong-based Arcadia Fund Management Group. While generative AI has focused on chatbots, content creation and software applications, the next phase is expected to bring intelligent systems into the physical world. Physical AI combines advanced AI models with robotics, allowing machines to interpret their surroundings, make decisions and perform tasks traditionally requiring human intervention. Introducing vision-based tactile sensing on the LinkerHand. 320 × 240 per fingertip. 0.05 mm spatial resolution. 0.1 N force sensitivity. More than 380,000 sensing points across the hand. Touch, made visible. #LinkerHand #LinkerBot https://t.co/0u9e0MMyd0 — Linkerbot (@LinkerbotHQ) September 27, 2026 Unlike conventional industrial robots, which are generally programmed for repetitive movements, the ambition is to develop machines capable of adapting to different situations. Applications could include robotic hands manipulating unfamiliar objects, autonomous machines working across production lines and robots assisting hospital patients. Mr Su said advances in computing power and AI models were making these capabilities increasingly possible. LinkerBot is developing robotic hands with built-in movement ability that could eventually be combined with sophisticated AI systems to perform a wider range of tasks. “We're going to have skill stores similar to the app stores,” Mr Su said. China's manufacturing scale could give its companies an advantage as the technology shifts towards commercial production. The country installed about 295,000 industrial robots in 2024, accounting for 54 per cent of global installations, according to the International Federation of Robotics . The figures refer to factory robots rather than humanoids, but demonstrate the scale of China's industrial automation industry and supporting supply chains. SK hynix held 50 per cent of the global high-bandwidth memory market by revenue in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung accounted for 33 per cent, according to Counterpoint Research data reported by the Yonhap news agency. Opportunities beyond robotics "Physical AI provides a lot of opportunities for investors,” said Mr Zeng, whose investments include ByteDance and Zhipu AI in China, as well as South Korea's SK hynix and Samsung. The next stage of AI would require advances in computing hardware and infrastructure, he added. He identified high-bandwidth memory, optical transceivers and robotics components among the technologies benefitting from rising investment. Health care could also become an important market. During a recent visit to Suzhou, near Shanghai, Mr Zeng said he encountered a company developing a voice-controlled robot designed to assist bedridden patients with repositioning and personal care. Mr Su said humanoid robots could eventually help to care for elderly people and children in smaller communities, where shrinking populations make it difficult to attract doctors and maintain healthcare services. While fully autonomous, general-purpose robots are still being developed, their potential to ease labour shortages, reduce care costs and extend essential services to underserved communities illustrates the social and economic impact physical AI could have beyond factories. For the Gulf, opportunities could include using autonomous systems in established industries. Mr Zeng highlighted electric and autonomous heavy-duty trucks for mining and industrial operations, alongside energy storage and cleaner power technologies. Energy is also becoming increasingly important to AI investment. Global data-centre electricity use is expected to more than double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency . The forecast highlights the importance of electricity generation, storage and cooling infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates. For Gulf countries with substantial energy resources and growing renewable power capacity, this creates another potential area of collaboration with Asian technology developers.

events.title: Judge orders White House to reinstate press access until litigation concludes
events.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday ruled the Trump administration must continue to grant CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the White House grounds while the lawsuit filed by the three news organizations continues. Why it matters: It marks a major win for the news outlets as it maintains their White House access and signals the judge believes their legal claims could succeed on their merits. Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Trump, awarded a temporary restraining order to the plaintiffs on Sept. 24 that mandated the White House reinstate the outlets' credentials for 14 days. Last week, Kelly extended that through Oct. 13. The preliminary injunction preserves the outlets' access until the case is resolved, which could take weeks, months or years. Zoom in: "Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House 'hard pass' press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO," the court order from Judge Kelly said. Yes, but: The judge's ruling doesn't guarantee that the plaintiffs have access to key areas, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One. The White House has continued to bar CNN and Politico journalists from press pool assignments onboard Air Force One, despite the temporary restraining order reinstating their credentials. A different White House lawsuit, brought by the Associated Press, could help clarify the extent of the president's power to bar reporters from those types of spaces. That case is ongoing . Catch up quick: The news outlets sued the White House, arguing it violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints. They also argued their Fifth Amendment rights were violated as they were banned without due process. The temporary restraining order and the preliminary injunction suggest the judge believes the plaintiffs have a strong case on the Fifth Amendment claims. Further legal proceedings, including a potential trial, would determine whether the White House violated the outlets' First Amendment rights. Reality check: Legal experts believe the news organizations have a strong case because of a precedent set by the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight case in which an appeals court ruled it was unconstitutional for the White House to arbitrarily revoke press credentials based on a journalist's reporting or viewpoint. They point to comments President Trump made to justify the ban, including, "They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration." What to watch: The broader White House press pool, which consists of outlets that cover the president and travel with him on rotation, has stood in solidarity with the barred outlets. The White House reached out to other outlets to fill CNN and Politico's spots in the press pool, but they have refused. Some outlets have indicated that they intend to continue withholding publication or distribution of images captured as part of the White House still photography pool, "until a court has the chance to hear arguments on the legal claims filed by those media organizations." Disclosure: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN.

events.title: What will it take for AI-powered purchases to become the norm?
events.summary: ‘Full-stack agent-native solutions’ key to wider business adoption, Ant International’s chief innovation officer says Anyone who has spent time on the internet researching goods and doing lengthy price comparisons will be intrigued by developments in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for agentic commerce. This new form of online shopping involves AI-powered agents – autonomous software systems that use reasoning, memory and external tools to complete multi-step tasks across different sites and platforms on their own. They can carry out each stage of the buying process, from the initial search to comparing different options from multiple sellers, perhaps even negotiating, and then complete a purchase based on broad customer prompts, or even without direct human intervention. However, the potential benefits of agentic commerce are not limited to online shopping. For businesses, AI agents can help humans execute tasks from end to end and support them on actions that have clear, measurable objectives and standard operating procedures. AI agents could organise an estimated US$3 trillion to US$5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030, according to a report published earlier this year by leading management consulting firm McKinsey & Company. The key to that will be ensuring payment functions are fully integrated with the rest of the ecosystem and are guaranteed to be secure, reliable and accessible around the clock anywhere in the world. “Businesses are already leveraging AI for faster, more efficient decision-making on a range of tasks,” says Jiangming Yang, chief innovation officer at Ant International, an affiliate of financial technology company Ant Group. He adds that in the past year, nearly 90 per cent of customers of Antom – a merchant payment and digitisation platform operated by Ant International – have already adopted agentic AI tools. “But to reach the next phase of agentic commerce – where AI can be used to generate new business opportunities – merchants need full-stack AI-native solutions [end-to-end systems where AI is built into every layer of the process] that allow agents to execute securely across functions like payments, accounting, foreign exchange, treasury and growth operations,” he says. Yang also believes that adoption is likely to take off more quickly in scenarios where results of agent deployment can be assessed easily, such as business-to-business purchasing and operations. With AI agents able to handle inquiries and transactions and resolve problems autonomously around the clock – based on clearly defined rules and boundaries – there is scope to cut operating costs, improve response times and increase all-round efficiency. However, to reach that point, a number of general challenges must still be addressed. One is the issue of trust and transparency, with users likely to be sceptical about autonomous agents making buying decisions and accessing their financial data when they first adopt the technology. “The agentic era creates new risks in finance,” says Yang, whose role at Ant International includes being responsible for anticipating customer needs and staying ahead of industry trends. “Accountability, safety and traceability are crucial considerations for merchants and users in adopting these technologies.” Ant International’s two-layered security architecture is key to meeting these needs, he says. It features a first layer that protects users from existing threats such as fraud and scams with a payment-specific AI model that can simultaneously interpret various types of data and user behaviours. The second layer, meanwhile, targets agent-specific risks through Ant International’s know-your-agent (KYA) framework, which verifies not only the agent’s digital identity, but also that it is acting within the authorised user-defined parameters such as the purpose or budget. Another issue is the so-called integration complexity, where fragmented payment systems can make the seamless deployment of AI agents technically challenging, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises with limited resources. Yang also stresses the importance of the use of an interoperable framework that can help businesses reduce duplicated work processes related to agentic commerce while maintaining trust and managing risks. One significant advance in AI agents enacting payments is Ant International’s Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP). Launched in April, the company describes the framework as the world’s first mobile-first, “wallet-agnostic” open protocol designed for cross-border agentic commerce. Last month, Ant International announced that 10 digital wallets within its Alipay+ digital cross-border payment network will support AMP in their own agentic payment architectures.

events.title: Conflicting advice left prospector stranded on outback tenement
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Goldfields prospector allowed to retrieve equipment after being stranded on outback tenement Dale Richardson's tenement and belongings he had to leave behind in March. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) Conflicting advice over whether he could or could not legally access his outback tenement left Goldfields prospector Dale Richardson stranded for almost a month. Mr Richardson says he was forced to break the law to leave the site, more than 1,000km north-east of Perth, to return home. He says the confusing situation highlights the need for reform of WA's Aboriginal heritage and access laws. A prospector was left stranded on a remote tenement with dwindling supplies for almost a month due to conflicting advice from WA's former Aboriginal Affairs Minister and the state's planning and heritage bureaucracy. Prospector Dale Richardson had approval for the tenement near Cosmo Newbery, about 1,000 kilometres north-east of Perth, since 2021 under the WA Mining Act. But he has faced more than two years of confusion over whether he can drive out to the ground he has pegged without breaching WA's Aboriginal Heritage and Planning laws. Dale Richardson says the experience has been confusing. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) In a move WA's peak mining and exploration body says highlights the need for reform of the laws, the confusion culminated in Mr Richardson being stranded on the tenement, unsure if he could leave without breaching the law. He was on the tenement on February 27 this year when he received advice from the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage that he could no longer drive along the remote White Cliffs-Yarmarna Road, contradicting previous advice he had obtained. He stayed until his supplies ran low, leaving on March 21, but left his caravan and most of his prospecting equipment behind. In September, Mr Richardson was told by the department that he had breached Section 31 of act by using the road, but no formal action would be taken against him. The road at the heart of Mr Richardson's situation passes through the Cosmo Newbery West and South Aboriginal Reserves, generally requiring permission to access under the Aboriginal Affairs Planning Authority Act. But in December 2024, former Aboriginal Affairs Minister Tony Buti wrote to Mr Richardson confirming he did not need a permit to travel along the road. That advice was reversed in February, when the department advised the minister's earlier ruling had been incorrect, based on an additional investigation and information provided by Central Desert Native Title Services. The department initially advised the road Mr Richardson was using did not meet the gazetted route, and he would be obliged to use a track that had not been maintained for more than 60 years. Dale Richardson says this is the track Don Punch said he had to use to access his tenements. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) But in a subsequent update, it ruled a Federal Native Title decision meant the road was no longer gazetted, and he would need a separate mining permit to use it. A Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage spokesperson said advice on road access had been based on the information available when access to the tenements was initially sought. "I've done everything that I was legally supposed to do," Mr Richardson said. "I've tried to get a permit, I've tried to negotiate an agreement, they're just not willing to do so for some reason." The Yilka Talintji Aboriginal Corporation, which represents the area's native title holders, declined to speak to the ABC. White Cliffs-Yamarna road, at the start of Cosmo Newberry Reserve. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) While not at risk of prosecution, Mr Richardson said he had been left with little opportunity to retrieve his caravan and equipment. Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch intervened late last week, granting the prospector a three-month permit to return to the site, remove his property and secure his prospecting equipment. The limited permission does not allow Mr Richardson to resume prospecting. Don Punch granted Mr Richardson a three-month permit to access the site and secure his equipment. ( ABC News: Briana Shepherd ) Labelling the matter complex and unusual, Mr Punch said the Aboriginal Lands Trust had only wished to grant Mr Richardson seven days' access, but he had opted to overrule the body. "Since being made aware of the matter, my office has remained engaged with the relevant parties," he said. Mr Richardson said he wanted to work and rehabilitate his tenements, actions he continues to hold a license for.

events.title: Failed caravan company AOR allegedly traded insolvent since 2023
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Failed caravan company Australian Off Road allegedly traded insolvent since 2023 Australian Off Road suddenly shut its doors in September, leaving dozens of staff unemployed. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Josh Dye ) Administrators for collapsed caravan company Australian Off Road have detailed fresh allegations against its directors. Nearly 50 customers who paid for caravans that were not built are among the creditors owed $14 million. Administrators say AOR may have been trading insolvently since 2023. A failed Queensland caravan manufacturer may have been trading while insolvent for three years, according to administrators, who say the company owes $14 million. Australian Off Road (AOR) shut its doors in September after 26 years operating on the Sunshine Coast, becoming the second local van manufacturer after Zone RV to collapse within a year. Nearly 50 customers face losing $2.25 million after making progress payments toward caravans that were not built. They include Sandra Muller from NSW Southern Highlands, who stands to lose $101,000. Sandra Muller has paid $101,000 towards her caravan, which was not built. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) In a report to creditors on Tuesday night, administrators DVT McLeods detailed fresh allegations against directors Russell Evans and Steve Budden and said AOR may have been insolvent for more than three years. Potential offences identified included insolvent trading, reckless or intentional dishonesty, failure to act in good faith, and improper use of position to gain advantage. "We have a preliminary view that the company traded whilst insolvent from at least 30 June 2023," the report stated. Administrators also said AOR's creditor bill had grown to $14 million, up from $9 million estimated last month . The administrators said further investigations were required and that the results would be reported to ASIC, the corporate regulator. The ABC has attempted to contact Mr Evans and Mr Budden. Mr Evans is one of two parties offering to purchase the company out of administration. He has pitched to investors seeking $2 million to resurrect AOR in a move that could leave existing customers empty-handed. It is legal for a director to buy and transfer a company's assets into a new business if the sale is approved by creditors. The ABC has seen an email from Mr Evans outlining his vision "to establish a new, financially disciplined premium off-road caravan manufacturing business". His proposal offered 20 cents in the dollar for the company's assets, while the existing company's debts would not carry across. The pitch pledged to "recognise customers who paid deposits" and "investigate practical solutions for affected customers" but did not clarify whether all progress payments would be honoured. Inside the Australian Off Road factory in China. ( Supplied ) Mr Evans said the new business would have "a clean financial structure" and "a clear pathway to sustainable profitability and growth". Mr Evans's proposal detailed projected annual revenue of $11.3 million with production of 84 caravans, or seven a month. The new venture would "create a new, low-cost and scalable caravan business", he wrote. Despite marketing itself as an Australian manufacturer and blaming imported Chinese vans for its demise, the ABC can reveal AOR was making chassis in China. A separate company with a factory north of Shanghai was established in 2025 to reduce AOR's production costs. The Chinese company is owed $518,000 but falls among the unsecured creditors. AOR made a loss in three of the past four financial years, and had a negative asset position of $3 million when it collapsed, the creditors report stated. Administrators engaged Argus Auctions to advertise the sale of the business or its assets. After receiving 200 enquiries, 20 parties signed non-disclosure agreements, with feedback that "stock was outdated and poorly managed" and there was a "lack of operational systems and structure". Russell Evans joined AOR about 2012 and became a director in 2021. ( Supplied ) Only two parties made offers to buy the company, including Mr Evans's proposal. The administrators said they were investigating allegations that caravans fully paid for by some customers had been delivered to other people. If you know more about this story, contact Josh Dye at dye.josh@abc.net.au The report noted the company's CCTV system ceased recording on September 9, the day the company stopped trading. "Due to the limited clarity and quality of the footage … we are unable to determine with certainty … whether any caravans were moved within or removed from the premises," the report stated.

events.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 03:05 BST Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday. The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said. Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC. The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning. "Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added. In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks." The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said. The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied. OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said.
