events.title: Reassessment of billion-dollar silver mine sparks tractor protest
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Opponents hold tractor protest as IPC begins reassessment of Bowdens silver mine Fifteen tractors and dozens of trucks and utes weave through Mudgee, honking horns and receiving waves of support from locals. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) is reassessing the proposed Bowdens silver mine near Mudgee. Protesters drove tractors through the town today to express their opposition to the development. Three days of hearings are being held by the IPC before a determination is made. Plans for a $1 billion silver and lead mine in Central West New South Wales are being reassessed as opponents take to the streets of Mudgee in tractors to protest. Approval of the Bowdens Silver Mines Limited project was deemed "void" by the NSW Court of Appeal in August 2024. It had been approved by the state's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) in April the previous year. That decision was overturned when the court ruled the IPC should have examined the potential environmental impacts of the project's transmission line. The IPC has now started three days of hearings as part of its reassessment. Silver Mines Limited managing director Jo Batershill told the panel today the merits of the project were now stronger than when it was approved in 2023. He said it was in the best interests of the local and regional economy, the state's strategic minerals goals and the nation's contribution to the global renewable energy transition. The proponents are seeking approval to extract 30 million tonnes of ore over 23 years. A group of protesters gathered in Mudgee ahead of the public hearing on the Bowdens silver project. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Today's "tractorcade" was similar to a protest held in 2023 when residents of Lue, about 26 kilometres east of Mudgee, disrupted traffic through the famous wine region. Protester Tom Combes, who farms sheep and cattle at Lue, described the mine proposal as "just nuts". Tom Combes was one of more than 40 residents outside the IPC hearing in Mudgee with signs and shirts voicing their opposition to the development. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) "All the people that live out there, all of their lifestyle, their health and their amenity is going to be destroyed," he said. Mr Combes is one of 97 speakers set to give evidence over the next three days. A conditional safeguard measure introduced by the IPC during the previous assessment saw Silver Mines Limited offer voluntary blood testing for residents and, in particular children at Lue Public School, 2 kilometres from the project. Janet Walk lives 9 kilometres from the proposed site and told the IPC the offer made her nervous. "You don't test children's blood unless you think the lead is going to appear in the blood," she said. "There is no safe level of lead in a child's blood. "The monitoring will tell us that the child has lead in their blood, but it won't stop it, it won't treat it." Janet Walk told the hearing that the mine could put children at risk. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Tractor protest participant Jamie Inglis, whose cattle property is 5 kilometres from the site, shared that fear. "There are a number of concerns… contamination of Lawson Creek, which is the lifeblood of our farmers," he said. "We don't need silver and we definitely don't need lead." Susannah White raised about the potential impact of lead on livestock. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) Susannah White was worried about the future of her beef farm on Lawson Creek, downstream of the proposed mine site. She referenced the Australian and New Zealand Food Standards Code, which stipulates that livestock cannot be sold or consumed if lead above 0.24µmol/L is detected in the animal. "If this mine is approved it means our business is unviable," she told the hearing. "These animals could need destroying because they can't be sold and they can't be moved. "What are the animal welfare implications when you run out of feed because you can't sell the animals like you normally would?" The 2023 IPC decision was successfully challenged by the Bingman Catchment Landcare Group. The court found the panel failed to consider the impacts of a 13km transmission line that the Department of Planning and Environment had deemed required a separate application. Dozens of people drove tractors from Lue to Mudgee, where the IPC is holding a three-day hearing into the Bowdens silver mine application. ( ABC Central West: Hamish Cole ) In response, the state government passed legislative changes that allow off-site infrastructure for state significant projects to be assessed separately.

events.title: An eerie trip inside Thailand’s oldest amusement park, deserted after flooding
events.summary: Siam Amazing Park was forced to close after rising water damaged rides and left parts of the park inaccessible With its mouth agape, the giant lion’s head is frozen in a roar. No water rushes down the log flume that descends from its heights, while at ground level, the vast amusement park stands empty of noise and activity except for leaves blowing in a light breeze. Welcome to Siam Amazing Park, billed as the longest-running amusement park in south-east Asia, and certainly in Thailand . Up to a million people rush in every year for thrills on rides like the Boomerang, an orange rollercoaster that loop-the-loops at 80km/h (50mph), or to splash around under the tropical sun in one of the world’s largest wave pools. It now stands empty, after being closed late last month when it started raining in Bangkok and did not stop for days . It could take more than six months for the park to reopen. Managing director Wuthichai Luangamornlert sits in an airconditioned conference room at the park’s entrance. Below his office, rows of turnstiles stand empty where just days before, thousands of tourists and local visitors were eagerly pushing through. He was not too alarmed when the rains began at the end of September . The area on the outskirts of Bangkok has seen heavy rains before – the megacity itself is built on floodplains and has a network of muddy canals and pumps to drain water. “When it rains a lot, it will dry off and the water will go away by the next morning,” he says. But the next morning came and it was still raining, and the day after, it was still raining. “The water level keeps rising. So that’s when we knew that it was not normal.” After three days, the sewers filled up and much of the park turned into a giant lake, with the water level reaching around knee height. Many of the motors and electrical systems that power the rides were damaged. Buildings around the park are still marked with lines of silt – the markers a flood leaves behind. Wuthichai’s father, Chaiwat, who opened the park in 1980, is famous in Thailand for his rags-to-riches tale, and kept prices discounted so the average Thai family could afford a rare visit. The son is now managing things, and says it is odd how rapidly his mindset changed from that of little concern to the reality of having the park closed for six months, or longer. “It happened within a few hours,” he says. This story of unstoppable rising water is one told across the city, where the government declared a flood disaster across all 50 districts. For days, people were forced to use boats to get to their destroyed homes, and those who did not have boats used inflatable pool toys. Weeks later, only puddles are left, although many canals are full and the rainy season is not over. Climate scientists warn the world is indeed experiencing a slow-moving crisis as the planet bakes due to human-induced heating, although it is too early to attribute Bangkok’s rains to climate breakdown, and the picture is complicated by an abnormally strong El Niño, a cyclical weather pattern that brings violent extremes. In the water section of the amusement park, dry water slides drop directly into murky flood waters, while deck chairs stand abandoned. Small fish have entered the once-chlorinated waters, making their home in waters turned green with algae which were previously bright azure. The wider park – which was built to be bursting with children, laughter and blaring music – remains spectacularly eerie. Stalls offering rice and spicy meat as well as American-style food such as hotdogs stand empty, although their price boards remain outside. Wuthichai says the park’s primary concern was their several hundred staff. The business is not as strong as it was before the Covid pandemic, he says, when they were forced to close but did not make redundancies. Several rollercoasters are foreign-made and need specialised parts and labour from Europe or Japan that could take months to arrive. At least the double-decker carousel at the park entrance is bespoke and locally made, he adds. The owners expect the cost of repair, and the lost revenue from being closed, to reach millions of US dollars. Short of cash, they have asked for a debt holiday from banks, help from the government, and are also considering offers to buy the park. “There are people who are still interested, still making appointments all the time,” says Wuthichai, who sits next to his adult son, the third generation of the family business. “We have not made a decision yet.”

events.title: Justice Department says North Koreans have infiltrated dozens of US companies
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The U.S. Department of Justice is warning that hackers working for the North Korean regime are increasingly relying on Americans to facilitate the hacking of U.S. companies. In an announcement on Tuesday, prosecutors said they have indicted and arrested at least two people, and conducted searches across dozens of suspected “laptop farms” in Texas. The computers were allegedly used by North Koreans to remotely hack into American companies and steal sensitive data. According to the DOJ, federal authorities seized over 180 computers that they believe American companies had shipped out to their newly hired employees, not realizing that they were sanctioned North Korean spies who had used stolen identities of U.S. citizens to gain employment. The DOJ said that it raided over 40 laptop farms across Texas, the largest disclosed number of homes and residences used for facilitating North Korean hacks, which were owned by at least two American facilitators. CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate and disrupt the latest North Korean operations, said that laptop farms are “vital” to North Korea in helping its hackers overcome physical, financial, and legal challenges of not physically being in the United States. The prosecutors said at least 70 U.S.-based companies had been infiltrated by the hackers, who are believed to have generated around $3 million in stolen funds. The DOJ did not name the affected companies, but described them as healthcare, cyber support, retail, communications, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio and 16 other states, including the District of Columbia. “Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals,” the Justice Department said . Oftentimes, North Korean hackers use real-looking email addresses, spoofed LinkedIn profiles, and extensive online and social media accounts as cover for their activities. In a separate public service announcement , the FBI said that there are “thousands” of North Korean state-controlled IT workers working at Western companies, which “pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.” This is the latest wave of arrests, indictments, and enforcement action targeting North Korean activities in the United States in recent years. The breakaway regime has used this “remote IT workers” scheme to allow North Koreans to gain employment with U.S. and European companies, earn a wage, and then steal sensitive information and intellectual property while as employees. The victim companies are then extorted into paying the hackers further. The remote IT workers’ scheme is one of several strands of illicit revenue that the North Korean regime aims to generate, including hacking crypto exchanges and open source developer projects , with the aim of funding its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. The regime is thought to have stolen at least $2 billion in crypto during 2025 alone. Experts on North Korea have put the number of hacked companies and the amount of stolen crypto as likely much higher than reported. Earlier this year, CrowdStrike said in a separate report that North Korean hackers were behind around half of all documented “hands-on-keyboard” intrusions over the past year, referring to hacks that are carried out by humans and not automated tools or AI. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Federal Court declares Commonwealth's blocking of NSW goldmine 'invalid' Regis Resources argued the Commonwealth's decision rendered its goldmine unviable in its current form. ( ABC News: Lani Oataway ) A Federal Court judge has found an Aboriginal protection order that halted an approved goldmine in NSW was "invalid". Regis Resources launched the legal action in 2024, challenging the Commonwealth's decision relating to its McPhillamys Gold Project. Justice James Stellios ruled that the project must be referred back to the federal minister for re-determination. The Federal Court has overturned a Commonwealth decision that halted a billion-dollar goldmine in New South Wales. Regis Resources launched legal action against then federal minister for environment and water Tanya Plibersek in November 2024, challenging the validity of an Aboriginal protection order she granted over part of its McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney. The order applied to 400 hectares of the site, including an area where the company wanted to build a tailings dam, which is used to hold mining waste. It was made after the mining project received approval in 2023 . At the time, Ms Plibersek said the order would protect the headwaters and springs of the Belubula River and that the company could construct its tailings storage elsewhere. But Regis Resources disputed this, saying the decision affected a critical area of the project development site and meant the project was "no longer financially feasible". The Belubula River originates at the mine site. ( ABC News: Xanthe Gregory ) Justice James Stellios has presided over the Federal Court challenge and held two days of hearings in December 2025 . He delivered his judgment during a short sitting today, which found that Regis Resources was successful in the judicial review and the minister's "declaration is invalid". The Aboriginal protection order was granted after Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds lodged an application to protect the area under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act in 2020. Tanya Plibersek granted the Aboriginal protection order over part of the McPhillamys mine site in 2024. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) The court heard the application was supported by the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC) and referred to a Dreaming story called the Blue Banded Bee. Justice Stellios told the court that this information "constituted a new application" and should have been referred to the government reporter for consideration and to carry out a public consultation process. "The court's decision and my reasons say nothing about the merits of the claim ... whether it's a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration ... those are matters within the authority of the minister ... not the jurisdiction of this court." In a statement the WTOCWAC said it was "disappointed by the court's decision" and will take time to consider the implications of the judgment. "This case has always been about protecting places of profound cultural and spiritual significance to Wiradyuri people," the group said. "The court's decision does not diminish the cultural significance of these places, nor does it alter our obligation to speak for and care for Country." Regis Resources took the office of the federal environment minister, now held by Murray Watt, to the Federal Court. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Justice Stellios said the appropriate remedy was for the proposal to be sent back to the federal minister for environment and water, a position now held by Murray Watt, for redetermination. He ordered the parties to provide written submissions on costs to be submitted by October 27. In a statement, Senator Watt said he respected the ruling. "The Judge specifically made the point that his decision did not concern the merits of the Minister's decision … instead, the court's decision was based on an error in the process used to grant the declaration," he said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told parliament during Question Time that the government was carefully considering the judgment. Senator Watt said it was "an example of how complex the current cultural heritage processes are for everyone involved". "We remain committed to working alongside [First Nations people, industry and state and territory governments] on a better system," he said. In a statement, Regis Resources said "after considerable delay and uncertainty, and more than two years of time lost" it was "eager to move forward" to advance one of the country's largest undeveloped gold projects.

events.title: MAS keeps Singdollar appreciation rate unchanged but warns of elevated inflation
events.summary: Unlike most central banks, which target interest rates, MAS uses S$NEER, a trade-weighted basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners. MAS kept Singapore dollar policy unchanged, but said the war-linked energy shock will keep inflation elevated until 2027. The bank said the S$NEER band will keep strengthening to curb imported inflation, after two policy tightenings in 2026. Core inflation rose to 2.1% in July to August, and MAS expects growth to stay steady as GDP grew 5.4% in the third quarter. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s central bank maintained its monetary policy stance, but warned that persistent energy price pressures from the Iran war will keep inflation elevated well into 2027. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Oct 14 that it will keep unchanged the rate of appreciation of the Singapore dollar’s trade-weighted value, also called the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) policy band. Unlike most central banks, which target interest rates, MAS uses S$NEER, which is a trade-weighted basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners. This is because, in a small and open economy such as Singapore’s – where gross exports and imports of goods and services are more than 300% of gross domestic product (GDP) and almost 40 cents of every dollar spent domestically is on imports – the exchange rate has a much stronger influence on inflation than interest rates. MAS said: “The current appreciating policy band will allow the S$NEER to continue to strengthen and lean against the anticipated near-term rise in imported inflation, ensuring the gradual easing of inflationary pressures in 2027.” Faced with sticky inflation amid an unresolved energy shock from the Iran war, MAS has tightened its policy stance twice in 2026 – in April and July – allowing for a stronger S$NEER that helps dampen the impact of rising import costs. Global crude oil benchmark Brent was trading around US$106 a barrel on Oct 14, up more than 70% since the start of the year, as supplies from the Middle East remained constrained amid the Iran war and the conflict between top oil exporter Saudi Arabia and Yemen. “Since September, energy commodity prices have risen anew and are projected to remain high in the near term,” said the central bank. Global and regional food prices are also expected to pick up as costlier inputs and adverse weather patterns impact food production. Firming imported cost pressures in Singapore will keep core and all-items inflation at the current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead, MAS said. Core inflation, which excludes the costs of accommodation and private transport from all-items inflation, rose to 2.1% on the year in July to August, from 1.5% in the second quarter. For 2026 as a whole, core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2%, while all-items inflation should come in around 2%. This is lower than MAS’ July forecast of 1.5% to 2.5% for both core and all-items inflation. MAS said inflation should ease more discernibly in the second half of 2027 as global energy prices gradually moderate. But with inflation running high all the way to mid-2027, both core and all-items inflation are projected to average 1.5% to 2.5% – higher than the historical average of 1.5 per cent. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Danish investment bank Saxo, said MAS’ decision to leave policy settings unchanged was a surprise relative to market expectations. However, the pause should not be seen as a pivot. “After two rounds of tightening in 2026, policymakers appear comfortable giving earlier measures more time to work rather than responding aggressively to every inflation risk,” Chanana said. DBS Bank’s senior economist Chua Han Teng said the pause likely reflected a softer-than-expected 2026 inflation outlook, with MAS lowering the top end of its previous forecast. However, the relatively higher projection for 2027 alludes to the persistent risk of energy prices remaining volatile for longer. “MAS likely kept the door open for another calibrated tightening if needed,” he said. For now, economic growth is not a worry for the central bank, with strong demand for Singapore’s AI-related exports, such as semiconductors, and an increase in production capacity across the technology sector. In its quarterly Macroeconomic Review report, also released on Oct 14, MAS said technology-related sectors have accounted for around 75% of overall growth. While there was some moderation in electronics output growth in early third quarter, it said this likely reflected capacity constraints in the global supply chain as underlying AI-related demand remained firm. The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry’s (METI’s) advance estimates released on Oct 14 showed Singapore’s overall GDP grew by 5.4% year on year in the third quarter. In August, METI projected Singapore’s GDP to grow 4.5% to 5.5% in 2026.

events.title: 'A lot of emotion:' First round of redundancies to hit Whyalla steelworks
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts First round of redundancies to exit Whyalla steelworks by end of week More than 250 Whyalla steelworks employees have accepted redundancies since the permanent closure of the blast furnace. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) The first of more than 250 Whyalla steelworks employees to accept redundancies will leave on Friday. The plant's direct workforce will be reduced due to the permanent closure of the blast furnace last month. Workers have told the ABC they feel uncertain about their future in the steelmaking town. The first of more than 250 workers to accept redundancies at the Whyalla steelworks will finish up this week — but those who want to stay are still facing an anxious wait. The permanent closure of the blast furnace last month will reduce the plant's direct workforce from 1,700 to 1,200, while at least another 300 contractor roles will also be affected. Australian Workers' Union organiser Shane Karger said he expected about 270 direct employees to accept "genuine redundancies" by the end of this month. The first group of those will exit by this Friday. Mr Karger said following that, voluntary redundancies and early retirement scheme applications would be processed. Genuine redundancy occurs when a worker's role is no longer required, for example, those who were working at the blast furnace. He said voluntary redundancies would go to workers in departments that would reduce their numbers but not shut down entirely. Shane Karger said it's been a emotional time for workers in Whyalla. ( ABC News ) Mr Karger said the final number of redundancies should be known by November. "[That] will then sort out how many positions are up for redeployment," he said. Even for those who stay on, it is unclear what the future will look like. The steelworks has been in administration since early last year, with the announcement of a buyer expected by the end of 2026. Mr Karger said unions have been working with administrators KordaMentha to make the process as fast and smooth as possible. "There's been a lot of emotion," he said. "You've got other workers that are looking forward to a well-earned rest after a very long career at the steelworks." The steelworks was forced into administration in February last year. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Several contractors have confirmed to the ABC that they have already laid off staff, with more than one closing down entirely. Jack Taylor, 30, has done manual labour at the steelworks for 10 years but will clock off for the final time this week. His was one of the roles being cut and he has opted not to apply for redeployment, instead accepting a redundancy. "It was a big decision to make," he said. "I own my house here in Whyalla so going for redeployment [would have] meant I'd have a chance of keeping a job, having income coming in." Jack Taylor accepted a redundancy. ( ABC News ) Mr Taylor said years of uncertainty over the future of the steelworks had taken a toll. "We've been through administration two times. "I'm just a bit over all of it, to be honest." He plans to apply for fly-in-fly-out jobs in the mining sector, and hopes to stay in Whyalla. "I've got my family, the footy club, all my friends and that here," he said. events.title: SoftBank junk bond sale raises stakes for CEO Son’s all-in AI bet
events.summary: The scale of Masayoshi Son’s investments, which include backing of about US$64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. SoftBank’s record US$11 billion junk-bond sale shows pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to prove his huge AI bet will pay off, especially through OpenAI. The company is borrowing at up to 9.75% to keep assets it expects to rise in value, while investors worry about concentration risk and possible AI market overheating. Analysts say SoftBank’s AI bets are far bigger and riskier than before, with mixed past results, but supporters believe AI could still bring major financial gains. TOKYO – SoftBank’s promise to pay its highest-ever yields in a record US$11 billion (S$14.1 billion) junk-bond offering highlights the pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to secure returns on his all-in bet on AI amid concerns about possible overheating in the market. The SoftBank debt issuance in September added to a sharp surge in corporate borrowing in 2026, including major bond sales from Amazon.com, Alphabet and Tencent. The scale of Son’s investments, which include backing totalling US$64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. Those fresh investments are now coming under sharper scrutiny by analysts and investors amid worries about the degree of concentration in SoftBank’s portfolio and whether a payoff from the expenditures by AI companies will come soon enough. SoftBank previously sold shares in Nvidia and T-Mobile US to fund its investments, but it is now borrowing at record yields of up to 9.75% to retain assets that it believes will appreciate, a senior SoftBank executive told Reuters. “We’ve borrowed money in large part because we don’t want to sell assets that we believe will keep rising in value,” said Alex Clavel, CEO of SoftBank Investment Advisers, which manages the Vision Funds. Sam Altman’s OpenAI is the core investment in the latest iteration of Son’s investment strategy, following lucrative bets on Chinese tech giant Alibaba and chip designer Arm. “Given OpenAI’s appreciation to date, 9.75% is still very reasonable,” Clavel said. Arm’s valuation has grown fivefold since it floated in 2023 and further listings from SoftBank’s private AI portfolio would clarify their value and more easily allow the assets to be monetised for additional investment activity. Altman has said OpenAI will not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns about artificial intelligence. It also faces competition from rival Anthropic and hyperscalers, as well as low-cost Chinese labs. SoftBank was previously “betting on a bunch of numbers at the roulette table. Now it’s red or black, either lose everything or gain everything”, said analyst David Gibson of MST Financial. Increased scrutiny of AI-related fundraising SoftBank will pay its highest-ever coupon of 9.75% on a bond issued in September that matures in 2034. That return compares with Alphabet offering 5.2% for a bond issued in August that matures in 2033. SoftBank’s shares surged to a record high of 8,632 yen in June, though they have fallen 38% since then, while its credit default swap spreads – the cost to insure its debt against a default or other credit event – jumped 24% over the same period. SoftBank’s higher yields reflect investor perceptions of their risk and concentration in large positions, analysts say. “The bets are much bigger than we’ve ever seen,” said Amir Anvarzadeh of Asymmetric Advisors, who recommends shorting the stock. James Athey, a fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough, said the fund was not allocating to high-yield bonds at this stage of the credit cycle, given current tight spread levels. “SoftBank is so aggressive, so concentrated and so all-in, I don’t think we’d be looking there first anyway,” he said. Clavel, however, says SoftBank’s OpenAI backing reflects their deep business ties. “We see OpenAI as a partner, building a relationship that can deliver strategic value as well as financial returns,” he said. OpenAI is also an investor in and customer of data centre company SB Energy, which SoftBank is looking to list and may seek a valuation of US$50 billion, Reuters has reported. “SoftBank is taking advantage of hyper-excitement around AI-driven businesses, applying very high valuations for relatively low revenues, and they are looking to capitalise,” said MST’s Gibson of the potential valuation. Son’s bets have a mixed track record – his investment in Chinese tech giant Alibaba was a major success, but Son also directed US$16 billion to Adam Neumann’s WeWork, which ultimately went bankrupt. Other setbacks included a crash in the value of its investments as central banks moved to hike rates in 2022. “OpenAI’s value appreciation to date far exceeds the losses in our 2021 vintage investments,” Clavel said.

events.title: Singapore’s GDP grew by 5.4% in third quarter of 2026
events.summary: On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the Singapore economy expanded by 1.1%, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter. Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter of 2026, slower than 6.2% in the previous quarter, said METI on Oct 14. Manufacturing rose 7.5%, while construction grew 8.8% as public and private projects increased. Services also grew, led by wholesale trade, transport, IT, finance and hotels. METI said fuller third-quarter GDP data, including inflation, jobs and productivity, will be released in the Economic Survey of Singapore in November 2026. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter, moderating from 6.2% in the previous quarter. This was higher than the 5.1% consensus estimate in a Bloomberg poll. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the economy expanded by 1.1%, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter, said the Ministry of Energy , Trade and Industry (METI) on Oct 14. The manufacturing sector grew by 7.5% year on year in the third quarter, slower than the 12.9% growth in the previous quarter. The construction sector expanded by 8.8% year on year in the third quarter, faster than the 6.1% growth in the preceding quarter, as both public- and private-sector construction output increased. Among the services sectors, the wholesale and retail trade, and transportation and storage sectors collectively grew by 8% year on year in the third quarter, extending the 6.9% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the retail trade sector. Growth in the wholesale trade sector was led by the machinery, equipment and supplies segment, which saw strong growth in tandem with the robust increase in electronics exports over the same period. Meanwhile, growth in the transportation and storage sector was supported largely by the water and air transport segments. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the wholesale and retail trade, and transportation and storage sectors as a whole grew by 2.2%, improving from zero growth in the second quarter. The group of sectors comprising the information and communications, finance and insurance and professional services sectors expanded by 4.3% year on year in the third quarter, easing from the 5.1% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group grew during the quarter. Growth in the information and communications sector was driven by the IT and information services segment, while that in the professional services sector was largely supported by the architectural and engineering, as well as the technical testing and analysis services segments. Growth in the finance and insurance sector was led by the fund management and banking services segments. On a quarter-to-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, this group of sectors expanded by 0.4%, moderating from the 2.8% growth in the second quarter. Growth in the remaining group of services sectors, comprising accommodation and food services, real estate, administrative and support services, and other services industries, came in at 2.1% year on year in the third quarter, extending the 2.4% growth in the preceding quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the food and beverage services sector. In particular, the accommodation sector grew on the back of an increase in gross lettings in the higher value-added hotel segments. On a quarter-to-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the sectors in this group collectively expanded by 0.6%, easing from the 0.8% growth in the second quarter. Selena Ling, chief economist and head of OCBC group research, said Singapore’s economic growth continued to be driven by AI- and electronics-related activity, trade and transportation services, as well as construction and infrastructure. She noted that construction growth accelerated sharply in the third quarter, supported by both public- and private-sector activity, while trade and transportation services strengthened on the back of robust regional trade and continued demand for AI-related electronics. Finance, information and communications, and professional services also continued to expand at a solid pace, but consumer-facing and other domestic services lagged. “This divergence creates a dual-speed expansion where businesses linked to construction, trade and advanced electronics may continue to benefit from strong demand, while consumer-oriented sectors face a more challenging environment, especially on the domestic cost front and tightening financial conditions,” she said. Zavier Wong, market analyst at trading platform eToro, said the strong economic growth has yet to translate into tangible benefits for many households. “Most households aren’t seeing that growth in their wallets,” he said.

events.title: Global standard-setting bodies publish final report on guidance for FMIs on general business risks and general business losses
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) CPMI and IOSCO issue their final report on FMIs’ management of general business risks and losses. The report provides supplemental guidance to the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for financial market infrastructures . The Bank for International Settlements’ Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) and the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) today published a final report on financial market infrastructures’ (FMIs) management of general business risks and general business losses. The report sets out guidance for FMIs and relevant authorities, including in the context of FMIs’ recovery and orderly wind-down, on: i. identifying, monitoring and managing general business risks; ii. determining the minimum amount of liquid net assets funded by equity to be held against potential general business losses; and iii. governance and transparency in managing general business risks. The final report builds upon the consultative report on general business losses published in November 2025. It takes into account the findings of the Level 3 assessment report on the implementation of PFMI Principle 15 (General business risk), which identified issues relating to FMIs' management of general business risks and the liquid net assets funded by the equity they hold to cover potential losses. Consultation responses can be found here . CPMI and IOSCO appreciate the thorough responses and engagement received from respondents.

( Supplied: HBO Max ) HBO's Girls will be back for five episodes. Production will begin in 2027, 10 years after the series finale. The core cast will make a comeback but it is unclear whether movie star Adam Driver will join them. HBO's Emmy-winning series Girls is returning for five episodes. The returning cast will include creator, star, writer and director Lena Dunham as Hannah, Allison Williams as Marnie, Jemima Kirke as Jessa, Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna and Andrew Rannells as Elijah. In a mock Zoom call, Dunham, Williams, Kirke, Mamet and Rannells committed to a limited run. "I have a question though," Dunham says. One unanswered question is whether Hollywood movie star Adam Driver will return to the fold. His breakout performance as Adam Sackler in Girls earned him three consecutive Primetime Emmy nominations. While Andrew Rannells (right) was part of the announcement, Adam Driver (left) was not. ( Supplied: HBO Max ) In a statement, Dunham said it was rare to get the chance to return to something that changed your life with the gift of hindsight and a whole new level of gratitude and understanding. "I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day. "Then, right around my 40th birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. "And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop." Dunham said new people were still discovering the show, reminding her why "we do this". The "why" being the joy of being together, as well as the chance to wear yellow mesh, she joked. Girls was considered groundbreaking. ( Supplied: HBO Max ) The cast of Girls will be dealing with a different world and different issues as they examine what it means to be in their 40s as opposed to their 20s. The show will be executive produced by Judd Apatow. Production will begin in 2027, a decade after the season six finale. Girls won two Emmys, including Outstanding Casting for a Comedy Series, and was nominated 19 times. Girls ran from 2012 to 2017 and was set in New York City. events.title: Mike Johnson's Latino voter problem keeps getting worse
events.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years. Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018. The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research. In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%. That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis , a leading authority on Latino voting behavior. Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP. In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown. The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters. Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys. Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living. 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue. 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans. That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February. The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. The Equis survey is the latest indication they could help Democrats take back Congress. Note: The Equis survey was conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2 via phone and text-to-web with 1,800 registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino nationally. The sample was weighted to match the composition of registered voters modeled as Latino by state, gender, age, education, vote history, voter registration date, VCH score and 2024 vote recall.

events.title: Democrats fear "more October surprises" after "bullshit" raid on Ilhan Omar's home
events.summary: Congressional Democrats' private text chains lit up with fear and anger on Monday after Department of Homeland Security agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home in Washington, D.C. Why it matters: The search came less than a month before the midterms , immediately setting off alarm bells among Democrats that "more October surprises" could be coming, as one senior Democrat told Axios. Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) told Axios: "We expect more of this kind of thing." Driving the news: Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" on Omar's home as part of an ongoing immigration probe, the Justice Department said in a statement. DOJ has not detailed the scope or subject of the search warrant. Fox News reported the investigation concerns Omar's immigration paperwork. She came to the United States in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee from Somalia. Omar's office and Democratic House leadership quickly denounced the action as an "abuse of power," with a spokesperson for Omar saying she "has done nothing wrong." What we're hearing: "People are outraged. ... [This is] what authoritarian tyrants and dictators do," said the senior House Democrat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to relay colleagues' private conversations. Another House Democrat told Axios "the chatter on texts" is that "folks are irate." Zoom out: Democrats allege the raid fits into a broader pattern of Trump using federal resources to boost Republicans and target his political opponents. DHS became embroiled in controversy just last week after a statement targeting Pennsylvania Democrat Janelle Stelson, which critics said violates federal laws restricting partisan activities by federal officials. Trump has also come under fire for using taxpayer funds to run campaign-style television ads touting him and his administration in the run-up to the midterms. What they're saying: "President Trump will keep trying to intimidate and bully Americans ahead of the midterms," said Balint, adding, "We suspect he will try anything to stay in power and in control." Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) said that "of course there will" be more like the Omar raid, saying Trump is "the pettiest, worst human being" and "can't help himself." Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios: "This is some serious hate-baiting bullshit. This administration is just despicable." Asked whether he expects more, Huffman said, "Of course." The other side: One congressional Republican cheered the raid on Omar, who has long been the target of right-wing attacks on her immigration status. "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and deported," Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) wrote in a post on X , also comparing Monday's raid to the 2022 FBI search of Mar-a-Lago . The White House, DOJ and DHS did not respond to a request for comment. What to watch: House Democratic leaders are already signaling plans to wrap this into their oversight agenda if they retake the majority. "We will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his deputies said in a statement. House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said in a statement: "We will be demanding transparency and accountability as to who authorized this abusive search and who carried it out."

events.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
events.summary: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027). At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system. While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework ( CVE-2026-108398 ) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug. Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs. “We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said. Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software. Tyler Reguly , associate director of security research and development at Fortra , notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first. “Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said. Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software. Oh to be a fly on the wall. Reply → Ron October 13, 2026 Why do I still own and use a computer for my business? Reply → Fred Flamer October 14, 2026 For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement……. Reply → General Flummery October 14, 2026 Fred: It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then: 1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it. Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital. I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen. events.title: An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
events.summary: An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday. Abdulrahman Alfozan, whom federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room. He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing. OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office. Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US District Court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest. FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but neither prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X . “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.” OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep. Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview , Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations. The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment. Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies. According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.” The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated. OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted. After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing. According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found. He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

events.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip , PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI). “The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.” Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers. While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable. Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease. “One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.” The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word. To use the device, patients undergo an hourlong procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors. “The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where … it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.” He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.” When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired. As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue. The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors. “In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.” Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI.

events.title: How long will humans be needed for translation?
events.summary: Google's translation service handles one trillion words per month Published 14 October 2026, 00:05 BST "Il pleut des cordes," say the French when it's raining hard. "It's raining ropes," is the direct translation. It's the kind of idiom which can trip up an AI translator. "You can imagine the dilemma this throws AI into," says François Yvon, a research director specialised in automatic translation with the French National Centre for Scientific Research CNRS. He says a well-trained system will know that ropes are not literally falling from the sky and use the English phrase "it's raining cats and dogs". "But is it going to find the equivalent when it's translating into Indonesian?" asks Yvon. A comment on the weather is pretty low-risk, but more and more translation is being done by machines, and on topics with higher stakes than the weather. In April, Google said people are now translating , external one trillion words a month with Google Translate. That doesn't count the others: DeepL, Microsoft, Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, not to mention made-to-measure corporate translation systems. Direct sales of machine translation , external (i.e. outside general AI subscriptions) were worth an estimated $1.4bn (£1bn) last year. AI translation is the "right call" in many cases says John Zimmerman "For plenty of use cases, raw AI translation is now the right call: multiplying your costs by 100 to catch the last few percent of errors isn't rational if you're translating internal documents or product listings," says John Zimmerman, founder of OKA (Open Knowledge Association), a Swiss non-profit that translates Wikipedia articles into other languages. "For an encyclopedia it's different. Wikipedia runs on trust. A wrong fact can sit there for years and get cited by journalists and AI systems," he says. With more than 10,000 published pieces, mostly into Spanish, Portuguese and English, OKA is, Zimmerman says, the single largest contributor of translated articles to the collaborative online encyclopedia. Which is something it absolutely could not have become without AI. "Translating 10,000 articles the traditional way would cost millions. In our process, the AI produces the draft, then a human translator checks every sentence," he explains. But that human input is required less and less. "The machine output is now good enough that skipping the human entirely has become a serious option, and a real temptation across the industry. Two or three years ago, with tools like DeepL, our translators still rewrote a good chunk of every draft. "Today the prose often doesn't need fixing at all. So, the question is no longer whether AI translation is good, it clearly is, but whether it's good enough to remove the human," says Zimmerman. Ariella Baltié is a translator and legal expert specialised in translating court documents from English into French. She was contacted recently by someone who'd already translated his documents with AI, asking her to check them. "There were two major errors right at the beginning," she said. The AI had translated "Le demandeur" (the plaintiff) as "the requester". "Totally awkward for legal papers," says Baltié. When the AI saw "Madame X, épouse Y" (Ms X, wife of Y'), it came up with "Ms X marries Y". In other words, it mistook a noun for a verb, completely losing the meaning of the phrase. The consequences of mistranslation in the legal sphere can be serious. In the US, for example, errors in machine-translated asylum applications have led to delays in the release of detainees. Ariella Baltié specialises in legal translation work Accuracy is a matter of life and death in the medical field. "The units for dosages and blood tests often include Greek letters," says Carol Bereuter, who is a specialist in medical translations. She came across one automatically-translated text that had translated the greek letter μ as milli (one thousandth) instead of micro (one millionth). "That's a serious error. If you give someone a milligram when it's meant to be a microgram, you are giving them a thousand times the dose," points out Bereuter. She also makes the point that, as AI translators have got better, catching errors has got more difficult. "Whereas in the past, with things like Google Translate, the sentence would jump out at you because there'd be a grammatical error or it would sound clunky, today it sounds perfectly legitimate. It sounds fluid. It sounds natural. So the errors are a lot harder to spot." Carol Bereuter is a specialist in medical translations "If it's something that will bear your signature, there's a risk for your reputation. And if decisions are going to be taken on the basis of a translation concerning a medical procedure, a contract you might sign or a major purchase you might make, the risk is even greater," warns François Yvon. Even sentences that seem quite clear to a human can trip up an AI service, he says.

events.title: US fines Bank of America US$1.2b for anti-money laundering violations
events.summary: The announcement marks a hit to Bank of America just a day before it reports its third-quarter earnings. US regulators fined Bank of America more than US$1.2 billion for anti-money laundering and sanctions breaches, saying it failed to report over US$5 billion in suspicious transactions. The Treasury said some activity involved Chinese money laundering networks, the south-west US border, and sanctions violations linked to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism. Bank of America must fix its controls, face independent reviews, and absorb a US$1.2 billion charge, while its shares fell 2.6% after the announcement. WASHINGTON – The US Treasury Department said on Oct 13 that it is imposing penalties of more than US$1.2 billion (S$1.54 billion) on Bank of America, citing “violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws”. The second biggest US bank failed to properly report more than US$5 billion in “suspicious transactions”, the department said. Some of these involved risks related to national security and other concerns, including transactions “indicative of Chinese money laundering networks” and illicit finance around the south-west US border. The overall charge involves US$1.2 billion assessed by the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. This includes a US$750 million civil penalty from a key bank regulator, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced a US$11.6 million settlement with the bank over “apparent violations of numerous sanctions programmes, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism”. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” he said. A Bank of America spokesperson told AFP its results would include a US$1.2 billion charge weighing on net income by around 17 US cents per share. They added that the institution is committed to finishing the work needed to address issues that regulators raised. “We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year,” the spokesperson said. US regulators have published a consent order requiring Bank of America to work with a third party to identify and report suspicious transactions that went undetected. The institution will also have to undergo an independent review of its programmes for monitoring suspicious activity, and on other forms of due diligence. The bank is subject to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order as well, calling for it to address issues in its anti-money laundering programme and compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act. But the Treasury noted on Oct 13 that the bank “failed to prioritise” compliance despite agreeing to the 2024 order. Due to Bank of America’s “egregious and continued” violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, the OCC imposed its biggest civil money penalty assessed against a bank, said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould. Bank of America shares were down 2.6% in after-hours trading, following the Treasury’s announcement. AFP

events.title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. In most factories, automation is fixed: robots and machines are programmed for one specific task and product. Changing a line means reprogramming and physical retooling, or swapping out equipment, which can take weeks or months. San Francisco-based Industrial Next says it’s changing that. The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor. The company announced onstage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing. Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix. The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills. After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt. “We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing — designing cars and designing self-driving systems — and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.” The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better. “I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.” Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability. Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks. “We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high-precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.” In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts. Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones.

events.title: Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman thinks the AI doomer narrative isn’t doing the industry any favors. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , the AI chipmaker exec quipped that “some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn’t be allowed to talk in public.” He’s referencing the negativity now spreading around the dangers of AI, from models breaking containment to AI insiders debating the percentage chance that AI may kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. The argument has become so mainstream that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was recently parodied in a skit on “Saturday Night Live,” where the fictional character summed up the discourse, saying, “We do not condone what we are doing.” Feldman, however, thinks the promise and potential that go hand in hand with AI developments are getting overlooked. He thinks AI leaders should spend more time telling people that AI could lead to a world where your grandkids will “never meet anybody who dies of cancer,” for instance, even if they have concerns about AI risks. Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company’s customers include big names working with the technology, like OpenAI, Block, Figma, pharmaceutical giant GSK, and Lovable. However, he’s pragmatic about weighing the trade-offs between risk and reward. “I don’t think there are powerful technologies that don’t come with the challenge of ‘what happens when powerful technologies are in the hands of bad people?’ I think you can’t make one and not have the other,” Feldman said during his interview at Disrupt. “I think what we have to say is that this technology is powerful,” he added. “We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably,” he added. The chipmaker CEO also suggested that some of the negativity around AI has to do with how the data center industry has approached the new buildouts created by AI demand. “As an industry, we weren’t super good for the past few years at working with local communities, particularly in the U.S. We — the industry — didn’t do what others have done in the power industry in oil and gas. They didn’t work with the community. They didn’t engage the community as they should have, and that was a problem,” Feldman said. He compared the NIMBY-ism — “not in my backyard!” — of what’s going on in the U.S. with other countries, naming Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico, and Sweden as markets where they’re encouraging companies to build data centers. Feldman also wasn’t concerned that efficiency improvements would create less demand for his chips, or those from other companies competing with Nvidia, as Cerebras is. “We can do our job as hardware vendors to make our compute more efficient, and then the model makers can do improved work in making their models more efficient to achieve the same goals.
