events.title: Emergency order by US to 'prevent blackouts' could affect data centres
events.summary: The US Department of Energy has issued an emergency order to try to prevent power cuts amid increasing demand. Monday's order prompted PJM Interconnection , a corporation that transmits electricity in parts of the US, to " direct data centres and other large-load customers to switch to back-up generation resources, if necessary". Data centres in the US are commonly blamed for a surge in electricity prices and have driven public opinion on AI to sour, according to polls. In issuing its emergency order, the Energy Department also gave "a high rate of planned generator outages during the autumn maintenance season" as a possible cause of blackouts. PJM has issued a Maximum Generation Alert and Load Management Alert for Oct. 13 ahead of expected tight system conditions caused by unusually warm fall weather and planned equipment outages required for maintenance and construction. This alert does not require any action from… pic.twitter.com/zH8QXo2Jwm — PJM Interconnection (@pjminterconnect) October 12, 2026 The order remains in effect until October 16. Energy Secretary Chris Wright was confident in his decision to order utility companies and others to take emergency measures. "This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including back-up power, available to use as needed," Mr Wright said. The Department of Energy said in a statement that the US had 35 GW of unused back-up generation available nationwide. PJM issued a maximum generation alert for October 13 and 14: "Emergency procedures took place as above-normal temperatures are forecast across much of the PJM region. Additional emergency procedures may be necessary pending system conditions." The company said the alert does not "require any action from customers". The warnings come before the US midterm elections, where energy policy, AI and data centres are key issues. Any blackouts or failure to adequately address them could add to friction between residents in the US and utility companies, as well as AI firms. President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed critics of AI in recent weeks and accused them of "hoaxes". But in February he tried to ease the strain data centres were putting on the grid by signing a non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which technology and data centre companies would provide their own electricity to operate. Meanwhile, the Department of Energy has pushed for the construction of more nuclear reactors to address AI energy needs.

events.title: MariBank courts younger customers with child accounts and global stock trading
events.summary: The idea for the child account was mooted by senior management and supported by findings from an internal survey, said MariBank’s head of consumer business Huo Haiyan. MariBank is launching child accounts and global stock trading targeting customers aged 16 to 28 to attract digitally savvy youth and promote financial literacy early. The bank, whose core user base is in its 20s and 30s, is also expanding its investment options to include US and global equities from early 2027. MariBank is expanding beyond Sea's ecosystem, addressing underserved banking needs and aiming to build trust as a primary bank over time. SINGAPORE – Sea-owned MariBank is rolling out child accounts and global stock trading targeted at customers aged 16 to 28, as it looks to capture a growing base of digitally savvy youth. The idea for the child account was mooted by the digital bank’s senior management and supported by findings from an internal survey, said its head of consumer business Huo Haiyan. Speaking to The Straits Times at MariBank’s office in Rochester Commons, Huo said several members of the senior management team were heavy users of the bank’s products. One of them, for instance, wanted a convenient digital method of giving his daughter an allowance, rather than handing her physical cash. Through an internal study involving parents, the bank found several common concerns, including how to manage children’s transactions and allowances, encourage saving and build financial literacy from a young age. Targeted for launch in the first quarter of 2027, the child account will let children make their own transactions within parent-set guard rails, with certain transactions, such as adding a debit card to a mobile wallet on a new device, requiring explicit parental approval. About 30% of MariBank customers have a Mari Invest account, with one in four Mari Invest customers in their 20s – highlighting growing interest in investing among younger customers. Among the investment products it offers, the bank said it is seeing a steady upward trend in take-up for its Mari Invest Singapore Equities product. It declined to share specific adoption or customer numbers. Making investing simple, reliable and rewarding for younger customers who are highly comfortable managing their finances digitally is key, Huo noted. The bank is also no longer subject to an individual deposit cap, allowing it to compete more aggressively with traditional lenders for consumer savings. Mari Savings account holders can now deposit more than $100,000, according to a thread on social media platform Reddit, which Maribank confirmed. Huo said that many users experienced inconvenience when their incoming transactions or payments could not be completed as their account balance had exceeded the cap. There were a few thousand such transactions being rejected monthly, due to customers hitting their balance caps. With the cap removed, customers can benefit from MariBank’s high-interest promotions, such as new-user rates and ShopeeVIP bonuses reaching up to 3.08% per annum. These apply directly to the customer’s full balance and there is no cap on the bonus interest that customers can earn. Huo said the ShopeeVIP partnership was the main driver of the bank’s deposit growth, with 18% of MariBank users being ShopeeVIP users as well. MariBank’s customer deposits rose from $1.54 billion in 2024 to $2.82 billion by 2025. Within one month of the ShopeeVIP partnership launch in July, users who claimed the ShopeeVIP bonus interest rates doubled their balances . While Singapore tech giant Sea’s ecosystem will remain one of MariBank’s most important and cost-efficient channels, Huo noted that there will always be “a ceiling and a limit”. Sea operates three core businesses through its digital entertainment arm Garena, e-commerce platform Shopee, and digital payments and financial services arm Monee, previously known as SeaMoney. Huo said: “We need to prepare ourselves to reach users outside the ecosystem. We are already trying to scale through other channels such as online marketing and referrals.” Efforts to leverage other channels have been successful, with more than 50% of MariBank customers now coming from outside Shopee, up from 50% previously. Entering a mature, heavily banked market where consumers had already established banking relationships also presented a significant challenge. MariBank therefore focused on addressing the needs of retail consumers and businesses that had not been fully met. “Our aim is to fill out the white spaces where we see underserved needs,” said Huo. She added that this includes making overseas money transfers more affordable for businesses and foreigners in Singapore. “As much as we can, we try to accommodate (these gaps) such that we make the transfer fees affordable, so they can bank with us.” The bank was also cognisant that building trust with users takes time, particularly as it sought to establish itself as more than a secondary banking option.

events.title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device in OpenAI office
events.summary: Prosecutors released CCTV images of the suspect allegedly checking on the secret recorder A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee. Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product. Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say. On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said. OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier". According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment. Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customising, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customis[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'". The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene. That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said. Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation. If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000). events.title: Topgolf saved over $11.3 million after leaving VMware
events.summary: Topgolf’s VMware costs were going to increase by 400 percent under Broadcom. To avoid that cost, the sports entertainment company moved 12,000 virtual machines (VMs) to VergeIO’s VergeOS and has saved over $11 million so far. Before migrating, Topgolf’s VMware connection “ran very deep,” Scott Forehand, Topgolf’s global infrastructure manager, told Ars Technica. Topgolf has over 100 locations worldwide featuring interactive golf games with real-time shot tracking and digital analytics. The company used vSphere and ESXi for decades and started using VxRail, the hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) platform that VMware co-engineered with Dell, in 2017. Topgolf employees previously participated in numerous VMware customer councils and have been interviewed for books on how Topgolf used vSphere and Horizon (now Omnissa Horizon), per Forehand, who is a leader of the Dallas/Ft. events.title: They're vital community hubs, but regional post offices face uncertain futures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Concerns for future of regional post offices laid out in Senate inquiry Topic: Postal and Delivery Services Tarpeena resident Shirley Little's mother used to run the town's post office. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) An inquiry into Australia Post's retail network has highlighted the challenges facing licensed post offices (LPOs) around the country. LPOs make up about two-thirds of the network, but Australia Post says almost 40 per cent of licensees plan to exit within three years. The committee's report is due to be released on October 22. Advocates say small-town post offices need to be kept alive as aging licensees and changing community needs threaten their future. A Senate inquiry is underway into Australia Post's retail network that will look into, among other factors, the role licensed post offices (LPOs) play "in delivering community services". An inquiry into Australia Post's retail network will report back this month. ( ABC News ) But in Tarpeena, in South Australia's south-east, locals already know what losing the local post office can mean. In 2022, the LPO running out of the local pub, the Pines Hotel, was closed, leaving the closest post office 20 kilometres away. Long-time postie Shirley Little's mother owned and managed the LPO for more than four decades, back when it operated alongside the local general store. Shirley Little at Tarpeena's post office in 2015. ( Danielle Grindlay ) "I think when the post office did eventually close down, the older people missed it because it was somewhere they could go every day and someone would say hello to them," she said. About two-thirds of the Australia Post network is made up of LPOs, with about 2,900 operating across the country. Unlike general post offices, which are run by Australia Post, LPOs are run by licensees either as a standalone post office or alongside another business. The peak body representing LPO licensees, LPO Group, said other post office services, such as banking, were being "run down" as focus shifted towards parcel services. LPOs make up two-thirds of Australia Post's retail network. ( ABC Pilbara: Louise Miolin ) "When you're in the rural and regional parts of Australia, that's one of the most important businesses in your town," LPO Group chair Scott Etherington said. Pines Hotel licensee Lynton Cram said after the post office moved into the hotel, it failed to attract business. Pines Hotel licensee Lynton Cram ran Tarpeena's post office for a few years. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) "During the week I had very little business, apart from delivering the mail and sorting it," he said. "As far as doing any other transactions like parcels or cash transactions, it was very minimal." In its submission to the inquiry, Australia Post said it faced growing challenges in the regions, including declining foot traffic, increasing costs and a lack of workers. It said 38 per cent of LPO owners were aged 60 or older, and 39 per cent in non-major cities intended to exit the network within three years. The post office in Tarpeena closed in 2022. ( ABC South East SA: Josh Brine ) An Australia Post spokesperson said it had been engaging with the inquiry, and would review and consider the committee's report. "We have expanded how and where customers can access our services. "We've done this by adding self-service options like parcel lockers, which are in addition to our reported retail outlets. These services complement post offices, not replace them." Australia Post says it's committed to continuing to serve regional communities. ( ABC Radio Brisbane: Anna Levy ) The spokesperson said Australia Post had paid $635 million in commissions to licensees in the previous financial year, and that those payments had increased each year for the past 15 years. "For the past two years, we have been engaging with licensees and their representative associations to update the current LPO model, which is more than 30 years old," they said. More than 140 published submissions have been made to the inquiry, with the committee's report due on October 22.

events.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn over claimed sanctions breaches
events.summary: Bank of America was ordered to pay more than $1.2 billion in fines after the US Treasury Department said the company breached anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, the agency said on Tuesday. The authority said the fine is the third-largest in its history. Bank of America was also ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest ever issued by the OCC. The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over 475 “apparent violations” of sanctions against “ Russia , Belarus, Iran , Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism”. Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US, with more than 70 million clients, and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for customers every year. It enables more than $450 trillion of payments in employee payrolls, supplier payments and corporate credit cards. It also processes an average of $1.9 trillion in wire transfers a day globally for clients. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire us financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law." The Treasury Department said Bank of America admitted it willfully breached the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to assist the Treasury in detecting and preventing money laundering. Bank of America said it has "invested billions of dollars" to tackle financial crime, and that it is "far along" in its remediation efforts with US regulators. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right", a Bank of America representative said. The department said the US bank failed to report to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with more than $1 billion implicating national security and other risks "indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border." The OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against the bank in 2024 over deficiencies related to its Bank Secrecy Act and compliance programmes. “The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable,” said Jonathan Gould, Comptroller of the Currency. Tuesday's fine followed an action from the OCC last week, in which American Express was fined $350 million after its compliance programme allowed about $13 billion in suspected money laundering activity to go undetected for more than a decade. Bank of America is due to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday. The bank said its third-quarter results will include a $1.2 billion non-tax deductible charge, reducing income by roughly 17 cents per share. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," a bank representative said.

events.title: US hits Bank of America with $1.2 billion fine, saying it violated money laundering, sanctions laws
events.summary: The fines amount to the third-largest amount in Treasury Department history. WASHINGTON -- The U.S. Treasury Department said Tuesday that it’s imposing $1.2 billion in fines on Bank of America for allegedly violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The fines on America’s second-biggest bank amount to the third-largest in the department’s history. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.” Treasury said Bank of America also reached an $11.6 million settlement with the department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control over “apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism." In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed the $1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.'' The penalty includes $750 million that will go to the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by that federal bank regulatory agency. Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated'' the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,’’ Bank of America said in a statement. “We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 (Comptroller of the Currency) Consent Order and FinCEN’s investigation. Both those historic actions happened as part of the Biden administration’s focus on anti-money laundering and efforts to promote compliance with the then-emerging virtual currency industry. events.title: Helix Carbon says it can make iron cheaper by recycling blast furnace pollution
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The iron and steel industries are among the biggest polluters in the world. Plenty of startups have tried to cut the industry’s emissions, mostly by developing new ways to make the metals. Helix Carbon thinks those startups have been going about it all wrong. “Any attempt to decarbonize the steel industry without dealing with the blast furnace is not going to work,” David Brown, Helix Carbon’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. A blast furnace is the giant furnace that turns iron ore into the iron used to make steel. Rather than replace blast furnaces, Helix wants to clean them up. Its approach promises to slash the steel industry’s carbon emissions while boosting profit margins for iron producers, a rare win-win for a dirty industrial process. Blast furnaces have made iron for centuries, using coke, a processed form of coal, to help turn raw iron ore (iron bound up with oxygen) into metallic iron. The burning coke supplies heat for the reaction but doesn’t take part in it directly. Instead, carbon monoxide produced from the combustion does the work of reducing the iron, meaning stripping away its oxygen atoms. The process releases tremendous amounts of carbon dioxide, or CO 2 , which is normally dumped straight into the atmosphere. But Helix Carbon has devised a way to turn that waste carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and recycle it back into the blast furnace. Helix Carbon’s process relies on an electrolyzer, a device that uses electricity and a catalyst to break off an oxygen atom from the carbon dioxide. Electrolyzers aren’t new, but Brown said the startup’s design can handle the entire exhaust stream from the blast furnace. Most electrolyzers are too delicate for raw exhaust like that. They work only on purified, concentrated carbon dioxide, so the exhaust typically has to be processed before they can use it. By injecting carbon monoxide into a blast furnace, iron producers can use less coke. How much, exactly, is still debated, Brown said. Some scientific papers suggest as much as 90% of the coke can be eliminated, while other studies suggest it’s more like 30% to 40%. Helix Carbon is proposing that iron producers start by replacing 33% of their coke. The company says using its technology to do so would save them $14 per ton of iron. “That may not seem like a lot, but margins in the iron industry are famously thin,” Brown said. The iron and steel industries are a combined $2 trillion market, according to Grand View Research , which makes the sector an appealing target for a young startup to chase. But it also moves slowly, in part because its equipment lasts so long. “There are blast furnaces that have lived for over 100 years,” Brown said. To bring in revenue earlier, Helix Carbon plans to court the specialty chemicals industry first. “We don’t need to capture the CO 2 first,” Brown said. “We just utilize it, and that opens up the door of making chemicals on-site right out of waste streams.” Helix Carbon presented live onstage on Tuesday in the Startup Battlefield pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, taking place this week from October 13-15. events.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering allegations
events.summary: The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for years of failures to report suspicious transactions and address shortcomings in its anti-money-laundering program. Why it matters: The action includes the third-largest penalty in Treasury history. What they're saying: "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release . The big picture: The civil action comes less than a week after federal regulators fined American Express $350 million over similar failures to detect and report suspected money laundering. Zoom in: Bank of America admitted to willfully violating federal anti-money-laundering laws — including requirements to maintain adequate safeguards and report suspicious transactions. Regulators said the bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in more than $5 billion in suspicious activity that was either unreported or reported late. More than $1 billion involved potential national security and other high-priority risks — including Chinese money-laundering networks and suspected trade-based money laundering linked to the U.S.-Mexico border, regulators said. Of note: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency also assessed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the agency's history. Treasury also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over hundreds of apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, including those targeting Russia and Iran. Flashback: Bank of America has been working to address deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering program since a December 2024 regulatory order. But regulators said significant problems persisted. Officials said the bank prioritized revenue while limiting compliance resources — at times relying on law enforcement and other outside sources to identify suspicious activity. The other side: In a statement, Bank of America said it has invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to fighting financial crime. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators." What to watch: Bank of America reports third-quarter earnings Wednesday. The bank said it will record a $1.2 billion, non-tax-deductible charge in those results. The bank said costs associated with its ongoing efforts to fix compliance problems are already reflected in its expenses. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

events.title: FBI arrests OpenAI employee accused of planting hidden recording device in conference room
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI after discovering that an employee allegedly planted a hidden recording device in one of the AI maker’s office executive conference rooms. The employee, named by federal prosecutors as Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was fired and arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. The company said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to understand the “sophisticated” device. OpenAI told TechCrunch that the device contained “advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring,” though it is unclear to what degree this device is technically distinct from other recording devices. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” said OpenAI in its post on X. OpenAI’s spokesperson, Nate Evans, confirmed that the employee started with the AI model maker in July 2025 and worked on the product team. Prosecutors with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California said Alfozan was charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications — effectively accusing him of covertly recording people’s voice audio without their permission. Prosecutors said OpenAI caught the device after it was inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in OpenAI’s San Francisco office. Per the prosecutors, Alfozan was caught looking behind the television where the recording device was placed, and where OpenAI had placed a camera that allegedly caught the employee. It’s not clear exactly for what purpose the recording device was used, but FBI director Kash Patel said the scheme was to “capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology.” Neither Alfozan nor his attorney could be immediately reached for comment. He faces five years in prison if convicted. When reached, a spokesperson for the FBI reiterated a statement made by Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” Patel said. events.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar under investigation by Jeanine Pirro's office
events.summary: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home. The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked." Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which her office said cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well." "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe. Catch up quick: Federal agents searched Omar's home before dawn Monday as part of a separate immigration probe, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reported. Omar described the search in an X post as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." Trump has repeatedly lashed out against Somali immigrants, including Omar — who he described in a post last year as "always wrapped in her swaddling hijab" and "the worst 'Congressman/woman'" in our Country." Zoom out: Omar's office pointed Axios to The Wall Street Journal's reporting last month that the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss allegations that she possibly violated House rules or law by reporting false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures. A disclosure filed last year listed Omar and her husband's assets as ranging from $6 million to $30 million. She later amended the form to reflect a much lower range, the Journal first reported, citing what her team said were accounting errors. Pirro's office did not respond to Axios's request for comment. What they're saying: After Pirro's appearance on Fox News, Trump shared a post on Truth Social suggesting, without evidence, that Omar benefited from fraud in Minnesota . events.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July. Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device. These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components. The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited. The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services. In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data. Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations. U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng. The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees. However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI. That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Volta’s $5 billion debt deal is a pulse check on the AI-financing boom
events.summary: The Scoop Lenders are feeling maxed out on data-center debt. When Volta, an AI infrastructure company, went out recently to raise $5 billion for a data center in Norway, the deal didn’t seem that different from the more than $450 billion in AI-related debt deals done so far this year. But as Volta’s bankers at JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs went out to sell it, some investors pushed back, saying they’re full up on data-center debt and demanding more security and a higher interest rate. The deal is expected to price later this week with a rate of at least 11%, unusually high for a data-center project, anchored by a $1.5 billion order from Apollo, people familiar with the matter said. Commitments for the deal are due this week and lenders are still in discussion about allocations, so details about the financing could change. Volta’s deal is a pulse check on the AI-financing world. Deals are still getting done, but less smoothly than they were earlier this year, with higher rates and more heavily negotiated terms, investors and bankers say. Volta was founded in February and the Norway data center is its first significant project. Some investors balked at its lack of a track record, while others were unnerved by Volta’s reliance on Anthropic to buy much of the data center’s compute. Anthropic doesn’t share much financial information with lenders and the exact level of its obligations struck some investors as unsettled. The deal includes an unusual provision to overcome that skittishness: The interest rate charged to Volta will decrease if Anthropic can get an investment-grade credit rating, some of the people said. The Financial Times reported last month that Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPO advisers were lobbying credit-rating agencies for blue-chip status, which would be almost unheard-of for companies as unprofitable as both AI labs are. JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs have also underwritten a $1.3 billion term loan to Volta. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Apollo declined to comment. Volta didn’t respond to a request for comment. Anthropic didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More September has been the second-lowest month this year for issuance for AI financings, as regulatory and political challenges weigh on data center construction, according to a report from Morgan Stanley. The fourth quarter is expected to slow down further, the analysts said.

events.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
events.summary: Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday. Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung . What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday. The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect. Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery. "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said. The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement. Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center. It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things. Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer. The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups. Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized." He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers. events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind , and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” “The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.” Find the technical paper here . October 2026. events.summary: The battle for Congress is shifting deeper into red territory as both parties deem some races essentially over. The Democratic group Senate Majority PAC is scaling back ads in Georgia and North Carolina as Republican spending there slows, signs both parties see the Democratic candidates — Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper — as increasingly favored to win. The GOP Senate Leadership Fund is spending more to assist Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, after boosting spending in Kansas and South Carolina. And the Congressional Leadership Fund, a House GOP leadership-aligned PAC, is redirecting resources from candidates in purple districts, like those represented by Reps. Tom Kean of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, toward GOP incumbents in districts more handily won by President Donald Trump in 2024, like Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas and Rob Wittman of Virginia. Republicans still have some bright spots on the map. Democrats pulled back on some ad spending in another red district in Arizona, and Republicans are still spending heavily to try to flip outgoing Rep. Jared Golden’s seat in Maine. — Burgess Everett and Nicholas Wu

events.title: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Fusion power usually conjures images of massive industrial facilities laced with large lasers or magnets, but a startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been quietly building a device that can fit on a tabletop. The optics of the device were on display behind Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries , while he chatted with me on a video call. The company has been operating in stealth out of a small lab near MIT, and Kai gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at the technology it has been developing. “We purposely built a small modular reactor. It’s tiny, it’s benchtop,” he told me. “Because it’s small, it makes everything easier.” The small size has allowed Cambridge Heavy to experiment and iterate quickly. “The small module nature can enable 50 to 80 experiments, 50 to 80 shots per day,” he said. Data from those experiments will feed simulations that use AI to optimize the design. That nimble approach has attracted investor attention. The startup recently raised a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures with participation from Overlay, Neta Foundation, P3A, MassCEC, and the Rothrock family. Cambridge Heavy’s fusion reactor uses lasers to compress a fuel target, similar to the groundbreaking experiment that proved controlled fusion reactions could produce more power than they consume. But unlike other inertial confinement designs, Cambridge Heavy’s minimizes the number of lasers required to spark fusion. The system uses two main lasers to drive ignition. One laser is split into multiple beam lines that deliver light in concentric rings. Those rings of laser light are timed to hit the flat, round fuel target successively, starting from the outside and working in. The first ring starts a compression wave within the target that starts traveling inward. The subsequent laser rings are timed to boost the wave at just the right moment to further compress the fuel. As the shock wave reaches the center of the target, a laser fires on the target, generating heat and producing a magnetic field. With the right amount of pressure and heat, fusion occurs. Cambridge Heavy’s design generates high pressures with relatively low laser power, Kai said. The concept emerged from the lab of Keith Nelson, a chemist at MIT. There, researchers used the laser pulses to study materials under extreme conditions. As they ramped up pressures, they realized they were approaching fusion-ready conditions. In about a decade, Cambridge Heavy plans to develop a power plant from the concept, though that’ll require scaling up the design. It will be larger than the current benchtop prototype, though not quite as large as other fusion power plants. Kai said it should be about the size of two basketball courts, and it will test whether the approach can generate enough energy to support a power plant. Before that happens, though, Cambridge Heavy plans to use its smaller-scale devices to make tritium, a rare isotope of hydrogen that will be used by nearly all fusion power plants in the works today. Tritium sells for around $30,000 per gram today. Each power plant won’t need a lot of tritium — on the order of grams per year — but the substance is so rare that only about 40 kilograms exist today. One recent study predicts that without new sources, the fusion power industry will be short by about 28 kilograms in 2054. At current prices, that’s about $840 million worth of tritium. Fusion startups are in the process of designing fuel systems that will help the reactors be largely self-sufficient when it comes to tritium supplies, though they may need occasional top-ups. But that process could take up to 10 years, Kai said, giving Cambridge Heavy years of potential revenue as it pursues its power plant. events.title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If fusion power pans out, and there are signs that it will , the world will need a lot more lithium. That’s the bet behind Licube , a startup that has licensed technology from Hirosaki University in Japan, to purify lithium-6, the form of lithium that fusion plants need to make their own fuel, out of naturally occurring lithium. The reason comes down to the fuel supply. A lot of things have to go right for fusion power to hit the grid, and one of them is the fuel. Most planned plants would run on a mix of two fuels, deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is easy to come by, but tritium is extremely rare in nature, and it’s an open secret in the fusion world that there isn’t enough of it to power every planned plant. The proposed workaround is to make tritium on site, inside the power plant itself. A fusion reaction gives off a stream of fast-moving particles called neutrons. Startups plan to surround the reactor with a blanket of lithium, so that when a neutron strikes a lithium atom, the atom splits into helium and tritium. The tritium can then be collected, purified, and fed back into the reactor as fuel. Not all lithium does this job equally well. It comes in two slightly different forms, lithium-6 and lithium-7, named for their weights. Lithium-6 is far better at capturing neutrons and producing tritium, but it makes up only about 7.5% of natural lithium, and the rest is the heavier lithium-7. Separating the two is difficult, and there is little capacity to do it today, so the world doesn’t have enough lithium-6 either. Licube sees a big market in solving that problem. “If fusion comes online, it should be a $50 billion market by 2040,” Yohei Kiguchi, co-founder and CEO of Licube, told TechCrunch. Licube is one of 20 startups that are presenting onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco as part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition. While fusion has the potential to capture a significant chunk of the multitrillion-dollar energy market, fusion startups are still years away from building their first power plants. “Fusion is the biggest market in the future, but we also understand the future might be late by a few years,” Kiguchi said. Until fusion becomes a major market, Licube plans to use the same technology to purify lithium for use in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission reactors, and spacecraft industries. The core technology is based on the electrolyzer, a device that uses electrical current to drive chemical reactions. In Licube’s case, lithium is dissolved in a liquid on one side of a ceramic membrane. As electrical current flows from one side of the membrane to the other, lithium-6 moves faster. Licube can then draw off that liquid and separate the lithium-6. The goal is to enrich the lithium to at least 99.995% lithium-6. Fusion companies can feed that highly enriched lithium into their fuel breeding systems. Kiguchi was inspired to start Licube after visiting ITER, the experimental fusion reactor being built in the south of France. He said he was living a couple of hours’ drive away in Monaco after retiring from his previous company, Enechange, an energy-switching platform network in Japan. “I found out that I was too young to retire,” he said. “I’m an energy guy. I want to do something bigger.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: Real estate agents urged to 'enhance responsibly' as AI use rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Real estate AI use grows with furniture and families altered in advertisements It has become a growing trend for the real estate industry to use AI-generated content to market homes. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The ABC has found several examples of AI being used in real estate advertising around the country. Experts say AI use is common in the industry and support its use as long as it is not misleading. Queensland's Office of Fair Trading encourages the industry to "enhance responsibly". Digitally altered furniture, families and songs about floor plans are some of the ways real estate agents use artificial intelligence (AI) to sell and rent homes. Marketing and consumer behaviour academic Sara Thaichon said the property industry was "one of the fastest adopters of AI in Australia". It has prompted one state regulator to issue a best practice guide to help the sector avoid misrepresentations. This image of a lounge room from a real estate website was generated using OpenAI tools. ( Supplied ) Ms Thaichon said "virtual staging" was common in real estate to help prospective buyers imagine the home's potential. "There's nothing wrong about that if it's done correctly, if the use of AI is disclosed," the Griffith University associate professor said. But she said using AI to enhance and create a false perception of a property can be considered "house-fishing". Sara Thaichon is an associate professor in the marketing department at Griffith University. ( ABC News: Glenn Mullane ) The ABC had found several examples of the technology being used in images on real estate websites around the country. When run through a SynthID detector, those images returned a positive result for OpenAI's invisible watermark, confirming the content had been generated with that tool. SynthID watermark result of an image of a bathroom from real estate website. ( Supplied ) Some real estate websites also feature AI-generated families in property listings. A Western Australia advertisement featured a digitally altered family of four and their dog having a picnic, with one child holding a wine glass. The image was tested with SynthID detectors, but none found a watermark. This image of a family outside a house featured in a Western Australia real estate advertisement. ( Supplied ) Google AI's tool determined the image showed "strong signs of digital manipulation or artificial generation," citing inconsistent lighting, the picnic mat's haloing, and the dad's slightly distorted grip on the bottle. A New South Wales agent used AI to turn several properties' floor plans into acoustic songs featuring lyrics such as "stone-top kitchen, gas and grace" and "four rooms full of little dreams". In one video, a female voice sang "this is where our future breathes" as the vision cut to the home's bathroom. Google's tool found these songs were created using AI music tools. It said the songs followed a standard "generative prompt structure" of address, features, and amenities, with vocals exhibiting synthetic processing and uniform pitch modulation common in AI music. Ms Thaichon said AI songs weren't "a big problem" if the lyrics were factually correct. events.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
events.summary: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta , both of which declined to back new legislation. The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework . The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.” OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said. However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.” The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.” While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI. MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said. Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.” In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over. Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said. When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so. “What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.” The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government , we will continue to do it.” The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access . The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.

events.title: Social Security benefits are rising again, but probably not enough to offset healthcare costs
events.summary: Increasing Social Security benefits annually helps millions of older Americans afford necessities. Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits are slated to find out on Oct. 14, 2026, how much their monthly check will rise. This cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities. I am a finance professor , and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices . And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face. The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026 , which the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, will also release on Oct. 14. It stood at 3.4% in August , according to the BLS. Experts have no doubt that the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 will be far above the 2.8% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2025 . Many forecasts range from 3.4% to 3.6% . But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured. Calculating the COLA The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices. The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers , known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index. The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January. If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same . That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015. Spending much of the bump on premiums One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation. Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College . For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA. More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are , helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation. Finding other options Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare , say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs. There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older , known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch. The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates. Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W. But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years . What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose. events.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days. How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause. Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines. Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today. “It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.” “Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha. Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model. “None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data. Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid). He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers. If you’re curious to learn more, Niobia will present onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt this afternoon in San Francisco. Join us to catch the company and the 19 startups against which it’s competing as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, happening today, Tuesday, through Thursday, October 15. events.title: Inside Trump, Netanyahu's dilemma: Strike Iran before elections or wait
events.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official. The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later. But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said. " Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said. A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said. Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations." Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran. According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets. Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute all of the various parts of its nuclear program. Israel is especially concerned about Iran potentially operating Pickaxe Mountain as a uranium enrichment site. Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Oct. 2 to discuss next steps in the war and the possibility of resuming strikes. Behind the scenes: An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant. A U.S. official said Trump has been going back and forth on the issue. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the leadership of U.S. Central Command are the strongest backers of resuming strikes in Iran, a source familiar with the discussions said. But most of Trump's advisers favor keeping up economic sanctions and other forms of pressure for now. "They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," the second U.S. official said. Between the lines: Renewed strikes would carry major political implications for both leaders. Resuming the war could dramatically affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke last week with Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and discussed the possibility of resuming full-scale fighting against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a source briefed on the call. Zamir said that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Caine's spokesman, Joe Holstead, declined to comment. It's a big dilemma for Zamir because a strike ahead of the elections could be seen as a political ploy by Netanyahu that would erode public trust in the military, which is largely viewed as apolitical. The intrigue: The White House is aware of Netanyahu's domestic political considerations. "Bibi's got an election before the midterms. He believes his strength is being a wartime prime minister," one of the U.S. officials said. In meetings with his security and intelligence chiefs in recent days, Netanyahu claimed it was Trump, not him, who initiated the discussion about possibly hitting Iran before the elections, an Israeli official said. According to this account, Trump asked Netanyahu if Israel would join. Resuming the war before the U.S. election could backfire on Trump by reminding voters of the unpopular conflict and potentially sending gas prices higher. The big picture: Qatari mediators are still waiting for Iran to respond to the latest U.S. counterproposal to end the war, which includes demands for nuclear concessions. "The negotiations are not really dead, but they're not really alive. We're just here, piling on the pressure and there's a belief that smarter heads will prevail over there," a U.S. official said. "The Iranians thought this president would back down because of the pressure and the midterms. He has shown them the error of their ways," the official added. Trump repeated a familiar refrain Tuesday, telling reporters that "Iran is a failed country" and "we will make a decision on Iran very soon."

events.title: Rivian’s startup Mind Robotics hires former Ford EV chief Doug Field
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Doug Field has worked on EVs at Ford and Tesla, the not-so-secret car project at Apple, and was employee No. 1 at Segway. Now the executive is turning his attention to Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe’s latest project: Mind Robotics . Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics, an industrial AI and robotics venture Rivian created last year. The news, shared onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 (taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco), is another sign that Mind Robotics is getting ready to scale up its early operations just one year after its founding. Scaringe will still be involved with Mind Robotics, but the day-to-day aspects of the business, including product, engineering, and operations, will be handled by Field. Mind Robotics, which has already amassed more than $1 billion in backing from Accel, Andreessen Horowitz, Eclipse, Kleiner Perkins, and the venture arms of Volkswagen and Salesforce, is building a full stack for industrial manufacturing. The purpose-built robots will run on foundation models with a goal of automating industrial and manufacturing tasks at scale. Unlike the humanoid robots being developed by Tesla and others, Scaringe says Mind Robotics won’t attempt to mimic all the biomechanics of a human . The startup is also using Rivian as “a live, high-volume manufacturing environment for model training and deployment,” with Rivian being Mind Robotics’ first customer. Scaringe said on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday that he wanted someone like Field to help run Mind Robotics, and so he called him up to ask for a recommendation. “Him and I then really began digging into how important it is that we really think deeply and very intentionally about how we develop robotics and deploy robotics into our society, into our economy, and we found such alignment in how we thought about this from the overall mission of the business, but even more important, we found really deep alignment just in how we both work and how we build teams,” he said. Field left Ford in April after five years shaping the automaker’s electric vehicle and technology strategies. His departure was part of a wider reorganization of the automaker’s leadership. Prior to Ford, Field led Apple’s Project Titan, the electric, autonomous car project that was canceled in 2024 . He also served as senior vice president of engineering at Tesla, where he oversaw development of the Model 3 and got the sedan through “production hell.” “Integrating AI and robotics is one of the most important — and difficult — engineering challenges of our time,” Field said in a statement. “Mind has assembled an exceptional team and has a unique advantage: the ability to deploy and learn inside a real, high-volume factory from day one. I’m thrilled to join RJ in building a team, culture, and technology that will redefine what we can make in America.” Mind Robotics is the second company that Scaringe created outside of Rivian, following Also , a micromobility play that’s starting with high-end e-bikes. Like with Field and Mind Robotics, Scaringe is involved as chairman at Also but has tapped someone to run the day-to-day: Chris Yu, the former chief product officer of Specialized. Mind Robotics and Also operate as stand-alone companies, but Rivian has minority stakes in both. The company reported owning about a third of each startup as of June 30, 2026 .
