events.title: Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says.

( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) Consumers are raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs. A government spokesperson said it had empowered the Clean Energy Regulator to monitor the industry closely. After waiting a year for a battery system that never showed up, Bob Emery's frustration boiled over. He says the installer, Lux Solar, "can't be trusted". Mr Emery paid a $1,000 deposit last October for a 48kwh system which he hoped would slash his power bills at his Perth home. After lengthy delays, he unsuccessfully requested a refund. The retired electrician also pursued his case with a consumer protection body and industry groups without resolution. He joins a growing number of customers raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. The program has sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025. Over four years, the scheme has covered estimated costs of more than $7.2 billion. There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs with the NSW energy and water ombudsman saying complaints in that jurisdiction had doubled since last year. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has several investigations underway and South Australia has announced a crackdown on "dodgy solar companies". Queensland's Office of Fair Trading confirmed Lux Solar is under investigation. It is the second solar company in as many months being probed for allegedly charging customers for deposits to install battery systems under the federal scheme that were never delivered. Bob Emery is still waiting for his solar battery. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) In June, Lux Solar was kicked out of the voluntary industry-run consumer protection scheme, the New Energy Tech Consumer Code (NETCC) for "major failures," including continuing to take payments without showing it could deliver the systems. The company has continued to advertise itself as an "approved seller" on its website, despite the Clean Energy Council requesting that wording be removed. Consumer advocate and CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre, Erin Turner, has called for the ad to be investigated. "That's really potentially misleading and I hope a regulator looks at it because that's a part of the consumer law where we can see really significant court actions with fines of up to $100 million," Ms Turner said. 'I don't have any trust in anyone installing it' In November 2025, Mr Emery was told the installation of his battery system was two to four weeks away. Two months later there was still no progress, so he emailed the salesman and asked for a refund. Bob Emery has waited over a year for his solar battery from Lux Solar. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) Again, he was told the "install team" would make contact within a week or two. Mr Emery grew alarmed when the salesman stopped answering his calls and voice messages with Lux Solar weren't returned. Lux Solar is based in Western Australia but also operates in Queensland and New South Wales. Mr Emery made a complaint to Consumer Protection WA but the watchdog said it was up to him to take the matter to court. "The government bodies need to lift their game," he said. "It's put me off the whole (federal battery) program, I don't have any trust in anyone installing it," he said. Lux Solar told customer Justin Albin that installer issues were the reason for delays getting his solar battery. ( ABC News: Brigham Edgar ) His frustration is shared by Brisbane man Justin Albin and his Queensland work colleague who both waited about a year after paying deposits to Lux Solar last October. In January, a salesman told Mr Albin there had been "some installer issues" but he would get his system as promised. He received an email which said Lux Solar had more installation teams "ramping back up" and confirmation would come soon. He sent a legal letter demanding Lux Solar install the system or he would start court proceedings. Justin Albin has waited about a year after paying a deposit last October. ( ABC News: Brigham Edgar ) Lux Solar offered him a refund which he rejected.

events.title: Outcry over council's 'extortionate' fee hike on short-stay homes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bass Coast short-stay holiday home owners call for rethink of council fee hike Phillip Island holiday home owner Lisa has described the council fee hike on her property as extortionate. ( ABC News: Georgia Lenton-Williams ) Holiday home owners in Victoria's south-east are urging a council to overturn an increase to its short-stay accommodation levy. The Bass Coast Shire Council says the extra fees are needed to cover the costs associated with tourism, including rubbish collection. More than 1,000 properties are registered as short-term rentals in the shire, but industry data has identified more than 2,300 listings on platforms such as AirBnB and Stayz. A coastal Victorian council has defended its move to increase fees for providers of short-stay rental accommodation as hundreds of community members urge it to rethink the decision. The Bass Coast Shire, which takes in holiday hotspots like Phillip Island on Victoria's south-east coast, is one of just a handful of Victorian areas with local laws regulating short-stay accommodation. The council says the extra fees are necessary to cope with additional costs created by the holiday accommodation industry, but tourism advocates warn it may deter holiday home owners from renting at all, meaning more homes will stay empty for longer. Lisa, who did not want her last name published, bought her Phillip Island holiday home with her partner two years ago and said they worked very hard to afford it. Lisa says she and her partner have worked hard to afford their Phillip Island holiday home. ( ABC News: Georgia Lenton-Williams ) The couple is currently renting the property using an online platform at a base rate of about $220 per night. "We thought we could just share the home with other people and let them enjoy it until we're fully ready to move down here full time," she said. Earlier this year, Bass Coast Shire Council increased its annual registration fee to short-stay providers like Lisa from $324 to $600 — or $900 for homes with more than five bedrooms. The fee hike caught Lisa off guard. "It seems a bit extortionate really," she said. The Bass Coast Shire takes in holiday hotspots like Phillip Island. ( Supplied ) While governments across Australia have taken different approaches to regulating the short-stay sector, a statewide levy of 7.5 per cent came into effect in Victoria in 2025 . Some councils, like Warrnambool, scrapped local fees after the levy was introduced, but a handful retained local laws. That includes the Bass Coast, which has had a registration process in place since 2023 and now has the highest fees in the state . The retention of the local fees has led some short-stay providers to accuse governments of "double-dipping". However, University of Sydney housing expert Nicole Gurran said the state booking levy was likely also being paid by consumers. "It may be a bit of both: a bit of a provider absorbing the cost and a bit of them adding them on to the fee paid by the customer," she said. Professor Nicole Gurran says local councils are facing several challenges with tourism population booms. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) Dr Gurran said short-stay rentals and sudden population booms over holiday periods were difficult for regional councils to deal with. "You've got increased costs associated with waste collection, for instance, associated with managing beaches, parks, public spaces," she said. Bass Coast Shire mayor Brett Tessari agreed, saying the fee was introduced to "control" issues related to short-stay accommodation, including complaints from permanent residents about disruptive behaviour. Bass Coast Mayor Brett Tessari says the new fee is an attempt to address issues associated with short-stay accommodation. ( ABC News ) "The waste, the rubbish, the anti-social behaviour — it's our regular permanents that put up with all that," he said. "The cost is quite significant and we realised before this increase that we were just nowhere near where we needed to be." While Victoria's statewide levy raised $85.8 million in 2025 , that money is directed towards social housing investment rather than being used used to cover local costs. Rental shortage after pandemic migration More than 1,000 short-stay properties in the Bass Coast region have registered with the council. However, data collected by AirDNA, a company that provides analytics on the short-term rental industry, identified more than 2,300 listings advertised across Airbnb and Stayz in the area in August.

events.title: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States. Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny , with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen. Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed. Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement , Axios' Marc Caputo reported. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired. Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center. . The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR . The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett . How a firing squad works State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves. How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood. A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head. The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner. If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss. Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method. For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank round, while South Carolina has three shooters, all with live ammunition. Hasan uses a wheelchair, potentially complicating how the execution would be carried out at Fort Hood. Yes, but: Firing squads don't always work as intended. Last year, prisoner Mikal Mahdi was executed in South Carolina by firing squad. An autopsy later found that only two bullets struck him and missed his heart. Where firing squad is legal The method is legal in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, according to the DPIC . It is the main execution method in Idaho as of this past summer. The only authorized method for capital punishment in Texas is lethal injection. Yes, but: State laws don't govern military executions. Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios What we know about the execution livestream Few specifics are known about the livestream execution, where it would streamed, or how people would watch it. It will happen on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 1pm CT, in Fort Hood. It's unclear if the execution would stream on social media or a website. TikTok and Kick said the event would violate their policies. What we're watching: The Army. Army Regulation 190-55 assigns the Army responsibility to choose the method, date and location of the execution.

Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently. According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time. The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences. Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses. The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences. The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025. Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them. events.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit. There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel .) And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space. Longshot Space Technology , a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission. When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs. The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far. The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says. These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.) “If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.” The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites. “The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes. But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price. It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.

events.title: Private school fees loophole a sticking point in Labor's trust tax plan Greens say
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Greens concerned private school fees paid out of trusts could escape Labor's 30pc tax Nick McKim has accused Labor of 'watering down' its trust taxation plans. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke/Matt Roberts ) The Greens say a "loophole" for private school fees is a sticking point in Labor's proposed trust laws. Jim Chalmers will introduce legislation for the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts on Wednesday, amid stiff business opposition. Labor requires the support of the Greens in the Senate to pass the tax hike, given that the Coalition is opposed. Parents who pay private school fees from their trust funds could escape Labor's proposed trust tax, in what the Greens say is a "loophole" that must be closed. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will today unveil a bill to impose the 30 per cent minimum tax on some trusts. The budget proposal has enraged the business lobby and unnerved Labor backbenchers anxious about small business hostility. The Greens, whose votes are required in the Senate, have the opposite concern. On Tuesday, the party called for a Senate inquiry into the bill, saying an early draft was "watered down" and the proposal would not get a "free pass". The ABC can reveal the Greens' main concern is an exemption for money paid from trusts to charities, non-profits and other tax-exempt entities, including private schools. "People who are wealthy enough to set up trusts should not get a tax break to pay for private school fees when this option is denied to people who can't afford expensive accountants," Greens economic spokesperson Nick McKim told the ABC. "The treasurer needs to knock this out of the legislation." In a draft proposal last month, the government indicated it would cap the amount of exempt money each year, but that cap has not yet been set. The proposal does not change the tax treatment of private schools, since this avenue already exists, but the Greens will argue that carving charitable payments out from the new higher rate of tax will make it more attractive. "There is far too much leniency," Senator McKim said. "Labor is just trying to funnel ever-increasing revenues into the private education system when public schools are being starved of funds." Mr Chalmers said the Greens had not raised their concerns with him directly but that there were "good reasons" for the charitable exemption. "We've tried to make sure that there are reasonable arrangements for charities, for not-for-profits … This is a very specific sliver of what's being proposed here," he told ABC Radio National. "We can't lose sight of why this reform is really important … There are legitimate reasons for trusts, but they also allow a small proportion of people to manage their tax in ways that are not available to most working Australians." The 30 per cent minimum tax applies only to so-called "discretionary" trusts, a term the tax office uses to identify trust structures that give their owners the flexibility to shift their money into the names of family members, holding companies, or others. Tax experts say these complicated structures allow a minority of very wealthy, highly motivated people to achieve dramatic reductions in the tax they pay. The government expects to raise $4.5 billion from the tax in its first year of operation. Government offers small businesses a trust tax workaround Those with discretionary trusts can be exempt from the new minimum 30 per cent tax if they agree to hold their trust distributions constant. But business lobbies and the opposition have argued discretionary trusts are used for a range of legitimate purposes, including by small business owners. The government has outlined several exemptions, including for family farms that are placed within trusts, charities that operate as trusts, and trusts that are set up to manage deceased estates. But Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said the tax still sent "the wrong message" and targeted business unfairly. "We urge all members of parliament to … listen to the views of those small businesses who will be affected: small and medium-sized home builders, family pharmacies, newsagents, small retailers, restaurants and cafes," he said on Tuesday. The government estimates that 350,000 active small businesses — roughly one in six — used discretionary trusts in 2022–23, the last year of available data. Treasury analysis suggests 140,000 of those would not need to pay the new tax.

events.title: What it takes to trust AI with real-world fixes
events.summary: Copilot to autopilot: Why no single safeguard is enough We designed a layered model that lets an AI agent resolve production network incidents on its own within defined identity, authorization, tooling, and human-approval boundaries. It’s 2:00 am. A pager goes off. A link somewhere in a datacenter has started flapping, a handful of alarms have correlated into one incident, and the on-call engineer is now doing what on-call engineers have always done: opening five tabs, one per system, and reconstructing what happened from fragments. We built an AI agent to do that reconstruction. It works. It pulls the device state, reads the telemetry, correlates the recent changes, classifies the failure, and writes a clean summary into the incident before the human has finished logging in. It also knows the fix. And that is where the demo stops being a demo. Because the agent “knows the fix,” the question is whether the system should allow it to shut a BGP session on a device that’s carrying live customer traffic. A “read” is something you can double-check. A “write” is an action that already happened. The moment an agent can change production, every property you were relaxed about at the read stage becomes a potential source of customer impact and risk. This post is about what we learned building an agent that’s trusted to take that action, as well as the uncomfortable conclusion we kept arriving at: There is no single thing you can build that makes an agent safe to run in production. Not a smarter model, not a stricter prompt, not a clever guardrail. Safe autonomy requires a stack. Ask 10 builders for a definition, and you’ll get 10 answers—and most of them are really examples (“You know, like a coding agent”) rather than definitions. That’s fine; we’re still in the relatively early days of agentic AI. But the fuzziness hides what matters here. An agent is not the model. The model is the brilliant, non-deterministic part in the middle. The agent is the deterministic software wrapped around it—the part that decides what the model is asked, what it may do with the answer, which tools it can reach, and what happens when it is wrong. The model supplies intelligence. The agent supplies judgment about how far to trust that intelligence and what to let it touch. Seen that way, the interesting engineering in an agentic system is usually the wrapper. And the whole safety question reframes with that distinction: Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it. Concretely, the harness we wrap around the model during execution is a mostly-deterministic workflow with a few narrow, schema-checked model steps inside it. It is what turns “the model worked something out once” into “these steps run the same way every time.” You don’t need its full mechanics yet—that’s another layer. For now, just hold the picture: a deterministic workflow with the model kept on a short leash inside it. Harness, agent, orchestrator, playbook, call it what you like. The load-bearing idea is the same: deterministic software putting a non-deterministic model to work, on purpose, within limits. The “holy grail” of agentic development is an agent that can investigate a problem, work out a fix, and carry it out without a human directing every step. But getting there in production means building safety into each step. More autonomy should not mean fewer controls. Imagine giving that agent a service account with broad access, a shell that can run anything, and a stern system prompt listing everything it must never do. It might have everything it needs to fix the problem. But what actually prevents it from taking an action it shouldn’t take? A broadly privileged service account can give the agent more access than the person who invoked it. An unrestricted shell can put anything that account and machine can reach within the impact radius. A system prompt helps guide behavior, but it can’t enforce permissions. The model can misinterpret an instruction or be influenced by malicious text in a log or tool response. Production safety can’t depend on instructions to the model alone. The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence. Modern models are frighteningly good at figuring out the fix. The real question is: “What is this thing allowed to do, under whose identity, through what interface, and with whose sign off?” It’s boring, it’s deterministic, and it’s the whole game. The mental model: Four boundaries, layered Once we started stacking boundaries, the architecture fell into four layers. Each answers a different question. None of them are sufficient alone, and that’s the point. Read bottom to top, it’s defense in depth across identity, tool, mutation, and time. Read as a sentence: The agent acts only as the human who summoned it (identity), reaches production only through a controlled interface (tool), can read freely but must pause before it changes anything (mutation), and gets less reliant on live reasoning the more it runs (time). Two of these are security controls in the literal sense: identity and tool access are where an attacker or a hallucination does its damage, so that’s where the hardest walls go. Layer 1: The agent never has more access than you The agent doesn’t get its own powerful account. It acts on behalf of the human who invoked it, bounded by that person’s real permissions. Where a service identity is unavoidable, it gets the narrower of the two. Identity is compound: the human plus the agent, and the stricter one wins. Access policies are owned by the teams that own each tool, defined per tool, and changed through a normal pull request (PR) with the tool team as a required reviewer. Merging a PR grants access; reverting it revokes access. Layer 2: One tool interface, not a bare shell The agent never gets a bare shell. Every capability it has sits behind a single typed tool interface, each tool is individually authorized, and each call is structured and logged. Note the careful wording: The enemy is not the command line; it is the unbounded one. A raw shell cannot be governed, because you cannot put a permission boundary, a schema, or a clean audit trail around bash. But a command line invoked as one narrow, declared tool, behind the interface, is fine. This is why the framing of “MCP vs. CLI” is a false dichotomy. You want both, chosen by trust level. Put everything behind the tool interface, then pick the implementation per call: a plain function or a sandboxed CLI for low-risk local work inside the trust boundary, and MCP for anything that crosses it, because MCP gives you least privilege, credential isolation, structured audit, human approval hooks, and rate limiting for free. You can secure a CLI, too, but only by paying for per-user sandboxes with tightly limited access, and even then, you can’t match per-tool granularity. Layer 3: Read freely, pause before you write Diagnostics run on their own.

events.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
events.summary: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting for them to halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision. Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off. events.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it. “Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said. Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon , October 13. Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. “I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision. “We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said. At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world. The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale. Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom. Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision. “It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.” While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop. “They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said. Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world. “There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.

events.title: Pluto Security raises $42M as AI gives enterprise security teams a new headache
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The problem with giving everyone in a company access to AI tools is that people will use them in unexpected ways. And that fact is steadily seeding fears that companies now have new, gaping security holes in their systems or, at least, will soon. Illustrating the pace of AI tool adoption within enterprises driving such fears, Shahar Bahat, CEO and co-founder of Pluto Security , says a newly announced AI tool can show up inside companies’ environment within a mere two hours of its release. And about 60% of the risks her company detects across its customer base are in tools vibe-coded by non-developers: Finance departments are the biggest source of such risks, she told TechCrunch, followed by marketing and legal teams. Developers rank fourth, she said. Her startup’s tools apparently found a vibe-coded app made by a finance employee at a Fortune 500 company to manage customer information and churn, but the app was left exposed to the internet. Pluto, fresh out of stealth with $42 million in funding, is the latest in a new crop of security startups that have quickly sprung up to help companies address those fears gaps, and all of them are raising big money from investors on the back of the conviction that only using existing security software to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, and usage is a square-peg-round-hole approach. Bahat tells TechCrunch her startup started selling only in April and has already found some takers for its tech, which helps companies gain context, risk analysis, visibility, and control over how their employees use AI tools. She said Pluto began selling in April and has already crossed $2 million in annual recurring revenue, with more than 30 enterprise customers, including Oscar Health, Workato, Sixt, and AlphaSense. Pluto’s funding spans an $8.5 million seed round led by TLV Partners, with cybersecurity firm Armis’ founders also investing. The company recently raised a Series A of $34 million led by Jump Capital, with Skinos (Check Point co-founder Shlomo Kramer’s venture firm), Ansa Capital, and other angel investors participating. That’s decent traction for a young startup, though not unique in this AI era. But it may be because the breadth of the risk isn’t isolated to large tech companies that lead the AI adoption charts. When I asked Bahat where she’s seeing the biggest risks, she said the issues are differentiated by the mindset of the CISO and how willing the organization is to adopt AI, but there were risks to be found anyway. “In general, I’ll say there was not one POC in which we entered and didn’t find malicious stuff,” she said. “Whether those are extension packages or skills — some of them had active live attacks while we did the POC. Which again, for me, product-wise is amazing. For the companies, it’s not very good.” Pluto’s entire bet is that securing such environments will require security tools to pay attention to what AI agents are doing in real time, in addition to keeping track of what and how employees are building and deploying. “We’re moving from user behavior to agent behavior,” Bahat said. In line with that vision, the startup’s software monitors the AI tools employees use, the skills, extensions, MCP servers, and other components those tools rely on, as well as the apps and agents being created. The company says it can identify risky components, spot potentially dangerous agent activity, and enforce security policies without stopping employees from using or making AI tools. To do all that, Pluto connects to endpoint security and device management systems and can deploy its own sensors through them or directly onto devices. It gathers information, including prompts, commands, running processes, permissions, and users’ previous activity, and uses its own “lightweight” models on endpoints to help assess what an agent is trying to do. What stood out is that Pluto’s system can intervene while an agent is working, Bahat said. If an agent tries to gain permissions beyond what a user intended, for example, the system can stop the action or add instructions into the session that prompt the agent to ask for confirmation. “We can inject context back to the session, and this way I can change how the agent is working,” Bahat explained. The startup also takes an unusual approach to finding customers. In April, it launched Plutonium , a free platform that lets anyone check risks associated with publicly available AI skills, connectors, and add-ons. There’s also an MCP scanner and a catalog of verified components. Bahat claims thousands of security professionals use Plutonium and that the community around it has become an important source of feedback and prospective customers.

events.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
events.summary: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. events.title: MIT startup says it can turn diesel trucks into cheaper hydrogen haulers — see it at Disrupt
events.summary: Disrupt 2026 has officially begun. Grab your pass now to be at the center of the startup epicenter. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Diesel fuel powers everything from shipping to agriculture, and with prices hitting record highs in recent weeks, governments around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout. For now, that’s meant releasing fuel from stockpiles, but in the coming years, the answer might be a new technology from an MIT startup called LNK Energies . LNK has created a way to convert existing heavy-duty trucks from diesel to hydrogen, slashing pollution and costs while shielding operators from the price spikes that result from geopolitical instability like the war in Iran. “If you look at total cost of ownership of a Class 8 truck, it’s 13% cheaper than diesel,” Alexis Huynh, chief technology officer at LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. (Class 8 is the heaviest category of trucks, including big rigs.) Automotive companies have been exploring the use of hydrogen in long-haul trucking in part because refilling a hydrogen tank is faster than recharging the massive batteries those trucks require. But hydrogen is challenging to move to refilling stations, and the pressure tanks required to store it on the truck are large and costly. LNK’s approach is to carry hydrogen chemically attached to another compound. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, or LOHCs, are liquids that can absorb and later release hydrogen, and they have been widely studied, but mostly for moving large quantities of hydrogen from refineries to fueling stations. The equipment needed to separate hydrogen from the LOHC, known as a reactor, has been too big to fit onto a truck. “A lot of the reactors that LOHC companies have today are really large. They’re about the size of a shipping container,” Huynh said. “We have shrunk that basically to the size of a mini fridge.” Moving the reactor onto the truck saves a surprising amount of energy. When hydrogen is stored on a truck, it must be pressurized to more than 11,000 psi (800 bar), roughly 800 times normal air pressure, and squeezing it that hard takes a lot of power. Because LNK’s fuel carries the hydrogen in liquid form and releases it on board as needed, that step goes away. “We’re eliminating the expensive compression step,” Sayandeep Biswas, co-founder and CEO of LNK Energies, told TechCrunch. In LNK’s system, once the hydrogen is released on the truck, it can be burned in a conventional internal combustion engine, the kind in today’s diesel trucks, with just a few modifications. The company uses waste heat from the engine to help power the on-board reactor. Or, if the trucking company wants to fully eliminate combustion emissions, it can use fuel cells instead, which convert hydrogen into electricity to power electric motors. The LOHC can be stored in a traditional fuel tank and dispensed using pumps, just like diesel. “The entire hydrogen infrastructure doesn’t need to exist,” Biswas said. “It’s just a standard diesel station.” Biswas and Huynh have a demonstration reactor working in the lab that can power an engine from a lawnmower. In 18 months, they plan to install a larger version in a commercial truck. The trucks will cost more up front, but promise to be cheaper to operate. The duo are confident that they can undercut diesel at a price of $6.50 per gallon after they’ve made just 50 to 100 trucks. None of their projections include government subsidies. “The idea isn’t to have a technology that is cheaper at scale, but one that is cheaper even during that adoption period,” Biswas said. events.title: US home sales rose in September, but slowed from a year earlier
events.summary: Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers. Existing home sales rose 1.5% last month from August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday. One of the factors in the monthly increase is that sales in August were revised lower. Sales fell 2.2% compared with September last year. The latest sales tally is slightly above the 3.98 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet. Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2-million. September is the second month in a row that the annual sales pace has remained below 4 million. Home prices continued to rise nationally last month. The U.S. median sales price increased 1.3% in September from a year earlier to $417,500, an all-time high for the month of September based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis for 39 months in a row. “This is a very tough market out there, especially with mortgage rates rising,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. This year, sales have been in a rut in large part due to rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have marched higher in the months since the war between the U.S. and Iran started in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher. The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage hit 7.4% last week , its highest level in nearly three years. It briefly dipped below 6% before the war started. Many of the homes purchased last month likely went under contract in August and July, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.43% to 6.69%, according to Freddie Mac. Mortgage rates are not likely to drop meaningfully any time soon, given the ongoing uncertainty over oil prices, geopolitical tensions, the exploding U.S. government debt and other factors that have been driving rates on home loans higher, Yun said. The sharp rise in mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, has led many would-be home shoppers to put their home shopping plans on hold. However, those who can afford to buy at current rates, or pay all cash, have a much wider selection of homes to choose from than they've had in years as properties sit on the market longer. Although home inventory levels remain below historical norms, there were 1.6 million unsold homes at the end of last month — the highest level of unsold inventory on the market since November 2019, NAR said. All told, unsold home inventory rose 1.9% last month from August and climbed 4.6% from September last year, NAR said. September’s month-end inventory translates to a 4.8-months’ supply at the current sales pace. Traditionally, a 4- to 6-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers. The more balanced market gives home shoppers potentially more leverage in negotiating better terms with sellers, especially if a property has not fetched offers in weeks or months. Consider, in September, the national median home listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250 as about 21% of listings had their initial price lowered, according to Realtor.com. “The market is clearly tilting in favor of buyers able to negotiate for better prices,” Yun said. events.title: CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle case over opioid prescriptions
events.summary: CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids WASHINGTON -- CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of prescribing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.” It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.” The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids. The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden's administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills," or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. Under the settlement, CVS must also "implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. events.summary: Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France PARIS -- Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France’s food supplies but acknowledged that the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” ″It was a wake-up call for everyone,” he said. The Paris prosecutor’s office said Tuesday that its cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack, including the extent of damage caused by spoiled food and possible fires. Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French grocery chain Cooperative U, said 80 of the company’s 2,000 stores were affected. Most managed to prevent disruptions to refrigeration, but some had to discard food, he said in a post on X. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products is an attack on the French food supply chain. It is unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable,” Schelcher said. Danish technology company Danfoss, which supplied the refrigeration management software, said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates. “Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall,” the company said. events.title: UK's Burnham weighs approval for oil and gas drilling in the North Sea
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces a crucial decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea LONDON -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing a key test of his environmental policies as he decides on whether oil and gas companies should be allowed to drill in the North Sea. Burnham's government has been under heavy pressure from climate campaigners and businesses over whether to approve two oil and gas fields in waters north of Scotland, including one said to be the U.K.'s largest untapped oil resource. Environmental groups have urged Burnham to refuse permission for the projects, known as Rosebank and Jackdaw, saying they would accelerate climate change at a time when the U.K., like the rest of Europe, faces record extreme heat linked to human actions including burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. But opposition politicians, the oil and gas industry and U.S. President Donald Trump have piled pressure on Burnham to give the green light, arguing it would protect jobs, cut household bills and boost Britain’s energy security. British officials have been expected to make a decision since August, when public consultations on the two projects closed. Rosebank is an oil field that also will produce gas. Located 80 miles (130 kilometers) north of Scotland's Shetland Islands, it is estimated to be the largest undeveloped oil and gas field in the U.K., reportedly with capacity to produce 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil within about 25 years. Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles east of Aberdeen on Scotland's northeast coast. Production there was expected to last under a decade. The Shell Group, one of the project's co-developers, predicts the field can produce around 6.5% of the U.K.’s gas production at its peak. The opposition Conservative Party, which has pushed for the developments to go ahead, said the Jackdaw field could start heating 1.4 million homes in the U.K. this winter if approved. The former Conservative government previously approved production at both sites, which were scheduled to start operations later this year. But a court in Edinburgh ruled last year that the approvals were unlawful, after considering a legal challenge from Greenpeace and another nonprofit. “The public interest in authorities acting lawfully and the private interest of members of the public in climate change outweigh the private interest of the developers,” judge Andrew Stewart ruled at the time. Critics have argued that the oil and gas reserves in Britain's North Sea holdings are small and would make little difference to energy bills because prices are decided by international markets. They contend that new developments would increase carbon emissions while failing to contribute to Britain's energy security. Analysts at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a London-based nonprofit, estimated that more than 90% of the oil and gas likely to be produced from the North Sea has already been extracted. “We’ve just had record-breaking heat waves this summer, wildfires, half of the country’s still in drought. We’re facing potential crop failures and food shortages this winter from a super El Niño ,” said Victoria Smith, a Fossil Free London activist protesting on Tuesday. events.title: White House pushes out Kimberly Guilfoyle after misconduct reports
events.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, announced her resignation Tuesday, shortly after the White House asked her to step down and following reports alleging misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The exit of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday that she was asked to resign during her first press briefing. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Driving the news: "My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote in a post on X on Tuesday. "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again." "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America." Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president. Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines. Zoom in: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador." A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true. Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025. What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun. Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath. events.title: Europe's alternative to Trump's China trade war
events.summary: Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0 , betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach. Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb. Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe. The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December. The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters . Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.) Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs. The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point." "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said. What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade official, tells Axios. Washington is pushing trading partners to join forces against China's industrial overcapacity. "It's really hard for any one country to make progress on that if you don't have allies on your side," Mullaney says. By the numbers: Chinese automakers ramped up hybrid shipments to Europe after the EU imposed steep tariffs on fully electric vehicles in 2024. New data released yesterday shows that China's global passenger vehicle exports surged 64% in September, to 919,000, even as domestic sales fell 27%. What to watch: Europe's deal could shift pressure to other industries — or perhaps even other nations — without addressing the underlying imbalances driving China's export boom. Economist Michael Pettis argued over the weekend that the agreement would do little for European manufacturing overall. "EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers," he wrote on X . The bottom line: Europe's deal may provide breathing room for its automakers. But China's industrial might — and the pressure it is inflicting on manufacturers around the world — is not going away.

events.title: Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'
events.summary: Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called "a bet on the future of humanity". Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a "women-first" chat rule. Bumble ditched the rule in August this year. Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble's founder and current chief executive, said she would remain "actively involved" with the business she set up 12 years ago. While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd's role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners. Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to "renew and accelerate businesses...in a world transformed by AI". They said: "Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfillment, human connection and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity." This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, with some experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity . Bumble's share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021 . Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023. In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app. Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had "exciting potential" in dating apps related to safety, and Bumble had been looking at research that found Gen Z and milliennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles. This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According to a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.
