events.title: Kroger to lay off 3K corporate employees over 3 years as it leans into AI
events.summary: Grocery store chain Kroger says it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations. “Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.” Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.” Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer. Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO . Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities. Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells. Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer, Vatican says Crew lands on remote island in search for Amelia Earhart Eyewitnesses describe rider's roller coaster fall: 'Everybody tried to save this man' Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon. Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed. A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value. Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee. Kroger shares fell 1.6% in morning trading Tuesday, to $61.66. events.title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
events.summary: Singh's clip of Sabrina Carpenter went viral Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year. The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral. "The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says. The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first. He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms. The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible. Eknoor Singh's successful social media video clips include one of popstar Dua Lipa With clippers able to earn up to $3 (£2.30) per 1,000 views across platforms, it can be very lucrative if a particular clip does take off. Singh says he got hooked on clipping last year when he made $300 from posting a short video of popstar Dua Lipa on Instagram. "I was like, 'OK, this is a lot of money for simply posting a video.' I instantly knew how lucrative it could be." Now he says he is earning "at least £10,000 a month". He adds that he looks for clips that are funny, quick to watch and engaging, such as a short video he made in May last year of Sabrina Carpenter's reaction to having the tails of her dress stepped on at the Met Gala in New York. Singh did not reveal who the client was. For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping. He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests. Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says. Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says. Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world". Ethan Weems says the income helps him continue to work from home Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick. The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max. For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs. That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos. In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips. "The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions". Eknoor Singh says he can make clips anywhere with just his mobile and a good internet connection Evan Stanfield, the founder and boss of Clipping Culture, is himself just 21. He set up the business last year after dropping out of the University of Kansas. Stanfield says that the website connects brands to more than 340,000 clippers from all over the world. He has a simple theory for the popularity of short videos: "People's attention spans are getting shorter and shorter." He adds that making the clips is a young person's game because "they're most of the consumers of short-form videos". Back in London, Eknoor Singh says he is "kind of clipping non-stop", wherever he is. "I could be anywhere. I could go on holiday and make money." I paid £30,000 for an 'influencer' degree.

Time: 10am – 11.30am | Location: Bank of England, 20 Moorgate, London, EC2R 6DA The Chair thanked members for attending and confirmed that the Minutes of the Money Markets Committee (MMC) June 2026 meeting had been published on the Bank’s website. footnote [1] The Chair updated on recent usage of the Bank’s market-wide repo facilities. Members were reminded that use of the Bank’s facilities, including against a broad range of eligible collateral, was consistent with the intended transition to a repo-led operating framework. The Chair provided a brief update on the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC’s) September decision on Quantitative Tightening footnote [2] , including the exchange of letters between the Governor and the Chancellor regarding QT and the APF. footnote [3] The Chair also noted the related announcements made by the Bank and HM Treasury that came out at the same time. footnote [4] Item 2 – Discussion on market conditions Members noted that money markets continued to function smoothly and that funding conditions remained stable, even during recent increased bond market volatility. Liquidity was reported to be ample, with limited signs of stress. Members also reported stable cross-currency funding conditions despite recent geopolitical developments and broader market volatility, with quarter-end and year-end conditions expected to remain orderly. While some highlighted the potential for volatility in outright asset markets to transmit into funding conditions through reduced risk appetite or position unwinds, the overall assessment was that money market functioning remained robust. Some nevertheless noted emerging funding pressures further out the euro curve as Eurosystem liquidity continued to decline. Members also discussed developments in European Commercial Paper (ECP) markets, noting increased issuance activity and growing use of these funding channels. Members also discussed the Financial Policy Committee’s proposed changes to the leverage ratio framework footnote [5] . Members generally welcomed the direction of the proposals but considered that leverage requirements are just one of a number of constraints on their activity including stress-testing assumptions, investor expectations and risk-weighted capital requirements. As a result, members considered that it was difficult to predict the extent to which the proposals would lead to a material increase in leverage or balance-sheet deployment in UK money markets in the near-term. Some noted that greater releasability of constraints in stress could support increased use of gilts and reverse repo within buffers. Members noted increasing competition for retail and corporate deposits. While this had not materially affected funding plans, some observed that sustained competition for deposits could increase wholesale funding requirements and funding costs over time. Members agreed this would remain an area to monitor. From a market infrastructure perspective, strong trading activity across gilt and international markets was reported, with no material change in cleared repo conditions. Members also welcomed the predictability provided by the MPC and Bank's recent balance sheet announcements and noted that the Bank's liquidity facilities continued to support confidence in firms' ability to manage reserves and liquidity needs.

events.title: Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K: What to know about smart hub and updated console
events.summary: Apple has introduced HomeView, a device that the company says incorporates artificial intelligence-driven Siri and an easy-to-use interface to help people at home. A video posted to Apple 's website and social media accounts shows a busy family in the kitchen using the device to answer questions, communicate with others and set reminders. “Siri, ping me my keys,” a woman asks HomeView as she tries to leave her home. The HomePod speaker causes her keys to give off a beeping noise, presumably with the help of Apple 's AirTag. In the video and on the HomeView webpage, Apple says the product is only “available in English to start”. The company says HomeView will be available on November 13 with prices starting at $299. Two options will be available: a device that rests on surfaces and a version that mounts on a wall. Before Apple's HomeView announcement, Anshika Jain, principal analyst for the technology market analysis firm Counterpoint , said that such a device would help the US technology giant strengthen its consumer product offerings. “The upcoming display-based device could become a central interface for controlling smart home products, accessing content and services, and interacting with Apple’s AI capabilities, potentially giving Apple a stronger foothold in the smart home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. Apple also seems prepared to allow devices made by other companies to work with HomeView. “Designed in collaboration with Apple and select brands, Apple Home Collection accessories – including smart cameras, thermostats and a door lock – are simple to set up, easy to use, and private with data that’s encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home,” the company posted to its site. It added that the collection of devices would arrive at a later date. Mohit Agrawal, research director with Counterpoint, said that this aspect was intriguing. “Rather than buying its way in, as Amazon did with Ring and Google with Nest, Apple is partnering with LG and Schneider Electric,” he explained. “This lets it fill out the home quickly, from the front door to the thermostat, while keeping control of the experience through Siri and the Home app.” Apple seems to be positioning the forthcoming HomeView product as a device that is used passively in day-to-day life. “HomeView does the heavy lifting when you’re busy around the house,” a description reads. “And with a vibrant display and powerful acoustics, your music, videos and calls look and sound amazing … meet the new heart of your home.” According to technology news outlet, The Verge , HomeView will be initially available in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and India. HomePod mini 2 Also on Tuesday, Apple announced its HomePod mini speaker devices would be getting an upgrade. “Siri on HomePod mini 2 puts a powerful, AI assistant right at the centre of your home,” the company said. “Once set up with your iPhone or iPad , Siri draws on broad world knowledge and your personal context to help you find what you need and get more done every day.” The HomePod 2 will be available on October 30, with prices starting at $149. Apple touts improved sound, touch controls, a mesh design and a woven power cord among the HomePod's improvements. “With Apple Intelligence and a more capable Siri, the company is positioning HomePod as an entry point into an AI-powered home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. “Still, shipment growth is likely to remain modest in low single digits YoY [year over year] as the market continues to face saturation and longer replacement cycles.” Apple TV Apple's TV console has gone several years without an update, but that changed on Tuesday with the unveiling of Apple TV 4K. The company says the updated console has an A19 processor that assists in delivering 4K video quality, and it will also have a Siri remote. Apple TV 4K will be available on November 13, with prices starting at $299. “Apple TV 4K delivers the ultimate cinematic experience, from shows and movies to games and workouts,” the company said. “With the new, more powerful Siri AI and built-in microphones, enjoying what you love is as easy as using your voice.”

events.title: Saudi attacks shake the confidence of foreign investors
events.summary: Oil prices ticked down on Tuesday as Saudi oil executives sought to reassure the market following a major attack on the capital’s airport. International energy bosses were largely absent from this week’s World Petroleum Council Energy Congress, held in Riyadh for the first time, after the Houthi attack. The CEOs of BP, Shell, and TotalEnergies, along with a host of international ministers, including US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, dropped out due to the strikes. That left a thinner-than-expected crowd, mostly made up of local executives, to hear the kingdom seek deeper international cooperation to secure energy supplies and trade routes. Saudi Arabia can build more pipelines and boost storage capacity, but “no one nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone,” Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said. His comments reflect the growing role of foreign investors in the region’s energy industry, already expanding even before the Iran war. Long relegated to minor roles, the Gulf energy companies increasingly see international energy firms and global investors as an integral part of their plans to lock in customers for their hydrocarbon exports, invest in their infrastructure, and bind other states into their security in a way that the old expectations of oil for security arrangements have failed to guarantee. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Trump’s Russian energy strategy could backfire
events.summary: Tim’s view The contradictory tangle of energy policy actions taken by US President Donald Trump toward Russia over the weekend risks repeating mistakes that he and his allies often slammed his predecessor for. On Friday, Trump announced the US would waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the spring and permit it to release 300,000 metric tons of diesel into the global market, before announcing an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv. The diesel deal was quickly condemned by a bipartisan group of senators , who argued that the volume was too small to make a difference — equal to less than a day of US consumption — and extended a “financial lifeline” to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This, they said, contradicted both a 2022 US ban on Russian energy imports and the spirit of the new sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to penalize countries like China and India for the very same kinds of purchases the president is now pursuing. The diesel relaxation, former State Department energy diplomat Geoff Pyatt told me, is “enough of a sweetheart deal to encourage [Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill] Dmitriev and Putin to keep fighting in hopes Trump will deliver Kyiv.” As for the “ceasefire,” Russia seems to have violated it almost instantly . A Ukrainian official told me on Monday that Kyiv was temporarily holding off on further long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries while it assessed Moscow’s behavior and was waiting for a chance, potentially later this week, to clarify details of Trump’s proposal with US officials. Axios reported the deal could apply only to refineries , which would make little sense for Ukraine to participate in given that it has only one barely-functional refinery. Kyiv is more worried about the power sector, which a recently leaked Russian military planning document makes clear is still directly in Moscow’s sights . Dangling a limited ceasefire deal that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy can’t accept sends the same message to the Kremlin as the diesel deal: Ukrainians are the problem in this war, and US resolve in support of Ukraine is barely paper-thin. The past few years have shown repeatedly that accommodating Putin pushes him away from the negotiating table, not toward it . Trump and his energy officials have criticized Biden often and loudly for authorizing, in 2022, a record release of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which they framed as an irresponsible stab at tamping down US fuel prices ahead of an election at the expense of long-term American security interests. They also criticized Biden’s decision in 2021 to relax sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline in the interest of repairing relations with Moscow, which helped embolden Putin to undertake the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With just three weeks until the midterms, Trump is clearly riled about diesel prices and the slow recovery of exports of refined products from the Persian Gulf. But it’s counterproductive to capitulate to Putin: In addition to the uncountable human toll, a longer war in Ukraine means more energy market distortion ahead. Notable A new poll found that even if Trump managed a political feat like ending the Iran war or bringing down gasoline prices by $1 ahead of November’s midterms , a majority of voters would not be more likely to vote Republican.

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI and built with privacy and security at its core CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today introduced Apple HomeView , designed to be central to the home and personal to everyone in it. With a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection, and smart home management together in one place, from playing music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and security at the core. 1 HomeView recognizes users by their faces, adapting so they can access their personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My. HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s profoundly more capable and conversational, with broad world knowledge that powers richer music discovery and onscreen awareness. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, it can also draw on a user’s personal context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant information across their apps, to provide more helpful, personalized responses. 2 Designed to fit in any space, HomeView can be placed on a tabletop as the center of the home or wall-mounted to fit in spaces like the entryway or hallway. Pre-orders start today, with availability beginning November 13. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. “It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home. And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.” Elegantly Designed for Any Space HomeView features a beautiful aluminum design with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display connected to a domed speaker base by a stainless steel hinge that provides a smooth tilt for comfortable viewing on tabletops of any height. The perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table, HomeView comes in four beautiful colors — silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray — each finished with a matching cable. The elegant design and Liquid Retina display seamlessly blend into any space while remaining clearly visible from across the room. It features adaptive display technologies, including True Tone, that react to changing light throughout the day. Automatic brightness adjusts from 500 nits — bright enough to stay vivid and easy to see even in a sunlit room — down to just 0.3 nits, making it ideal for the nightstand. The HomeView interface intelligently adjusts based on the user’s distance, showing simpler information that’s viewable from across the room and richer detail as they step closer. A separate wall-mounted HomeView model — available in space gray and silver — offers the same 7-inch Liquid Retina display, powerful set of features, and rich audio. It can be attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home HomeView recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Each user gets their own personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests. Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon. With broad world knowledge, anyone in the home can ask Siri about virtually any topic and get an answer.

Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K , delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience. 1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free. 2 The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes. 3 The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13. “The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.” An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.” A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing. Faster Performance, Smarter Remote The A19 chip in the new Apple TV 4K delivers up to 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance than the previous generation, for greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations. The A19 chip also includes a new, dedicated AV1 decoder, enabling more efficient, high-quality streaming while using less bandwidth. The new Siri Remote keeps its familiar design while adding Find My support with Precision Finding and an option to play a sound on the remote — making it far easier to locate. 4 Apple’s Most Immersive Home Theater Ever Pairing HomePod with Apple TV 4K already offers users an immersive viewing experience that’s easy to set up, and the new Apple TV 4K takes it even further. For the first time, users can create a four-speaker surround sound experience with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and HomePod mini 2. HomePod (2nd generation) can also be used in this four-speaker setup for the ultimate audio experience, as long as the front and rear speaker pairs match. 5 An Even Smarter Home Hub The new Apple TV 4K continues to serve as a powerful home hub, giving users control of their smart home accessories from anywhere. 6 With a compatible doorbell, notifications appear directly on the TV so users can see who’s at the door, speak with them, and control other accessories like unlocking the door — all without interrupting what they’re watching. Apple TV 4K supports automations, guest mode, and secure local processing of HomeKit Secure Video, now enhanced with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity video descriptions and summarized notifications. Users can also use Siri AI to control smart home accessories and turn scenes on or off hands-free. And with built-in Wi-Fi and Thread, Apple TV 4K can seamlessly connect and control a user’s smart home. events.title: A pioneering Jeddah schoolhouse show reaches Frieze Masters in London 58 years later
events.summary: It took 58 years for a pioneering Jeddah schoolhouse show to reach Frieze Masters in London. In 1968, two female artists hung their paintings at a school in Jeddah called Dar Al-Tarbia Al-Hadetha, in one of the first exhibitions women had ever held in Saudi Arabia. One of them, Mounirah Mosly , spent the decades that followed — long before Vision 2030 set off a boom in Saudi art — designing Aramco publications, helping run its children’s art competitions, and working dyes, snakeskin, and rope into collages about war and Palestine, until her death in 2019. This week, her creations go on display at Frieze Masters , Frieze London’s fair for art made before 2000, where a slot reads as a verdict that the work now belongs to history. Jeddah’s Athr Gallery is debuting with Mosly and a second pioneer of Saudi modernism, Abdulrahman Alsulaiman. Her work hangs in the fair’s Feminist Legacies section. — Manal Albarakati

events.title: AI is an inflation problem, Fed’s Goolsbee says
events.summary: The News Inflation tied to the AI boom is “jumping out of its lane” and starting to push up prices in unrelated corners of the economy, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said. “Prices are going up in spaces that are not just components in data centers and the directly adjacent industries,” he said on Semafor’s . “I’m getting increasingly nervous that that’s just straight, old-fashioned overheating demand.” Prices for land, electricity, water, construction, and electrical components used in data centers have surged. Those spikes don’t appear to have yet hit consumer pain points — for example, the cost of groceries or a haircut — but economists are closely watching how AI’s wealth, from paper millionaires in Silicon Valley to higher-paid construction workers, is being spent. Fed Governor Lisa Cook warned last month about “some economy-wide pressure from AI-fueled demand” but said that so far the boom looks like “a shift in demand toward AI-related sectors rather than an increase in economy-wide demand.” Fighting that kind of sector-specific inflation with rate hikes “could be a mistake,” she said. Goolsbee isn’t a member of the Fed committee that sets interest rates, but will join it in 2027. He and other economists have been trying to parse how much of today’s stubborn inflation — 3.4% in August, with September’s numbers due out this week — is from higher oil prices triggered by the war in the Middle East, which the Fed can’t do much about, and how much is coming from hotter demand across the economy for goods and services. “If inflation remains persistent, then I think it’s clear what the Fed has to do,” he said, when asked whether the central bank should raise interest rates again when it meets later this month. Liz’s view The Fed’s problem is that its best tool for fighting inflation doesn’t seem to be denting the demand for AI inputs. Hyperscalers aren’t slaphappy consumers who might be deterred by higher interest rates. They are locked in a must-win battle and don’t seem to mind higher debt costs. Companies like Alphabet and Meta have cash-cow advertising businesses that can support a few extra basis points of interest. It’s a broader problem for the Fed: Big parts of the US economy no longer respond to rising interest rates. There may be a pain point for the hyperscalers, but it’s likely to be intolerable for the rest of us. Room for Disagreement The issuance of new AI-linked debt fell in August, according to Morgan Stanley, which could show investors tapping on the brakes, even if corporate executives don’t want to. Transcript Liz Hoffman: Austan Goolsbee, welcome to the show. Austan Goolsbee: Thank you for having me. Liz: You are a great communicator in a world of wonks, literally a champion talker. Kevin Warsh wants the Fed to talk less and to force investors to look at the numbers and make their own decisions. What do you think? I’m an old friend and fan of Chairman Warsh. I worked with him back in the financial crisis. Before he ever got there, I’m uneasy with people expressing what we’re now calling forward guidance, that is saying, “Here’s what I think will happen at the next meeting. Here’s what I think four months from now the interest rate should change.” Most of the discussion about communication seems to have been about that, and I kind of agree with we should phase out that kind of communication. I’m engaged in a demystification project about the Federal Reserve. Here’s what we do. We’re not the bad guys. We’re the Guardians of the Galaxy. I’m going to stay on that for sure. Liz: Getting to those numbers that you would all like the market to put more stock in and make their own decisions about, even if they were prepared to be weaned off the commentary, does the data that you’re seeing right now lay out a clear picture? I like how you phrased that. I would say no, not a super clear picture because inflation’s still way too high. I have been worrying publicly about the potential for supply shocks like tariffs, like oil prices to shove us into a stagflationary kind of a trade-off. There is one sense in which it hasn’t been ambiguous. It hasn’t been stagflationary. The job market still looks very stable to me. Growth has been solid, consumer spending solid. We’re falling down on the inflation side of the mandate. But the ambiguity comes, is the inflation getting better on its own as it might if a supply shock kind of worked through or if you had a tariff that was just a one-time increase in the level of prices that should fade away and it hasn’t really been fading away. And you’ve seen inflation in services kicking up and that’s not really from tariffs, that’s not really mostly from oil. So that’s where you start to get the ambiguity in it and it’s not totally clear. Rohan Goswami: How much of that is AI, which obviously it’s driving a huge investment boom that’s sending up the price of inputs, power, land up. But at the same time, there is this deflationary promise that it’ll make everything cheaper. How do you think about those two things? This dynamic where there is great promise to come that is factored into massive stock market valuations and massive incentives for companies to engage in business investment. All of those things, the bigger the hype, the greater the chance that you overheat the economy in the short run, that for the day job of the Fed, the more promise there is, the more temptation, the more tendency to spend today based on the promise of what is to come. And that you got to be careful about because that’s just old-fashioned overheating right now. Rohan: What would a financial unwind of that trade, of the AI trade actually look like from where you sit? If it’s a discovery that the fundamentals are not there and it’s a bubble, that we have had bubbles in US history in the past, including in the recent past, and their unwinds can get ugly depending how much leverage is associated with those bubbles. It could be more like the popping of the internet. Now, Rohan, you’re not old enough. You don’t remember it, but if you back up, if you’re older than dirt like me, you’ll remember we had an experience with the internet that they were building out the infrastructure premised on growth rates of 20% per year. And when the growth rate came in, well, it’s only going to be 7% per year, that’s still a pretty strong growth rate, but they were massively overbuilt. And so we kind of had this overhang. That’s slightly different than... Finding out the fundamentals are different is slightly different than just a old-fashioned bubble in my view. Liz: But Alan Greenspan, I think, said basically that the Fed cannot deflate a bubble in real time without making life miserable for everybody else. Do you think that’s still true? There is a very significant debate among economists about the question, should the Fed try to prevent bubbles, pop bubbles, just clean up after the bubble pops? All of those things. events.title: How the Houthis’ Zaydi heritage influences their strikes in Iran
events.summary: The Houthis firing missiles at Riyadh are not just Iranian proxies — they’re heirs to a 1,000-year-old Zaydi imamate that ruled northern Yemen on and off until the modern state was established in 1962. Zaydism holds that power belongs to the Prophet’s descendants, not elected officials. In an explainer video , Baraa Shiban, a RUSI fellow who sat on Yemen’s National Dialogue before being exiled for criticizing the group’s abuses, describes how, after a 1995 trip to Iran, the group’s founder, Hussein al-Houthi, fused the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam with Tehran’s revolutionary doctrine and built a militia in Hezbollah’s image. The group seized Sanaa in 2014, a decade after its founder was killed. Rather than replace the state, the Houthis hollowed it out, Shiban said, assigning a “supervisor” to sit over every ministry and neighborhood, extorting businesses, indoctrinating the public, and recruiting children as soldiers . They now rule most of Yemen’s population and sit on one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. — Manal Albarakati

events.title: Five things to watch after Trump's Russian diesel deal
events.summary: President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down. Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. A few things to watch... The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement. Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes. The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers. Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter. "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba. The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard. Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. The law. It's not clear if any Russian barrels will reach U.S. shores — or whether it's legal if they do. A bipartisan group of seven senators, in a statement , say the decision runs afoul of a 2022 law barring U.S. imports of Russian oil and petroleum products. Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence said it is acting "in compliance with all applicable laws." Meanwhile, the White House faces an Oct. 18 deadline to begin implementing a more recent law — named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — that imposes fresh sanctions on Russia and trade penalties on buyers of Russian energy. But the law gives the White House discretion to waive key provisions. Ukraine. Trump is pushing Ukraine and Russia to ease attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has criticized Trump's deal, said Russia has continued its barrages even as he maintained Ukraine held back early this week. events.title: Ecuador’s former president tried to kill dollarization. Here’s what that means for Venezuela, Argentina and the Rest of Latin America
events.summary: Ecuador’s experience with dollarization matters beyond Quito. The possibility of mothballing local currencies and replacing them with the dollar is a hot topic in Latin America. It’s also on the agenda in Washington, D.C., where there is renewed interest in promoting the use of the greenback. Ecuador is an ideal natural experiment in how a dollarized system holds up against a hostile government. Rafael Correa, who holds a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois, opposed dollarization before it was adopted in Ecuador and before he became president. He led the country for a decade but could not dismantle Ecuador’s dollarized system because it produced excellent results and garnered widespread public support. The collapse In 1999, Ecuador’s sucre began a catastrophic plunge. At the end of 1998, it traded at 6,825 sucres to the U.S. dollar. By the end of 1999, it had plunged to 20,243 sucres to the dollar, losing two-thirds of its value against the greenback in one year. The losses did not stop there. During the first week of 2000, the sucre shed another 27.7% and hit an all-time low of 28,000 to the dollar. Faced with a currency in free fall, a banking crisis, and an imploding economy, President Jamil Mahuad announced on January 9, 2000, that Ecuador would replace the sucre with the dollar at 25,000 sucres to the dollar. President Bill Clinton and Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers had encouraged the move. Dollarization worked. Inflation dropped sharply, deposits flowed back into the banking system, and the economy switched from negative to positive growth with a surge in exports leading the way. With a system immune to currency crises, stability was established in Ecuador, and while stability might not be everything, everything is nothing without stability. A durable regime Today, dollarization enjoys roughly 90% approval. It is the longest-lived Ecuadorian currency regime since independence in May 1830, and it has lasted longer than any constitution. Its resilience is all the more notable because it survived Correa’s presidency (January 2007 to May 2017). Before entering politics, Correa published papers denouncing dollarization and sketched a plan to unwind it. As president, he called it “an immense error” and “monetary suicide.” Yet he knew an open attempt to dedollarize would trigger bank runs, economic collapse, and perhaps his impeachment. So, Correa repeatedly assured voters that abandoning the dollar would be catastrophic and was not on his agenda. What Correa did instead Below the surface, his actions told a different story. In his first year in office, he dismantled one of dollarization’s natural complements, a fiscal anchor. Ecuador had built an oil reserve fund, which, together with the dollar, had delivered the country’s first run of concurrent fiscal surpluses since it began pumping oil. Correa scrapped the fund. That same year, Correa introduced a series of economic policies that cut against dollarization’s logic. He closed the economy to foreign capital, which runs contrary to the principles of a dollarized system. He selectively defaulted on Ecuador’s foreign debt despite record oil revenues. He imposed an exit tax on every dollar leaving the country and sharply raised import tariffs. To exert control over private banks, he forced them to repatriate 45% of their liquidity and park it at the central bank. Correa also introduced a central bank electronic money program. It was billed as a tool for financial inclusion, since it let Ecuadorians pay by mobile phone. But because the central bank, not private banks, issued the balances, the government could have used it to pay its bills in digital credits not fully backed by dollars. The public wanted nothing to do with it, and the program was shut down. Most egregiously, the central bank began lending directly to the treasury. In effect, this allowed Correa to print unbacked “ecuadollars.” Central bank financing of the government peaked at about 10% of GDP, according to the IMF, with the heaviest lending in 2009–2014. The loans were of questionable legality and ran contrary to the tenets of a dollarized system. The legacy Correa was convicted of bribery in the Sobornos case and sentenced to eight years in prison. He lives in Belgium, outside the reach of that sentence. His legacy lingers. The full benefits of dollarization are not realized in Ecuador today because the central bank still sets interest rates and directs bank lending toward favored sectors. In addition, remaining capital controls restrict Ecuador’s access to the world’s deepest pool of international dollar liquidity. For countries weighing dollarization, the lesson is clear: the dollar does its job. For 26 years, Ecuador has remained immune from the plague of a currency crisis and has sustained respectable economic growth, low inflation, and surging exports. events.title: Car finance compensation payments delayed until next year
events.summary: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, regulators have announced. Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed. Who could receive car finance compensation? The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest. Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024. The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period. In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them. The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much. Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan. Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders. How much compensation could victims receive? Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement. The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn. How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered. For some customers - especially if their contact details have changed - it could take many months before compensation is paid. What do victims need to do to claim compensation? Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything. The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company. The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts. Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation . The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external . lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027 those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees. FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers. When will drivers receive compensation and who will pay? Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027. But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme. Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 to 26 February. It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes. The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme.

events.title: Americans are stressed about grocery prices, so why do they toss or overlook so much ‘misfit’ food?
events.summary: Shoppers are much more inclined to buy misshapen produce if they can be assured the quality is good. Carly Reeves on Unsplash , CC BY There’s a paradox that drives the shopping decisions of many Americans: Almost three-quarters say they’re feeling stressed out about skyrocketing grocery bills . But they keep discarding large quantities of food that’s safe to eat, from crooked carrots to surplus yogurt to “best before” items pulled from shelves early. Overall, the U.S. government estimates that 30% to 40% of all food – from consumers, retailers and producers – is thrown out. That’s not just a massive missed opportunity for people experiencing food insecurity , but it’s also a significant contribution to global warming. According to the United Nations, 8%-10% of carbon emissions globally result from food waste. In recent years, however, a market to rescue discarded groceries and repurpose food scraps and by-products has grown dramatically. This ranges from marketing “ugly” produce to appeal to more consumers to upcycling food by-products . I study how consumers evaluate product value and quality, and my research suggests that American shoppers are much less fixated on prices or environmental impact. Instead, they care about quality. Even when perfectly good “misfit” produce is deeply discounted, for example, many shoppers assume that the low price reflects poor quality and either walk away or reach for a fruit or vegetable they think looks better. What does this mean for reducing food waste and shedding these purchasing biases? My research has found that smarter and more effective labeling can make a big difference. A discount or promise of lower carbon emissions isn’t enough by itself – people have to believe the food is good first. Making ‘ugly’ food attractive A whole retail sector is now dedicated to marketing misfit food. “Ugly produce” delivery companies like Hungry Harvest and Misfits Market are rescuing and reselling food to shoppers who want to save and reduce their carbon footprint. Misfits Market alone has rescued more than 265 million pounds (about 120 million kilos) of food since 2018 and sells it at an average discount of 35%. Companies that sell ‘misfit’ produce have seen a surge of consumer interest in recent years. Jintao Zhang , CC BY Another example is Too Good To Go , an app that sells “surprise” bags of surplus food at about one-third of the retail price. It estimates that it has saved more than 26 million meals, including through partnerships with more than 530 Whole Foods stores . And the app Flashfood encourages grocers to list meat, dairy and produce nearing their best-before date at around half price and directs shoppers, including those on public food assistance, to those deals. Consumers appear to be responding. Too Good To Go users in the U.S. saved 8.1 million meals in the first seven months of 2025, a 67% jump from the year before , while Misfits Market rescued 27 million pounds of food (about 12 million kilos) in 2025, up from 23 million (about 10 million kilos) in 2019, its first full year of operation. This market is also using smarter labeling to grow its appeal. Shoppers who believe that food appearance is important tend to judge misshapen produce as lower quality. But labeling these offerings as “ugly” actually reduces that bias because it signals that the only flaw is cosmetic. Another study found that in-store messages that raise shoppers’ self-esteem can also make a different: In field tests, a “ Different Outside. Same Inside ” message successfully urged people to overlook external appearance when making judgments, whether on people or food. The upcycling boom This sustainability push is also playing out in the processed and semi-processed foods market, where would-be waste is converted into upcycled products. Examples include flour milled from soybean pulp, snacks that leave the fruit peel on, and “bites” made from rescued bananas . Companies that want to market these goods can get third-party certification through Upcycled Certified if they pass an audit of their supply chain. More than 600 products from over 100 brands now carry it, and sales of certified products grew 17% from 2024 to 2025. Here, too, perceptions of quality matter. In research on consumers’ acceptance of these foods, my co-authors and I found that they made their purchase decision based largely on whether they believed the product was as good as its conventional counterpart. But in this case, in contrast to “ugly” produce, these products tend to be pricier, so they can’t compete through discounting. Rather, they usually sell at a premium – like this small bag of specialty flour going for $7. That means that it’s even more important they signal higher quality so they can appeal to less price-constrained shoppers. Generational attitudes differ on this point, our research found . Gen Z, millennials and baby boomers are more willing to buy foods certified as upcycled if they agree that the quality and environmental appeal are worth it. But Gen Xers – those who were born between 1965 and 1979 – show less enthusiasm, citing a perception of lower quality. That result fits what we generally know about Gen X shoppers. We discovered they are hard to persuade and cost-conscious, and they tend to rely much more on their own judgment. Gen Xers are also least likely to eat out or go shopping for groceries online, preferring instead to cook for themselves. That means they tend to scrutinize foods more closely in the store. A “green” benefit won’t beat these skeptics. They need an assurance of quality from brick-and-mortar retailers they trust, rather than from online platforms. When logos matter The encouraging news from our research is that it sometimes doesn’t take much to change beliefs. In two experiments, my co-authors and I tested whether a simple logo could shift shoppers’ perceptions of foods made from rescued ingredients. We designed one version that was round, green and descriptive, following established design principles: Circular logos signal higher quality , while descriptive ones lift brand evaluations . The other was hexagonal, monochrome and bare. Shoppers respond more favorably to logos that provide information and incentives, research has found. From Jintao Zhang. , CC BY We found that shoppers who saw products with the well-designed logo rated those foods higher in quality and were more willing to buy them than those who saw the same products with no logo. The poorly designed logo, meanwhile, made no difference. It was the increase in perceived quality, in our view, that made people more willing to buy. A logo that looks credible, explains itself and signals care can change what shoppers believe. A forgettable one might as well not be there. Closing this gap in perceptions, in short, doesn’t require shoppers to care more about the planet. It requires them to believe the food is good. events.title: Poundland in rescue talks as owners seek buyer
events.summary: Retail chain Poundland is in talks with potential buyers as it seeks a rescue deal, it has confirmed. Executives are working with an Irish property development group on a management buyout, as first reported by Sky News , external . But a union representing shopworkers warned that the retailer could fall into administration if that deal falls through, putting thousands of jobs at risk. This outcome would be "a disaster for our members", the Usdaw union said. Poundland has about 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and 12,000 employees. The chain has been struggling for a number of years due to pressures including rising costs and competition. However, it expects sales to have grown more than 3% in 2026 compared with the previous year, which managing director Barry Williams said earlier this month was evidence that its recovery plan "is working". The retailer was sold for £1 last summer by previous owner Pepco to US investment firm Gordon Brothers. The current owners are in the process of seeking buyers, with the Poundland management attempting a buyout, a spokesman said. Mr Williams, along with the firm's leadership team and Andy Bond, a former chairman of Pepco, have been working with Irish real estate firm Martin Property Group on a management buyout. Martin Property Group is the management team's "preferred partner", the spokesman said, but the team will "work with whoever can deliver the best result for the business, colleagues and suppliers and build on the successful recovery that's already taking shape," he added. However, Bally Auluk, a national officer at Usdaw, said there are "deep concerns that the business could go into administration" should this buyout fail. "We are aware that a management buy-out has been attempted and we are told that their offers are being turned down," he added. A Poundland source disputed this, however, saying the Martin Property Group is part of the sale process and remains the management team's preferred partner. Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth said there were "tough times" on the High Street for all retailers. She said retailers were struggling with "significantly subdued consumer confidence as prices continue to rise" due to higher fuel costs. Poundland itself faces intense competition from rivals including B&M, Aldi, Lidl and from online retailers including Temu and TikTok Shop. The business "lost its strong £1 identity leaving shoppers to think it was getting too expensive", Shuttleworth said, and a costly expansion into clothing and frozen food under past management had not been successful. However, increased sales this year showed a deal with Mr Williams as boss "would make good sense", she added. Are you a Poundland customer? Do you think it is doing well, or badly? Get in touch here. events.title: Du and etisalat unveil new services boosting UAE push towards 6G
events.summary: UAE telecoms operators du and etisalat have unveiled new services to boost mobile phone communications as the nation accelerates its push towards 6G technology . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . U6GHz – the new spectrum for the next generation of mobile connectivity – is expected to enhance the cloud, artificial intelligence, digital experiences and connected environments. The U6GHz band was identified for international mobile telecoms in the Europe, Middle East and Africa region, several Asian countries, as well as China, Brazil and Mexico, according to global technology advisory Omdia. U6GHz combines a wide contiguous spectrum bandwidth with characteristics closer to that of existing bands than that of other higher candidate bands, making it the “sweet spot” that balances capacity and coverage, the UK-based research firm said. Placing U6GHz “into the hands of customers … [will be] unlocking new opportunities for consumers, businesses and emerging digital applications”, Saleem Alblooshi, chief technology officer of Dubai-based du, said in a statement. Separately, Abu Dhabi's etisalat said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. The company – which recently rebranded back from e& – is using 2x2 Mimo, a wireless technology that allows the transmission of two data streams between mobile devices and cellular base stations. That new capability is exclusive on compatible smartphones on etisalat UAE’s 5.5G network and will be useful in sending high-resolution photos, videos and large files faster, in addition to harnessing the abilities of AI-powered applications, the company said. “Mobile experiences are changing,” said Marwan bin Shakar, chief technology officer of etisalat UAE. “Smartphones are no longer primarily consuming content – they are creating, sharing and increasingly sending richer data to AI and cloud applications in real time. That changes what we need from the network. By bringing this capability … we are increasing upload capacity where it matters.” Last month, etisalat claimed it had launched the world’s first mobile network operating on U6GHz. Mr bin Shakar said this was key to “accelerating the nation's transition to the 6G era”. Sixth-generation technology , or 6G, will offer faster speeds and data transfers for users of smartphones, tablets, laptops and other devices. Though the announcement does not mean 6G cellular technology has officially arrived, the UAE telecoms company's U6GHz mobile network makes use of several innovations that “elevate the 5G-advanced experience” and pave the way for it to become standard. The announcements from du and etisalat are the latest in a series of developments in the UAE related to the eventual adoption of 6G. Last month, du and Khalifa University said they had carried out field trials for the new technology. In 2024, the UAE's Telecommunications and Digital Regulatory Authority announced plans to allocate 600MHz and 6GHz bands, a move that helped accelerate the development of 6G services in the Arab world's second-largest economy. South Korea's Samsung, one of the world's largest manufacturers of smartphones, has predicted widespread adoption of 6G networks by 2030, with “completion of standards and early commercialisation by 2028".

events.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
events.summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 . Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark. New and upcoming RTX Spark updates — among the thousands of apps, games and models available at launch — include: New agent features, models and tools that enhance local agents on RTX Spark: Updates to top agent apps including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy streamline setup on RTX Spark, improve security with OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), and enable hybrid local and cloud AI routing. The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15. NVIDIA PAIR moves out of beta and adds llama.cpp support. Top creative apps optimized for RTX Spark: Up to 2x performance is coming soon to Adobe’s top apps. NVIDIA and Adobe have collaborated to rearchitect Photoshop for GPU-accelerated compositing and Premiere for playback, rendering, effects and more. The NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 release brings new Video Super Resolution, Video Frame Generation, offline file processing and agent Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls to the app. NVIDIA RTX Video Frame Generation and high dynamic range (HDR) capabilities are available now in ComfyUI to accelerate AI generative video workflows. NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction will be available in Blender 5.3 in November to improve interactivity in the viewport. Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark: Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries. GitHub Copilot, Pi and other coding agents are now optimized for RTX Spark. Llama.cpp adds support for decision models, and releases a Windows app. Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus: A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta . Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, the third-generation small language model (SLM) for NVIDIA ACE AI game characters, releases Friday, Oct. 23. The latest RTX Remix update, including DLSS 5 support, releases on Friday, Oct. 23. Advancing Local AI Agents With New Apps, Models and Tools AI is changing the way people interact with PCs. Agent popularity skyrocketed this year, with projects such as OpenClaw and Hermes topping popularity charts on GitHub. Local large language models (LLMs) surpassed the intelligence threshold to power agents, with models like Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next catching up to frontier cloud models released just a few months ago. As a result, local LLM downloads are already 5x higher than all of last year. From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents. Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app. These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC. MXC delivers operating system-level security, while OpenShell makes it simpler for agents to adopt MXC and adds advanced capabilities such as credential protection and security monitoring. Hermes Agent will integrate granular OpenShell controls and MXC by the end of the month. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot now support MXC. After installing an agent, setting up local AI is also now seamless in GitHub Copilot, Hermes Agent, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy. The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks. Many users want the best of both worlds — local models for free iteration, and cloud models for frontier intelligence. NVIDIA Switchyard, an open source model router library, enables agents to intelligently route queries between local and cloud LLMs, allowing the user to minimize cloud usage but still obtain similar results to just running on cloud. Hermes will be adding Switchyard later in October, and other agents like Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot have integrated their own routing solutions. Software providers have made it simple for agents to connect to top Windows apps, with easy-to-use MCP libraries and command line interfaces (CLIs). NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills . NVIDIA is also releasing AI playbooks for RTX Spark, available on Friday, Oct 16. Users can set up their first agent, build an AI chief of staff, configure their system for development or design a creative assistant. Meet Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B: Built for Local Agents on RTX Spark NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, available Thursday, Oct. 15, is a new LLM purpose-built for running local agents on RTX Spark. This model is a 74B parameter, 9B-active-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, packed into 24GB using 2-bit quantization with advanced quantization-aware training techniques to retain quality. It aims to achieve the optimal balance between speed and intelligence, being faster than most popular dense models while smarter than most popular MoE models with a similar memory footprint. Users will be able to run Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B at launch through llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio. It will also be directly accessible via agents such as Hermes and OpenClaw. Like other Nemotron models, Bolt 74B is fully open source — including training data, weights and recipes — so developers can fine-tune and customize their own agents. Local AI doesn’t have to run on just one PC. NVIDIA PAIR , a personal AI router, is officially moving out of beta today, making it easier to tap into the total AI compute of compatible PCs on a local network. The free, open source software tool automatically discovers and connects devices, installs AI models and inference engines, and distributes AI workloads across available systems. The official release adds llama.cpp support, direct model downloads from Hugging Face, customizable inference engine settings and RTX Spark support, along with a variety of inference and user experience improvements. PAIR works on Windows, Linux and macOS.

events.title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify. The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology. Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems . —Grace Huckins This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here .  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power Fervo Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places. Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? Read the full story to find out . —Eshan Raul Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from sustainable cement to shipping containers packed with old EV batteries.  The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets Temperatures rose to 120°F, spoiling food and sparking fires. ( BBC ) + The attack has sparked alarm about cyber threats to food security. ( FT $) + It joins a recent wave of cyberattacks and cybercrimes. ( CNBC ) + AI is exacerbating the threats. events.title: El Niño supercharges storms, leaving thousands without power in US and Mexico
events.summary: Powerful hurricanes killed several people and left thousands without power in the US and Mexico, as experts warned that this year’s supercharged El Niño risked making storms longer and more destructive. The climate phenomenon, which originates in the Pacific and leads to warmer global temperatures, has upended weather across the world, fueling extraordinary storms in the Americas. “ It’s been berserk, ” an expert told the Associated Press. Elsewhere, however, this year’s record El Niño has been welcome news: Forecasts for a warmer-than-usual winter have eased pressures on European and Asian economies — including some of the world’s biggest LNG importers — which are scrambling to contain soaring winter energy bills as expanding global conflicts drive up fuel prices. — Jeronimo Gonzalez
