events.title: Xi’s ‘death watch’ will become a global spectacle
events.summary: Andy’s view The Australian sinologist Geremie R. Barmé wrote that “autocrats and patriarchs share a fateful dilemma”: Once in power “the countdown to their demise is on.” Mao Zedong’s long descent into ill health and madness brought China to the brink of civil war. Deng Xiaoping went out peacefully, though the decade before he died was marked by political upheavals, including the Tiananmen Square protests. Now, the Xi Jinping “death watch” has begun. Of course, the big difference is that today China is at the center of everything. As it drags on, the Xi “death watch” will become a global spectacle, moving markets, affecting investment flows, and shaping defense priorities. China’s internal risks are now the world’s risks. Xi’s physical condition is one thing. At 73, he’s visibly slowing; he looked fragile descending the stairs of his plane at Air Base Andrews when he arrived for a summit with US President Donald Trump last month, clasping the hand of his wife, Peng Liyuan, for support. The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese officials made a highly unusual request for a “ hold room ” for Xi at the White House where he could take breaks between meetings, and his talks with Trump were surprisingly brief. But the pressures building inside the Chinese system are largely unseen: Leadership politics, including the health of the top man, are as much a black box today as they were in the Deng era. But we can assume that from now on, everything that happens behind the high red walls of the leadership compound in Beijing will be connected, one way or another, to the vexed issue of how a post-Xi China will be governed. Political transitions are the midnight hour for all autocratic regimes. But Xi’s dilemma is particularly acute: If he names a successor now to carry forward his policies and protect his legacy, he risks triggering a political knife fight years before he’s ready to relinquish power. Wait too long, though, and he creates a dangerous political vacuum. Either way, Xi will have to pick a relative unknown — all the current members of the Politburo Standing Committee are too old to step into his shoes — raising a host of troubling questions. Would a designated successor catapulted to the top be strong enough to command the loyalty of the powerful military? Could he hold the Party together? Or could Xi himself turn on the chosen one? One of Mao’s designated successors, Liu Shaoqi, died of diabetes and pneumonia in solitary confinement, lying in his own filth. Deng cycled through two successors before settling on Jiang Zemin. Xi has grown paranoid about those around him, his ruthless purges targeting some of his oldest, and most trusted, comrades. That doesn’t bode well for any potential second-in-command. China now faces a period of prolonged political uncertainty. Carl Minzner, a US legal scholar and senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, predicted a “ long twilight ” with the economy sagging, social discontent rising, and the state using “grid management” — surveillance techniques used to maintain control over Xinjiang and other restive border areas. A succession struggle is unlikely to remain within China’s borders, Tyler Jost, a professor at Brown University, and Daniel Mattingly of Yale University argued in Foreign Affairs last year, noting that Xi’s prize goal is unification with Taiwan and “if he hears the succession clock ticking, he could become more willing to gamble on war .” I’m betting that the end of the Xi era will look a lot less like Deng’s, whose passing created hardly a ripple — by then, he’d handed over power and put in place a system to ensure smooth leadership transfers — and more like Mao’s, a drama that involved a bloodless coup (the arrest of the so-called “Gang of Four” led by Mao’s widow), intervention by the People’s Liberation Army, and show trials. We had a foretaste of this kind of turmoil when Xi took power in 2012. A carefully constructed power transfer was upended by the arrest of Xi’s main Politburo rival, and there were wild internet rumors of a military coup, tanks in the streets of the Chinese capital, and gunfire near the leadership compound. Xi has wrenched China back to an era of one-man rule. But having attained the pinnacle of power — next year he’ll likely get a fourth five-year term in office — Xi now has to reckon with the consequences for his country. As Deng himself warned, “building a nation’s fate on the reputation of one or two people is very unhealthy and very dangerous. Notable In 2025, during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Beijing, a hot mic picked up a conversation between Putin and Xi in which the two discussed organ transplants and the possibility of living forever. Musing on such procedures, Putin told Xi (through a translator) that with modern technology organs could be transplanted again and again so that “ (you can) even achieve immortality .” While a largely hypothetical conversation, it hinted that staving off old age and death — maybe for eternity — is top of mind among the world’s most powerful autocrats.

events.title: Hundreds of scientists call for greater AI security in new open letter
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More than 300 scientists call for greater AI security through new international body The open letter says immediate change is needed as future AI-related incidents may expose critical infrastructure. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) More than 300 scientists from across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania are calling for greater AI safety measures in an open letter. The letter gave three recommendations, including establishing an international body to record and publish security incidents caused by AI. The federal government is finalising its national AI standards and plans to legislate new rules in 2027. A group of 350 scientists from more than 30 countries has written an open letter calling for greater AI security by establishing an international body to record and publish security failures due to AI. In several incidents in recent months, both overseas and in Australia, AI models have hacked into the systems of external organisations, including startup Hugging Face and multiple government websites . "[These incidents] can also be seen as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures," the open letter reads. The scientists are from 31 countries, including Australia, and are based across Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania. They said without immediate change, future incidents could expose critical infrastructure. The letter had three recommendations: Adopting high-assurance containment systems, and initially defaulting to air-gapping, which means disconnecting from the internet, for cyber-capable AI models. Creating an international body to record and track AI containment failures. Reporting security incidents to the body and making them public. Toby Walsh, chief scientist at the University of New South Wales AI Institute, was among the signatories and said now was the time to act. "But you can imagine what would happen if an AI [model] was trying to hack into the air traffic control system. It could easily cause significant harms to our day-to-day lives." Safeguards will ensure incidents won't repeat Following the Hugging Face hack, where an AI model broke into the company's systems, OpenAI described it as a "warning shot", saying without proper safeguards AI agents could take "dangerous actions" without human direction. But Professor Walsh said one of the recommendations in the open letter would have prevented the hack entirely. "We wouldn't have had the Medicare hack if they'd been careful about giving the agents minimal permissions for the task it was needed to do. "I mean, these are all incredibly basic things." Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism' Parents warned of lifelong risks as students 'subcontracting learning' to AI Data centre companies to pay into new Tasmanian local community fund Real estate agents urged to 'enhance responsibly' as AI use rises Professor Walsh said the most important element of the open letter was the creation of an international body to provide both information sharing and oversight of incidents. He said similar bodies existed for industries such as banking, aviation and pharmaceuticals. "Every time there's an aviation accident, independent inspectors go in and find out what happened, so that everyone can learn and not make that same mistake again," he said. "We could do the same with AI because it's advancing rapidly and we need to make it as safe as possible." International cooperation needed to prevent incidents Last week, Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton echoed those sentiments surrounding regulating AI similar to banking and aviation in a speech . Regulate AI like banks and airlines The federal government is looking to banking and aviation regulation as it develops laws that would make AI companies demonstrate they can identify and manage risks. The government is finalising its national AI standards, and plans to legislate the new rules next year. But Professor Walsh said there needed to be broad international consensus on AI because the technology was not being developed in isolation. "So we need to cooperate internationally … in terms of perhaps reporting of incidents and sharing of information that doesn't mean that we have to regulate internationally," he said. Cybersecurity improved after it became a requirement for companies to report incidents, Professor Walsh said. "[Otherwise] no-one knew what was happening and we weren't able to learn from all of the mistakes that companies made," he said.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Germany's Nuremberg Airport reopens after glitch causes hijack alert An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. ( AP: Tizian Gerbing ) An aviation emergency has halted flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system". The airport said flight operations have returned to normal. One of Germany's biggest international airports says that flight operations have resumed after they were suspended following an aviation emergency. A flight from Corfu to Germany landed safely as planned in Nuremberg after a hijack alert issued from the cockpit was put down to a "malfunction in the radio communication system", according to the airline. Corendon Airlines said it wanted to "emphasise that no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger". The incident forced a brief suspension of operations at Nuremberg Airport, where the plane was planned to land, the airport said. Flight operations later returned to normal. "From the cockpit, the code '7500' (hijacking case) was transmitted, and furthermore, the pilot could no longer be reached by radio," police said earlier on X. "For safety reasons, various alarm scrambles were then triggered." The alert comes less than a month after the co-pilot of a jet flying from Dubai to Israel attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe. An aviation emergency halts flights at one of Germany's biggest international airports. ( Reuters: Michaela Rehle ) The airline said the emergency code had been transmitted on Tuesday while the plane, a Boeing 737-800, was in Croatian airspace "due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system". "The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made. The aircraft landed safely at Nuremberg Airport," it said. An airport spokesperson had no additional information. Crash axe used in flydubai attack on pilot The co-pilot who allegedly attempted to down a flydubai plane had been barred from flying in his home country of Oman. German authorities have also been on heightened alert since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia. A possible drone sighting had already disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Tuesday, the airport said in a separate statement. Three pilots independently reported an object they had seen during take-off or landing, the German media outlet Bild reported. An airport spokesperson said six flights were delayed and two inbound flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution. Authorities across Europe have stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks amid an increasing number of mostly mysterious drone incidents. Germany says Russia responsible for Leipzig airport drone attack Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says that after assessing the technology used and other intelligence information "the government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack". In August, a drone disrupted flights overnight at Hanover Airport, located in northern Germany. The incident came a week after an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport . Runways at the airport were closed for 90 minutes before normal operations resumed. The Der Spiegel weekly, citing an internal police report, reported that "the possibility of a hybrid activity cannot be excluded". The drone went undetected by authorities and airport staff, flying freely for about two hours. German authorities use the term "hybrid attack" to describe a wide range of incidents — including sabotage and espionage as well as propaganda operations — that have increased since the start of the war in Ukraine and are mostly blamed on Russia. According to the magazine, the police report concludes that it is "currently impossible" to link the Hanover incident to the explosive drone found at Leipzig Airport. Following the Leipzig incident, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt warned of "a new dimension of threat" and mentioned a potential "hybrid attack scenario" without blaming anyone or any state in particular. Germany has become Ukraine's leading military backer in Europe following the 2022 Russian invasion.

events.title: IMF warns UK of risk of inflation ahead of government’s first budget
events.summary: The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday. The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget. It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies , said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023. “The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported. Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported. The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported. The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. Previous governments have failed to achieve the same goal. Energy crisis Britain is facing a prolonged energy squeeze after the price of European gas surged more than 150 per cent this year. Dwindling gas reserves threaten to keep British consumers' costs high through winter. The price increase brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on the UK's fragile economy. Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage, which leave it vulnerable supply disruptions and global market price volatility. Inflation impact In its latest World Economic Outlook published on Tuesday, the Washington-based IMF said debt-burdened economies such as the UK should restrict any public relief to “targeted and temporary” measures so they can still be able to pull inflation back. The multilateral lender expects UK inflation to climb to 3.3 per cent this year and ease to 2.8 per cent next year. The UK aims to bring inflation back to its 2 per cent target and the market expects the Bank of England to start raising rates from next month. Rebuilding the fiscal space is “urgent”, given elevated debt as well as higher borrowing costs and increasing demands on public budgets, against an ever-worsening global geopolitical backdrop, the latest IMF report warned. “Support measures should be used sparingly, designed in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy, and unwound rapidly as the shock dissipates,” the report advised economies supporting elevated debt levels. The fund expects the UK economy to grow 1.3 per cent this year, an upward revision of 0.5 percentage points from the fund’s projections in April. Growth, however, is estimated to edge lower to 1.2 per cent next year as “higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”, the IMF added. “The IMF projections draw attention to both the resilience and the fragility of Britain’s economic prospects,” said Valentin Boboc, chief economist at Institute of Economic Affairs. “Despite stronger-than-expected growth this year, the longer-term outlook remains disappointing due to high taxes, expensive energy and other impediments to investment.” Before the budget, the Chancellor needs to focus on “removing obstacles to growth” and should restrain spending, Mr Boboc said. The country must restore business confidence and “recognise that Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity”, he added.

events.title: Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues
events.summary: Alex Gibney’s Musk Has a Unique Perspective on Daddy Issues Only one person agreed to be in Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary immediately: Musk’s father. “We had Errol Musk at ‘hello,’” Gibney says. Eventually, the director would speak with scores of Musk’s associates for his film. His first wife, Justine Musk, appears, as does his ex-girlfriend Ashley St. Claire. Journalist Kara Swisher, LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman, myself, and WIRED global editorial director Katie Drummond also spoke to Gibney for Musk , which hits theaters nationwide on Friday. But landing Errol Musk, with whom the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a complicated relationship, was a watershed. “Everybody else took a lot of persuasion,” Gibney says. “It was very difficult to get people to appear because the risk profile for talking about Musk in a way that was honest was high.” Once Gibney interviewed all of his subjects, he had enough material to make a documentary that runs nearly four hours, including a 10-minute intermission. It’s a damning portrait of the trillionaire CEO, detailing how much of his genius is based on his formidable ability to promote his own mythology—and the stock price of his public companies. Musk never agreed to an interview with Gibney. Instead, the director’s team researched every public comment Musk ever made and created a simulated Elon Musk who appears throughout the film. I spoke with Gibney earlier this month about his experience making the film, why he decided to make his simulated Elon attractive, and what material he had to leave on the cutting room floor. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. ZOË SCHIFFER: Alex Gibney, thank you so much for being with us today. This shouldn’t spoil anything, but in the four years that you spent making Musk , Elon Musk never agreed to sit down with you for an interview. Instead, your team looked back through the archives of everything he has said publicly, and you put together a sort of simulated interview, which appears throughout the film as a through line. Basically, it plays into Musk’s idea that we are all, in fact, living in a simulation. How did you decide on this approach for the film? Well, what were we gonna do? He’s the main character. I actually thought because he’d been so outspoken about this idea of a simulation, that cinematically we should lean into that. We should play in Elon’s sandbox and have a simulated interview. As we began to develop that idea, by using his real words, his actual audio recordings, but placing them in a kind of avatar which we would design, I think there became all sorts of thematic reasons to do it. One was because he himself had said we’re living in a simulation. But two was the importance of this notion in the Elon Musk story of the shifting sands between what is real and what is unreal. Then also, because a lot of the film deals with his issues of AI, that discomfiting relationship that we’re beginning to explore, all of us on planet Earth, with these AI LLMs and how we begin to project things on these computer interfaces, it felt like this might be something interesting to do. By the way, you’ll notice that when Elon is talking to people in a normal interview situation, he rarely looks at the interviewer or at the camera. He’s always looking this way or that way. So we designed this in a very different way, where he’s looking right down the barrel of the lens directly at the viewer, and we thought that that would be OK. We’re gonna give Elon a break, and actually, I thought our avatar made him look pretty good compared to some of the recent images of him. I have a question about that because your simulated Elon Musk—I think it’s fair to say—looks a lot hunkier than present day Elon Musk. He’s kind of chiseled and tan, and … It is kind of a two-day growth of beard. Exactly. Was that an intentional choice? And if so, can you just talk about why that was? It was. I joke about this, but he’s the star of my movie, I want my star to look good. But I think also it would’ve been a mistake to go into slop AI territory, like some of the images that Elon’s fans are posting about me right now, to sort of denigrate him visually. Also, to some extent, the story is also about image building, too. So I thought, “OK, let’s have some fun with that as well.” Because we had a lot of choices. I mean, we started out with the design firm, like how should he look? What should he be dressed in? You know, we put him in a gamer chair, a leather jacket. There were conscious choices. That extends to some of the comments he makes, where I don’t find like the most bumbling comments that Elon ever made. When we have somebody speaking about something, I want a rejoinder from Elon. We looked for the best rejoinders, like how can he come back at us? Now, later on in the film, his statements become more and more fantastical, but that also is part of what happens. I think it really worked for the film.

events.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
events.summary: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here . Late last month, Anthropic released a report arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.  These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. “I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth. What are the benefits of open models? Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.  Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so. If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications. Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a recent report from Mozilla . And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure. But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.” Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it. Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience. But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations. Mark Zuckerberg himself has said that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models. “I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.” Are open models riskier than closed ones? events.title: Scammers Are Stealing Millions From Food Stamp Recipients. Congress Could Fix It — but Won’t.
events.summary: Jovelle Tamayo/ProPublica. Source images: Zaydee Sanchez/ProPublica, Tina Russell for ProPublica, MPfoto71/Alamy. It wasn’t the kind of call a grocery store gets every day. A customer with a thick Eastern European accent was on the phone saying he wanted to buy several thousand cans of Red Bull. Could the store have them in stock in a few days? Also, did they have equipment to move all those stacks of energy drinks into the parking lot, where two minivans would be waiting? When the day came, Oct. 19, 2022, employees at the Smart & Final store in San Diego sold 3,960 cans of Red Bull and 720 of Monster Energy to two men and two women, all with the same accent, and helped them wheel the pallets out back. To pay for it all — the bill came to $10,747.05 — the group pulled out piles of plastic. These weren’t credit or debit cards; they looked more like hotel-room keys. There were 25 cards in all, each with a different amount loaded onto it, and the four people took turns swiping one after another. Then, the payment complete, they drove off. In the days that followed, people as far away as New York and Florida made panicked calls to the store. They wanted to know why their food-stamp accounts (containing their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits) had been drained at this seemingly random location in San Diego. It would turn out that what became known as the Red Bull Crew had gotten ahold of their SNAP data and used the funds to buy the energy drinks, which they then sold online or to smaller stores. It was hardly an isolated event. From September through November of that year, the same crew, part of a criminal syndicate based in Romania, bought at least $305,274.52 in energy drinks, using SNAP account information and PINs stolen from at least 174 victims nationwide, according to court documents and federal investigators. To hear the Trump administration tell it, the SNAP program is under siege by well-heeled recipients of food stamps. Vice President JD Vance, upon being named “Fraud Czar” this spring, said : “There are people who have Lamborghinis who currently receive SNAP benefits.” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, whose agency oversees the program, regularly goes on TV and social media to allege that masses of SNAP recipients are scamming the system, driving Bentleys, Ferraris, Maseratis and, yes, Lamborghinis. The federal government’s own statistics tell a different story. Confirmed cases of intentional program violations — fraud — committed by SNAP recipients account for $64 million a year, or about 0.08% of all benefits issued annually, according to the most recent 50-state reports compiled by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Meanwhile a far bigger fraud wave has exploded over the past five years: organized theft from SNAP recipients. In 2025, $470 million was stolen electronically from beneficiaries — and thus from the U.S. taxpayer — according to data supplied to ProPublica by Propel , a company that provides a mobile app for SNAP recipients to check their account balances and transaction histories. More than 990,000 households that received food assistance last year had benefits stolen. (The reason it’s necessary to use data from a private company: The federal government has stopped tracking rates of this crime.) ProPublica interviewed nearly 100 victims of SNAP theft, federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, USDA officials, caseworkers and other experts to understand what’s behind this phenomenon and why more isn’t being done to stop it. The victims are almost all working people with families, or retirees, who have struggled to afford groceries in the current economy. Most didn’t learn about the crime until they were in a checkout line, only to have their benefit card declined. Jared Chesnut, a laid-off software developer in Hoover, Alabama, had $893 in SNAP benefits stolen from him in December: “I ate rice and grits the rest of the month.” Rita Harper for ProPublica Upon reporting the disappearance of their food assistance, victims are informed that nothing can be done under current federal law. “The only thing they said was that [my benefits] cannot be refunded unless they were lost due to a natural disaster,” said one SNAP theft victim in Ohio. “They told me they’d add my name to the list,” said another in rural Oregon. “They advised if I feel the place is sketchy, don’t run my card there,” a victim in Philadelphia said. Still another, in Virginia, added, “They even charged me $2 for a replacement card.” Perhaps the most vexing aspect of all: The federal government knows how to prevent the vast majority of this crime in a single step. Congress just hasn’t been willing to take it. SNAP theft is an old scheme applied to a new target. For years, scammers would surreptitiously install skimming devices on card readers at ATMs, gas pumps and corner stores. These devices could read the data on people’s cards as they swiped — while a pinhole camera or overlay keypad captured their PINs — all of which could be picked up later or sent via Bluetooth to someone sitting in a nearby cafe or parking lot. This pilfered data, in turn, was used to make online purchases, or it was loaded onto cloned cards to withdraw cash. Skimming became exponentially more difficult when credit and debit card companies installed digital microchips in the 2010s and then introduced tap-to-pay. But one kind of card did not get the new chips: Electronic Benefits Transfer, or EBT, cards, which people use to access SNAP and other public assistance. These still rely on the 1960s-era magnetic-stripe technology that skimmers can easily read. EBT cards are not a particularly high-value target compared with bank cards. (The average monthly SNAP benefit is about $350 per household.) But funding boosts to SNAP during the pandemic temporarily increased benefit amounts, and profits could be considerable if you skimmed hundreds of people’s card information every month. Skimming teams, often run by Romanian gangs, pivoted. With cloned magnetic-stripe cards, they started buying up huge quantities of SNAP-eligible products like energy drinks and baby formula that are easy to store and resell. “We’ve started many, many briefings saying that one of the biggest ways we’re going to fight this is to just get chips in the cards,” said Michael Peck, assistant special agent in charge of the Secret Service’s Criminal Investigative Division. Among the Secret Service’s lesser-known functions is investigating many financial crimes, and Peck leads its efforts against benefit theft. He said he and his team have delivered this message on Capitol Hill both at committee meetings and to individual members of Congress. Yet congressional leadership has continually blocked legislation that would fund chip EBT cards nationally, despite universal support for the measure among Democrats and significant support among the Republican rank and file. events.title: Axios-Ipsos poll: "Medicare for All" support surges
events.summary: Supporters of "Medicare for All" now outnumber opponents by nearly 2-to-1, according to a new survey of U.S. adults from the Axios-Ipsos American Health Index . The big picture: Two-thirds of all survey respondents — and half of Republicans — said the federal government should be willing to spend more tax dollars to lower health care costs for Americans. Why it matters: With three weeks to go before the midterm elections, and private health insurance premiums and prescription prices crushing voters, these findings suggest a path for swing-state candidates who embrace socialized medicine. But the public's openness is driven more by desperation than by confidence in government. Affordability is foremost on most Americans' minds, and health care brings almost daily reminders of economic pressure. Between the lines: Survey respondents say they want more government intervention — but they trust those leaders less than ever. Trust in President Trump for health-related information fell to a survey low of 20%. Trust in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fell to a survey low of 25%. Trust in congressional Republicans (20%) and Democrats (25%) also were at lows. By the numbers: 43% of Americans said they support the idea of establishing a "Medicare for All" program to provide government-run health insurance to all, largely replacing private health insurance; 24% oppose the idea and 32% say they aren't sure. Nearly half of independents (47%) support it, as do 62% of Democrats. 21% of Republicans support Medicare for All, and 27% are undecided, compared with 52% who oppose the idea. The other side: Opponents said their top reason is they fear Medicare for All would have a worse quality of care than private insurance. Other reasons were feeling it would become too expensive for taxpayers; that government should not be providing health care; or that it would expand the size of government too much. But resistance to the idea has changed markedly from recent campaign cycles, when centrist Democrats were likelier to embrace a public health insurance option or a version of Medicare for All with a role for private insurance. What we're watching: Respondents said they'd be more likely to support congressional candidates this year if those candidates favored expanding government subsidies of health care costs, reinstating enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired at the beginning of this year and expanding prescription drug discount platforms. Republicans are less supportive than Democrats and independents. But the GOP is divided over expanding government subsidies for health care costs, with 31% more likely to back a candidate who supports the idea, 29% less likely and 31% saying it would make no difference. Half of respondents said they'd be less likely to support a candidate backed by pharmaceutical and drug companies, compared with 7% saying they'd be more likely. What they're saying: "Health care is one of the significant ways that people experience economic pressure every day," said Mallory Newall, Ipsos senior vice president for U.S. public affairs. "'Medicare for All' is still something that many Americans have questions on" and "the amount of Americans answering 'not sure' tells me people's sentiments aren't fully formed," Newall said. Still, the current level of support is "noteworthy — and it is not solely driven by members of the Democratic Party," she added. Depending on the candidate's party affiliation or the makeup of their district, "Maybe they don't call it 'Medicare for All,'" Newall said. But expanding federal programs to cover more Americans' health costs "is a message that can connect with voters during this cycle." Methodology: This Axios-Ipsos Poll was conducted Sept. 25 – 28, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,122 general population adults age 18 or older. The margin of sampling error is +/-3.0 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults. Editor's note: This story has been updated to correct Mallory Newall's title.

events.title: Qatar's government revenue fell 42% in first half due to Iran war, Emir says
events.summary: Qatar's revenue fell 42 per cent in the first half of this year, as exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) dropped due to the impact of the Iran war, Emir Sheikh Tamim said during a Shura Council meeting. LNG exports from Qatar, the world’s second-largest supplier before the conflict, has fallen sharply due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz as well attacks on its Ras Laffan complex . “The crisis naturally had an adverse impact on public finances, with total revenues falling by 42 per cent during the first half of the year, while public expenditures decreased by 14 per cent – all without compromising essential services or development priorities,” Sheikh Tamim said. “We decided against curtailing essential services and chose not to alter development priorities, aiming to sustain the economic momentum Qatar is experiencing.” Measures taken before the crisis, such as strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, adopting conservative oil-price assumptions in the budget and developing non-oil revenue, helped Qatar absorb the economic fallout, he said. About 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG capacity is offline after Iranian strikes damaged two of its 14 export trains, removing 12.8 million tonnes a year from the market. QatarEnergy has said repairs will take three to five years, meaning even a safe reopening of Hormuz would restore access to only part of Qatar’s prewar supply. Gas prices have soared globally due to the disruption. Disruption to Qatar's energy sector affects markets and consumers worldwide, the Emir said on Tuesday. “The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, along with direct damage to some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, has disrupted a significant portion of the country's exports,” he said. However, the economic fallout is concentrated mainly in the energy sector, while non-hydrocarbon industries continue to grow, accounting for about 80 per cent of real gross domestic product, he added. “This reflects the national economy's ability to withstand and continue growing under exceptional and complex circumstances,” Sheikh Tamim said. Economies across the Gulf are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue, the World Bank said last week. Qatar's economy is estimated to be hit the hardest among all countries in the region, facing a 20.9 per cent contraction this year, compared to 1.8 per cent growth in 2025, the World Bank said. The estimate would represent the country's weakest economic performance in five decades, after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund in its update this week said it expects Qatar's economy to contract by 15.6 per cent this year, before rebounding to growth of 18.8 per cent in 2027. Investments of $60.7 billion However, Qatar will emerge from the regional crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes, Sheikh Tamim said. “We have a portfolio of projects and investment opportunities valued at approximately 221 billion riyals [$60.7 billion] over the next five years,” he said. Planned investments will cover infrastructure, public-private partnerships and private-sector projects in real estate and hospitality, he added. Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had faced three simultaneous responsibilities during the crisis: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in global energy and economic security, and keeping diplomatic channels open. “Our strategy for shouldering these responsibilities consisted of four main elements: first, firmly defending the homeland without being drawn into war; second, maintaining services, supply chains and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and open waterways; and fourth, encouraging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful solutions to the conflict,” he said. Sheikh Tamim said the goal is “not merely to return to the pre-crisis status quo, but to use recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities”. “God willing, Qatar will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes,” he added.

events.title: A golden age of corporate profits
events.summary: Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax profit data includes inventory and capital depreciation adjustments. Corporate America is raking in record profits, luxuriating in luscious margins and capturing the largest chunk of the country's income on record. Why it matters: The corporate bonanza is bolstering the stock market, but it may also be playing a role in the persistently sour sentiment among the American electorate. The latest: Tuesday is the unofficial start of third-quarter earnings season as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and others report results. Zoom in: Wall Street expects the members of the blue-chip S&P 500 index to continue to make it rain. Third-quarter earnings per share are expected to grow roughly 29% for the index, compared with the quarter in 2025, according to estimate data collected by FactSet. That's after a massive 50% annual increase in second-quarter earnings that was supercharged by the giant, non-operating gains on valuations of tech investments reported by Amazon and Alphabet. (Amazon, for example, penciled in its stake in Anthropic as boosting its profit by more than $50 billion.) But even without those enormous gains, the numbers were quite strong, thanks to the AI boom that analysts expect to keep powering giant profits. What they're saying: The market is still all about AI, but the gains are extremely concentrated . "At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3," wrote Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity analyst with Goldman Sachs. Snider noted that more than two-thirds of the total growth in S&P 500 earnings for the quarter is expected to come from just 10 stocks. What's more, Micron Technology and Nvidia alone are expected to generate more than one-third of the growth in earnings for the blue chips, Snider wrote. The big picture: Broader measures of U.S. corporate profitability captured by economic — rather than stock market — data also seem to show remarkable strength. For the economy as a whole, after-tax corporate profits in Q2 jumped 18.2% compared with the same quarter of 2025. And key measures of corporate profit margins across the entire U.S. economy are some of the fattest on record. Data: FactSet, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax U.S. corporate profits, including inventory and capital consumption adjustments as a share of gross value added of U.S. corporate business. Reflects profits made within the U.S.; does not include profits produced overseas. The other side: Boom times for corporate America have a flip side, however, with the so-called labor share of national income collapsing to some of the lowest levels on record. The labor share tells you what percentage of the giant paycheck produced by the U.S. economy goes to workers in the form of wages and benefits, rather than to corporate profits, dividends, rents and interest paid to other economic actors, commonly summarized as "capital." The bottom line: That decline helps explain the persistently sour mood of the American public toward the economy and its deep skepticism toward the AI boom that's producing this bonanza for American corporations.

events.title: Trump AI directive sparks questions
events.summary: The newly minted Super Intelligence Task Force is telling AI companies to report and immediately remediate any instances of rogue behavior involving their products, a rare effort by the Trump administration to exert more power over the firms developing the advanced technology. An Anthropic incident in which a testing model submitted visa applications, according to a State Department spokesman, spurred the task force’s first “action,” which it’s referring to as a “notification and remediation process.” Frontier AI labs largely do this sort of disclosure and incident reporting already, and Trump’s task force has not laid out exactly what will count as an “incident” that must be reported going forward. Still, the administration’s decision to make an example of Anthropic is likely to trigger more disclosures than before. “Our message to all SI companies is clear: delayed notification, inadequate corrective action, and a failure to take responsibility will not be tolerated,” task force leaders Jay Clayton, Andrew Ferguson, Scott Kupor, and Emil Michael said in a statement. The effectiveness and scope of the new requirements will depend in part on how the task force defines an “incident,” how quickly it must be disclosed, who it must be reported to, and the consequences for not doing so. Officials have yet to lay out these details, and companies are seeking more clarity. Anthropic contacted the task force to disclose the latest incident and has a history of reporting security episodes publicly and tweaking models to prevent more harm. — Ashley Gold

events.title: Why would anyone want this job?
events.summary: Ben’s view On May 13, 2022, then-White House Middle East envoy Brett McGurk asked his boss how he liked his job. Joe Biden, he’d noticed, had been a chatty, expressive vice president, but had grown quieter in a way that wasn’t just about his age. “There’s no joy in it,” Biden responded. “That’s the difference. No joy in this job.” McGurk’s new memoir cataloguing two grim years of trying to negotiate between American and regional officials is, among other things, a set of portraits of miserable world leaders: There’s the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who “seemed annoyed to be there” when the Americans showed up to ask for help with oil prices. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, pressed by Biden to negotiate, “seemed lost, used to meetings that started nowhere and ended there.” Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “looked down at his shoes shuffling on the carpet” as “something was weighing on him.” Biden took out his own irritation on the short-lived Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid, telling him, “Don’t be a phony, man.” Lapid, in turn, “recoiled.” And so on. In McGurk’s account, only the “smug” and inscrutable Benjamin Netanyahu isn’t obviously unhappy. This narrative of the woes of leadership could serve as a cautionary tale for the few dozen men and women in both of America’s political parties currently searching their souls and consulting their spouses about whether to run for president. Journalists typically treat these deliberations as theater. But even the people most obviously preparing to run take them more seriously than you’d imagine. Win or lose, a candidate’s campaign will consume their life and their loved ones’; a victory guarantees their life will change forever. So while Vice President JD Vance’s aides right now appear quite confident he’ll run, they also sincerely believe that he hasn’t yet — totally — decided. Vice presidents are special: They have already paid the price of national office, getting far less in return than their bosses. But one Republican elder who likes Vance is advising against it: He suggests Vance return to Ohio, get to work reinventing trade education or some other worthy task, and run for president as the guy, rather than Donald Trump’s shadow. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s supporters, meanwhile, swear he hasn’t taken any steps toward running, much less decided on it. They also caution people against saying he’s not running, however: He hasn’t decided anything. On the Democratic side, we assume they’re all running — California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Sens. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Cory Booker, D-N.J., and the rest. But they might want to read McGurk’s book and think about whether they really want the job. Because oddly, of all the distinguishing qualities of successful presidential candidates, ambition turns out to be perhaps the most salient. One former Biden administration official recently quipped that their money was on Maryland Gov. Wes Moore for the Democratic nomination, because he has the single quality you most need to become president: really, really wanting to be president. Room for Disagreement The potential candidates will also hear more cynical arguments in favor of running no matter what. ABC News observed in 2024 : “there are also a lot of benefits, even if you lose: better job opportunities, increased public profiles and the chance to build up a war chest for the next run.”

events.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
events.summary: The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance. Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control. The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power. Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services. The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex. The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives. Google has been developing its own Tensor Processing Units for years, with its latest generation including separate versions optimized for training AI models and running inference. OpenAI is developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom, initially focusing on inference workloads. The company said in August that its first chip was outperforming Nvidia hardware on certain workloads and that it was already developing subsequent generations. Amazon has its own ⁠ Trainium family of AI chips, which are being used by customers including Anthropic. OpenAI has also committed to using Amazon's custom silicon as part of a massive infrastructure agreement. Anthropic confirmed in August that it is exploring its own chip designs, even as it continues to rely on chips from Nvidia, Amazon and other suppliers. Meta also has an internal chip development program, while continuing to buy substantial computing capacity from Nvidia and other suppliers. Between the lines: Nvidia isn't necessarily losing business just because its customers are developing competing chips. Nvidia's revenue more than doubled to $96 billion in the second quarter, a reminder that overall demand for AI computing leaves room for Nvidia chips and new offerings from Microsoft and others. Like Microsoft, most Nvidia competitors are focused on inference, where margins are highest, while Nvidia remains dominant for training. Still, Nvidia has begun to leverage its balance sheet to bankroll the AI buildout , so any competition that even slightly reduces its strength is noteworthy because it could weaken its centrality to continued growth. What they're saying: Building competitive AI hardware requires designing entire systems, optimizing everything from memory and networking to software and power consumption, Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, told Axios. "We prioritize Maia for inference," Borkar said, describing it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing and an area where Microsoft can distinguish itself on cost and efficiency. "For us, it's not an either-or strategy," she said. "We want a broad ecosystem while investing deeply in our first-party silicon." Yes, but: Microsoft's plans to make Maia its primary inference platform apply specifically to Microsoft's own services, not necessarily to third-party Azure customers, including OpenAI. Borkar also cautioned that the shift won't happen overnight. Maia 300 deployments will begin in 2027, but reaching multi-gigawatt scale will take time, extending beyond next year. Reality check: As Axios ⁠ previously reported , companies developing their own chips remain dependent on the same limited manufacturing capacity, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia relies on. That means even if custom chips can reduce dependence on Nvidia, they don't eliminate broader supply-chain constraints. The bottom line: Nvidia remains central to the AI boom, but its biggest customers increasingly want to control more of the technology powering their own services — and capture more of the economic benefits for themselves.

events.title: Dems' red-state showings raise prospect of a bigger 2028 map
events.summary: Data: RealClearPolitics , American Presidency Project ; Note: Nebraska's Senate race is between a Republican and an independent; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Move over Wisconsin and Arizona. With Democrats making Republicans sweat in a host of red-state Senate races , a new batch of swing states may be emerging. Why it matters: Some of the closest Senate races are in Nebraska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and even Kansas. Sure, this could be a blip — or a reminder that it's a 50-50 moody nation, even in a bunch of red states. The conditions that helped Barack Obama carry conservative states like Indiana and North Carolina in 2008 — an unpopular war, a bruising economy, an electorate hungry for change — could resonate again in 2028. State of play: Democratic and Republican Senate candidates are running margin-of-error races in red states that not long ago were thought to be forbidding, or even a wasted effort, to many Democrats. The Senate races in Kansas and Ohio are tied. So is Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn is trying to knock off Sen. Pete Ricketts. Democrat James Talarico has consistently led polls in Texas, though that race appears to be tightening as money pours into the state on behalf of Republican Ken Paxton. Alaska is also a toss-up. President Trump won all these states by double digits in 2024. Zoom in: Republican operatives told Axios they're far from convinced that what's happening now will create a new slate of swing states in the 2028 race for the White House. They see the current campaign as more of a one-off — a combination of dismay with Trump, high prices and uninspiring candidates. "None of those states will be targeted [by Democrats] in the 2028 presidential. I will bet big money on that. But … all are in danger this year," one GOP consultant told Axios. "It's a function of the atmosphere that we're playing defense in R+15 states. There's lethargy on our side," a Republican pollster said. "I don't think they're the new swing states per se." But Democrats say better-than-expected performances by their candidates in several red states would at least open the door to an expanded map — with a big "if." "An opening, yes," Obama's former chief strategist, David Axelrod, told Axios. "A guarantee, hardly." Obama, he said, spent an enormous amount of time in rural communities and got to know voters. The Democrats who are faring well in those places this year have made a point of speaking with, not at, conservatives. Yes, but: There's no certainty that Democrats will prevail in red states this year, much less set a path for 2028. Polls are narrowing in several other Senate battlegrounds besides Texas, and the polling industry has had enough misses and challenges in recent elections to raise questions about whether we're getting an accurate picture of the political landscape at this time. Either way, it's safe to say Democrats have made things interesting for the Nov. 3 election. The big picture: The backlash against Trump has set the tone in many of these surprisingly competitive Senate surprise states, but Democrats also have also benefited from factors specific to each race. In Ohio, former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is better known than the incumbent, Sen. Jon Husted (R). In Texas, Democrats have a seminarian candidate in James Talarico who's emphasized the Bible's teachings as Republicans have tried to tag him as a radical leftist. His opponent, Ken Paxton, has been dogged by corruption allegations throughout the race. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is the pastor of the largest United Methodist church in the country. His opponent, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, has been hurt by reports that his former medical practice sued patients for even small unpaid bills, and that his 2020 campaign stiffed a bakery on a $700 bill. What we're watching: To build on any openings Democrats might realize this year, the party will need a 2028 candidate who can appeal to center-right voters the way Democrats in red states have this year, Axelrod said. "Part of the long-term problem for Democrats has been that it's still a party of working people, but it often approaches working people — especially in small towns in rural areas, in the spirit of missionaries and anthropologists," Axelrod said. Like, "we're here to help you become more like us." So in 2028, he added,"it depends on who the candidate is, and what kind of bonds of trust that candidate can build."

events.title: What Flock Actually Costs Cities Across the Country
events.summary: In 2020, the police department of picturesque Covington, Georgia, paid Flock Safety , the surveillance technology company, $40,000 to maintain 20 cameras around the city. The next year, it paid the same amount. In 2022, that cost went up to $81,250. Fifteen new “Falcon” cameras, which Flock says have more sophisticated technology for reading license plates, accounted for $37,500. Another $3,750 went toward installing the new cameras, and the rest was spent maintaining the initial fleet. WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from public records requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism . Then, in 2024, the department paid Flock $113,225. Of that, $87,500 was to maintain its existing 35 cameras, a rate it agreed to pay for the next five years, and the remainder went toward eight new Falcon cameras. The next year, Covington paid Flock $159,000 for a combination of camera maintenance and enrollment in its Drone as First Responder program, which uses drones to fly to emergency scenes and stream footage back to the police station. It’s unclear how much Covington will wind up paying Flock in 2026, but through August, it has paid $201,000—$100,000 to maintain its existing cameras, $800 to replace one, and another $100,200 for new software products. The Covington Police Department did not respond to a request for comment. Overall, Flock is a small fraction of the Covington police department’s $12,488,733 budget for June 2025 to July 2026. But amid fierce blowback about Flock’s surveillance practices, contracts with the company are now being scrutinized in cities across the country. Flock did not provide a comment for this story. WIRED obtained documents via public record request from a dozen Flock customers across the country and compared them to publicly available information from more than a dozen others. The documents shed light on how much Flock can actually cost communities, the way many of those deals are structured, and how the deals can expand over several years—leaving taxpayers on the hook year after year, with no end in sight. “Once you let police officers try a tool,” says Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, “it becomes really hard to get the political will and motivation to take that tool away from them.” When Flock was founded in 2017, it originally sold its license plate readers to private homeowner associations (HOAs). By the time the company decided to sell to police departments in 2019, it had an in: Rather than starting a camera network from scratch, police could start by accessing the cameras that HOAs were already using. A version of this story played out in Alpharetta, Georgia . In 2020, the city’s police department paid Flock $17,680 for five Falcon cameras and logins for Flock software called Wing, which can extract vehicle and license plate data from off-brand camera footage. The next year, when Alpharetta bought a few more Flock cameras, a payment justification noted that “several” local private homeowner associations had already purchased Flock and granted them camera access. “We are looking to add more city cameras into the Flock system,” the justification read. According to the city, “other vendors” would “not integrate with our existing Flock system.” Over the next several years, Alpharetta expanded its work with the company significantly. By 2025, the city’s annual Flock bill had ballooned to $381,000. As in other industries, companies that sell technology to police often use financial incentives to get customers in the door. Clearview AI , Ring , and Taser have all ponied up enticing offers to agencies around the country. “A lot of these police surveillance vendors have learned the lessons of general old salesmanship,” Guariglia tells WIRED. In other words, deals and discounts work. In some cases, this looks like new and increasingly expansive Flock products. In 2025, for instance, Alpharetta paid for an upgrade to the Elite Package of FlockOS, which Flock describes as a real-time crime-center platform. Other products are first offered with a free trial; Alpharetta took advantage of one 90-day window last year to try a new product dubbed Nova. Flock also expands its contracts by offering discounts if departments sign a multiyear contract. In 2024, Alpharetta locked into a five-year contract with Flock that would cost $254,250 the first year and $238,000 for each successive year. The agreement was $232,500 less than five one-year agreements, which could be subject to higher rates. The Alpharetta Police Department declined to comment. Five-year agreements are common among Flock customers, which the company has sometimes marketed as a “price-lock promotion.” In a November 2023 email, Flock customer success manager Gwen Saltal used this framing to offer a five-year deal to New York’s Albany County Sheriff’s Office.

events.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
events.summary: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”  Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data , including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker , this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.  Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.
