events.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
events.summary: Microsoft to expand Azure Maia system to multi-gigawatt deployments Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027 As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. Maia 200: Driving the workloads that Microsoft runs at scale The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. Maia 300: Scaling more useful AI within every megawatt AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. That density allows Microsoft to serve more simultaneous AI interactions and larger workloads from each rack, improving datacenter capacity and the economics of expanding AI services. Maia 300 will begin production deployments in 2027. For more information on Maia 300 architectural details, read our technical paper . Azure Maia is at the heart of our Frontier Transformation The future will not be defined by a single model or a single piece of silicon or a single innovation. Model and silicon choice are inherent in our vision for Frontier Transformation. Our focus is on developing responsible, affordable and scalable platforms that will help everyone amplify their intelligence to drive breakthrough outcomes that matter for them.

events.title: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem
events.summary: Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise. Why it matters: The agreement President Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin Friday is designed to ease the cost of living for U.S. consumers. But Republicans who pleaded for help with fuel prices now face a fresh dispute over Russia, with energy analysts questioning whether the deal will deliver the relief Trump is promising. The big picture: With three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are trying to answer voter anger while keeping up with a president whose proposed fixes keep becoming political liabilities of their own. Trump's decision to lock arms with Putin adds another complication. Driving the news: Weeks after signing a sweeping Russia sanctions law, Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets. The next day, Trump blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced, even as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities. Republicans who just supported squeezing Moscow have three options in the final sprint for control of Congress: defend Trump's reversal, break with him or stay quiet. Zoom out: The diesel deal packs some of the GOP's biggest liabilities into one decision: the Iran war's economic fallout, the party's split over Russia and a president determined to make the election about himself. The deal also reverses Trump's own pressure campaign. Last year, he slapped an extra 25% tariff on India for buying Russian oil. On Oct. 2, he and other G7 leaders pledged to keep sanctions on Russia. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will do much for diesel prices, which averaged $6.28 a gallon Oct. 11, up 71% from a year earlier. What they're saying: The White House pushed back on criticism of Trump's record: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. A senior administration official said Trump is "laser-focused on bringing down costs, whether it's diesel with the Russians or importing Argentine beef. Some people might not like it, but he's thinking of what Americans are paying and what he can do about it." Friction point: The internal pushback has been swift. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed to force a House vote blocking the oil purchases. Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Michael McCaul (R-Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), already criticized the deal by Sunday. Tillis told NBC News' "Meet the Press" that Trump's deal may violate a law that requires the White House to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. Even MAGA ally Laura Loomer denounced the deal as not only funding Russia but indirectly helping Iran by putting "money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran." Yes, but: Some Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso , backed the deal. How we got here: Farm-state Republicans have pleaded with the White House to deliver diesel relief. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and others urged Trump to ban diesel exports, something the president embraced before the White House abruptly reversed and ruled out a ban. GOP candidates in key Senate races, like Iowa's Ashley Hinson and Michigan's Mike Rogers , have called for ending the Iran war after previously supporting it. Instead, Trump has defended it in vivid terms, saying Iran might have attacked Los Angeles and San Diego if not for his war. Between the lines: Trump's unpopular positions collide with voter sentiment as he touts the war with Iran, the rise of data centers and his own popularity. His efforts to give Republicans something to campaign on leave candidates exposed through big promises, about-faces and proposals that won't materialize before voters cast their ballots. Data centers: Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) has faced Democratic attacks over data centers, an issue the National Republican Senatorial Committee has identified as a vulnerability. Yet Trump used a Husted rally last week to defend the projects: "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." Dividend checks: Voters have also rejected Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend checks that analysts say would cost $1.3 trillion . A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans disapproved. Trump: Trump has insisted the midterms should be a referendum on his presidency, telling Republicans at last month's convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." But a Pew Research Centerpoll released Thursday found 44% of registered voters view their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 19% who see it as a vote for him. Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed oil prices, the Iran war and the midterm convention for falling poll numbers. The bottom line: For Republican candidates, the challenge isn't just selling Trump's record. It's keeping up with a president who continues to give them new decisions to defend.

events.title: Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
events.summary: When Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development. Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today. The Muse Wonder models will be available through an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent . Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky , with some researchers not sticking around for long. Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups. But the company fell behind after delivering several disappointing versions of the model, and as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google rapidly introduced more capable models. Meta announced the first model from its new lab, Muse Spark , in April of this year. The company has also released a small open-weight model called Muse Glimmer , and says it plans to release larger open-weight models in the future. It did not disclose details of how new Muse Wonder models were built or trained. Muse Wonder was built to compete with the very best, however. Meta says the largest version of the new model outperforms Anthropic’s second-best model, Claude Fable 5.1, and ranks just below its best, Claude Opus 5.5, on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , a widely used aggregated score of model capabilities. Meta says the model outperforms OpenAI’s best model, GPT-6 Astra, and both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on some specialized benchmarks, including ones that measure a model’s ability to work with legal documents and to build software. Benchmarks are not always a reliable measure of real-world performance, but this is still a significant step forward for Meta’s models. Muse Wonder also includes two novel features designed to help make agents more effective and less inclined to misbehave. The new features, called Active Memory and Active Focus, are designed to keep the model locked into a stated goal and prevent it from becoming confused. This can be a challenge when AI performs complex research or builds a large software project, for example, and can lead to expensive mistakes or compounded errors. Meta says it has put significant effort into training Muse Wonder to refuse to generate dangerous outputs, such as recipes for building bioweapons or help with hacking. It says the company scores well on several benchmarks designed to measure how resilient models are to those prompts. A series of recent incidents involving rogue AI agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others also shows how easily powerful AI models can stray when given open-ended commands. Meta did not disclose whether it has seen agents powered by Muse Wonder misbehave in testing or what it has done to mitigate this issue specifically. Zuckerberg said in a post on X last month that the company had delayed the release of its Muse models to work on safety. Meta also revealed a framework designed to ensure that it scales its models’ capabilities safely in a blog post earlier this month. Muse Wonder may add more fuel to an already furious race to develop more capable AI, however. It certainly suggests that Meta is once again competitive in the increasingly high-stakes AI race. events.title: Britain faces looming energy crisis as gas reserves dwindle
events.summary: Britain faces a deepening energy crisis as a result of dwindling reserves and the possible closure of its largest storage site. With a 150 per cent surge in European gas prices before the seasonal dip in temperatures, the prospect of another inflationary shock is casting a shadow over the October 28 Budget. The prospect of losing Rough, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, threatens to further weaken the country's ability to withstand supply disruptions as Europe heads into winter with depleted reserves. Underground gas storage in Britain was only 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to only 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity equals about seven days of average winter demand. The problem of limited UK reserves is compounded by uncertainty over the future of Rough, which could close next year unless the government backs a £2 billion redevelopment proposed by its owner, Centrica. Chris O'Shea, chief executive of Centrica, which also owns British Gas, stepped up pressure on the government on Tuesday, warning that the site, which accounts for about half of Britain's gas storage capacity, would close at the end of the first quarter without a plan to support investment. "The commercial decision will be that this facility will close at the end of the first quarter," Mr O'Shea told the BBC, rejecting the government's position that Rough's future was a commercial matter for the company. He said Centrica was seeking a regulatory framework similar to those available to other critical infrastructure operators, providing more predictable returns in exchange for lower investment risk. Mr O'Shea described Rough as "the biggest battery in the UK", saying the proposed investment could create up to 5,000 jobs while safeguarding almost 1,000 existing positions. The company has also offered to make the site available as a temporary strategic gas reserve this winter but has yet to receive a response from the government, he said. "Our system is not resilient. Without energy security, we have no national security," Mr O'Shea said, pointing to increasingly frequent electricity supply margin notices. Britain’s grid operator sought emergency assistance from France on Monday, requesting as much as 1,200 megawatts of additional electricity through an undersea interconnector to help maintain the security of the power system. Britain will probably not run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House. “The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said. Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”. European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf. The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group. “It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters. Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels. EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves. A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further. Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high. The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

events.title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
events.summary: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations. Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era. NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics. NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs. Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP 🔗 NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories. NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory 🔗 NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: NVIDIA Config Manager : Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/ NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine : Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins NVIDIA Rack Management Service : Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management. Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller : Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days. Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories 🔗 For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on. At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for.

events.title: NVIDIA and Cisco Introduce New Pluggable Optics Form Factor to Scale AI Factories
events.summary: Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) is designed to be the first module to support 400Gb/s-per-lane electrical signals, enabling capacity up to 12.8Tb/s so AI factory builders can scale Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a proven deployment model across multiple generations of data center networks. USFP delivers 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of 200Gb/s-per-lane optics so AI factories can connect more computing systems without adding network tiers, while using less power to move each bit of data. NVIDIA and Cisco are working with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build a multi-source hardware ecosystem around USFP. NVIDIA and Cisco today announced plans for Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), a new high-density 400Gb/s-per-lane optical module designed to equip the hardware ecosystem for the next generation of AI factories using pluggable transceivers. As AI models grow and inference demand expands, AI factories must connect more computing systems while managing network complexity, power and costs. Moving more data per watt and per switch helps operators make better use of their infrastructure investments. Scaling AI factories requires more bandwidth per connection and more connections per switch. When a switch reaches its capacity, further network expansion can require additional switch layers and optical links, increasing latency, power consumption and costs. USFP is designed to enable AI factory builders to scale from 200 Gb/s per lane to 400Gb/s-per-lane Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a deployment model proven at scale across multiple generations of data center networks. With USFP, customers can embrace next-generation optical technology and meet the performance demand of AI workloads without overhauling their data center infrastructure. The first planned USFP-based transceivers will pack 16 full-duplex lanes in an octal small form factor (OSFP)-sized footprint supporting both switches and SuperNICs, with the ability to expand to 32 and more lanes in the future. By doubling both the lane count and bandwidth per lane, USFP enables AI fabrics to connect more 1.6Tb/s endpoints without adding network tiers. Customers will be able to achieve 12.8Tb/s of overall capacity with USFP. Comparable with an OSFP-sized module, it delivers 4x the bandwidth and front-panel bandwidth density, with approximately 1.3x the power efficiency, versus 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable modules. This means AI builders can increase their compute scale within the same network footprint, while decreasing networking’s share of the overall AI factory power budget. “Building the world’s largest AI factories starts with rethinking the smallest of connections,” said Gilad Shainer, senior vice president NVIDIA. “With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco are building an ecosystem to reinvent pluggable optics — connecting more computing with greater efficiency to power the next generation of AI factories.” “AI builders need an interconnect architecture that can scale performance without locking them into a more complex operating model,” said Bill Gartner, senior vice president and general manager of optical systems and optics at Cisco. “Cisco and NVIDIA recognized that scaling pluggable optics to 400Gb/s per lane would require more than another incremental extension of today’s module designs. Through our collaboration, USFP is designed to deliver a new level of bandwidth density while preserving the serviceability, deployment flexibility and operational simplicity of pluggable optics. By taking a full-stack approach — from silicon and systems to optics and the network operating system — we can optimize every layer to deliver the performance and scale the next generation of AI networks will require.” More AI Infrastructure From Every Switch Designed for electrical signals of 400Gb/s per lane, USFP uses a new two-dimensional array connector with a two-step insertion design that engages high-speed contacts after the module is inserted, reducing contact wear, improving signal integrity and making insertion force more predictable. The connector technology allows for further scaling of lane count to 32 full duplex lanes and more in the future. Because the connector is designed for 400Gb/s performance, it also offers improved performance at 200Gb/s per lane. USFP supports power dissipation of up to 100 watts without needing a separate, dedicated embedded cooling circuit within the transceiver, reducing switch design complexity and improving reliability. Together, these capabilities enable higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the mature deployment, serviceability and manufacturability of existing pluggable transceivers. All USFP configurations support optical designs that reduce latency and power consumption by simplifying signal processing. Support for a broad range of optical technologies and connection distances gives system designers the flexibility to meet unique AI factory deployment needs. A Hardware Ecosystem for Next-Generation AI Factories NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build USFP cages, connectors and modules, with additional partners expected to join. The shared form factor gives suppliers a common foundation for developing high-density pluggable infrastructure for 400Gb/s-per-lane fabrics to build a robust ecosystem for AI factory builders. The collaboration builds on NVIDIA and Cisco’s existing work to ensure NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking and Cisco Silicon One-based Ethernet networks work together seamlessly, simplifying AI infrastructure deployment for enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign clouds. NVIDIA and Cisco plan to create an open industry specification for USFP through an upcoming community-led multi-source project. For more than 40 years, Cisco has securely connected the world. events.title: OPay readies $4B New York IPO
events.summary: The News OPay, the Lagos-based fintech firm backed by Softbank and Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui, more than doubled its revenue in the first half of 2026 as lending overtook payments as its top source of income, according to a filing ahead of a planned New York listing likely set for next month. The company has applied to trade under the ticker OPAY, with a potential Nigerian secondary listing to follow. The filing lays out a business growing rapidly after jumping 137% to $467 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 while net income rocketed by over 300% to $91 million. OPay launched in Nigeria as a payments company in 2018 backed by Chinese investors and later funded by venture investors led by Softbank. OPay hadn’t disclosed an IPO price range or a listing date as Semafor was going to press but based on the normal sequence of filings and roadshows, investors will be expecting pricing to be revealed in mid-November. Previous reports have put the initial valuation estimates around $4 billion. The fintech firm also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. Know More A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise and presence to expand across Africa. Step Back OPay took off in 2019 in Nigeria with ambitions to be a super app that offered various features, including motorcycle taxi bookings, food deliveries, and quick loans. But it narrowed its focus to financial services in recent years and raised $570 million in venture funds between 2018 and 2021. A handful of African tech companies have successfully listed in the US, notably e-commerce platform Jumia and telecom towers provider IHS but have had mixed performances. An OPay listing in the US would be the first by a fintech company with a mostly Nigerian customer base.

events.title: Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon. [Read more]
events.summary: Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon. Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services. And we’re introducing Maia 300, which delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems. We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot. Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet. Read more: https://lnkd.in/g68XQtxE This is encouraging. If AI is going to become part of practically every product and workflow, the cost of running it has to come down significantly. More efficient hardware could open the door to use cases that simply aren't economical today. Spot on, Satya Nadella! Transitioning toward custom silicon and multi-gigawatt infrastructure deployments represents a fundamental milestone in redefining enterprise AI economics and operational scalability. Maximizing tokens per watt through proprietary hardware architecture is critical for mitigating latency and curbing the exponential energy demands of large-scale agentic AI. Integrating full-stack silicon efficiency directly into cloud services sets a new benchmark for sustainable enterprise IT. As hyperscalers aggressively pivot toward custom silicon to optimize inference economics, what core engineering or supply-chain challenge do you view as the primary bottleneck for scaling multi-gigawatt deployments over the next cycle? "Tokens per watt". What an absurd metric. As if there's a uniform, consistent definition of a token or a generic correlation to compute. Not. And such a metric would inherently reward verbosity. Utterly stupid. I'm assuming this is good news. Anyone else consider themselves "tech savvy" and dont understand much of what they just read? It seems great though! Good job Microsoft: more power is always good:) 40% more tokens per watt, but at what context length? The workloads you named, sustained multi-step agents, carry long contexts, and every agent's working memory grows with each step. At that point the binding constraint is memory, not compute, and the specs that lead this launch are memory specs. Tokens per watt measured on short contexts says little about tokens per watt once agent memory dominates. The bigger announcement may be co-design. With Maia as the primary engine, Copilot's models get shaped around Maia and each next Maia around Copilot's workloads. That's where the gain compounds, and it's very hard to copy from outside. It also splits the market: integrated model-plus-chip stacks on one side, open models on general-purpose GPUs on the other. As agents multiply token demand, that gap becomes the price difference between closed and open AI. Who gives open models what Maia gives Copilot? I’d love to be in the room for Microsoft’s next GPU pricing negotiation when NVIDIA knows Maia is already running Copilot workloads 😅 Having a credible alternative at that scale might be worth almost as much as the efficiency gains themselves. Incredible milestone, mr.Satya! As custom silicon scales to multi-gigawatt deployments with Maia 300, optimizing tokens-per-watt highlights a critical industry truth: physical thermal management at the hardware level is becoming just as vital as architectural efficiency. We’ve been tackling this exact frontier through advanced passive thermal architectures designed for high-density AI hardware. If you or your silicon team are ever open to a brief exchange on bypassing the thermal wall at scale, I'd love to share a few notes. Exciting times ahead for full-stack optimization!" Werden die Effizienzgewinne von Maia zeitnah auch in günstigere PTU-Reservierungen für Enterprise-Kunden weitergegeben, oder bleibt die Hardware primär für Microsofts eigene SaaS-Dienste reserviert? Gerade bei fest gebuchten Kapazitäten entscheidet am Ende der Preis pro garantiertes Token über den tatsächlichen Nutzen im produktiven Betrieb. Tokens per watt is the number I watch from Manila, where available power decides where AI capacity can go. A 40% gain stretches the same megawatts further. In markets like ours, that makes it easier to run inference in-country, close to the users and their data, and every in-country deployment pulls demand into local data center space and domestic fiber. The question that sits underneath the announcement is not about efficiency. You are about to run multi-gigawatt inference for agents that act — that buy, sign, dispatch, approve, execute — across Teams, Copilot, and the Azure estate. Every one of those actions will commit against a real target at some point. The tokens-per-watt number tells us how cheap the compute is. It does not tell us what stands between an agent's decision and the consequence when the agent has valid credentials, valid authority, and intent to exceed scope. The industry has spent two years building the layer above the action: monitoring, containment, audit, oversight. Every incident in that window had the same shape. The credentials were valid. The policy was configured. The action fired anyway. Whoever solves that layer first owns the next decade of enterprise AI. It is not the model layer, it is not the silicon layer, and it is not the SaaS layer. It is the layer between the decision and the consequence. You have the biggest bet on the silicon. That is the correct place to be building. But the layer that makes agents safe to run at scale is not on the roadmap you just published. events.title: Ecobank agrees to join Chinese payment platform
events.summary: Ecobank agreed a partnership with China’s payment system to enable transaction settlements in the yuan currency. The Togo-based bank, which operates in 34 African countries — more than any other continental lender — will sign an agreement this month to join the China Interbank Payments System (CIPS). South Africa’s Standard Bank and the African Export Import Bank have taken the same step in the last year. The move follows increasing demand from businesses on the continent to transact and settle deals using China’s currency. An 18% rise in China-Africa trade last year — marked by a surge in the continent’s imports of Chinese solar power equipment — underscored the growing commercial relationship between both parties, highlighting the appeal of financial systems that make transactions easier to complete. China this year removed tariffs for imports from all African countries except Eswatini. Its move to increase bank integrations with its payments system furthers a push led by the BRICS bloc against the US dollar’s dominance in international trade. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics
events.summary: STOCKHOLM -- American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. “The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise." For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. “This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “ stagflation ’’ of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. “Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view," Hall and Woodford’s research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’ Hall studied the way that consumer decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. “If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote. “The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead,” Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’ Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.’’ Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing. During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.” The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896.

events.title: First Utility-Scale Enhanced Geothermal Plant Goes Live
events.summary: This article was originally published by Canary Media . The geothermal startup Fervo Energy is now selling power to the grid from its Cape Station project in Utah—marking the first time a utility-scale, next-generation geothermal facility has achieved such a feat worldwide. The Houston-based firm turned on an initial 33-megawatt unit late last week and has been testing and ramping up output since. On Thursday, Fervo will officially begin commercial operations, supplying carbon-free electricity to Shell Energy, a retail power provider in California. Cape Station, a $2 billion project that will eventually be 500 MW, is unique among the world’s commercial geothermal plants. While other facilities draw on naturally occurring hot water and steam, Fervo has engineered its own geothermal resource deep underground. The startup uses drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to create reservoirs in hot, dry rocks that generate steam to produce electricity. “Traditional geothermal would have never been done in southern Utah,” sa ys Dawn Owens , Fervo’s senior vice president and head of development and commercial markets. With the first unit online, Fervo sa ys it is working to commission two more 33-MW power blocks by 1 Jan uary , 2027. The project’s remaining 400 MW—which is supported by a new agreement with Google —is under construction and slated to come online in 2028. Fervo’s Next-Generation Geothermal Journey Fervo already operates a 3.5-MW commercial pilot plant in Nevada, which went online in late 2023. Owens sa ys the pilot, called Project Red, was important for demonstrating the technology itself. But firing up Cape Station proves that Fervo’s approach can achieve utility scale and export power to wider markets. “This is massive for both Fervo and the geothermal industry at large,” she sa ys . Fervo , which went public in May, is leading the fast-growing movement to develop clean, always-on geothermal power to meet soaring demand from data centers and balance growing supplies of intermittent solar and wind energy. Next-generation geothermal firms have raised billions of dollars in private capital in recent years to develop and deploy technologies that can harness energy in harsh, deep environments. Drilling continues at Fervo Energy’s Cape Station geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah, where the company plans to ramp up production to 500 MW. Fervo Energy Today, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation every year. Expanding geothermal’s share of the mix will require not just building more projects like Cape Station but also tackling high upfront drilling costs and other economic and regulatory barriers —all while working to limit potential impacts on communities and the environment, experts say. “ Fervo’s first power achievement shows investors the size and scale of the opportunity to fuel many more such milestones across developers and sites in the future,” sa ys Mitchell Smith , who serves as grid lead for the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium. The bipartisan initiative is calling for increased public and private financing “ to help bring more projects online responsibly and at the speed of demand,” he added. Enhanced Geothermal Energy Gets Cheaper Fervo has declined to disclose the terms of its power purchase agreements for in-progress and future development, which together represent about 1,000 MW, or enough to power roughly 1 million U.S. homes every year. Phase 1 of Cape Station is set to deliver power at $7,000 per kilowatt, while Phase 2 should come at $5,500 per k ilowatt , the company previously told Canary Media. (By comparison, the average cost to build a natural gas–fired power plant was $2,157 per k ilowatt in 2025.) Along with slashing drilling costs, enhanced geothermal projects could improve their economics by delivering power when it’s most valuable to utilities, according to researchers . While geothermal plants traditionally provide around-the-clock, baseload power, next-generation facilities might operate flexibly during certain periods—like in the evening, when solar output declines—to reduce overall grid costs. Geothermal plants could also operate “ behind the meter” to directly power data centers so that the costs of adding new electricity capacity aren’t passed on to utility customers, Owens sa ys . “We’ve been saying all along that our technology makes geothermal more scalable and affordable in more places,” she sa ys . On Cape Station’s powering-up, she add s , “ That’s just something no next-generation geothermal company has ever been able to do before.”

events.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
events.summary: Dolly Parton waves to her fans at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in March 2024. Amy Harris/Invision via AP Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings , had been her head of security for many years. But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death . This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going. Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate . She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “ an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate . He denies the allegations. As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike. Following Dolly Parton’s death, there has been turmoil in her management involving her nephew Bryan Seaver. Managing celebrity estates after death Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works , such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights , which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit. These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests. Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs . It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate , which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights. Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide , which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities. Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met. Marilyn Monroe’s will is seen on display at Julien’s Auctions in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2012. Joe Klamar/AFP via Getty Images Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge? Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies. A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer. Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it. As one study found, family managers often have a “ sense of kinship obligation ” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival. By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company . Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.” Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business . Death can be bad for business When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one. But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen. In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power. According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death. Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether. The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning. events.title: Business faces a more interventionist Washington post-midterms
events.summary: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." Get the 16-page FGS report .

events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday 21 October!   10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals Brimstone is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer. During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated. Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks. Discover how it’s making strides on two industrial problems . —James Temple Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from geothermal power plants to smart turbines and semi-solid-state cells. events.title: Trump privately expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
events.summary: President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said. A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally . In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions: At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening. Later that night, Trump was more nuanced : "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision." On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source. "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others. "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said. Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures. "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr." Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.) Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth. They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran , to the leadership of the Army . Advisers say the men have a good relationship. Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed. Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR . Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast. Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center. The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11. A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization. The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it. "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do." "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

events.title: Israel mints tech unicorns. Can it keep them from leaving for New York?
events.summary: The Scene Israel has produced more tech unicorns per citizen than any country in the world, twice as many as the US. Ittai Ben-Zeev’s job is getting them to stay there. The CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is tasked with convincing the next Wiz, Monday.com, and Fiverr, which all went public in New York or sold to US rivals, to list at home instead. He’s also courting global investors whose money will help boost trading and valuations. His biggest tailwind, he said, is the takeover of US markets by a handful of AI giants. Israeli startups worth a few billion dollars can’t get the attention of investors rhapsodizing about trillion-dollar IPOs from SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI. “New York is no longer an option,” said Ben-Zeev, the exchange’s CEO since 2016. After the Oct. 7 attacks, 7% of its workforce was called up for military service and the bear case for its stock market was obvious. Since Oct. 8, 2023, the TA-125 has beaten the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite by 23. The country is on track this year for a record 30 IPOs . Foreign holdings of Israeli shares more than doubled from September 2023 to the beginning of this year. Ben-Zeev dismissed wartime nationalism as a reason for Israeli founders to list at home, or for Israeli investors to buy their shares. “Israelis will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange,” he said. But he said the Jewish diaspora has increased its investments. Bill Ackman and his Israeli-born wife, Neri Oxman, bought 4.9% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2024 after a 45-minute meeting with management, Ackman said in an interview. “Owning a stock exchange is the purest way to bet on a country,” he said, taking a minute to run the numbers: His $23 million investment is worth $230 million today. He said AI’s productivity-enhancing potential will overcome Israel’s economic weakness, its small population. “There will be a trillion-dollar company coming out of Israel, and that value will be shared among a tiny country.” The war also gave TASE cover to move its Sunday-to-Thursday trading to Monday through Friday. It wasn’t an easy pitch in a country that takes Shabbat seriously, but a way “to signal the world that we are part of it” and gain entry into global indexes that have long snubbed it, Ben-Zeev said. Anti-Israel sentiment and antisemitism are fueling campaigns at many US institutions to divest from Israel. Politicians will politick, he said, but “investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return.” Q&A Liz Hoffman: Israel has produced more tech unicorns per capita than any other country in the world, but they all want to go public in New York. How do you hold onto them? Ittai Ben-Zeev: It used to be that a tech company with $100 million [in annual revenue] could IPO in New York. That’s no longer the case. The $100 million became $500 million. And because of the gigantic IPOs that are coming, for most Israeli tech companies, New York is no longer an option. Six or seven years ago, if an Israeli company couldn’t do an IPO on Nasdaq or NYSE, they were looking at Singapore, Toronto, Australia. We managed to change the perception. And I believe that in 2027, maybe before the end of 2026, we’ll start seeing global investment banks leading global IPO offerings on TASE, and only for TASE. I’m mindful, speaking to you the week of the anniversary of Oct. 7 — is patriotism part of the pitch? No. Post-Oct. 7, I see a genuine change in the way that Jewish people in the diaspora, especially in the States, want to invest in Israel, not only to make a return but also to get a broader connection to Israel. But that’s not the case with the Israeli entrepreneurs. Israelis, I have to tell you, will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange. Then what’s the pitch? You are Israeli. You don’t understand the American mentality. The American market can be brutal. You miss your estimates by one cent, your share price goes down, and then what? Start in the Israeli market and, once you’re ready, you can always do a dual listing. Think about TASE as a stop on the way to New York. You’ve also courted global companies to dual-list in Tel Aviv. Palo Alto Networks did that after buying [Israeli startup] CyberArk, but why would most companies bother? We have data that shows you get more liquidity and more demand for your shares. You can argue that it’s not significant enough, but it’s a free option. And not too many people are aware of it, but if you look at the amount of money Israelis have in cash deposits in Israeli banks and you compare it to GDP, we are No. 1 of any western society. That’s money that is just ready to be invested. You’re in New York this week, selling the Israeli economy to investors. But the Middle East is a volatile place to invest right now, and there are big anti-Israel divestment campaigns at some US institutions. In the old days, people would ask me: What will happen to Israel if something happens in Iran? I remember being in New York a couple of years ago, telling one of those American investors that if something happened in Iran, you should be more worried about your American portfolio than your Israeli portfolio. Israel is more well-positioned than it used to be, and I’m not sure that everybody fully understands it. In terms of BDS [the push for boycotts, divestment, and economic sanctions against Israel], there are politicians all over the world. Investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return. And the Israeli market is a good marketplace to make a return. Also, I think Israel can do a better job of PR. This is part of what we tell companies: You need to know how to sell the pitch. It’s not only about facts; it’s also about storytelling. As a country, this is something we need to do better. You shifted trading from Sunday to Thursday to Monday to Friday. Was that a hard sell? We were in the middle of a war. Everybody understood that it’s important for us to signal the world that we are part of it. We needed to get aligned to global standards, and this is what we did this year. What’s it like having Bill Ackman on your cap table? For sure it has helped change the perception. Israeli tech guys, they look to New York. When they will read what you’re writing, they will give it much more credit than what the Israeli newspaper writes. So a very successful businessman like Bill talking about the Israeli economy, putting faith in the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, helps my pitch.
